items.text: משנת הפתיחה: זמני קריאת שמע בערבין
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Time for Evening Shema
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents three opinions on the time for reciting the evening Shema: from when priests enter to eat terumah until the end of the first watch (Rabbi Eliezer), until midnight (the Sages), and until dawn (Rabban Gamliel). A story illustrates Rabban Gamliel's lenient ruling, and the Mishnah extends this principle to other mitzvot whose proper time is until dawn, explaining that the Sages set midnight as a safeguard.
items.desc: המשנה פותחת בשאלה מאימתי קוראים את שמע בערבין, ומביאה שלוש דעות: רבי אליעזר אומר עד סוף האשמורה הראשונה, חכמים אומרים עד חצות, ורבן גמליאל אומר עד שיעלה עמוד השחר. מסופר מעשה שבני רבן גמליאל באו מבית המשתה והורה להם לקרות כל עוד לא עלה עמוד השחר, ומכליל שכל מצוות חכמים שאמרו 'עד חצות' מצוותן עד עמוד השחר, והטעם להרחיק אדם מן העבירה.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the question of when the evening Shema may be recited, and presents Rabbi Eliezer's opinion: from the time priests enter to eat their תרומה (priestly portion) until the end of the first watch.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בשאלת זמן קריאת שמע בערבית ומביאה את דעת רבי אליעזר.

sub.desc_en: The Sages rule that the evening Shema may be recited until midnight.
sub.desc: חכמים חולקים על רבי אליעזר וקובעים שזמן קריאת שמע עד חצות.

sub.desc_en: Rabban Gamliel rules that the evening Shema may be recited until dawn.
sub.desc: רבן גמליאל מרחיב את הזמן עד עלות השחר.

sub.desc_en: A story illustrates Rabban Gamliel's lenient ruling: when his sons returned late from a wedding feast and had not recited the Shema, he told them they were still obligated if dawn had not yet arrived.
sub.desc: מסופר מעשה בבני רבן גמליאל שחזרו מבית המשתה והורה להם לקרוא כל עוד לא עלה השחר, ומכליל זאת לכל מצוות חכמים עד חצות.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah extends the principle that the proper time for certain מצוות (commandments) is until dawn, and explains that the Sages set midnight as a safeguard (הרחקה) to keep people from sin.
sub.desc: מסופר מעשה בבני רבן גמליאל שחזרו מבית המשתה והורה להם לקרוא כל עוד לא עלה השחר, ומכליל זאת לכל מצוות חכמים עד חצות.

items.text: Gemara's First Question: Why Begin with Evening?
items.text_en: Gemara's First Question: Why Begin with Evening?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Tanna begins with the evening Shema rather than the morning Shema, given that the verse mentions "when you lie down" before "when you rise." It answers that the Tanna is expounding the verse, which lists lying down first.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks where the Tanna is positioned to begin the Mishnah with 'From when?'
The Gemara further asks why the Tanna teaches the evening Shema first rather than the morning Shema.
The Gemara answers that the Tanna is expounding the verse 'בשכבך ובקומך' (when you lie down and when you rise), which mentions lying down first.

items.text: Alternative Answer and Further Question
items.text_en: Alternative Answer and Further Question
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative answer: the Tanna learns from the order of creation (evening then morning). It then questions why the Mishnah's later section (about blessings) lists morning before evening, and resolves that the Tanna first discusses evening, then morning, and while still on morning explains its laws before returning to evening.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative answer: the Tanna learns from the order of creation (evening then morning), as it is written 'וַיְהִי עֶרֶב וַיְהִי בֹקֶר יוֹם אֶחָד' (and there was evening and there was morning, one day).
The Gemara questions: if the order is evening then morning, why does the Mishnah's later section (about blessings) list morning before evening? It should have listed evening first.
The Gemara resolves: the Tanna first discusses evening, then morning, and while still on morning explains its laws before returning to evening.

items.text: בירור משמעות 'משעה שהכהנים נכנסים לאכול בתרומתן'
items.text_en: Why 'When Priests Enter' Rather Than 'Nightfall'?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah says "from the time the priests enter to eat their terumah" instead of simply "from nightfall." It explains that the Mishnah teaches incidentally that priests eat terumah after nightfall, and that atonement does not delay eating terumah, citing a verse about sunset and purification.
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת: מדוע לא שנה התנא במפורש 'משעת צאת הכוכבים'? ומתרצת שהתנא לימד אותנו דרך אגב שכהנים אוכלים בתרומה משעת צאת הכוכבים, ושכפרה אינה מעכבת. מביאה ברייתא הדורשת את הפסוק 'ובא השמש וטהר' – ביאת שמשו מעכבתו מלאכול בתרומה, ואין כפרתו מעכבתו. ומבררת שהכוונה ב'ובא השמש' היא ביאת השמש ממש, ו'וטהר' הוא טהר יומא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah says 'from the time the priests enter to eat their terumah' instead of simply stating 'from the time the stars come out'.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מדוע המשנה לא אמרה במפורש 'משעת צאת הכוכבים', שהרי כהנים אוכלים בתרומה רק אז?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah incidentally teaches that priests eat terumah after nightfall and that atonement (כפרה) does not delay eating terumah, citing a baraita about the verse 'וּבָא הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ וְטָהֵר' (the sun sets and he is pure).
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת: המשנה מלמדת אגב אורחא שכהנים אוכלים בתרומה רק משעת צאת הכוכבים, ושכפרה אינה מעכבת אכילה בתרומה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the verse's 'וּבָא הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ' means the actual sunset and 'וְטָהֵר' means the day becomes pure (i.e., nightfall).
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא המפרשת את הפסוק 'ובא השמש וטהר' להוכחה שטבילת יום אינה מעכבת אכילת תרומה.

items.text: קושיית הגמרא על 'וְטָהֵר'
items.text_en: Resolving the meaning of 'and the sun sets'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether 'and the sun sets' means the sun's actual setting or its light's departure, and whether 'and he becomes pure' refers to the person or the day. Rabbah bar Rav Sheila argues that if it meant the person, the verse would use 'yit'har' (active), so 'v'taher' means the day becomes pure, as people say 'the sun set and the day became pure'.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה על הפסוק 'וּבָא הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ וְטָהֵר' – האם הכוונה לביאת אורו (שקיעת החמה) וטיהור הגבר, או לביאת שמשו (צאת הכוכבים) וטיהור היום. רבה בר רב שילא מתרץ שהלשון 'וְטָהֵר' מורה על טהרת היום, כלשון בני אדם.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether 'and the sun sets' refers to the sun's actual setting or its light's departure, and whether 'and he becomes pure' refers to the person becoming pure.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: שמא 'ביאת השמש' פירושה ביאת אורו (שקיעה), ו'וטהר' פירושו טהרת הגבר?

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Sheila argues that if the verse meant the person, it would use 'yit'har' (active), so 'v'taher' means the day becomes pure, as people say 'the sun set and the day became pure'.
sub.desc: רבה בר רב שילא מתרץ: אילו הכוונה לטהרת הגבר, היה כתוב 'ויטהר'; 'וטהר' מורה על טהרת היום, כלשון בני אדם.

items.text: בעיית המערבא ופתרונה מברייתא
items.text_en: The Westerners' question and resolution from a baraita
items.desc_en: In the West, they did not hear Rabbah bar Rav Sheila's teaching and debated the same question. They resolved it from a baraita that gives the sign for the time as 'the emergence of the stars', proving that 'and the sun sets' means the sun's actual setting and 'and he becomes pure' means the day becomes pure.
items.desc: במערבא לא שמעו את דברי רבה בר רב שילא, ושאלו אם 'וּבָא הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ' הוא ביאת שמשו או ביאת אורו. לבסוף פשטו מברייתא שהסימן הוא צאת הכוכבים, ומכאן שביאת שמשו היא וטיהור היום.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that in the West, Rabbah bar Rav Sheila's teaching was unknown, and they inquired whether 'and the sun sets' means the sun's actual setting or its light's departure, and whether 'and he becomes pure' refers to the day or the person.
sub.desc: בני מערבא, שלא שמעו את תירוץ רבה בר רב שילא, שואלים: האם 'ביאת השמש' היא ביאת שמשו (צאת הכוכבים) וטהרת היום, או ביאת אורו וטהרת הגבר?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the inquiry from a baraita: since the baraita states 'the sign for the matter is the emergence of the stars', it proves that 'and the sun sets' means the sun's actual setting and 'and he becomes pure' means the day becomes pure.
sub.desc: בני מערבא פושטים את הבעיה מברייתא: הסימן 'צאת הכוכבים' מוכיח שביאת השמש היא ביאת שמשו, וטהרת היום.

items.text: הרמת המשנה על זמני קריאת שמע
items.text_en: First contradiction: Mishnah vs. baraita on the poor man
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah says the time for Shema is from when priests enter to eat terumah, but a baraita says it is from when a poor man enters to eat his bread with salt. The Gemara questions whether the beginning of the baraita contradicts the Mishnah, but resolves that the poor man and the priest have the same time.
items.desc: הגמרא מעלה סתירה בין המשנה שקובעת זמן קריאת שמע משעת כניסת כוהנים לאכול בתרומה, לבין ברייתא האומרת 'משהעני נכנס לאכול פתו במלח'. הגמרא דוחה שהסיפא חולקת, אך הרישא אינה חולקת כי עני וכוהן שיעור אחד להם.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a contradiction: the Mishnah says the time for the evening Shema is from when priests enter to eat their terumah, but a baraita says it is from when a poor person enters to eat his bread with salt until he finishes his meal.
sub.desc: הגמרא מעלה סתירה בין המשנה לברייתא האומרת 'משהעני נכנס לאכול פתו במלח'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the end of the baraita certainly disagrees with the Mishnah, and asks whether the beginning also disagrees.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת האם הרישא של הברייתא חולקת על המשנה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the poor person and the priest have the same time, so the beginning of the baraita does not disagree with the Mishnah.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה את הסתירה בטענה ששיעור העני והכהן שווה.

items.text: ברייתא נוספת וסימן צאת הכוכבים
items.text_en: Second contradiction: Baraita with Rabbi Meir and Sages
items.desc_en: A baraita states that Rabbi Meir says the time for Shema is from when people enter to eat on Shabbat eve, while the Sages say it is from when priests are permitted to eat terumah, with the sign being the emergence of stars. The Gemara explains the additional verse citation to counter the claim that twilight is still day.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא נוספת עם מחלוקת רבי מאיר וחכמים על זמן קריאת שמע, וסימן צאת הכוכבים. הגמרא שואלת על הפסוק הנוסף 'וְהָיוּ לָנוּ הַלַּיְלָה מִשְׁמָר', ומסבירה שאין ראיה גמורה אלא זכר לדבר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that presents the positions of Rabbi Meir and the Sages regarding the time for the evening Shema, with the Sages providing a sign of the emergence of stars and an allusion from Nehemiah.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא הכוללת את שיטת רבי מאיר (משעה שבני אדם נכנסים לאכול בערבי שבתות) ואת שיטת חכמים (משעה שהכהנים זכאים לאכול בתרומה, סימן: צאת הכוכבים), ומביאה פסוק מספר נחמיה כ'זכר לדבר'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the baraita adds a second verse with 'and it says'.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מדוע הוסיפו חכמים לשון 'ואומר' לפני הפסוק השני, לכאורה מיותרת.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the second verse is needed to counter the objection that the workers might have worked into twilight, proving that the day ends only with the emergence of stars.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת: הפסוק הראשון לבדו אינו ראיה גמורה, כי ייתכן שהפועלים האירו והקדימו לעבוד גם בלילה; הפסוק השני מוסיף ומוכיח שהלילה נקבע למשמר והיום למלאכה, ומכאן ש'עד צאת הכוכבים' הוא יום גמור.

items.text: דחיית הסתירה בין עני לבני אדם
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction between the two baraitot
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes that the poor man and 'people' have the same time, leading to a contradiction between Rabbi Meir and the Sages. It then concludes that the poor man and the priest have the same time, but the poor man and 'people' do not, resolving the contradiction.
items.desc: הגמרא מעלה קושיה: אם עני וכוהן שיעור אחד, הרי חכמים הם רבי מאיר? ומתרצת שעני וכוהן שיעור אחד, אך עני ובני אדם אינם שיעור אחד, ולכן אין סתירה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection: if the poor man and the priest have the same time, then the Sages' opinion would be identical to Rabbi Meir's.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם עני וכוהן שיעור אחד, הרי חכמים הם רבי מאיר, ומדוע נחלקו?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: the poor man and the priest have the same time, but the poor man and 'people' do not, thus the Sages and Rabbi Meir disagree.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה את הקושיה ומתרצת: עני וכוהן שיעור אחד, אך עני ובני אדם אינם שיעור אחד, ולכן אין סתירה.

items.text: ברייתא רביעית והוכחת שיעורים נפרדים
items.text_en: Third contradiction: Baraita with multiple opinions
items.desc_en: A baraita lists opinions: Rabbi Eliezer (from when the day is sanctified on Shabbat eve), Rabbi Yehoshua (from when priests are pure to eat terumah), Rabbi Meir (from when priests immerse), Rabbi Yehuda's objection, Rabbi Chanina (from when a poor man eats), and Rabbi Achai (from when most people recline). The Gemara proves that the poor man's time is distinct from the priest's time, as otherwise Rabbi Chanina would duplicate Rabbi Yehoshua.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא עם מחלוקת רבי אליעזר, רבי יהושע, רבי מאיר, רבי יהודה, רבי חנינא ורבי אחאי. מוכח שעני וכוהן שיעורים שונים, אחרת רבי חנינא יהיה כרבי יהושע. המסקנה: שיעור עני לבד ושיעור כוהן לבד.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita listing multiple opinions: Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda's objection, Rabbi Chanina, and Rabbi Achai/Acha, each giving a different time for the evening Shema.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: האם באמת שיעורו של עני ושיעורו של כהן זהים? ומביאה ברייתא הסותרת זאת.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the poor person and the priest have the same time, then Rabbi Chanina's opinion would be identical to Rabbi Yehoshua's.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם שיעור עני ושיעור כהן זהים, הרי שרבי חנינא הוא כרבי יהושע, וזו סתירה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes definitively that the poor person and the priest have different times.
sub.desc: הגמרא מסיקה: מכאן ששיעור עני לעצמו ושיעור כהן לעצמו, ואינם זהים.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda objects to Rabbi Meir, arguing that priests immerse while it is still daytime.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: האם באמת שיעורו של עני ושיעורו של כהן זהים? ומביאה ברייתא הסותרת זאת.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina states the time is from when a poor person enters to eat his bread with salt.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם שיעור עני ושיעור כהן זהים, הרי שרבי חנינא הוא כרבי יהושע, וזו סתירה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Achai (or some say Rabbi Acha) says the time is from when most people recline for their meal.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: האם באמת שיעורו של עני ושיעורו של כהן זהים? ומביאה ברייתא הסותרת זאת.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the poor person's time and the priest's time are the same measure, then Rabbi Chanina's opinion would duplicate Rabbi Yehoshua's.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם שיעור עני ושיעור כהן זהים, הרי שרבי חנינא הוא כרבי יהושע, וזו סתירה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes: learn from this that the poor person's measure is distinct and the priest's measure is distinct.
sub.desc: הגמרא מסיקה: מכאן ששיעור עני לעצמו ושיעור כהן לעצמו, ואינם זהים.

items.text: קביעת איזה שיעור מאוחר
items.text_en: Determining which time is later
items.desc_en: The Gemara determines that the poor man's time is later than the priest's time, because if it were earlier, Rabbi Chanina would duplicate Rabbi Eliezer. Therefore, the poor man's time is later.
items.desc: הגמרא קובעת ששיעור העני מאוחר יותר, כי אם היה מוקדם, רבי חנינא היה כרבי אליעזר. לכן מסתבר ששיעור העני מאוחר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which of the two times (poor person or priest) is later.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת: איזה מהשיעורים מאוחר יותר – של עני או של כהן? ומסיקה ששיעור עני מאוחר, שאם לא כן רבי חנינא היה זהה לרבי אליעזר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reasons that the poor person's time is later, because if it were earlier, Rabbi Chanina's opinion would be identical to Rabbi Eliezer's, so it must be later.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת: איזה מהשיעורים מאוחר יותר – של עני או של כהן? ומסיקה ששיעור עני מאוחר, שאם לא כן רבי חנינא היה זהה לרבי אליעזר.

items.text: דיון בטבילת כוהנים ובין השמשות
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's objection to Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Meir's response
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda objects to Rabbi Meir's opinion that priests immerse at the time of Shema, noting that priests immerse while it is still day. Rabbi Meir responds that he refers to the twilight of Rabbi Yosei, which is as fleeting as the blink of an eye, impossible to pinpoint.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה בדברי רבי יהודה לרבי מאיר על טבילת כוהנים מבעוד יום, ומסבירה שרבי מאיר התכוון לבין השמשות של רבי יוסי, שהוא כהרף עין, ולא לבין השמשות של רבי יהודה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Yehuda's objection to Rabbi Meir: do not priests immerse while it is still day?
sub.desc: הגמרא מצטטת את דברי רבי יהודה שהקשה לרבי מאיר: והלא כהנים טובלים מבעוד יום, כלומר לפני בין השמשות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Yehuda's objection to Rabbi Meir is valid.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת: האם קושיית רבי יהודה על רבי מאיר נכונה?

sub.text_en: Rabbi Meir's response (as explained by the Gemara)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Meir's response: he was referring to the twilight period according to Rabbi Yosei, which is as brief as an eye blink, and impossible to pinpoint precisely.
sub.desc: רבי מאיר משיב לרבי יהודה: אני מתכוון לבין השמשות של רבי יוסי, שהוא כהרף עין, ולא לבין השמשות שלך.

items.text: Resolving contradictions in Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Resolving contradictions in Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction in Rabbi Meir's statements and resolves it by positing two Tanna'im who hold his view. Similarly, a contradiction in Rabbi Eliezer's statements is resolved either by two Tanna'im or by suggesting that the beginning of the mishnah is not Rabbi Eliezer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between two statements of Rabbi Meir.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by positing two Tanna'im who transmit Rabbi Meir's view.
The Gemara raises a similar contradiction between two statements of Rabbi Eliezer.
The Gemara offers the same resolution: two Tanna'im transmit Rabbi Eliezer's view.
An alternative resolution: the beginning of the mishnah is not attributed to Rabbi Eliezer.

items.text: Question on Rabbi Eliezer's wording
items.text_en: Question on Rabbi Eliezer's wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Eliezer's phrase 'until the end of the first watch.' If he holds there are three watches, he should say 'until four hours'; if four watches, he should say 'until three hours.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Eliezer's phrase 'until the end of the first watch,' arguing that if he holds there are three watches he should say 'until four hours,' and if four watches he should say 'until three hours.'

items.text: Answer: Three watches and their signs
items.text_en: Answer: Three watches and their signs
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that Rabbi Eliezer indeed holds there are three watches, and he teaches that there are watches in heaven and on earth. A baraita describes the signs for each watch: the first watch, a donkey brays; the second, dogs bark; the third, a baby nurses and a woman talks with her husband.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that Rabbi Eliezer holds there are three watches, and teaches that there are watches in heaven and on earth, citing a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer describes God roaring like a lion each watch.
A baraita provides signs for each watch: first watch a donkey brays, second dogs bark, third a baby nurses and a woman talks with her husband.

items.text: Clarifying the signs: which part of the watch?
items.text_en: Clarifying the signs: which part of the watch?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions which part of the watches the signs refer to. It concludes that the signs refer to the end of the first watch, the beginning of the last watch, and the middle of the middle watch. Alternatively, all signs refer to the end of each watch, with the last watch being unnecessary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions which part of the watches Rabbi Eliezer's signs refer to, noting that the beginning of the first watch is obvious (night) and the end of the last watch is obvious (day).
The Gemara answers that the signs refer to the end of the first watch, the beginning of the last watch, and the middle of the middle watch.
An alternative answer is offered: all signs refer to the end of each watch, with the last watch being unnecessary but still mentioned.

items.text: Practical application of the signs
items.text_en: Practical application of the signs
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the practical relevance: for one sleeping in a dark house who does not know the time for reciting Shema, when he sees a woman talking with her husband and a baby nursing, he should get up and recite Shema.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical halachic application emerges from the signs of the watches.

The Gemara answers: the signs are useful for one sleeping in a dark house who does not know the time for reciting Shema; when he sees a woman talking with her husband and a baby nursing, he should get up and recite Shema.

items.text: אמרת רב יצחק בר שמואל
items.text_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel's teaching on God's lament
items.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel reports in the name of Rav that during each of the three watches, God sits and roars like a lion, saying, 'Woe to Me that I destroyed My house, burned My Temple, and exiled My children among the nations.'
items.desc: רב יצחק בר שמואל בשם רב מוסיף שהקב"ה שואג כאריה בכל משמר ואומר 'אוי שהחרבתי את ביתי'.

sub.text: רב יצחק בר שמואל משם רב
sub.text_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel reports in the name of Rav that during each of the three watches of the night, God sits and roars like a lion, lamenting the destruction of the Temple and the exile of Israel.
sub.desc: רב יצחק בר שמואל אומר משם רב: שלוש משמרות, ובכל אחת הקב"ה שואג כארי ואומר אוי שהחרבתי ביתי.

items.text: מעשה רבי יוסי ואליהו
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Yosei in a ruin with Elijah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei recounts entering a ruin in Jerusalem to pray, where Elijah guarded the entrance. Elijah taught him three lessons: one should not enter a ruin, one may pray on the road, and one should pray a short prayer. Elijah also revealed that a heavenly voice laments three times daily, and when Israel responds 'Y'hei Shmei Rabba,' God nods and laments the exile of His children.
items.desc: מסופר על רבי יוסי שנכנס לחורבה להתפלל, ואליהו שמר עליו ולימדו שלושה דברים: אין נכנסים לחורבה, מתפללים בדרך, ומתפללים תפילה קצרה. כמו כן שמע בת קול המנהמת כיונה על חורבן הבית, ואליהו גילה שהיא אומרת כן שלוש פעמים ביום, ושהקב"ה מנענע ראשו בשעה שישראל עונים 'יהא שמיה הגדול מבורך'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei recounts entering a ruin in Jerusalem to pray, with Elijah guarding the entrance until he finished.
sub.desc: מביא ברייתא המספרת שרבי יוסי נכנס לחורבה להתפלל, ואליהו לימדו שצריך להתפלל בדרך תפילה קצרה.

sub.desc_en: Elijah asks Rabbi Yosei why he entered the ruin, and Rabbi Yosei answers that he entered to pray.
sub.desc: אליהו שואל על בת הקול, ומספר שהיא אומרת כן שלוש פעמים ביום, וכשעונים 'יהא שמיה הגדול מבורך' הקב"ה מנענע ראשו.

sub.desc_en: Elijah teaches that one should pray on the road with a short prayer rather than entering a ruin.
sub.desc: מביא ברייתא המספרת שרבי יוסי נכנס לחורבה להתפלל, ואליהו לימדו שצריך להתפלל בדרך תפילה קצרה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei summarizes the three lessons learned from Elijah: not to enter a ruin, to pray on the road, and to pray a short prayer.
sub.desc: רבי יוסי מסכם את שלושת הדברים שלמד מאליהו: אין נכנסים לחורבה, מתפללים בדרך, ומתפללים תפילה קצרה.

sub.desc_en: Elijah asks what sound Rabbi Yosei heard in the ruin, and Rabbi Yosei reports hearing a heavenly voice (בת קול) moaning like a dove.
sub.desc: אליהו שואל על בת הקול, ומספר שהיא אומרת כן שלוש פעמים ביום, וכשעונים 'יהא שמיה הגדול מבורך' הקב"ה מנענע ראשו.

sub.desc_en: Elijah reveals that the heavenly voice laments three times daily, and when Israel responds 'Y'hei Shmei Rabba,' God nods and laments the exile of His children.
sub.desc: אליהו שואל על בת הקול, ומספר שהיא אומרת כן שלוש פעמים ביום, וכשעונים 'יהא שמיה הגדול מבורך' הקב"ה מנענע ראשו.

items.text: ברייתא על איסור כניסה לחורבה
items.text_en: Three reasons not to enter a ruin
items.desc_en: The Rabbis taught that one should not enter a ruin for three reasons: suspicion (of illicit activity), danger of collapse, and danger from demons. The Gemara questions why suspicion is listed separately from collapse.
items.desc: הברייתא מונה שלושה טעמים לאי-כניסה לחורבה: חשד, מפולת ומזיקין, והגמרא מקשה מדוע צריך את כולם.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that one should not enter a ruin for three reasons: suspicion (of illicit activity), danger of collapse, and danger from demons.
sub.desc: ברייתא: מפני שלושה דברים אין נכנסים לחורבה: חשד, מפולת, ומזיקין. והגמרא מקשה: תיפוק ליה משום מפולת?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the reason of suspicion is listed separately, since the danger of collapse alone should suffice to forbid entry.
sub.desc: ברייתא: מפני שלושה דברים אין נכנסים לחורבה: חשד, מפולת, ומזיקין. והגמרא מקשה: תיפוק ליה משום מפולת?

items.text: דיון בטעמי המשניות על תפילת ערבית
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's reasons for not reciting Shema after midnight
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah lists specific reasons (mazikin, hashd, mappolet) for different scenarios, and resolves the apparent redundancies by specifying the exact circumstances: a new house, two people, a ruined building, etc. It concludes with an alternative explanation that the Mishnah refers to a new house in a desert where only mazikin are a concern.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה בטעמים השונים שניתנו במשנה לתפילת ערבית: מפני חשד, מפני מזיקין, ומפני מפולת. היא מביאה תירוצים שונים להסביר מדוע לא חוששים לכל הטעמים יחד, תוך התחשבות במצבים שונים כמו יחיד, שנים, חורבה חדשה, ומקום כשרים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah's reason of mazikin (harmful spirits) is needed for a new house, since even with one person, the concern of hashd (suspicion of adultery) would apply.
sub.desc: תירוץ ראשון: המשנה הראשונה עוסקת בחורבה חדשה, ולכן חשש מפולת אינו רלוונטי.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah refers to two people, where hashd is not a concern.
sub.desc: קושיה: מדוע לא חוששים למזיקין בחורבה חדשה? תירוץ: מדובר בשניים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that with two people, hashd is also absent, so why mention mazikin? The answer is that the two are פריצי (immoral), so hashd still applies.
sub.desc: קושיה: אם בשניים, מדוע לא חוששים לחשד? תירוץ: בשניים פרוצים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah mentions mappolet (collapse) for a ruined building, since hashd and mazikin would also apply.
sub.desc: קושיה: במשנה השנייה (מפני המפולת) מדוע לא חוששים לחשד ומזיקין? תירוץ: בשניים כשרים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the case involves two כשרים (upright people), so hashd is not a concern, and mazikin are not feared in a ruined building.
The Gemara questions why the Mishnah mentions mazikin for a new house, since hashd and mappolet would also apply.
sub.desc: קושיה: במשנה השלישית (מפני המזיקין) מדוע לא חוששים לחשד ומפולת? תירוץ: בחורבה חדשה ובשניים כשרים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the case is a new ruined building with two upright people, so only mazikin are a concern.
The Gemara objects that with two people, mazikin are also not a concern; the answer is that in their place (a desert), we do fear mazikin.
sub.desc: קושיה: אם בשניים, מדוע חוששים למזיקין? תירוץ: במקומן חוששים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: the Mishnah always refers to one person in a new ruined building in a desert, where hashd is absent but mazikin are feared.
sub.desc: תירוץ חלופי: לעולם ביחיד, בחורבה חדשה העומדת במדבר, שאין חשד כי אין אשה מצויה, אך יש חשש מזיקין.

items.text: מחלוקת רבי ורבי נתן במספר משמרות הלילה
items.text_en: Debate on the number of night watches: Rabbi vs. Rabbi Natan
items.desc_en: The Tannaim debate whether the night is divided into four or three watches. Rabbi Natan derives three watches from the verse about Gideon's 'middle watch', while Rabbi holds that 'middle watch' means one of the middle watches among four. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi supports Rabbi's view with verses about David's midnight prayers. Rabbi Natan aligns with Rabbi Yehoshua's opinion that the night has only three watches. Rav Ashi adds that even a watch and a half can be called 'watches'.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא שבה נחלקו רבי ורבי נתן: רבי סובר ארבע משמרות, ורבי נתן סובר שלוש. מובאים טעמים לכל אחד: רבי נתן מסתמך על הפסוק 'ראש האשמורת התיכונה', ורבי דורש 'תיכונה שבתכונות'. הגמרא מביאה גם ראיה של רבי יהושע בן לוי לפסוקים, ודברי רב אשי על קריאת 'משמרה ופלגא' בשם 'משמרות'.

sub.desc_en: The Tannaim state the dispute: Rabbi holds the night has four watches, Rabbi Natan says three.
sub.desc: הברייתא פותחת במחלוקת בין רבי לרבי נתן על מספר משמרות הלילה.

sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Natan's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Natan's proof from the verse about Gideon's 'middle watch' (אשמורת התיכונה), which implies only three watches.
sub.desc: רבי נתן מביא ראיה מהפסוק 'ראש האשמורת התיכונה' שיש שלוש משמרות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi interprets 'middle watch' as one of the middle watches among four.
sub.desc: רבי דורש 'תיכונה' כתיכונה שבתכונות, כלומר אחת מארבע.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Natan objects that the verse says only 'middle watch', not 'middle of the middle watches'.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה על רבי: הפסוק כתוב 'תיכונה' סתם, לא 'תיכונה שבתכונות'.

sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's support for Rabbi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi cites two verses about David's midnight prayers to prove the night has four watches.
sub.desc: רבי מביא ראיה משני פסוקים: 'חצות לילה אקום' ו'קדמו עיני אשמורות', המלמדים על ארבע משמרות.

sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution aligning Rabbi Natan with Rabbi Yehoshua
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Natan holds like Rabbi Yehoshua, who says the night has only three watches based on the timing of the morning Shema.
sub.desc: רבי נתן סובר כרבי יהושע שזמן קריאת שמע עד שלוש שעות, ומכאן שלוש משמרות.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi adds that even a watch and a half can be called 'watches', reconciling the terminology.
sub.desc: רב אשי מיישב: גם משמרה וחצי נקראת 'משמרות', ולכן אין סתירה.

items.text: דין אמירת דברי תורה בפני המת
items.text_en: Discussion on speaking before the dead
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zerika quotes Rabbi Ami quoting Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that one should only speak words of the deceased in their presence. Rabbi Abba bar Kahana limits this to words of Torah, while another version extends it even to mundane matters.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה דין בשם רבי יהושע בן לוי שאין אומרים בפני המת אלא דבריו של מת. רבי אבא בר כהנא מגביל זאת לדברי תורה, ויש גורסים שאפילו בדברי תורה אסור, וכל שכן בדברי חול.

sub.text: רבי זריקא בשם רבי אמי בשם רבי יהושע בן לוי
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zerika quoting Rabbi Ami quoting Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zerika in the name of Rabbi Ami citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules that before a dead person one should only speak words of the deceased.
sub.desc: רבי יהושע בן לוי קובע שאין אומרים בפני המת אלא דבריו של מת.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Kahana limits the prohibition to words of Torah, but mundane matters are permitted.
sub.desc: רבי אבא בר כהנא מגביל את האיסור לדברי תורה, אבל דברי חול מותרים.

sub.text: יש אומרים בשם רבי אבא בר כהנא
sub.text_en: Alternative version of Rabbi Abba bar Kahana
sub.desc_en: An alternative version extends Rabbi Abba bar Kahana's statement to include even words of Torah, and certainly mundane matters.
sub.desc: יש גורסים שרבי אבא בר כהנא החמיר אף בדברי תורה, וכל שכן בדברי חול.

items.text: בירור זמן קימת דוד בחצות הלילה
items.text_en: Clarifying David's midnight prayer and the meaning of 'neshef'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether David actually rose at midnight, citing a verse that he rose 'in the neshef' (twilight). It initially suggests 'neshef' means evening, but a contradiction arises from another verse. Rava resolves this by explaining there are two twilights: one that brings night and one that brings day.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה האם דוד קם בחצות הלילה או קודם לכן, על סמך הפסוק 'קדמתי בנשף'. היא מביאה דעות שונות: רב אושעיא בשם רבי אחא מסביר שדוד אמר שמעולם לא עבר עליו חצות בשינה; רבי זירא ורב אשי מתארים את סדר יומו. לבסוף, רבא מיישב את הסתירה בפסוקי 'נשף' בכך שיש שני נשפים: נשף לילה ונשף יום.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether David actually rose at midnight, suggesting instead that he rose at evening (אורתא).
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה על הפסוקים: מדוד שכתב 'קדמתי בנשף' משמע שקם באורחה, ולא בחצות הלילה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse where David says he rose 'in the neshef' (twilight) and proves that 'neshef' means evening from another verse.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה על הפסוקים: מדוד שכתב 'קדמתי בנשף' משמע שקם באורחה, ולא בחצות הלילה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Oshaya in the name of Rabbi Acha explains that David meant he never slept past midnight, not that he rose exactly at midnight.
sub.desc: רב אושעיא בשם רבי אחא מסביר שדוד אמר שמעולם לא עבר עליו חצות הלילה בשינה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira says David dozed like a horse until midnight and then strengthened himself like a lion.
sub.desc: רבי זירא ורב אשי מתארים את סדר יומו של דוד: עד חצות התנמנם או עסק בתורה, ומחצות התגבר כארי או עסק בשירות ותשבחות.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi says David studied Torah until midnight and then engaged in songs and praises.
sub.desc: רבי זירא ורב אשי מתארים את סדר יומו של דוד: עד חצות התנמנם או עסק בתורה, ומחצות התגבר כארי או עסק בשירות ותשבחות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that 'neshef' can also mean morning, citing a verse about David's battle from 'neshef' until evening.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: הרי 'נשף' משמעו בוקר, ככתוב 'ויכם דוד מהנשף ועד הערב', ומשמע מצפרא ועד ליליא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the objection, interpreting the verse as from evening to evening.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה: אפשר לפרש 'מהנשף ועד הערב' מאורחה ועד אורחה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if 'neshef' meant evening, the verse should have used a clearer phrase like 'from neshef to neshef' or 'from evening to evening'.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם הכוונה מאורחה לאורחה, היה לכתוב 'מהנשף ועד הנשף' או 'מהערב ועד הערב'.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction by explaining there are two twilights: one that brings night and one that brings day.
sub.desc: רבא מיישב: יש שני נשפים – נשף לילה שבא יום, ונשף יום שבא לילה.

items.text: How David knew the exact time of midnight and the story of his nightly routine
items.text_en: How David knew the exact time of midnight and the story of his nightly routine
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how David knew when midnight was, given that even Moses was uncertain. It explains that David had a sign: a lyre hung above his bed that would play by itself at midnight, waking him. The Gemara then recounts how David would study Torah until dawn, after which the sages would come to discuss the nation's needs, consulting Achitofel, the Sanhedrin, and the Urim veTumim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how David knew the exact time of midnight, given that even Moses was uncertain about it.
The Gemara answers that David had a sign: a lyre hung above his bed that would play by itself at midnight, waking him to study Torah until dawn.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Bizna citing Rabbi Shimon Chasida
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Bizna citing Rabbi Shimon Chasida
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Bizna in the name of Rabbi Shimon Chasida provides the tradition about David's lyre that played by itself at midnight.
The Gemara recounts how after dawn the sages came to David to discuss the nation's needs, and he instructed them to go to war.
The Gemara describes how David's advisors consulted Achitofel, the Sanhedrin, and the Urim veTumim.
Rav Yosef cites a verse to support the narrative about David's consultations.

items.text: Identification of Benaiah and Evyatar
items.text_en: Identification of Benaiah and Evyatar
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies Benaiah ben Jehoiada with the Sanhedrin and Evyatar with the Urim veTummim, explaining the names Kereti and Peleti as referring to their decisive and extraordinary words.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies Benaiah ben Jehoiada with the Sanhedrin and Evyatar with the Urim veTummim, and explains the names Kereti and Peleti as referring to their decisive and extraordinary words.

items.text: David's waking at midnight
items.text_en: David's waking at midnight
items.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Adda cites a verse indicating David would wake at midnight to praise God.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Adda (or Rabbi Yitzchak bar Rav Idi)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Adda (or Rabbi Yitzchak bar Rav Idi)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Adda cites a verse from Psalms to support the idea that David woke at midnight.

items.text: Moses and David's knowledge of midnight
items.text_en: Moses and David's knowledge of midnight
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira explains that both Moses and David knew the exact time of midnight. David used a harp to wake himself, while Moses said 'about midnight' to avoid Pharaoh's astrologers accusing him of falsehood.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira opens by stating that both Moses and David knew the exact time of midnight.
The Gemara asks: since David knew the exact time, why did he need a harp?
The Gemara answers: the harp was to wake him from his sleep.
The Gemara asks: since Moses knew the exact time, why did he say 'about midnight'?
The Gemara answers: Moses was concerned that Pharaoh's astrologers might err and accuse him of falsehood, citing the principle that one should say 'I don't know' to avoid being caught in a lie.

items.text: Rav Ashi's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that Moses was speaking at the beginning of the night of the 14th of Nisan, saying that at midnight the next day God would go out into Egypt.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that Moses was standing at the midpoint of the night of the 13th entering the 14th, and said that tomorrow at about this time God would go out in Egypt.

items.text: David's claim of piety
items.text_en: David's claim of piety
items.desc_en: Levi and Rabbi Yitzchak debate David's statement 'I am pious'. One says David woke at midnight while other kings slept; the other says David's hands were soiled with blood and afterbirth to purify women, and he consulted Mephibosheth in halakhic matters.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'To David: Guard my soul for I am pious' and introduces the debate between Levi and Rabbi Yitzchak regarding David's claim of piety.
Levi explains that David claimed piety because he woke at midnight to praise God while other kings slept until three hours into the day.

Rabbi Yitzchak explains that David claimed piety because his hands were soiled with blood and afterbirth to purify women for their husbands, and he consulted Mephibosheth in all halakhic matters without shame.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehoshua brei d'Rav Idi's proof
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua brei d'Rav Idi's proof
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua brei d'Rav Idi cites the verse 'And I will speak of Your testimonies before kings and not be ashamed' to support David's claim of consulting Mephibosheth without shame.

items.text: Mephibosheth's name and David's son Kilav
items.text_en: Mephibosheth's name and David's son Kilav
items.desc_en: A beraita explains that Mephibosheth was actually named Ish Boshet, but called Mephibosheth because he shamed David in halakha. Rabbi Yochanan says Kilav was actually Daniel, called Kilav because he shamed Mephibosheth in halakha, and Solomon praised him.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna (תנא) reports that Mephibosheth's real name was Ish Boshet, not Mephibosheth.
The beraita explains Mephibosheth's name as meaning he shamed David in halakha, so David merited having Kilav as his son.
Rabbi Yochanan asserts that Kilav's real name was Daniel.
Rabbi Yochanan explains the name Kilav as meaning he shamed Mephibosheth in halakha.
Solomon praised Kilav in his wisdom with verses showing that such a wise son brings joy and shames detractors.

items.text: David's uncertainty about his portion
items.text_en: David's uncertainty about his portion
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether David called himself pious, citing a verse where he was uncertain about his portion in the World to Come due to sin, as illustrated by Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi's contradiction about Jacob's fear and the principle that sin can cause failure of miracles.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether David called himself pious, citing the verse 'לוּלֵא הֶאֱמַנְתִּי' (Unless I had believed) and the tradition from Rabbi Yosei that David was uncertain about his portion in the World to Come.
The Gemara explains that David's uncertainty was due to the possibility that sin might cause failure, not a lack of piety.
Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi raises a contradiction about Jacob's fear despite God's promise, showing that sin can cause failure of miracles.
A baraita teaches that Israel was worthy of a miracle in Ezra's time like in Joshua's time, but sin caused it to fail, supporting the principle that sin can prevent divine protection.

items.text: The Sages' position on the Shema time
items.text_en: The Sages' position on the Shema time
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: the Sages say the Shema may be recited until midnight; whose opinion do they follow? If they follow Rabbi Eliezer, they should say so explicitly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the position of the Sages who say until midnight, asking why they do not follow Rabbi Eliezer's opinion.

items.text: Explanation for the Sages' ruling of 'until midnight'
items.text_en: Explanation for the Sages' ruling of 'until midnight'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Sages who say the Shema may be recited only until midnight actually agree with Rabban Gamliel that it is valid until dawn, but they set an earlier limit to prevent people from delaying and falling asleep. A baraita illustrates how a person returning from the field might procrastinate and miss the recitation entirely.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Sages agree with Rabban Gamliel in principle but set the limit at midnight as a fence to prevent transgression.
A baraita illustrates the concern: a person returning from the field might procrastinate and fall asleep, so the Sages made a fence to prevent this.
The baraita concludes that one who violates the words of the Sages is liable to death.

items.text: Why the severe penalty of death is stated here
items.text_en: Why the severe penalty of death is stated here
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita specifically states that one who violates the words of the Sages is liable for death, unlike other contexts. Two answers are given: because of the danger of falling asleep (an unavoidable circumstance), and to refute the opinion that the evening prayer is optional, teaching that it is obligatory.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why this baraita uniquely states that one who violates the words of the Sages is liable for death, unlike other contexts.
The first answer explains that the death penalty is stated because of the danger of falling asleep, an unavoidable circumstance.
The second answer says the death penalty is stated to refute the opinion that the evening prayer is optional, teaching that it is obligatory.

items.text: The dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi on juxtaposing redemption to prayer
items.text_en: The dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi on juxtaposing redemption to prayer
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita supports Rabbi Yochanan's view that one should recite the Shema and then immediately pray the evening prayer, juxtaposing redemption to prayer. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi argues that prayers were established in the middle (between redemption and prayer). The dispute is analyzed through both logical reasoning and a biblical verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita supports Rabbi Yochanan's view that one should recite the Shema and then immediately pray, while Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi argues that prayers were established in the middle.
The Gemara asks: On what basis do they disagree?
The Gemara offers two possible bases for the dispute: a verse or logical reasoning.

The Gemara explains the logical reasoning: Rabbi Yochanan holds that redemption exists at night but is not complete until morning, while Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi holds that since it is only from morning, it is not a complete redemption.

The Gemara explains the verse-based reasoning: both derive from the verse 'בשכבך ובקומך' (when you lie down and when you rise), but Rabbi Yochanan compares lying down to rising to require prayer after Shema, while Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi compares them only to require Shema close to bedtime.

items.text: Resolving the challenge from the blessing 'Hashkiveinu'
items.text_en: Resolving the challenge from the blessing 'Hashkiveinu'
items.desc_en: Mar bar Ravina challenges Rabbi Yochanan's view by noting that the evening service includes the blessing 'Hashkiveinu' between the Shema and the Amidah, breaking the juxtaposition. The Gemara answers that 'Hashkiveinu' is considered an extended redemption, just as the morning service's introductory verses are considered an extended prayer.

sub.desc_en: Mar bar Ravina challenges Rabbi Yochanan's view by citing the Mishnah that in the evening one recites two blessings before the Shema and two after, including 'Hashkiveinu' between the Shema and the Amidah, which breaks the required juxtaposition of redemption to prayer.
The Gemara answers that since the Sages instituted 'Hashkiveinu' as an extended redemption (גאולה אריכתא), it does not interrupt the juxtaposition; it is considered part of the redemption itself.

items.text: The merit of reciting 'Ashrei' three times daily
items.text_en: The merit of reciting 'Ashrei' three times daily
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Avina states that one who recites 'Tehillah LeDavid' (Psalm 145) three times daily is assured a place in the World to Come. The Gemara explores the reason, rejecting suggestions that it is due to its alphabetical structure or the verse 'Poteach et yadecha', and concludes it is because it contains both.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Avina
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Avina
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Avina states that one who recites 'Tehillah LeDavid' three times daily is assured a place in the World to Come.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind this assurance.
The Gemara rejects the suggestion that the merit is due to the alphabetical structure of the psalm, noting that 'Ashrei Temimei Derech' has an eightfold alphabetical structure.
The Gemara rejects the suggestion that the merit is due to the verse 'Poteach et yadecha', noting that 'Hallel HaGadol' also contains a similar verse about God providing sustenance.
The Gemara concludes that the merit is because the psalm contains both the alphabetical structure and the verse about God's sustenance.

items.text: The missing letter Nun in 'Ashrei' and its restoration
items.text_en: The missing letter Nun in 'Ashrei' and its restoration
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that the letter Nun is omitted from the alphabetical acrostic of Psalm 145 because it alludes to the downfall of Israel's enemies. The Gemara in the West resolves the verse positively, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak notes that David later restored it through the Holy Spirit in the verse 'Somech Hashem lechol hanofelim'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asks why the letter Nun is omitted from the alphabetical acrostic of Psalm 145 (Ashrei), explaining that it alludes to the downfall of Israel's enemies, as the verse says 'נָפְלָה לֹא תוֹסִיף קוּם בְּתוּלַת יִשְׂרָאֵל' (Fallen, she will not rise again, the virgin of Israel).

The Gemara in the West (Eretz Yisrael) resolves the verse positively: 'נָפְלָה וְלֹא תּוֹסִיף לִנְפּוֹל עוֹד, קוּם בְּתוּלַת יִשְׂרָאֵל' (She has fallen but will not fall again; arise, virgin of Israel).
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak states that even so, David restored the letter Nun through the Holy Spirit in the verse 'סוֹמֵךְ ה׳ לְכָל הַנֹּפְלִים' (The Lord supports all who fall).

items.text: The flight speeds of Michael, Gabriel, Elijah, and the Angel of Death
items.text_en: The flight speeds of Michael, Gabriel, Elijah, and the Angel of Death
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Avina notes that what is said about Michael is greater than what is said about Gabriel, as Michael is described as flying with one wing while Gabriel requires two. A baraita elaborates: Michael in one, Gabriel in two, Elijah in four, and the Angel of Death in eight, but during a plague, in one.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Avina asserts that what is said about Michael is greater than what is said about Gabriel, citing verses showing Michael flies with one wing while Gabriel requires two.
The Gemara asks how we know that the 'one' in the verse refers to Michael, and Rabbi Yochanan answers with a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from another verse where Michael is explicitly called 'one'.
A baraita elaborates the flight speeds: Michael in one, Gabriel in two, Elijah in four, and the Angel of Death in eight, but during a plague, in one.

items.text: The mitzvah to recite Shema on one's bed
items.text_en: The mitzvah to recite Shema on one's bed
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states that even if one has recited the Shema in the synagogue, it is a mitzvah to recite it again on one's bed. Rabbi Yosei cites the verse 'Tremble and sin not; say in your hearts upon your beds and be still, Selah' as support. The daf ends with Rav Nachman beginning a statement.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states that even if one has recited the Shema in the synagogue, it is a mitzvah to recite it again on one's bed.

Rabbi Yosei cites the verse 'רִגְזוּ וְאַל תֶּחֱטָאוּ אִמְרוּ בִלְבַבְכֶם עַל מִשְׁכַּבְכֶם וְדֹמּוּ סֶלָה' (Tremble and sin not; say in your hearts upon your beds and be still, Selah) as a biblical support for the practice.
Rav Nachman begins a statement, but the daf ends before its content is given.

items.text: Abaye's ruling on a Torah scholar's bedtime prayer
items.text_en: Abaye's ruling on a Torah scholar's bedtime prayer
items.desc_en: Abaye states that even a Torah scholar must recite a verse of mercy before sleep, such as 'Into Your hand I entrust my spirit'.

sub.desc_en: Abaye rules that even a Torah scholar must recite a verse of mercy before sleep, citing the example of 'Into Your hand I entrust my spirit'.

items.text: Resh Lakish's three-step strategy against the evil inclination
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's three-step strategy against the evil inclination
items.desc_en: Rabbi Levi bar Hama in the name of Resh Lakish advises that one should first provoke the good inclination against the evil one; if that fails, engage in Torah study; if that fails, recite Shema; and if that fails, remember the day of death.

sub.text: Rabbi Levi bar Hama citing Resh Lakish
sub.text_en: Rabbi Levi bar Hama citing Resh Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Levi bar Hama in the name of Resh Lakish presents a four-step strategy: first provoke the good inclination against the evil one; if that fails, engage in Torah study; if that fails, recite Shema; if that fails, remember the day of death.

items.text: Resh Lakish's exposition of the tablets and Torah
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's exposition of the tablets and Torah
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish interprets a verse to show that the tablets, Torah, Mishnah, Prophets, Writings, and Talmud were all given to Moses at Sinai.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish interprets the verse 'And I gave you the tablets of stone and the Torah and the commandment' to show that all parts of the Oral and Written Law were given to Moses at Sinai.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak on the benefits of reciting Shema on one's bed
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak on the benefits of reciting Shema on one's bed
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak teaches that reciting Shema on one's bed is like holding a double-edged sword that protects from harmful spirits, citing verses from Psalms.

sub.desc_en: רבי יצחק (Rabbi Yitzchak) states that reciting קריאת שמע (Shema) on one's bed is like holding a double-edged sword, citing the verse 'רוֹמְמוֹת אֵל בִּגְרוֹנָם וְחֶרֶב פִּיפִיּוֹת בְּיָדָם' (High praises of God in their mouths, and a double-edged sword in their hands).

The Gemara asks how the verse relates to Shema, and מר זוטרא (Mar Zutra) or רב אשי (Rav Ashi) answers that it is derived from the preceding verse 'יַעְלְזוּ חֲסִידִים בְּכָבוֹד יְרַנְּנוּ עַל מִשְׁכְּבוֹתָם' (Let the pious exult in glory; let them joyously sing upon their beds), which refers to reciting Shema on one's bed.

רבי יצחק (Rabbi Yitzchak) adds that reciting Shema on one's bed causes demons to stay away, interpreting the verse 'וּבְנֵי רֶשֶׁף יַגְבִּיהוּ עוּף' (and the sparks fly upward) where 'עוּף' (fly) refers to Torah and 'רֶשֶׁף' (sparks) refers to demons.

items.text: Resh Lakish on Torah study warding off suffering
items.text_en: Resh Lakish on Torah study warding off suffering
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish states that engaging in Torah study keeps suffering away, interpreting the same verse about 'reshef' as referring to suffering.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish states that engaging in Torah study keeps suffering away, interpreting the verse 'ובני רשף יגביהו עוף' (and the sparks fly upward) by equating 'עוף' (fly) with Torah and 'רשף' (sparks) with suffering.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's correction: suffering for those who can study but don't
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's correction: suffering for those who can study but don't
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan objects that even schoolchildren know Torah protects from suffering; rather, suffering comes to those who can study Torah but neglect it.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan objects that even schoolchildren know Torah protects from suffering; rather, suffering comes to those who can study Torah but neglect it.

items.text: God's unique joy in giving the Torah
items.text_en: God's unique joy in giving the Torah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira (or Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa) contrasts human commerce, where the seller is sad and buyer happy, with God who rejoiced in giving the Torah to Israel.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira (or Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira (or Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira (or Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa) contrasts human commerce, where the seller is sad and buyer happy, with God who rejoiced in giving the Torah to Israel.

items.text: Rava's three-step diagnosis of suffering
items.text_en: Rava's three-step diagnosis of suffering
items.desc_en: Rava (or Rav Chisda) teaches that when suffering comes, one should first examine their deeds; if no sin is found, attribute it to neglect of Torah; if still not, it is yissurin shel ahavah (afflictions of love).

sub.desc_en: Rava (or Rav Chisda) opens: when one sees suffering coming, they should examine their deeds.

items.text: Rav Huna on God's desire to crush the beloved with suffering
items.text_en: Rav Huna on God's desire to crush the beloved with suffering
items.desc_en: Rav Huna states that God crushes those He desires with suffering, but only if accepted knowingly; reward includes seeing offspring, long life, and enduring Torah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna opens by stating that the Holy One crushes with suffering those He desires, citing the verse 'וה׳ חפץ דכאו החלי' (and the Lord desired to crush him, He made him ill).
The Gemara raises a question: could this apply even if one does not accept the suffering out of love? It then introduces a limiting teaching.

The Gemara answers by citing the verse 'אם תשים אשם נפשו' (if you make his soul a guilt-offering), deriving a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy): just as a guilt-offering is brought knowingly, so too suffering must be accepted knowingly.

Rav Huna concludes: if one accepts suffering knowingly, the reward is seeing offspring, long life, and that his Torah study endures in his hand, as per the verse 'וחפץ ה׳ בידו יצלח' (and the Lord's desire will prosper in his hand).

items.text: Two opinions on the definition of yissurin shel ahavah
items.text_en: Two opinions on the definition of yissurin shel ahavah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi and Rabbi Acha bar Chanina disagree: one says afflictions that do not interrupt Torah study, the other says those that do not interrupt prayer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between two sages over the definition of יסורין של אהבה (afflictions of love).

One sage (Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi) defines יסורין של אהבה (afflictions of love) as those that do not interrupt Torah study, citing the verse 'אַשְׁרֵי הַגֶּבֶר... וּמִתּוֹרָתְךָ תְלַמְּדֶנּוּ' (Happy is the man whom You afflict... and from Your Torah You teach him).

The other sage (Rabbi Acha bar Chanina) defines יסורין של אהבה (afflictions of love) as those that do not interrupt prayer, citing the verse 'בָּרוּךְ אֱלֹהִים אֲשֶׁר לֹא הֵסִיר תְּפִלָּתִי וְחַסְדּוֹ מֵאִתִּי' (Blessed is God who did not turn away my prayer and His kindness from me).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's resolution: both are yissurin shel ahavah
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's resolution: both are yissurin shel ahavah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that both types are afflictions of love, and the verse 'from Your Torah teach us' implies that Torah itself teaches this lesson.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan (via Rabbi Abba bar Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan (via Rabbi Abba bar Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that both types of suffering are יסורין של אהבה (afflictions of love), citing the verse 'כי את אשר יאהב ה׳ יוכיח' (for whom the Lord loves He rebukes), and then reinterprets 'ומתורתך תלמדנו' (from Your Torah teach us) as 'תלמדנו' (teach us) — implying that Torah itself teaches this lesson.

items.text: Kal vachomer from tooth and eye to suffering
items.text_en: Kal vachomer from tooth and eye to suffering
items.desc_en: A kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument: if a tooth or eye frees a slave, how much more so suffering that purifies the entire body. Resh Lakish adds that suffering, like salt, is a covenant that atones for all sins.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument: if a tooth or eye, which are single limbs, can free a slave, then suffering that purifies the entire body should certainly atone for all sins.

Resh Lakish (רבי שמעון בן לקיש) adds a supporting argument: just as salt is called a 'covenant' (ברית) that sweetens meat, so too suffering is called a 'covenant' that purifies all of a person's sins.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's three gifts given through suffering
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's three gifts given through suffering
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai teaches that Torah, the Land of Israel, and the World to Come are three precious gifts given to Israel only through suffering, each supported by a verse.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai (רבי שמעון בן יוחאי)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai (רבי שמעון בן יוחאי)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai (רבי שמעון בן יוחאי) opens by stating that three precious gifts were given to Israel only through suffering.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai (רבי שמעון בן יוחאי)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai (רבי שמעון בן יוחאי)
sub.desc_en: He lists the three gifts: Torah, the Land of Israel, and the World to Come.

items.text: Opening of a baraita on Torah and gemilut chasadim
items.text_en: Opening of a baraita on Torah and gemilut chasadim
items.desc_en: A tanna begins a baraita before Rabbi Yochanan about one who engages in Torah and acts of kindness, but the text cuts off.

sub.desc_en: A tanna begins a baraita before Rabbi Yochanan about one who engages in Torah and acts of kindness, but the text cuts off.

items.text: Atonement for burying one's children
items.text_en: Atonement for burying one's children
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how burying one's children atones for sins, given that Torah and acts of kindness are already known to atone. A Sage answers via a verbal analogy between the word 'avon' in the verse about atonement and in the verse about visiting the iniquity of fathers upon children.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who buries his children is forgiven all his sins.
Rabbi Yochanan questions how burying one's children atones, given that Torah and acts of kindness already atone via the verse 'בְּחֶסֶד וֶאֱמֶת יְכֻפַּר עָוֹן'.

sub.text: A certain elder in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.text_en: A certain elder in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.desc_en: A certain elder answers in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai, deriving a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'עָוֹן' — the same word appears in the atonement verse and in the verse about visiting the iniquity of fathers upon children.

items.text: Afflictions of love: leprosy and children
items.text_en: Afflictions of love: leprosy and children
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that leprosy and the death of children are not afflictions of love. The Gemara objects that leprosy is an altar of atonement, but distinguishes between atonement and afflictions of love. It then resolves the contradiction regarding children by distinguishing between those who never had children and those who had and lost them.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that leprosy and the death of children are not afflictions of love.
The Gemara objects that leprosy is explicitly called an altar of atonement in a baraita.
The Gemara distinguishes: leprosy provides atonement (כפרה) but is not classified as afflictions of love.
Alternatively, the baraita refers to us (Babylonians) while Rabbi Yochanan's statement refers to them (Palestinians).
Alternatively, the baraita refers to private leprosy (which is atonement) while Rabbi Yochanan refers to public leprosy (which is not an affliction of love).
The Gemara objects: if children died, Rabbi Yochanan himself called such a case 'this bone of a tenth son' (a great affliction).
The Gemara resolves: Rabbi Yochanan's statement refers to those who never had children (not an affliction of love), while the case of having and losing children is indeed an affliction of love.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan heals Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba and himself
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan heals Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba and himself
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan visits the sick Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba, who says he does not desire suffering. Rabbi Yochanan heals him by taking his hand. Later, when Rabbi Yochanan himself falls ill, Rabbi Chanina heals him. The Gemara explains why Rabbi Yochanan could not heal himself: a prisoner cannot free himself from prison.

sub.desc_en: The narrative opens with Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba falling ill.
Rabbi Yochanan visits Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba and asks if he desires suffering; Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba responds that he does not want them or their reward.
Rabbi Yochanan asks for Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's hand and raises him, healing him.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yochanan could not heal himself when he later fell ill.
The Gemara answers with a proverb: a prisoner cannot free himself from prison.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's weeping and healing
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's weeping and healing
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan visits the sick Rabbi Elazar, who is weeping in a dark room. Rabbi Yochanan illuminates the room and asks why he weeps. Rabbi Elazar explains he weeps over his beauty that will decay. Rabbi Yochanan agrees, and then heals him after Rabbi Elazar says he does not desire suffering.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar falls ill; Rabbi Yochanan visits him in a dark room and illuminates it by baring his arm.
Rabbi Yochanan sees Rabbi Elazar weeping and asks if it is over insufficient Torah study, lack of livelihood, or childlessness, offering consolations for each.
Rabbi Elazar explains he weeps over his beauty that will decay in the dust; Rabbi Yochanan agrees and they both weep.
Rabbi Yochanan asks if Rabbi Elazar desires suffering; Rabbi Elazar declines, and Rabbi Yochanan heals him by taking his hand and raising him.

items.text: Rav Huna's wine turns to vinegar
items.text_en: Rav Huna's wine turns to vinegar
items.desc_en: Rav Huna's four hundred barrels of wine turn sour. The Sages suggest he examine his deeds. He denies suspicion, but they argue that God does not punish without cause. They recall that he did not give a vine shoot to his sharecropper. Rav Huna accepts to give it, and the vinegar either turns back to wine or becomes valuable.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna's four hundred barrels of wine turn sour, setting the scene for the story.
The Sages visit Rav Huna and suggest he examine his deeds for a possible sin.
Rav Huna objects, denying that he is suspected of any wrongdoing.
The Sages reject his denial, arguing that God does not punish without cause.
Rav Huna asks if anyone has heard of a specific sin he committed.
The Sages report that Rav Huna did not give a vine shoot (שבישׁא) to his sharecropper.
Rav Huna objects that the sharecropper steals everything anyway, so why give him a shoot?
The Sages reject his objection with a proverb: 'After a thief, steal, and you will taste the taste [of theft].'
Rav Huna accepts to give the vine shoot to the sharecropper.
One version says the vinegar turned back into wine.
Another version says the vinegar became valuable and was sold at the price of wine.

items.text: Abba Binyamin's prayer and bed placement
items.text_en: Abba Binyamin's prayer and bed placement
items.desc_en: Abba Binyamin says he was distressed about two things: that his prayer be before his bed and that his bed be placed north-south. The Gemara clarifies 'before his bed' means near it, not literally in front. Rabbi Chama bar Chanina says placing the bed north-south yields male children, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds that his wife will not miscarry.

sub.desc_en: Abba Binyamin states he was distressed about two things: that his prayer be before his bed and that his bed be placed north-south.
The Gemara asks what 'before my bed' means.
The Gemara objects that if 'before' is literal, it contradicts the rule that nothing may interpose between the worshipper and the wall.
The Gemara resolves that 'before my bed' means 'near my bed,' not literally in front.
The Gemara cites the second clause of Abba Binyamin's statement about bed placement.

sub.text: Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina citing Rabbi Yitzchak states that placing the bed north-south yields male children, citing a verse.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds that such bed placement also prevents miscarriage, citing a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from the word 'בטנם' (their belly).

items.text: Punishment for not waiting for a fellow worshiper
items.text_en: Punishment for not waiting for a fellow worshiper
items.desc_en: Abba Binyamin teaches that if two enter to pray and one finishes first without waiting for the other, his prayer is torn in his face and causes the Divine Presence to depart from Israel. The Gemara then asks what reward one receives for waiting.

sub.desc_en: Abba Binyamin teaches that if two enter to pray and one finishes first without waiting for the other, his prayer is torn in his face, citing a verse.
Abba Binyamin adds that such a person also causes the Divine Presence to depart from Israel, citing another verse.
The Gemara asks what reward one receives for waiting for a fellow worshiper.

items.text: Harmful spirits and their effects
items.text_en: Harmful spirits and their effects
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina teaches that one who listens to mitzvot merits blessings. Abba Binyamin states that if permission were given to see, no creature could withstand the harmful spirits. Abaye, Rav Huna, and Rava describe their prevalence and effects, and a method is given to see them, with a cautionary tale about Rav Beivai bar Abaye.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina teaches that one who listens to mitzvot merits blessings, citing a verse.
Abba Binyamin states that if permission were given to see, no creature could withstand the harmful spirits.
Abaye says the harmful spirits are more numerous than us and surround us like a mound around a pit.
Rav Huna says each person has a thousand spirits on his left and ten thousand on his right.
Rava attributes various physical discomforts—crowding at weddings, weakening knees, wear of rabbinic garments, and swelling feet—to the harmful spirits.
The gemara describes a method to see the harmful spirits and recounts that Rav Beivai bar Abaye tried it, was harmed, and was healed through the rabbis' prayers.

items.text: Prayer is heard in the synagogue
items.text_en: Prayer is heard in the synagogue
items.desc_en: Abba Binyamin teaches that a person's prayer is only heard in the synagogue, citing a verse that links prayer to the place of song.

sub.desc_en: Abba Binyamin states that a person's prayer is heard only in the synagogue, citing the verse 'לִשְׁמֹעַ אֶל הָרִנָּה וְאֶל הַתְּפִלָּה' to prove that prayer belongs in the place of song.

items.text: The Shekhinah is present with various groups
items.text_en: The Shekhinah is present with various groups
items.desc_en: Ravin bar Rav Adda quotes Rabbi Yitzchak to prove that God is present in the synagogue, with ten, three, two, and even one person studying Torah. The Gemara explains the distinctions: two have their words recorded, three involve judgment which is also Torah, and ten cause the Shekhinah to come early.

sub.text: Ravin bar Rav Adda citing Rabbi Yitzchak
sub.text_en: Ravin bar Rav Adda citing Rabbi Yitzchak
sub.desc_en: Ravin bar Rav Adda quotes Rabbi Yitzchak, citing a verse to prove that the Shekhinah is present in the synagogue.
The Gemara deduces from the same verse that the Shekhinah is with ten people praying.
The Gemara deduces from a verse that the Shekhinah is with three judges sitting in judgment.
The Gemara deduces from a verse that the Shekhinah is with two people studying Torah together.

Rav Ashi explains the phrase 'וּלְחֹשְׁבֵי שְׁמוֹ' (and for those who think of His name) from the verse, teaching that one who intends to perform a mitzvah but is prevented is credited as if they performed it.
The Gemara deduces from a verse that even one person studying Torah has the Shekhinah with them.
The Gemara questions why two are needed if even one has the Shekhinah, and answers that two have their words recorded in the book of remembrance, while one does not.
The Gemara questions why three are needed if even two have the Shekhinah, and answers that one might think judgment is merely peacemaking, but it teaches that judgment is also Torah.
The Gemara questions why ten are needed if even three have the Shekhinah, and answers that with ten the Shekhinah comes early, while with three it comes only after they sit.

items.text: God's tefillin and their contents
items.text_en: God's tefillin and their contents
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avin bar Rav Adda quotes Rabbi Yitzchak that God wears tefillin, which contain verses praising Israel. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak asks Rav Chiya bar Avin what is written in them, and the answer is 'Who is like Your people Israel'. The Gemara details the verses in each compartment, resolving a question about the number of compartments.

sub.text: Rabbi Avin bar Rav Adda citing Rabbi Yitzchak
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avin bar Rav Adda citing Rabbi Yitzchak
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avin bar Rav Adda in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak opens by asking from where we know that God wears tefillin, citing the verse 'נִשְׁבַּע ה׳ בִּימִינוֹ וּבִזְרוֹעַ עֻזּוֹ' (The Lord has sworn by His right hand and by His mighty arm).
The Gemara interprets 'בִּימִינוֹ' (His right hand) as the Torah and 'וּבִזְרוֹעַ עֻזּוֹ' (His mighty arm) as tefillin, citing verses to support each identification.
The Gemara proves that tefillin are a strength for Israel from a verse, and cites a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer HaGadol identifies the 'name of God' in that verse as the head-tefillin.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's question to Rav Chiya bar Avin
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's question to Rav Chiya bar Avin
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak asks Rav Chiya bar Avin what is written in God's tefillin, and receives the answer: 'וּמִי כְּעַמְּךָ יִשְׂרָאֵל גּוֹי אֶחָד בָּאָרֶץ' (Who is like Your people Israel, one nation in the land).

The Gemara objects: does God really praise Himself with Israel's praise? It resolves by citing verses showing a reciprocal relationship: Israel made God one in the world (Shema), and God makes Israel one in the world (the same verse).

sub.text: Rav Acha brei d'Rava's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha brei d'Rava's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha brei d'Rava asks Rav Ashi: it is fine for one compartment (of God's tefillin), but what is written in the other compartments?
Rav Ashi answers that the other compartments contain the verses: 'כִּי מִי גוֹי גָּדוֹל', 'וּמִי גוֹי גָּדוֹל', 'אַשְׁרֶיךָ יִשְׂרָאֵל', 'אוֹ הֲנִסָּה אֱלֹהִים', and 'וּלְתִתְּךָ עֶלְיוֹן'.

The Gemara objects that this would be too many compartments, and resolves by pairing similar verses: 'כִּי מִי גוֹי גָּדוֹל' and 'וּמִי גוֹי גָּדוֹל' in one compartment, 'אַשְׁרֶיךָ יִשְׂרָאֵל' and 'וּמִי כְּעַמְּךָ יִשְׂרָאֵל' in one, 'אוֹ הֲנִסָּה אֱלֹהִים' in one, and 'וּלְתִתְּךָ עֶלְיוֹן' in one.

items.text: Opening: Reward for regular synagogue attendance
items.text_en: Opening: Reward for regular synagogue attendance
items.desc_en: Ravin bar Adda quoting Rabbi Yitzchak states that one who regularly attends synagogue but misses a day is questioned by God, citing Isaiah 50:10. The Gemara clarifies that this applies to one who goes for a mitzvah, not for personal benefit.

sub.text: Ravin bar Adda quoting Rabbi Yitzchak
sub.text_en: Ravin bar Adda quoting Rabbi Yitzchak
sub.desc_en: Ravin bar Adda in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak states that one who regularly attends the synagogue but misses a day is questioned by God, citing Isaiah 50:10.
The Gemara clarifies that the verse's darkness applies only if the absence was for a non-mitzvah purpose, but if for a mitzvah, the person receives light.
The Gemara asks why the verse concludes 'let him trust in the name of the Lord,' and answers that it is because he should have trusted but did not.

items.text: Gemara's first question: Trust in God vs. human effort
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: Trust in God vs. human effort
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse says 'let him trust in God's name' — it implies one should trust in God, not in oneself. Rabbi Yochanan explains that when God enters a synagogue and finds fewer than ten, He is angry, citing Isaiah 50:2.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse says 'let him trust in God's name' — it implies one should have trusted in God but did not.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that when God enters a synagogue and finds fewer than ten, He becomes angry, citing Isaiah 50:2.

items.text: Second answer: Establishing a fixed place for prayer
items.text_en: Second answer: Establishing a fixed place for prayer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chelbo quoting Rabbi Huna states that one who establishes a fixed place for prayer is aided by the God of Abraham. When such a person dies, they are praised as humble and pious, a disciple of Abraham.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chelbo in the name of Rabbi Huna states that one who establishes a fixed place for prayer (קובע מקום לתפילתו) receives divine assistance from the God of Abraham.
Rabbi Chelbo adds that upon death, such a person is eulogized as humble, pious, and a disciple of Abraham our father.

items.text: Proof from Abraham: He established a place for prayer
items.text_en: Proof from Abraham: He established a place for prayer
items.desc_en: The Gemara proves Abraham established a prayer place from Genesis 19:27, where 'stood' implies prayer. Various rabbis list rewards for different synagogue activities: running (Rabbi Zeira), pressure (Abaye), understanding (Rava), silence (Rabbi Papa), charity (Mar Zutra), eulogy (Rabbi Sheshet), wedding joy (Rabbi Ashi).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that Abraham established a fixed place for prayer, and answers by citing Genesis 19:27, interpreting 'standing' as prayer.
Rabbi Chelbo in the name of Rav Huna rules that one leaving the synagogue should not take large steps, but Abaye adds that entering requires running, citing Hosea 6:3.

Rabbi Zeira recounts that he initially thought rabbis running to a lecture on Shabbat were violating Shabbat, but after hearing Rabbi Tanchum citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that one should always run to a matter of halacha even on Shabbat, he too began running.
Rabbi Zeira states that the reward for attending a lecture (פִּרְקָא) is the running itself.
Abaye states that the reward for attending a wedding (כַּלָּה) is the pressure/crowding.
Rava states that the reward for engaging in Torah study (שְׁמַעְתָּא) is the understanding.
Rav Papa states that the reward for attending a house of mourning (בֵי טַמְיָא) is the silence.
Mar Zutra states that the reward for a fast day (תַעֲנִיתָא) is charity.
Rabbi Sheshet states that the reward for a eulogy (הֶסְפֵּדָא) is the lifting up (of the mourner).
Rav Ashi states that the reward for attending a wedding celebration (בֵי הִלּוּלֵי) is the words (of Torah or pleasant conversation).

items.text: Warning against praying behind the synagogue
items.text_en: Warning against praying behind the synagogue
items.desc_en: Rabbi Huna says one who prays behind the synagogue is called wicked, citing Psalms 12:9. Abaye clarifies this applies only if one does not face the synagogue. A story: Elijah killed a man praying behind the synagogue without facing it, appearing as a Arab traveler.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Huna states that one who prays behind the synagogue is called wicked, citing Psalms 12:9.
Abaye qualifies that the ruling applies only if one does not face the synagogue, but if one faces it, there is no issue.
A story is told of a man who prayed behind the synagogue without facing it, and Elijah, disguised as an Arab, killed him with a sword.

items.text: Interpretation of 'Kerum Zulut'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'Kerum Zulut'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Bibi bar Abaye (or Rabbi Bibi to Rabbi Nachman bar Yitzchak) asks the meaning of 'Kerum Zulut' (Psalm 12:9). Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar say: when one needs people, their face changes like a 'kerum' (a sea bird that changes colors in sunlight).

sub.text: Rabbi Bibi bar Abaye (or Rabbi Bibi to Rabbi Nachman bar Yitzchak)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Bibi bar Abaye (or Rabbi Bibi to Rabbi Nachman bar Yitzchak)
sub.desc_en: A certain rabbi asks Rabbi Bibi bar Abaye (or Rabbi Bibi asks Rabbi Nachman bar Yitzchak) the meaning of the verse 'כְּרֻם זֻלּוּת לִבְנֵי אָדָם' (Psalm 12:9).

sub.text: Rabbi Bibi bar Abaye (or Rabbi Nachman bar Yitzchak)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Bibi bar Abaye (or Rabbi Nachman bar Yitzchak)
sub.desc_en: The rabbi answers: these are matters that stand at the height of the world (i.e., are of supreme importance), yet people treat them lightly.
Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar both explain: when a person needs others, his face changes like a 'כְּרוּם' (a sea bird), citing the same verse.
Rav Dimi explains the metaphor: there is a bird called 'כְּרוּם' in the coastal cities that changes colors in the sunlight, illustrating the change in a person's face.
