items.text: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi: Like judged by fire and water
items.text_en: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi: Like judged by fire and water
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi say the needy person is as if judged by both fire and water, citing Psalm 66:12. This continues the theme of human dependence and divine judgment.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi state that a person who depends on others is as if judged by both fire and water, citing Psalm 66:12.

items.text: Emphasis on Mincha (afternoon) prayer
items.text_en: Emphasis on Mincha (afternoon) prayer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chelbo quoting Rabbi Huna stresses the importance of Mincha prayer, citing Elijah's answer only at Mincha (1 Kings 18:36-37). Rabbi Yochanan adds that evening prayer also has precedent (Psalm 141:2), and Rabbi Nachman bar Yitzchak says morning prayer too (Psalm 5:4).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chelbo in the name of Rabbi Huna urges constant care regarding the Mincha (afternoon) prayer, citing that Elijah was only answered at the Mincha time, as per the verse.
The gemara explains Elijah's double plea 'עֲנֵנִי' (answer me): one for fire from heaven, the other to dispel accusations of sorcery.
Rabbi Yochanan adds that the evening prayer (ערבית) also has a biblical precedent, citing Psalm 141:2.
Rabbi Nachman bar Yitzchak adds that the morning prayer (שחרית) also has a biblical precedent, citing Psalm 5:4.

items.text: Reward for rejoicing at a wedding
items.text_en: Reward for rejoicing at a wedding
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chelbo quoting Rabbi Huna says one who benefits from a wedding feast without rejoicing violates five 'voices' (Isaiah 62:5). If one rejoices, they merit the Torah given with five voices (Exodus 19:16-19). Rabbi Joshua ben Levi adds: one who rejoices merits the Torah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chelbo in the name of Rabbi Huna states that one who benefits from a wedding feast without rejoicing violates five 'voices' (קולות) cited from Jeremiah 33:11.
The Gemara asks what reward one receives if they do rejoice with the bridegroom.
Rabbi Joshua ben Levi answers that one who rejoices merits the Torah, which was given with five voices (קולות) as described in Exodus 19:16-19.

items.text: Clarification on the five voices
items.text_en: Clarification on the five voices
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the five voices refer to the thunder at Sinai. Rabbi Avahu says it is like offering a thanksgiving sacrifice (Psalm 116:17). Rabbi Nachman bar Yitzchak says it is like rebuilding Jerusalem ruins (Jeremiah 30:18).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: how can the five voices at Sinai be the reward, when the verse says the people saw the voices (קולות), implying they were visible phenomena, not audible blessings?
The Gemara answers: those voices (קולות) were before the giving of the Torah, so they are a different set of voices, not the five voices of the reward.
Rabbi Avahu says the reward for rejoicing with a bridegroom is considered as if one offered a thanksgiving sacrifice (תודה), citing the verse 'מביאים תודה בית ה׳'.
Rabbi Nachman bar Yitzchak says the reward is considered as if one rebuilt one of the ruins of Jerusalem, citing the verse 'כי אשיב את שבות הארץ כבראשונה אמר ה׳'.

items.text: Fear of Heaven ensures words are heard
items.text_en: Fear of Heaven ensures words are heard
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chelbo quoting Rabbi Huna says one with fear of Heaven has their words heard, citing Ecclesiastes 12:13. Rabbi Elazar says the entire world was created only for such a person. Rabbi Abba bar Kahana says such a person outweighs the whole world. Rabbi Shimon ben Azzai (or Zoma) says the world was created only to accompany this person.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chelbo quoting Rabbi Huna states that anyone with יראת שמים (fear of Heaven) has his words heard, citing Ecclesiastes 12:13.
The Gemara asks the meaning of the phrase 'כי זה כל האדם' (for this is the whole man) from the verse.
Rabbi Elazar explains that the Holy One, blessed be He, says the entire world was created only for the sake of this person who fears Heaven.
Rabbi Abba bar Kahana adds that such a person is equivalent in weight to the entire world.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Azzai (or ben Zoma)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Azzai (or ben Zoma)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Azzai (or some say Rabbi Shimon ben Zoma) says the entire world was created only to accompany this person.

items.text: Final ruling: Greeting one known to be a regular giver of shalom
items.text_en: Final ruling: Greeting one known to be a regular giver of shalom
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chelbo quoting Rabbi Huna concludes: one who knows a friend regularly gives greetings should initiate greeting, citing Psalm 34:15. If the friend does not return the greeting, they are called a robber, citing Isaiah 3:14.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chelbo quoting Rabbi Huna rules that one who knows a friend regularly gives greetings should initiate greeting, and if the friend does not return it, they are called a robber.

items.text: God's prayer and its content
items.text_en: God's prayer and its content
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites Rabbi Yosei that God prays, proven by the verse 'My house of prayer'. The Gemara asks what God prays, and Rav Zutra bar Toviyah quotes Rav: 'May it be My will that My mercy suppress My anger...'

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei proves from the verse 'בֵּית תְּפִלָּתִי' (My house of prayer) that God prays.
The Gemara asks: What does God pray?

sub.text: Rav Zutra bar Toviyah citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviyah citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviyah in the name of Rav answers that God prays: 'May it be My will that My mercy suppress My anger, and that I deal with My children with mercy beyond the line of strict justice.'

items.text: Rabbi Yishmael's vision and the blessing of God
items.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael's vision and the blessing of God
items.desc_en: A baraita recounts Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha entering the Holy of Holies and seeing God, who asks for a blessing. Rabbi Yishmael blesses Him with a similar prayer, and God nods, teaching that a commoner's blessing should not be taken lightly.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha recounting his entry into the Holy of Holies to offer incense.
Rabbi Yishmael describes seeing God seated on a high and exalted throne.
God asks Rabbi Yishmael to bless Him.
Rabbi Yishmael responds with a blessing that God's mercy overcome His anger and that He treat Israel with compassion beyond strict justice.
God nods in response to the blessing.
The baraita concludes by teaching that one should not take the blessing of a commoner lightly.

items.text: Do not appease a person in anger
items.text_en: Do not appease a person in anger
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei derives from the verse 'My face will go and I will give you rest' that one should not appease a person during their anger, as God told Moses to wait until the 'face of wrath' passes.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei states that one should not appease a person during their anger.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei
sub.desc_en: He cites the verse 'My face will go and I will give you rest' as a prooftext.
The Gemara explains that God told Moses to wait until the 'face of wrath' passes, demonstrating the principle.

items.text: The nature and timing of God's anger
items.text_en: The nature and timing of God's anger
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether anger exists before God, citing a verse that He is angry daily. It discusses the duration of His anger (a moment), its precise measure, and that only Balaam knew its timing. The Gemara explains that God did not get angry during Balaam's time, and derives the duration of a 'moment' from verses. It concludes with Abaye's description of the time of anger.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether anger exists before God.
The Gemara answers yes, citing a baraita that God is angry daily, and describes the duration of His anger as a 'moment' (reg'a), known only to Balaam.
The Gemara objects: if Balaam did not even know his donkey's mind, how could he know God's mind?
The Gemara resolves that Balaam knew only the precise moment of God's anger, not His general knowledge.
Rabbi Elazar explains that God refrained from anger during Balaam's time as an act of righteousness toward Israel.
The Gemara cites Balaam's statement to Balak that God did not express anger during that period.
The Gemara asks for the precise measure of a 'moment' (reg'a).
Rabbi Avin (or Rabbi Avina) states that a 'moment' is as its name implies — an instant.
The Gemara cites verses to prove that God's anger lasts only a moment.
The Gemara asks when God becomes angry.
Abaye describes the time of anger as the first three hours of the day, when the rooster's comb is white and it stands on one leg, with no red streaks.

items.text: A heretic's failed attempt and God's mercy
items.text_en: A heretic's failed attempt and God's mercy
items.desc_en: A heretic who tormented Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi tried to curse God at the moment of anger using a rooster, but fell asleep. Rabbi Yehoshua concluded it is improper to act thus, citing 'His mercies are over all His works' and 'It is not good to punish the righteous'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a heretic who tormented Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and planned to curse God at the moment of anger using a rooster.
The heretic fell asleep at the critical moment, leading Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi to conclude it is improper to act thus.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi cites two verses: 'His mercies are over all His works' and 'It is not good to punish the righteous' to support his conclusion.

items.text: God's anger at idolatry and the value of rebuke
items.text_en: God's anger at idolatry and the value of rebuke
items.desc_en: A baraita from Rabbi Meir states that when kings bow to the sun, God becomes angry. Rabbi Yochanan then says that one rebuke in the heart is better than many lashes, citing a verse, and Resh Lakish says it is better than a hundred lashes.

sub.text: Baraita in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Baraita in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: A baraita in the name of Rabbi Meir teaches that when all kings bow to the sun at sunrise, God immediately becomes angry.
Rabbi Yochanan states that one rebuke in the heart is better than many public lashes, citing a verse.
Resh Lakish says that one rebuke in the heart is better than a hundred lashes to a fool, citing a different verse.

items.text: Moses' three requests and theodicy
items.text_en: Moses' three requests and theodicy
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan reports that Moses asked three things and received them: the Shekhinah resting on Israel, not on idolaters, and knowledge of God's ways. The Gemara discusses the meaning of 'righteous and good to him' etc., initially explaining it as based on parentage, but then rejecting that due to verses about collective punishment. It reinterprets it as referring to a completely righteous vs. not completely righteous person. Rabbi Meir holds that only two requests were granted.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei states that one rebuke in a person's heart is better than many lashes, citing the verse about the wife who returns to her first husband.
Reish Lakish adds that one rebuke is better than a hundred lashes, citing a different verse.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei reports that Moses asked three things from God and received them, beginning with the request that the Shekhinah rest on Israel.
Moses' second request was that the Shekhinah not rest on idolaters, and it was granted.
Moses' third request was to know God's ways, asking why there is a righteous person who has good, a righteous person who has bad, a wicked person who has good, and a wicked person who has bad.
God answers Moses that the categories are based on parentage: a righteous person with good is a righteous child of a righteous parent, etc.
The Gemara objects to the parentage-based explanation, citing the contradictory verses about visiting the iniquity of fathers on children and that children shall not be put to death for fathers.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the verse about visiting iniquity applies when children continue their fathers' deeds, and the other when they do not.
The Gemara reinterprets God's answer: the categories refer to a completely righteous person, a not completely righteous person, a not completely wicked person, and a completely wicked person.
Rabbi Meir disagrees, holding that only two of Moses' requests were granted, not the third, citing the verse about God's grace and mercy even to the undeserving.

items.text: Moses' request to see God's face and its aftermath
items.text_en: Moses' request to see God's face and its aftermath
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses God's refusal to show His face, with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha saying God told Moses 'when I wanted, you did not want; now that you want, I do not want'. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani says Moses merited seeing God's 'back' through his earlier actions. Rabbi Chana bar Bizna explains that God showed Moses the knot of tefillin. Finally, Rabbi Yochanan states that any good word from God, even conditionally, is not retracted, as demonstrated by Moses' descendants multiplying.

sub.text: Tanna quoting Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
sub.text_en: Tanna quoting Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a baraita quoting Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha that God told Moses: 'When I wanted, you did not want; now that you want, I do not want.'
The Gemara notes that this disagrees with Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan, who says Moses merited three things for three actions.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani details the three rewards: for hiding his face, Moses merited a shining face; for fearing, others feared to approach him; for refraining from looking, he merited seeing God's likeness.

sub.text: Rabbi Chana bar Bizna citing Rabbi Shimon Chasida
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chana bar Bizna citing Rabbi Shimon Chasida
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chana bar Bizna explains that God showed Moses the knot of tefillin, interpreting 'my back' as a reference to the tefillin knot.
Rabbi Yochanan states a principle: any good word that comes from God, even conditionally, is never retracted.
The Gemara proves the principle from Moses: God's conditional promise to make Moses a great nation was fulfilled in his descendants, as shown by the verse about Moses' sons multiplying.
Rav Yosef teaches that 'above' in the verse means more than 600,000, derived from a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) between 'multiplied' here and 'multiplied' in the Exodus verse.

items.text: אברהם קורא לה' 'אדון' ודניאל נענה בזכותו
items.text_en: Abraham first called God 'Adon'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan teaches that no one called God 'Adon' until Abraham. Rav adds that Daniel was answered only because of Abraham, who first used this title.
items.desc: רבי יוחנן משם רבי שמעון בן יוחי אומר שאברהם היה הראשון שקרא לה' 'אדון'. רב מוסיף שדניאל לא נענה אלא בזכות אברהם, כפי שדרש מהפסוק 'למען אדני'.

sub.text: רבי יוחנן משם רבי שמעון בן יוחי
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan teaches that no one called God 'Adon' until Abraham, citing the verse where Abraham says 'Adonai Elohim'.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן בשם רבי שמעון בן יוחי קובע שאברהם היה הראשון שקרא להקדוש ברוך הוא 'אדון'.

sub.desc_en: Rav adds that Daniel was answered only because of Abraham, who first called God 'Adon', as implied by the verse 'for the sake of Adonai'.
sub.desc: רב מוסיף שגם דניאל לא נענה אלא בזכות אברהם, ומביא ראיה מהפסוק 'למען אדני'.

items.text: אין מרצין לאדם בשעת כעסו
items.text_en: Do not appease a person in anger
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan teaches that one should not try to appease a person during their moment of anger, citing a verse where God says 'My face will go and I will give you rest.'
items.desc: רבי יוחנן משם רבי שמעון בן יוחי דורש מהפסוק 'פני ילכו והנחותי לך' שאין לרצות אדם בשעת כעסו.

sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan teaches that one should not appease a person during their anger, citing the verse 'My face will go and I will give you rest.'
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן בשם רבי שמעון בן יוחי דורש מהפסוק 'פני ילכו והנחותי לך' שאין לרצות אדם בשעת כעסו.

items.text: Leah first to thank God
items.text_en: Leah first to thank God
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan teaches that no one thanked God until Leah, who named her son Judah, saying 'This time I will thank the Lord.'

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan teaches that no one thanked God until Leah, who named her son Judah, saying 'This time I will thank the Lord.'

items.text: Reuben contrasted with Esau
items.text_en: Reuben contrasted with Esau
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains that Leah named Reuben to contrast her son with Esau: Esau sold his birthright and hated Jacob, but Reuben, though Joseph took his birthright, did not hate him and saved him.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar introduces the contrast between Reuben and Esau, citing Esau's sale of the birthright and his subsequent hatred of Jacob.
Rabbi Elazar contrasts Reuben's behavior: despite Joseph taking his birthright, Reuben did not hate him and saved him from his brothers.

items.text: שמה של רות ושמות גורמים
items.text_en: Ruth and the significance of names
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that Ruth merited David, who 'satiated' God with songs. Rabbi Eliezer derives from a verse that names have significance, reading 'shammot' as 'shemot'.
items.desc: רבי יוחנן דורש את שמה של רות כמי שזכתה להוליד את דוד שריווה לה' בשירות. רבי אליעזר דורש מהפסוק 'אשר שם שמות בארץ' ששמות גורמים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the meaning of the name 'Ruth'.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בשאלה על משמעות שמה של רות.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that Ruth merited David, who 'satiated' God with songs and praises.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן דורש את שמה של רות כמי שזכתה להוליד את דוד שריווה לה' בשירות.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer derives from a verse that names have significance, reading 'shammot' as 'shemot'.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן דורש את שמה של רות כמי שזכתה להוליד את דוד שריווה לה' בשירות.

items.text: תרבות רעה בבית קשה ממלחמת גוג ומגוג
items.text_en: Evil upbringing worse than Gog and Magog
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan teaches that evil upbringing in one's home is worse than the war of Gog and Magog, citing David's flight from Absalom. The Gemara questions why the psalm is called a 'song' and resolves it with a parable about a debtor who rejoices after paying.
items.desc: רבי יוחנן משם רבי שמעון בן יוחי אומר שתרבות רעה בבית קשה ממלחמת גוג ומגוג, ומביא ראיה ממזמור דוד בברחו מאבשלום. רבי שמעון בן אבישלום מסביר מדוע דוד אמר 'מזמור' ולא 'קינה'.

sub.text: רבי יוחנן משם רבי שמעון בן יוחי
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that evil upbringing in one's home is worse than the war of Gog and Magog, citing the psalm of David fleeing Absalom and contrasting it with the psalm about Gog and Magog.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן בשם רבי שמעון בן יוחי קובע שתרבות רעה בבית קשה ממלחמת גוג ומגוג, ומביא ראיה ממזמור דוד בברחו מאבשלום.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the psalm is called a 'song' (מזמור) when it should have been called a 'lament' (קינה), given the tragic context of David fleeing his son.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מדוע דוד אמר 'מזמור' על בריחתו מאבשלום, ולא 'קינה'?

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Avishalom answers with a parable: a debtor is sad before paying his debt but rejoices after paying it.
sub.desc: רבי שמעון בן אבישלום מתרץ במשל: כשדוד ראה שהרעה היא מאבשלום בנו, שמח שיצאה הרעה ממשפחתו, ולכן אמר מזמור.

sub.desc_en: The parable is applied to David: he was sad when God decreed evil from his house, fearing the rebel would be a slave or mamzer, but rejoiced when he saw it was Absalom, his own son, hence he called it a 'song'.

items.text: התגרות ברשעים: מחלוקת ותירוצים
items.text_en: Permissibility to contend with the wicked
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan permits contending with the wicked, supported by a baraita. The Gemara raises a contradiction from Rabbi Yitzchak, who says not to contend if fortune smiles on the wicked. Multiple resolutions are offered: distinguishing between personal and heavenly matters, between a wicked person with or without good fortune, and between a completely righteous person and one who is not.
items.desc: רבי יוחנן משם רבי שמעון בן יוחי מתיר להתגרות ברשעים. רבי דוסתאי מסכים. רבי יצחק חולק ואומר שאם השעה משחקת לרשע אין להתגרות בו. הגמרא מיישבת את הסתירות בתירוצים שונים: בדברי שמיים לעומת דברי עצמו, רשע שהשעה משחקת לו, וצדיק גמור לעומת צדיק שאינו גמור.

sub.text: רבי יוחנן משם רבי שמעון בן יוחי
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai that it is permissible to contend with the wicked in this world, citing a verse.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן בשם רבי שמעון בן יוחי פותח וקובע שמותר להתגרות ברשעים בעולם הזה, ומביא ראיה מן הפסוק.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi Dostai bar Rabbi Matun supports the same ruling and explains that the verse 'אַל תִּתְחַר בַּמְּרֵעִים' means not to be like them, not to avoid contending with them.
sub.desc: ברייתא תומכת בדברי רבי יוחנן: רבי דוסתאי בר רבי מתון אומר שמותר להתגרות ברשעים, ומתרץ את הפסוק הסותר 'אל תתחר במרעים' שאינו אוסר התגרות אלא אזהרה שלא להיות כמותם.

sub.desc_en: An additional verse is cited to reinforce the permissibility of contending with the wicked.
sub.desc: הברייתא מוסיפה פסוק נוסף 'אל יקנא לבך בחטאים' המחזק את ההיתר להתגרות ברשעים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from Rabbi Yitzchak, who says not to contend with a wicked person whose fortune smiles upon him, citing verses that show such a person succeeds in judgment and sees his enemies fall.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מדברי רבי יצחק הסותרים: אם רשע מצליח, אל תתגרה בו, כי הוא זוכה בדין ורואה בצריו.

sub.desc_en: The first resolution distinguishes between personal matters, where one should not contend, and heavenly matters, where one may.
sub.desc: תירוץ ראשון: אין קושיה, כי רבי יוחנן מדבר בדברי שמיים (מצוות) ורבי יצחק בדברי עצמו (ענייני חול).

sub.desc_en: The second resolution distinguishes between a wicked person whose fortune smiles upon him, where one should not contend, and one whose fortune does not smile upon him, where one may.
sub.desc: תירוץ שני: גם בדברי שמיים, יש לחלק בין רשע שהשעה משחקת לו (אין להתגרות) לבין רשע שאין השעה משחקת לו (מותר להתגרות).

sub.text_en: Third answer with Rav Huna's support
sub.desc_en: The third resolution distinguishes between a completely righteous person, whom the wicked cannot swallow, and one who is not completely righteous, whom the wicked can swallow, citing Rav Huna's interpretation of a verse.
sub.desc: תירוץ שלישי: גם ברשע שהשעה משחקת לו, יש לחלק בין צדיק גמור (שאינו נבלע) לבין צדיק שאינו גמור (שנבלע), על פי דברי רב הונא.

sub.desc_en: The fourth answer states that when fortune smiles upon the wicked, the case is different and one should not contend.
sub.desc: תירוץ רביעי: שעה משחקת לרשע שאני, כלומר דין מיוחד לרשע שהשעה משחקת לו, ולכן אין להתגרות בו.

items.text: קביעת מקום לתפילה ואויבים נופלים
items.text_en: Fixed place for prayer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan teaches that one who fixes a place for prayer will have his enemies fall before him. Rav Huna notes a contradiction in verses about 'afflicting' and 'destroying,' resolving that initially they afflict, but ultimately they are destroyed.
items.desc: רבי יוחנן משם רבי שמעון בן יוחי אומר שכל הקובע מקום לתפילתו אויביו נופלים תחתיו. רב הונא מרמה בין 'לענותו' ל'לכלותו' ומיישב: בתחילה לענותו ולבסוף לכלותו.

sub.text: רבי יוחנן משם רבי שמעון בן יוחי
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan teaches that one who fixes a place for prayer (קובע מקום לתפילתו) will have his enemies fall before him, citing a verse about God establishing a place for Israel.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן בשם רבי שמעון בן יוחי קובע שכל הקובע מקום לתפילתו אויביו נופלים תחתיו, ומביא פסוק תומך.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna raises a contradiction between two versions of the verse: one says 'to afflict him' (לענותו) and the other says 'to destroy him' (לכלותו).
sub.desc: רב הונא מקשה סתירה בין הכתוב 'לענותו' לכתוב 'לכלותו' בפסוק.

sub.desc_en: The gemara resolves the contradiction: initially the enemies afflict Israel, but ultimately they are destroyed.
sub.desc: מיישב את הסתירה: בתחילה לענותו ולבסוף לכלותו.

items.text: גדולה שימושה של תורה יותר מלימודה
items.text_en: Serving Torah scholars greater than studying
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan teaches that serving Torah scholars is greater than studying, citing Elisha who 'poured water on Elijah's hands.' Rabbi Yitzchak asks Rav Nachman why he doesn't come to synagogue; Rav Nachman says he cannot, and Rabbi Yitzchak suggests gathering a minyan or having the messenger inform him, prompting Rav Nachman to ask why all this is necessary.
items.desc: רבי יוחנן משם רבי שמעון בן יוחי אומר ששימושה של תורה גדול מלימודה, מדרשה של אלישע. רבי יצחק שואל את רב נחמן מדוע אינו בא לבית הכנסת, ומציע פתרונות. רב נחמן מסרב, ורבי יצחק מקשה עליו.

sub.text: רבי יוחנן משם רבי שמעון בן יוחי
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan teaches that serving Torah scholars (שימוש) is greater than studying Torah (לימוד), citing the verse about Elisha pouring water on Elijah's hands.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן בשם רבי שמעון בן יוחי קובע ששימושה של תורה גדול מלימודה, ומביא ראיה מהפסוק על אלישע.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak asks Rav Nachman why he does not come to the synagogue to pray.
sub.desc: רבי יצחק שואל את רב נחמן מדוע אינו בא לבית הכנסת להתפלל.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman answers that he is unable to go to the synagogue.
sub.desc: רב נחמן משיב שאינו יכול לבוא.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak suggests gathering a minyan of ten for Rav Nachman to pray at home, but Rav Nachman says it is too burdensome.
sub.desc: רבי יצחק שואל את רב נחמן מדוע אינו בא לבית הכנסת להתפלל.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak alternatively suggests that Rav Nachman ask the prayer leader to inform him when the congregation prays, so he can pray at the same time.
sub.desc: רבי יצחק שואל את רב נחמן מדוע אינו בא לבית הכנסת להתפלל.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman asks why all this effort is necessary.
sub.desc: רב נחמן משיב שאינו יכול לבוא.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak answers by citing Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai (the teaching about serving Torah scholars being greater than studying), implying that attending synagogue is a form of service.
sub.desc: רב נחמן משיב שאינו יכול לבוא.

items.text: מעלת תפילת הציבור
items.text_en: The time of divine favor is when the congregation prays
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens by asking when is the 'time of favor' for prayer, citing verses to show that God accepts prayer when the community prays together. Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Acha bar Rabbi Chanina each bring a prooftext, and a baraita from Rabbi Nathan reinforces that God does not reject the prayer of the many, and that one who engages in Torah, acts of kindness, and prays with the community is considered as if he redeemed God and His children from the nations.
items.desc: הגמרא פותחת בשאלה מתי היא עת רצון, ומביאה מקורות לכך שתפילת הציבור אינה נמאסת. רבי יוסי ורבי אחא מביאים פסוקים, ורבי נתן מוסיף שכל העוסק בתורה, גמילות חסדים ומתפלל עם הציבור – מעלה עליו הכתוב כאילו פדאו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks when is the 'time of favor' for prayer, and answers that it is when the congregation prays together.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהו זמן הרצון לתפילה, ומשיבה שזה בשעה שהציבור מתפלל.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina cites a verse (Isaiah 49:8) to prove that the time of favor is when the community prays.
sub.desc: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא מביא פסוק מספר ישעיהו להוכחה שתפילת הציבור היא עת רצון.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Acha bar Rabbi Chanina cites verses (Job 34:10, Psalms 55:19) to show that God does not reject the prayer of the many.
sub.desc: רבי אחא ברבי חנינא מביא פסוק מאיוב ופסוק מתהלים להוכחה שהקב"ה אינו מואס בתפילת רבים.

sub.desc_en: A baraita from Rabbi Nathan reinforces that God does not reject communal prayer, and that one who engages in Torah, kindness, and prays with the community is considered as if he redeemed God and His children from the nations.
sub.desc: ברייתא מביאה את דברי רבי נתן המוכיח מהפסוקים שהקב"ה אינו מואס בתפילת רבים, ומוסיף שהעוסק בתורה ובגמילות חסדים ומתפלל עם הציבור נחשב כמי שפדה את הקב"ה ובניו מבין האומות.

items.text: השכן הרע שאינו נכנס לבית הכנסת
items.text_en: The one who does not pray in the synagogue is called a 'bad neighbor'
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that anyone who has a synagogue in their city and does not enter to pray is called a 'bad neighbor', and furthermore causes exile for themselves and their children, citing verses from Jeremiah.
items.desc: ריש לקיש קובע שמי שיש לו בית כנסת בעירו ואינו נכנס להתפלל נקרא 'שכן רע', וגורם גלות לו ולבניו.

items.text: שכר הקדימה והאחור לבית הכנסת
items.text_en: Elders in Babylonia and the merit of coming early to synagogue
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan is told there are elders in Babylonia and is initially surprised, since the verse about long life applies only to the Land of Israel. But when told they come early and stay late to the synagogue, he says that is what benefits them. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi then instructs his children to come early and stay late to the synagogue to merit long life, and Rabbi Acha bar Chanina cites a verse from Proverbs.
items.desc: רבי יוחנן תמה על זקנים בבבל, אך כששמע שמקדימים ומאחירים לבית הכנסת – הסביר שזהו שכרם. רבי יהושע בן לוי מצווה לבניו להקדים ולאחור לבית הכנסת כדי להאריך ימים, ורבי אחא מביא פסוק לכך.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that people told Rabbi Yochanan there are elders in Babylonia.
Rabbi Yochanan is surprised, citing the verse that promises long life only on the Land of Israel, implying it does not apply outside the Land.
When they tell him that the elders come early and stay late to the synagogue, Rabbi Yochanan says that is what benefits them.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi instructs his children to come early and stay late to the synagogue in order to prolong their lives.

sub.text: Rabbi Acha bar Chanina's verse citation
sub.text_en: Rabbi Acha bar Chanina's verse citation
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Acha bar Chanina cites a verse from Proverbs to support that frequenting the synagogue brings life.

items.text: שיעור כניסה לבית הכנסת
items.text_en: Entering the synagogue the distance of two doors before praying
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda says a person should always enter the synagogue the distance of two doors before praying. The Gemara clarifies that this means a measure of two doors, not literally two doors.
items.desc: רב חסדא אומר שייכנס אדם שיעור שני פתחים בבית הכנסת ואחר כך יתפלל, ומבואר שהכוונה לשיעור ולא לשני פתחים ממש.

items.text: פירושי 'לעת מצוא'
items.text_en: Interpretations of 'לְעֵת מְצֹא'
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents multiple interpretations of the phrase 'לְעֵת מְצֹא' from Psalms. Rabbi Chanina says it refers to a wife, citing 'מָצָא אִשָּׁה מָצָא טוֹב'. In the West, they ask whether it is 'מָצָא' or 'מוֹצֵא'. Rabbi Nathan says it refers to Torah, citing 'כִּי מֹצְאִי מָצָא חַיִּים'. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says it refers to death, citing 'לַמָּוֶת תּוֹצָאוֹת', and a baraita elaborates on the 903 types of death. Rabbi Yochanan says it refers to burial, and Rabbi Chanina cites a verse. Mar Zutra says it refers to the bathroom, and the Westerners say this is the best of all.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה פירושים שונים לפסוק 'לעת מצוא': רבי חנינא – אשה, רבי נתן – תורה, רב נחמן בר יצחק – מיתה, רבי יוחנן – קבורה, ומר זוטרא – בית הכסא. מובאת ברייתא על מיני מיתה, ומעשה במערבא על נישואין.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse from Psalms as the basis for the discussion.
sub.desc: רבי חנינא מפרש 'לעת מצוא' כאשה, על פי הפסוק 'מצא אשה מצא טוב'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina interprets 'לְעֵת מְצֹא' as referring to a wife, citing the verse 'מָצָא אִשָּׁה מָצָא טוֹב'.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן מפרש 'לעת מצוא' כקבורה, ומביא ראיה מפסוק. רבה בר רב שיילא מוסיף פתגם עממי על בקשת רחמים עד קבורה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports a custom in the West where they ask a groom whether his marriage is a 'מָצָא' (finding good) or 'מוֹצֵא' (finding bitter), citing contrasting verses.
sub.desc: הגמרא מוסיפה מנהג מערבא: כשנושאים אשה שואלים 'מצא' או 'מוצא', ומביאים פסוקים לכאן ולכאן.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Nathan interprets 'לְעֵת מְצֹא' as referring to Torah, citing the verse 'כִּי מֹצְאִי מָצָא חַיִּים'.
sub.desc: רבי נתן מפרש 'לעת מצוא' כתורה, על פי הפסוק 'כי מוצאי מצא חיים'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak interprets 'לְעֵת מְצֹא' as referring to death, citing the verse 'לַמָּוֶת תּוֹצָאוֹת'.
sub.desc: רב נחמן בר יצחק מפרש 'לעת מצוא' כמיתה, על פי הפסוק 'למות תוצאות'.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's interpretation, stating that 903 types of death were created, with the hardest being אסכרה (croup) and the easiest being נשיקה (a kiss).
sub.desc: ברייתא תומכת בדברי רב נחמן: תשע מאות ושלשה מיני מיתה נבראו בעולם, ומפרטת את הקשה והנוחה שבהן.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan interprets 'לְעֵת מְצֹא' as referring to burial, and Rabbi Chanina cites a supporting verse.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן מפרש 'לעת מצוא' כקבורה, ומביא ראיה מפסוק. רבה בר רב שיילא מוסיף פתגם עממי על בקשת רחמים עד קבורה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Sheilah adds a folk saying that one should pray even for the last clod of earth (burial).
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן מפרש 'לעת מצוא' כקבורה, ומביא ראיה מפסוק. רבה בר רב שיילא מוסיף פתגם עממי על בקשת רחמים עד קבורה.

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra interprets 'לְעֵת מְצֹא' as referring to the bathroom.
sub.desc: מר זוטרא מפרש 'לעת מצוא' כבית הכסא, ובמערבא אמרו שדבריו עדיפים מכולם.

sub.desc_en: The Westerners declare that Mar Zutra's interpretation is the best of all.
sub.desc: מר זוטרא מפרש 'לעת מצוא' כבית הכסא, ובמערבא אמרו שדבריו עדיפים מכולם.

items.text: מעלת ארבע אמות של הלכה ובית הכנסת
items.text_en: The importance of synagogues and study halls
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rafram bar Papa to share fine sayings from Rav Chisda about synagogues. Rav Chisda says God loves gates that are distinguished in halakha more than synagogues and study halls. Ulla says that since the Temple's destruction, God has only the four cubits of halakha. Abaye relates that he used to study at home and pray in the synagogue, but after hearing Ulla's statement, he prayed where he studied. Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi, despite having thirteen synagogues in Tiberias, prayed only among the pillars where they studied.
items.desc: רבא מבקש מרפרם בר פפא דברים טובים משם רב חסדא בענייני בית הכנסת. רב חסדא אומר שה' אוהב שערים המצוינים בהלכה יותר מבתי כנסיות. רבי חייא בר אמי משם עולא אומר שאין לה' בעולמו אלא ארבע אמות של הלכה. אביי משנה ממנהגו להתפלל במקום לימודו, ורבי אמי ורבי אסי מתפללים בין העמודים שם למדו.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rafram bar Papa to share fine sayings from Rav Chisda about synagogues.
sub.desc: רבא מבקש מרפרם בר פפא שיאמר דברים טובים בשם רב חסדא בענייני בית הכנסת.

sub.text: רפרם בר פפא בשם רב חסדא
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda says that God loves gates distinguished in halakha (הלכה) more than synagogues and study halls.
sub.desc: רב חסדא דורש את הפסוק 'אוהב ה' שערי ציון' – שהשערים המצוינים בהלכה חביבים על ה' יותר מבתי כנסיות ומדרשות.

sub.text: רבי חייא בר אמי בשם עולא
sub.text_en: Ulla's statement via Rabbi Chiya bar Ami
sub.desc_en: Ulla says that since the Temple's destruction, God has only the four cubits of halakha (הלכה) in His world.
sub.desc: רבי חייא בר אמי בשם עולא מוסיף שמחורבן בית המקדש אין לה' בעולמו אלא ארבע אמות של הלכה.

sub.desc_en: Abaye relates that he used to study at home and pray in the synagogue, but after hearing Ulla's statement, he prayed where he studied.
sub.desc: אביי משנה ממנהגו ומתפלל במקום לימודו, בעקבות דברי עולא על מעלת ארבע אמות של הלכה.

sub.text_en: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi's practice
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi, despite having thirteen synagogues in Tiberias, prayed only among the pillars where they studied.
sub.desc: רבי אמי ורבי אסי, אף שהיו להם שלושה עשר בתי כנסת בטבריה, לא התפללו אלא בין העמודים במקום לימודם.

items.text: גדול הנהנה מיגיעו ודירת אדם במקום רבו
items.text_en: The one who benefits from his labor and dwelling near one's teacher
items.desc_en: Ulla says that one who benefits from his labor is greater than a God-fearing person, as the verse for the former includes both 'ashrecha' and 'tov lach', while for the latter only 'ashrei'. Ulla also says a person should always dwell near his teacher, as Shlomo did not marry Pharaoh's daughter while Shimi ben Geira was alive. The Gemara notes a contradiction with a baraita that says one should not dwell near his teacher, and resolves it: if the student is submissive to the teacher, he may dwell near him; if not, he should not.
items.desc: רבי חייא בר אמי משם עולא אומר שגדול הנהנה מיגיעו יותר מירא שמים. עוד אומר שתמיד ידור אדם במקום רבו, ומביא ראיה משמעי בן גרא. הגמרא מקשה מברייתא שאומרת 'אל ידור', ומתרצת: הא דכייף ליה, הא דלא כייף ליה.

sub.text: רבי חייא בר אמי משם עולא
sub.text_en: Ulla via Rabbi Chiya bar Ami
sub.desc_en: Ulla states that one who benefits from his own labor is greater than a God-fearing person, because the verse for the former includes both 'ashrecha' and 'tov lach', while for the latter only 'ashrei'.
sub.desc: רבי חייא בר אמי בשם עולא פותח ואומר שגדול הנהנה מיגיעו יותר מירא שמים, ומסביר את הפסוקים המוכיחים זאת.

sub.text: רבי חייא בר אמי משם עולא
sub.text_en: Ulla via Rabbi Chiya bar Ami
sub.desc_en: Ulla further says that a person should always dwell near his teacher, citing that as long as Shimi ben Geira was alive, Shlomo did not marry Pharaoh's daughter.
sub.desc: רבי חייא בר אמי בשם עולא מוסיף ומביא ראיה משלמה ושמעי שצריך לדור במקום רבו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that says one should not dwell near his teacher.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מברייתא האומרת 'אל ידור', בניגוד לדברי עולא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction: if the student is submissive to the teacher, he may dwell near him; if not, he should not.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שאין קושיה: הא דכייף ליה (שנכנע לרבו) – ידור, הא דלא כייף ליה – לא ידור.

items.text: הלכות קריאת התורה והשלמת פרשיות
items.text_en: Leaving the synagogue during Torah reading and completing the weekly portion
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Menachem in the name of Rabbi Ami says that 'those who forsake God will perish' refers to one who leaves a Torah scroll and goes out. Rabbi Avahu would leave between one person and another (during Torah reading). Rav Papa asks about leaving between one verse and another, and the Gemara says 'teiku'. Rav Sheshet would turn his face and study, saying 'we are engaged in our own, and they in theirs'. Finally, Rav Huna bar Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Ami says a person should always complete his weekly portions with the congregation, reading the text twice and the translation once.
items.desc: רב הונא בר יהודה משם רבי אמי מפרש 'ועוזבי ה' יכלו' – זה המניח ספר תורה ויוצא. רבי אבהו יוצא בין גברי לגברי, ורב פפא מסתפק בין פסוקא לפסוקא – תיקו. רב ששת מחזיר פניו ולומד. רב הונא בר יהודה משם רבי אמי אומר שישלים אדם פרשיותיו עם הציבור: שנים מקרא ואחד תרגום.

sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Menachem in the name of Rabbi Ami
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehuda cites a chain of tradition interpreting the verse 'ועוזבי ה' יכלו' (those who forsake God will perish) as referring to one who leaves a Torah scroll and goes out.
sub.desc: רב הונא בר יהודה בשם רבי מנחם ורבי אמי מפרש את הפסוק 'ועוזבי ה' יכלו' כמניח ספר תורה ויוצא מבית הכנסת.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu would leave the synagogue between one person and another during Torah reading, indicating a leniency.
sub.desc: רבי אבהו נוהג לצאת מבית הכנסת בין גברא לגברא, דוגמה להתנהגות המותרת.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa asks whether leaving between one verse and another during Torah reading is permitted.
sub.desc: רב פפא שואל מה הדין לגבי יציאה בין פסוקא לפסוקא בתוך קריאת התורה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara responds with 'תיקו' (let it stand unresolved), indicating the question remains unanswered.
sub.desc: הגמרא מותירה את השאלה בתיקו, ללא הכרעה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet would turn his face away and study during Torah reading, saying 'we are engaged in our own, and they in theirs'.
sub.desc: רב ששת מחזיר פניו ולומד בשעת קריאת התורה, בטענה שעניינו בפני עצמו.

sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Ami
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Ami rules that a person should always complete his weekly Torah portions with the congregation, reading the text twice and the translation once.
sub.desc: רב הונא בר יהודה בשם רבי אמי פוסק שישלים אדם פרשיותיו עם הציבור, שנים מקרא ואחד תרגום.

items.text: פתיחה: שכר השלמת פרשיות עם הציבור
items.text_en: Completing portions with the community
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that even the portions of 'Atarot and Divon' (which are short) should be completed with the community, and whoever does so is granted long life.
items.desc: הגמרא פותחת באמירה כללית שכל המשלים פרשיותיו עם הציבור מאריכין לו ימיו ושנותיו, ומביאה דוגמה של עטרות ודיבון.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that even the short portions 'Atarot and Divon' should be completed with the community, and whoever does so is granted long life.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת באמירה כללית שכל המשלים פרשיותיו עם הציבור מאריכין לו ימיו ושנותיו, ומביאה דוגמה של עטרות ודיבון.

items.text: מעשה רב ביבי: השלמת פרשיות בערב יום כיפור
items.text_en: Rav Beivai's plan to complete portions on Yom Kippur eve
items.desc_en: Rav Beivai bar Abbaye considered completing the entire year's portions on Yom Kippur eve. A baraita taught by Chiyya bar Rav from Diftei cites a verse to show that eating and drinking on the ninth of Tishrei is considered as if one fasted on both the ninth and tenth. Another elder taught that one must not advance or delay the completion.
items.desc: רב ביבי בר אביי רצה להשלים את כל הפרשיות בערב יום כיפור, אך חייא בר רב מדיפתי לימדו פסוק המלמד על מעשה האוכל והשותה בתשיעי. רב ביבי רצה להקדים, וזקן אמר לו ששנינו שלא להקדים ולא לאחר.

sub.desc_en: Rav Beivai bar Abbaye considered completing the entire year's Torah portions on Yom Kippur eve.
sub.desc: רב ביבי בר אביי התכוון להשלים את כל פרשיות השנה בערב יום כיפור.

sub.text_en: Baraita taught by Chiyya bar Rav from Diftei
sub.desc_en: A baraita cites the verse 'וְעִנִּיתֶם אֶת נַפְשֹׁתֵיכֶם בְּתִשְׁעָה לַחֹדֶשׁ בָּעֶרֶב' and explains that eating and drinking on the ninth is credited as if one fasted on both the ninth and tenth.
sub.desc: רב ביבי בר אביי התכוון להשלים את כל פרשיות השנה בערב יום כיפור.

sub.desc_en: When Rav Beivai considered advancing the completion, an elder taught a baraita that one must not advance or delay the completion.
sub.desc: רב ביבי רצה להקדים את הפרשיות, וזקן אמר לו ששנינו שלא להקדים ולא לאחר.

items.text: צוואת רבי יהושע בן לוי לבניו
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's instructions to his sons
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi instructs his sons to complete their portions with the community, reading the text twice and the translation once. He also warns them to be careful with the veins (as per Rabbi Yehuda) and to respect an elder who has forgotten his learning due to circumstances, as both the tablets and their broken pieces are placed in the Ark.
items.desc: רבי יהושע בן לוי מצווה את בניו להשלים פרשיות עם הציבור שנים מקרא ואחד תרגום, ולהיזהר בוורידין כרבי יהודה, ולהיזהר בזקן ששכח תלמודו מחמת אונסו.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi instructs his sons to complete their Torah portions with the community by reading the text twice and the translation once.
sub.desc: רבי יהושע בן לוי מצווה את בניו להשלים פרשיות עם הציבור שנים מקרא ואחד תרגום.

sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi (citing Rabbi Yehuda)
sub.desc_en: He warns them to be careful with the veins, citing Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that one must slaughter the veins.
sub.desc: רבי יהושע בן לוי מזהיר את בניו להיזהר בוורידין כדעת רבי יהודה, ומביא ברייתא כראיה.

sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi (with Gemara's statement)
sub.desc_en: He warns them to respect an elder who has forgotten his learning due to circumstances, as both the tablets and their broken pieces are placed in the Ark.
sub.desc: רבי יהושע בן לוי מזהיר את בניו להיזהר בזקן ששכח תלמודו מחמת אונסו, ומביא אמירה כללית של הגמרא על לוחות ושברי לוחות המונחים בארון.

items.text: צוואת רבא לבניו: איסורים שונים
items.text_en: Rava's instructions to his sons and the story of Rav Pappa
items.desc_en: Rava instructs his sons not to cut meat on the hand (due to danger or spoiling the meal), not to sit on a gentile's bed (with various explanations), and not to pass behind a synagogue during prayer. The Gemara recounts the story of Rav Pappa who discovered a dead child under a gentile's bed, leading to the prohibition.
items.desc: רבא מצווה את בניו שלא לחתוך בשר על גב היד, שלא לשבת על מיטת ארמית, ושלא לעבור אחורי בית הכנסת בשעת תפילה. מובאים טעמים שונים לאיסורים, ומעשה רב פפא עם ארמית שגילה תינוק מת מתחת למיטה.

sub.desc_en: Rava warned his sons about veins, citing Rabbi Yehuda's rule that slaughter must cut the veins.
sub.desc: רבא פותח בציווי לבניו שלא לחתוך בשר על גב היד.

sub.desc_en: Rava instructs his sons not to sit on a gentile's bed, with three explanations: not to sleep without reciting the Shema, not to marry a convert, or because of the actual gentile woman.
sub.desc: רבא פותח בציווי לבניו שלא לחתוך בשר על גב היד.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts the story of Rav Pappa who discovered a dead child under a gentile's bed, leading the Sages to prohibit sitting on a gentile's bed.
sub.desc: רבא פותח בציווי לבניו שלא לחתוך בשר על גב היד.

sub.text_en: Supporting statement of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling that one may not pass behind a synagogue while the congregation is praying, supporting Rava's instruction.
sub.desc: רבא פותח בציווי לבניו שלא לחתוך בשר על גב היד.

sub.desc_en: Abaye qualifies the prohibition: it applies only when there is no other entrance, no other synagogue, and the person is not carrying a load, running, or wearing tefillin.
sub.desc: רבא פותח בציווי לבניו שלא לחתוך בשר על גב היד.

items.text: איסור מעבר אחורי בית הכנסת בשעת תפילה
items.text_en: The prohibition of passing behind a synagogue
items.desc_en: The Gemara supports Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling that one may not pass behind a synagogue during prayer. Abaye qualifies this: it applies only if there is no other entrance, no other synagogue, and if one is not carrying a load, running, or wearing tefillin.
items.desc: הגמרא מסייעת לרבי יהושע בן לוי האוסר לעבור אחורי בית הכנסת בשעת תפילה, ואביי מוסיף חריגים: אם יש פתח אחר, בית כנסת אחר, או אם נושא משא, רץ או מניח תפילין.

sub.desc_en: Rava instructs his sons not to pass behind a synagogue while the congregation is praying.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה את הברייתא האוסרת מעבר אחורי בית הכנסת בשעת תפילה, ומציינת שהיא מסייעת לרבי יהושע בן לוי.

sub.text_en: Gemara's support for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's explicit prohibition against passing behind a synagogue during prayer, supporting Rava's instruction.
sub.desc: הגמרא מציינת שהברייתא מסייעת לדברי רבי יהושע בן לוי האוסר מעבר אחורי בית הכנסת בשעת תפילה.

sub.desc_en: Abaye qualifies the prohibition: it applies only when there is no other entrance, no other synagogue, and when one is not carrying a load, running, or wearing tefillin.
sub.desc: אביי מוסיף חריגים לאיסור: אם יש פתח אחר, בית כנסת אחר, או אם האדם נושא משא, רץ או מניח תפילין – מותר לעבור.

items.text: שבח המדיים והפרסיים
items.text_en: Praise for Medes and Persians
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva praises the Medes for three customs: cutting meat on a table, kissing on the hand, and giving counsel in the field. Rabban Gamliel praises the Persians for three things: modesty in eating, in the bathroom, and in another matter. Rav Yosef interprets a verse as referring to the Persians who are sanctified and destined for Gehinnom.
items.desc: ברייתא מביאה דברי רבי עקיבא האוהב את המדיים בשלושה דברים, ורב אדא בר אהבה מביא פסוק. ברייתא נוספת מביאה דברי רבן גמליאל האוהב את הפרסיים בשלושה דברים, ורב יוסף דורש פסוק על הפרסיים שהם מקודשים לגיהנם.

sub.desc_en: A baraita quotes Rabbi Akiva praising the Medes for three customs: cutting meat on a table, kissing on the hand, and giving counsel in the field.
sub.desc: רבי עקיבא מביא ברייתא האוהבת את המדיים בשלושה דברים: חיתוך בשר על השולחן, נשיקה על גב היד, וייעוץ בשדה.

sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava's scriptural support
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava cites a verse (Genesis 31:4) to support the Medes' custom of giving counsel in the field.
sub.desc: רב אדא בר אהבה מביא פסוק המוכיח שיעקב ייעץ עם נשותיו בשדה, כמנהג המדיים.

sub.desc_en: A baraita quotes Rabban Gamliel praising the Persians for three things: modesty in eating, in the bathroom, and in another matter.
sub.desc: רבן גמליאל מביא ברייתא האוהבת את הפרסיים בשלושה דברים: צניעות באכילה, בבית הכסא, ובדבר אחר.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef interprets a verse (Isaiah 13:3) as referring to the Persians, who are sanctified and destined for Gehinnom.
sub.desc: רב יוסף דורש את הפסוק 'אני ציוויתי למקודשי' על הפרסיים, שהם מקודשים ומזומנים לגיהנם.

items.text: הלכה כרבן גמליאל
items.text_en: Halakha like Rabban Gamliel
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel that the halakha follows Rabban Gamliel.
items.desc: רב יהודה אמר שמואל שהלכה כרבן גמליאל, כנראה בהמשך למחלוקת קודמת בעניין קריאת שמע.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel ruled: The halacha follows Rabban Gamliel.
sub.desc: רב יהודה בשם שמואל פוסק שהלכה כרבן גמליאל, ובכך מביא סיוע לדעתו במחלוקת הקודמת.

items.text: קריאת שמע פעמיים: מחלוקת רבי שמעון וקושיות הגמרא
items.text_en: Debate on reciting Shema near dawn
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai says one can recite Shema twice at night, once before dawn and once after, fulfilling both day and night obligations. The Gemara questions this, noting the contradiction in calling the time both night and day. It resolves that it is night, but people are awake then. Rav Acha bar Chanina rules like Rabbi Shimon. An alternative version has Rabbi Shimon citing Rabbi Akiva about reciting twice during the day, with a similar contradiction.
items.desc: ברייתא של רבי שמעון בר יוחאי אומרת שפעמים שאדם קורא קריאת שמע פעמיים בלילה ויוצא ידי חובת יום ולילה. הגמרא מקשה על סתירה פנימית בברייתא, ומתרצת. רב אחא בר חנינא אמר רבי יהושע בן לוי שהלכה כרבי שמעון. יש גרסה אחרת שבה רבי שמעון אומר משם רבי עקיבא שקורא פעמיים ביום, וגם שם הגמרא מקשה.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's position that one may recite Shema twice at night, once before dawn and once after, fulfilling both the day and night obligations.
sub.desc: ברייתא מביאה את דברי רבי שמעון בר יוחאי, שאדם יכול לקרוא קריאת שמע פעמיים בלילה ולצאת ידי חובת יום ולילה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the baraita calls the time after dawn 'night' for the first recitation, but then calls it 'day' for the fulfillment of the day obligation.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה סתירה פנימית בברייתא: מצד אחד היא קוראת לזמן 'לילה', ומצד שני היא קוראת לקריאה 'של יום'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that it is indeed still night, but it is called 'day' because people are awake at that hour.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שהזמן הוא באמת לילה, והקריאה נקראת 'של יום' משום שיש אנשים שעומדים באותה שעה.

sub.text: רב אחא בר חנינא בשם רבי יהושע בן לוי
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Chanina citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Chanina reports in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai.
sub.desc: רב אחא בר חנינא בשם רבי יהושע בן לוי פוסק שהלכה כרבי שמעון בר יוחאי.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version presents Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai citing Rabbi Akiva, saying one recites Shema twice during the day, once before sunrise and once after, fulfilling both obligations.
sub.desc: מובאת גרסה אחרת שבה רבי שמעון בר יוחאי אומר משם רבי עקיבא שקורא קריאת שמע פעמיים ביום.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a similar contradiction in the alternative version: the time before sunrise is called 'day' for the first recitation, but then called 'night' for the fulfillment of the night obligation.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה שוב סתירה פנימית בגרסה השנייה: הזמן נקרא 'יום' אך הקריאה נקראת 'של לילה'.

items.text: Clarification of 'night' for the evening Shema
items.text_en: Clarification of 'night' for the evening Shema
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the time referred to as 'night' for the evening Shema is actually daytime, but it is called night because some people sleep at that hour.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction by explaining that the time referred to as 'night' for the evening Shema is actually daytime, but it is called night because some people sleep at that hour.

items.text: The halakha follows Rabbi Shimon and the condition of not saying Hashkiveinu
items.text_en: The halakha follows Rabbi Shimon and the condition of not saying Hashkiveinu
items.desc_en: Rabbi Acha bar Rabbi Chanina reports in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon citing Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Zeira adds the condition that one should not recite the blessing 'Hashkiveinu.' However, when Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef arrived, he clarified that this ruling was not stated explicitly but was inferred from an incident where Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi ruled that one may rely on Rabbi Shimon in a time of pressure.

sub.text: Rabbi Acha bar Rabbi Chanina citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Acha bar Rabbi Chanina citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Acha bar Rabbi Chanina reports in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon who spoke in the name of Rabbi Akiva.
Rabbi Zeira adds the condition that one should not recite the blessing 'Hashkiveinu' when relying on Rabbi Shimon's leniency.
Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef clarifies that Rabbi Acha's statement was not explicitly stated but inferred from a case.

The gemara recounts an incident where a pair of rabbis who got drunk at Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's son's wedding came before him, and he ruled that Rabbi Shimon is reliable enough to rely on in a time of pressure.

items.text: Introduction of the Mishnah's story
items.text_en: Introduction of the Mishnah's story
items.desc_en: The Gemara quotes the Mishnah's account of Rabban Gamliel's sons returning late from a wedding and asking about the Shema.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara quotes the Mishnah's story of Rabban Gamliel's sons returning late from a wedding.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rabban Gamliel's response
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rabban Gamliel's response
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the sons did not already know Rabban Gamliel's ruling. It explains that they were asking whether the Sages disagreed with him, and if so, whether the halakha follows the majority. Rabban Gamliel responded that the Sages actually agree with him, and the earlier time of midnight was only to distance people from transgression.

sub.desc_en: The גמרא (Gemara) asks in surprise whether the sons of רבן גמליאל (Rabban Gamliel) had not previously heard his explicit ruling about the evening Shema (קריאת שמע של ערבית) being permitted until dawn (עלות השחר).

sub.text: Gemara's answer and Rabban Gamliel's response
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer and Rabban Gamliel's response
sub.desc_en: The גמרא (Gemara) explains that the sons were actually inquiring whether the Sages disagreed with רבן גמליאל (Rabban Gamliel), and asks whether the הלכה (law) follows the majority; רבן גמליאל (Rabban Gamliel) answers that the Sages agree with him, and the earlier time of midnight (חצות) was only enacted לכתחילה (as an ideal) to distance people from transgression (להרחיק אדם מן העבירה).

items.text: Clarification of 'Not only this did they say'
items.text_en: Clarification of 'Not only this did they say'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah adds 'Not only this did they say,' and explains that Rabban Gamliel was telling his sons that even according to the Sages who say until midnight, the proper time is until dawn, and midnight is only to distance from transgression.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah adds the phrase 'Not only this did they say,' given that Rabban Gamliel himself holds the time is until dawn, not midnight.

The Gemara explains that Rabban Gamliel was telling his sons that even according to the Sages who say until midnight, the proper time is until dawn, and midnight is only to distance a person from transgression.

items.text: Contradiction regarding the time for eating the Passover offering
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding the time for eating the Passover offering
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the burning of fats and limbs until dawn but omits eating the Passover offering. The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that states the eating of the Passover offering is until dawn.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's list of items that are valid until dawn, noting that the eating of the Passover offering is omitted.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that states the eating of the Passover offering is valid until dawn.

items.text: Resolution through the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer ben Azariah and Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Resolution through the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer ben Azariah and Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef resolves the contradiction by attributing the two views to Rabbi Eliezer ben Azariah and Rabbi Akiva. A baraita is cited where Rabbi Eliezer ben Azariah uses a gezerah shavah to limit the eating of the Passover to midnight, while Rabbi Akiva argues from the verse 'in haste' that it extends until the time of haste. The Gemara then explains the necessity of the word 'this' for each opinion.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef resolves the contradiction by attributing the two views to Rabbi Eliezer ben Azariah and Rabbi Akiva, citing a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer ben Azariah uses a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) to limit the Passover eating to midnight.
The baraita continues with Rabbi Akiva arguing from the verse 'בחפזון' (in haste) that the eating extends until the time of haste, and explaining that 'בלילה' (at night) excludes daytime eating.
The Gemara asks: for Rabbi Eliezer ben Azariah, the word 'הזה' (this) is needed for the גזירה שווה (verbal analogy), but what does Rabbi Akiva do with the word 'הזה'?
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Akiva uses 'הזה' (this) to exclude another night, teaching that the Passover is eaten only on this night and not on another night.

items.text: Alternative derivation for Rabbi Eliezer ben Azariah and defense of Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Alternative derivation for Rabbi Eliezer ben Azariah and defense of Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Eliezer ben Azariah needs a gezerah shavah when the verse 'Do not leave any until morning' could suffice. Rabbi Akiva responds that 'morning' might mean the second morning. Rabbi Eliezer counters that every 'morning' in the Torah means the first morning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Eliezer ben Azariah needs a גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) when the verse 'לא תותירו עד בקר' (do not leave any until morning) could already teach the same lesson.
Rabbi Akiva responds that from that verse alone one might think 'בקר' (morning) means the second morning, so the גזירה שוה is necessary.
Rabbi Eliezer counters that every 'בקר' (morning) in the Torah means the first morning, so the alternative derivation from 'לא תותירו' is sufficient without the גזירה שוה.

items.text: Another tannaitic dispute about the time of eating the Passover
items.text_en: Another tannaitic dispute about the time of eating the Passover
items.desc_en: A baraita presents a dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua regarding the timing of slaughter, eating, and burning the Passover. Rabbi Abba explains that all agree the redemption began at evening but the actual exodus was in the morning. The dispute is about the 'time of haste': Rabbi Eliezer ben Azariah holds it refers to the Egyptians' haste, while Rabbi Akiva holds it refers to Israel's haste.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita about the timing of the Passover sacrifice, linking it to the previous dispute.
The baraita cites Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua disputing the timing of slaughter, eating, and burning the Passover.
Rabbi Abba explains that all agree the redemption began at evening but the actual exodus was in the morning.
The Gemara asks what the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer ben Azariah and Rabbi Akiva is about.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Eliezer ben Azariah holds 'time of haste' refers to the Egyptians' haste, while Rabbi Akiva holds it refers to Israel's haste.

items.text: Supporting baraita and the request for vessels
items.text_en: Supporting baraita and the request for vessels
items.desc_en: A baraita supports the idea that redemption began at night, citing the verse 'He brought you out by night.' The Gemara then begins to discuss the request for silver and gold vessels from the Egyptians, quoting the verse 'Speak now in the ears of the people.'

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports the idea that redemption began at night, citing the verse 'הוֹצִיאֲךָ ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ מִמִּצְרַיִם לָיְלָה' (the Lord your God brought you out of Egypt by night) and clarifying that they only left by day, but the redemption began in the evening.

Beit Rabbi Yannai interprets the word 'נָא' (please) in the verse 'דַּבֶּר נָא בְּאָזְנֵי הָעָם' (Speak now in the ears of the people) as a request, explaining that God asked Moses to request the Israelites to ask the Egyptians for silver and gold vessels, so that the righteous patriarch Abraham would not say that God fulfilled the prophecy of enslavement but not the promise of wealth.

items.text: Aggadic exposition on the Exodus and the borrowing from Egypt
items.text_en: Aggadic exposition on the Exodus and the borrowing from Egypt
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the righteous one (Joseph) fulfilled the prophecy of affliction but not the prophecy of leaving with great wealth. The Israelites preferred immediate freedom over wealth. Rabbi Ammi teaches that the Egyptians lent their vessels against their will, with a dispute over whose will was overridden. The verse 'vayenatzlu et Mitzrayim' is interpreted as making Egypt like a trap without grain or a net without fish.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the righteous one (Joseph) fulfilled the prophecy of affliction but not the prophecy of leaving with great wealth.
The Sages respond that the Israelites preferred immediate freedom over wealth, illustrated by a parable of a prisoner who wants release today without money.
Rabbi Ammi teaches that the Egyptians lent their vessels against their will, with a dispute over whose will was overridden.
The first opinion supports the Egyptians' coercion with a verse, while the second opinion attributes the coercion to the Israelites due to the burden.
Rabbi Ammi interprets the verse as making Egypt like a trap without grain, and Resh Lakish says like a net without fish.

items.text: God's name 'Ehyeh asher Ehyeh' and Moses' response
items.text_en: God's name 'Ehyeh asher Ehyeh' and Moses' response
items.desc_en: God tells Moses to tell Israel that He was with them in this servitude and will be with them in future servitudes. Moses objects that it is enough for the trouble to come at its time, so God instructs him to say only 'Ehyeh sent me to you.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces God's instruction to Moses: tell Israel that He was with them in this servitude and will be with them in future servitudes.
Moses objects that it is enough for the trouble to come at its time, so God should not mention future suffering now.
God accepts Moses' objection and instructs him to say only 'Ehyeh sent me to you' without mentioning future servitude.

items.text: Elijah's double plea 'Aneini' on Mount Carmel
items.text_en: Elijah's double plea 'Aneini' on Mount Carmel
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu explains why Elijah said 'Aneini' twice: once for fire to descend from heaven, and once to divert the people's minds so they would not attribute the miracle to sorcery.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu asks why Elijah said 'עֲנֵנִי' twice on Mount Carmel.
Rabbi Avahu explains that the first plea was for fire to descend, and the second was to divert the people's minds so they would not attribute the miracle to sorcery.

items.text: Mishnah: Time for morning Shema
items.text_en: Mishnah: Time for morning Shema
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the morning Shema may be recited from when one can distinguish between blue and white. Rabbi Eliezer says between blue and green. One may finish until sunrise; Rabbi Yehoshua says until the third hour, as kings arise at that time. One who recites later does not lose the reward, like one reading Torah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the question of when the morning Shema may be recited, and gives the first opinion: from when one can distinguish between תכלת (blue) and white.
Rabbi Eliezer gives his own criterion: between תכלת (blue) and כרתי (green).
The Mishnah states the first deadline for completing the Shema: until sunrise (הנץ החמה).
Rabbi Yehoshua extends the deadline to the third hour, because kings (who are exempt from early recitation) arise at that time.
The Mishnah concludes that one who recites the Shema after the deadline does not lose the reward, but is like one reading Torah.

items.text: Gemara: Defining the distinction between blue and white
items.text_en: Gemara: Defining the distinction between blue and white
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the distinction is not between a white wool clump and a blue one, which is recognizable at night, but between the blue and white threads in the same tzitzit. A baraita records other definitions: Rabbi Meir says between a wolf and a dog, Rabbi Akiva says between a donkey and a wild ass, and Acheirim say when one can recognize a friend at four cubits.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the distinction between blue and white means, and rejects the possibility that it refers to a clump of white wool versus a clump of blue wool, since that is recognizable even at night.
The Gemara answers that the distinction is between the blue thread and the white thread within the same tzitzit.
A baraita records alternative definitions: Rabbi Meir says between a wolf and a dog, Rabbi Akiva says between a donkey and a wild ass, and Acheirim say when one can recognize a friend at four cubits.

items.text: Halakhic ruling and the practice of the vatikin
items.text_en: Halakhic ruling and the practice of the vatikin
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules like Acheirim. Abaye distinguishes: for tefillin, follow Acheirim; for Shema, follow the vatikin, who finished with sunrise. A baraita supports this, citing the verse 'yira'ucha im shamesh'. Rabbi Yosei ben Elyakim testifies that one who juxtaposes redemption to prayer is unharmed all day. Rabbi Zeira objects that he did so and was harmed, but is told his harm was from not paying a fee to see the king, as per Rabbi Yochanan's advice to run to greet kings.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that the halakha follows the opinion of Acheirim regarding the time for reciting Shema.
Abaye distinguishes: for tefillin, follow Acheirim; for Shema, follow the vatikin (pious ones) who finished reciting it at sunrise, as Rabbi Yochanan stated.
A baraita supports this: the vatikin would finish Shema at sunrise to juxtapose redemption to prayer and pray during the day.
Rabbi Zeira cites the verse 'יִירָאוּךָ עִם שָׁמֶשׁ' (They will fear You with the sun) to support the practice of finishing Shema at sunrise.
Rabbi Yosei ben Elyakim testifies on behalf of the holy community of Jerusalem that one who juxtaposes redemption to prayer is unharmed all day.
Rabbi Zeira objects: he himself juxtaposed redemption to prayer and was harmed, contradicting the testimony.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Zeira's harm was due to not paying a fee to see the king, as per Rabbi Yochanan's advice to run to greet kings of Israel and even of the nations.

items.text: The problem of juxtaposing redemption to prayer and the solution
items.text_en: The problem of juxtaposing redemption to prayer and the solution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ila'a tells Ulla to greet Rav Brona, who rejoiced in mitzvot and once juxtaposed redemption to prayer and laughed all day. The Gemara questions how he could do so given the requirement to say 'Hashem sefatai tiftach' before prayer and 'Yihyu leratzon' after. Rabbi Elazar suggests it refers to the evening prayer, but Rabbi Yochanan says one who juxtaposes evening redemption to prayer merits the World to Come. Rabbi Elazar then suggests the afternoon prayer. Rav Ashi answers that even for all prayers, since the Sages fixed 'Yihyu leratzon' within the prayer, it is considered a long prayer, just as 'Hashkiveinu' is considered a long redemption.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ila'a tells Ulla to greet Rav Brona, who once juxtaposed redemption to prayer and laughed all day.

The Gemara questions how one can juxtapose redemption to prayer given the requirement to say 'ה׳ שְׂפָתַי תִּפְתָּח' (Lord, open my lips) before prayer and 'יִהְיוּ לְרָצוֹן אִמְרֵי פִי' (May the words of my mouth be acceptable) after.
Rabbi Elazar suggests that the verse 'ה׳ שְׂפָתַי תִּפְתָּח' (Lord, open my lips) should be recited only in the evening prayer, not the morning.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yochanan said one who juxtaposes the redemption of the evening prayer to the evening prayer merits the World to Come, so the verse cannot be omitted there either.
Rabbi Elazar revises his answer, suggesting that the verse should be recited only before the afternoon prayer.
Rav Ashi resolves that even if the verse is recited before all prayers, since the Sages fixed it within the prayer, it is considered an extended prayer and does not interrupt the juxtaposition.

Rav Ashi supports his claim with an analogy: just as 'הַשְׁכִּיבֵנוּ' (Help us lie down) is considered an extended redemption and does not interrupt the evening juxtaposition, so too the verse fixed by the Sages is considered an extended prayer.

items.text: Why 'Yihyu leratzon' was placed after the Amidah
items.text_en: Why 'Yihyu leratzon' was placed after the Amidah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why 'Yihyu leratzon' was instituted after the eighteen blessings rather than at the beginning. Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi answers because David said it only after eighteen chapters (in Psalms). The Gemara objects that there are nineteen chapters, but resolves that 'Ashrei ha'ish' and 'Lamah ragshu' are one chapter. Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi further notes that David said 103 chapters without 'Halleluyah' until he saw the downfall of the wicked. The Gemara again counts 104, but concludes that 'Ashrei ha'ish' and 'Lamah ragshu' are one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse 'יִהְיוּ לְרָצוֹן אִמְרֵי פִי' (May the words of my mouth be acceptable) was instituted after the eighteen blessings of the Amidah rather than at the beginning.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi
sub.desc_en: רבי יהודה בריה דרבי שמעון בן פזי (Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi) answers that David said this verse only after eighteen chapters of Psalms, so the Sages instituted it after the eighteen blessings of the Amidah.
The Gemara objects that there are nineteen chapters before the verse, not eighteen.
The Gemara resolves that 'אַשְׁרֵי הָאִישׁ' (Happy is the man) and 'לָמָּה רָגְשׁוּ גוֹיִם' (Why are the nations in an uproar) constitute a single chapter, making the count eighteen.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi
sub.desc_en: רבי יהודה בריה דרבי שמעון בן פזי (Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi) further supports this by noting that David said 103 chapters without 'הללויה' (Halleluyah) until he saw the downfall of the wicked, as per the verse 'יִתַּמּוּ חַטָּאִים' (Let sinners cease).
The Gemara objects that there are 104 chapters, not 103.
The Gemara concludes that 'אַשְׁרֵי הָאִישׁ' (Happy is the man) and 'לָמָּה רָגְשׁוּ גוֹיִם' (Why are the nations in an uproar) are one chapter, resolving the count.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: רבי שמואל בר נחמני (Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani) in the name of רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) begins to provide additional support, though the statement is cut off at the end of the daf.

items.text: Opening statement about David's favorite psalms
items.text_en: Opening statement about David's favorite psalms
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that every chapter that was beloved to David began and ended with 'Ashrei', citing Psalm 1 and Psalm 2 as examples.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that every chapter beloved to David began and ended with 'Ashrei', citing Psalm 1 and Psalm 2 as examples.

items.text: Bruriah's advice to Rabbi Meir about praying for sinners
items.text_en: Bruriah's advice to Rabbi Meir about praying for sinners
items.desc_en: Bruriah corrects Rabbi Meir's interpretation of 'יִתַּמּוּ חַטָּאִים' (let sins cease) as referring to sinners, not sins, and advises him to pray for their repentance instead of their death. Rabbi Meir follows her advice and they repent.

sub.desc_en: Beruriah challenges Rabbi Meir's prayer for the death of troublemakers, arguing that the verse 'יִתַּמּוּ חַטָּאִים' (let sinners cease) refers to sins, not sinners.
Beruriah adds that the verse's continuation 'וּרְשָׁעִים עוֹד אֵינָם' (and the wicked are no more) implies that once sins cease, the wicked repent, so Rabbi Meir should pray for their repentance.
Rabbi Meir heeds Beruriah's advice, prays for the troublemakers, and they repent.
Rabbi Meir follows Bruriah's advice, prays for their repentance, and they indeed repent.

items.text: Bruriah's response to a heretic about 'Rani akara'
items.text_en: Bruriah's response to a heretic about 'Rani akara'
items.desc_en: A heretic challenges Bruriah on the verse 'Rani akara lo yalada' (Sing, O barren one who has not given birth), questioning why a barren woman should rejoice. Bruriah explains that the verse refers to the congregation of Israel, which is like a barren woman who has not borne children for Gehinnom like the heretics.

sub.desc_en: A heretic asks Beruriah why the verse 'רָנִּי עֲקָרָה לֹא יָלָדָה' (Sing, barren one who has not borne) commands joy for not bearing children.
Beruriah rebukes the heretic and points to the verse's continuation, which promises that the desolate woman will have more children than the married one.
Beruriah explains that the verse refers to the congregation of Israel, which is like a barren woman who has not borne children for Gehinnom like the heretics.

items.text: Rabbi Avahu's answer about the order of David's psalms
items.text_en: Rabbi Avahu's answer about the order of David's psalms
items.desc_en: A heretic asks Rabbi Avahu why the psalm about fleeing from Absalom is placed before the one about fleeing from Saul, even though Saul's event occurred earlier. Rabbi Avahu explains that those who do not expound on 'semuchim' (adjacent verses) find this difficult, but those who do, do not, citing Rabbi Yochanan's teaching that 'semuchim' are from the Torah.

sub.desc_en: A heretic asks Rabbi Avahu why Psalm 3 (about Absalom) precedes Psalm 57 (about Saul) in the Psalms, even though Saul's event occurred first.
Rabbi Avahu explains that those who do not interpret adjacent verses (סמוכין) find this difficult, but those who do interpret them find no difficulty.
Rabbi Yochanan cites a verse to prove that interpreting adjacent verses (סמוכין) is a valid Torah principle.

items.text: Reason for juxtaposing Absalom and Gog and Magog
items.text_en: Reason for juxtaposing Absalom and Gog and Magog
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the section about Absalom is placed next to the section about Gog and Magog: to answer those who question how a servant can rebel against his master, by pointing out that a son can rebel against his father, and yet it happened.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the story of Absalom is placed next to the prophecy of Gog and Magog: to answer the question of how a son can rebel against his father, just as a servant can rebel against his master.
The Gemara answers that just as a son can rebel against his father and it happened, so too a servant can rebel against his master, and it happened with Absalom.

items.text: David's five worlds and five 'Bless the Lord' psalms
items.text_en: David's five worlds and five 'Bless the Lord' psalms
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai explains that Solomon's verse 'פִּיהָ פָּתְחָה בְחָכְמָה' refers to David, who dwelled in five worlds and sang a song in each: in his mother's womb, upon emerging and seeing stars, while nursing, upon seeing the downfall of the wicked, and upon seeing the day of death. Each world is linked to a verse from Psalms beginning with 'בָּרְכִי נַפְשִׁי'.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan introduces that Solomon's verse 'פִּיהָ פָּתְחָה בְחָכְמָה' refers to David, who lived in five worlds and sang praise.
David sang praise while in his mother's womb, citing Psalm 103:1.
David sang praise upon entering the world, looking at the stars and constellations, citing Psalm 103:20-21.
David sang praise while nursing, looking at his mother's breasts, citing Psalm 103:2.
Rabbi Avahu explains that 'all His benefits' refers to God placing breasts in the place of understanding.
Rav Yehuda explains that breasts are placed there so the infant does not look at the place of nakedness.
Rav Matna explains that breasts are placed there so the infant does not nurse from a place of filth.

sub.text: Fourth world: seeing the downfall of the wicked
sub.text_en: Fourth world: seeing the downfall of the wicked
sub.desc_en: David sang praise when he saw the downfall of the wicked, citing Psalm 104:35.

sub.text: Fifth world: the day of death
sub.text_en: Fifth world: the day of death
sub.desc_en: David sang praise when he contemplated the day of death, citing Psalm 104:1.
The Gemara asks how we know that Psalm 104 refers to the day of death, and Rabbah bar Rav Sheila answers by citing the continuation of the verse about God hiding His face.

items.text: The soul's fivefold likeness to God
items.text_en: The soul's fivefold likeness to God
items.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ukva (or Mar Ukva) asks Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi about the verse 'בָּרְכִי נַפְשִׁי אֶת ה׳'.
