Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explains that just as God fills the world, sees without being seen, sustains all, is pure, and dwells in hidden chambers, so too the soul fills the body, sees without being seen, sustains the body, is pure, and dwells in hidden chambers. Therefore, the one with five attributes (the soul) should praise the One with five attributes (God).

sub.text: Rav Shimi bar Ukva's question to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Rav Shimi bar Ukva's question to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ukva asks Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi about the meaning of Psalm 103:1.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's first answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's first answer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explains that unlike a human artist, God forms a figure within a figure and imbues it with spirit, soul, and internal organs.
The Gemara interprets 'אֵין צוּר' as 'there is no artist like our God.'
Rabbi Yehuda bar Menasya interprets 'כִּי אֵין בִּלְתֶּךָ' as 'there is no one who wears you out,' unlike humans whose creations wear them out.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's second answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's second answer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explains that David's five 'בָּרְכִי נַפְשִׁי' psalms correspond to God and the soul.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi draws five parallels between God and the soul: both fill the body/world, see without being seen, sustain, are pure, and dwell in hidden chambers.

items.text: Hezekiah's illness and the lesson of prayer even in dire straits
items.text_en: Hezekiah's illness and the lesson of prayer even in dire straits
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna explains the verse 'מִי כְּהֶחָכָם' as referring to God's wisdom in mediating between Hezekiah and Isaiah. Hezekiah refused to visit Isaiah, and Isaiah refused to visit Hezekiah, so God brought illness upon Hezekiah and sent Isaiah to visit him. Isaiah told Hezekiah he would die for not having children, but Hezekiah explained he saw through prophecy that his children would be wicked. Isaiah told him not to worry about God's mysteries and to do his duty. Hezekiah then asked for Isaiah's daughter in marriage, and despite the decree, he did not refrain from prayer. The Gemara concludes with the principle that even if a sharp sword is on one's neck, one should not refrain from mercy, as stated by Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Eliezer.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna introduces the verse 'מִי כְּהֶחָכָם' and explains that it refers to God's wisdom in mediating between Hezekiah and Isaiah.
The Gemara describes how God brought illness upon Hezekiah and sent Isaiah to visit him, with the prophecy that he would die in this world and not live in the next.
Hezekiah asks why he deserves such a harsh decree, and Isaiah responds that it is because he neglected procreation.
Hezekiah explains that he refrained from procreation because he saw through prophecy that his children would be wicked.
Isaiah rebukes Hezekiah for delving into God's mysteries and instructs him to simply do his duty.
Hezekiah asks for Isaiah's daughter in marriage, and despite Isaiah's claim that the decree is sealed, Hezekiah insists that Isaiah cease his prophecy and leave.
Hezekiah cites a tradition from his ancestors that even if a sharp sword is on one's neck, one should not refrain from prayer.
The Gemara adds that Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Eliezer both state the same principle, citing the verse 'הֵן יִקְטְלֵנִי לוֹ אֲיַחֵל'.

items.text: Opening: Even a dream of death should not prevent prayer
items.text_en: Opening: Even a dream of death should not prevent prayer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ḥanan teaches that even if a dream tells a person he will die tomorrow, he should not refrain from prayer, citing the verse 'For in many dreams and vanities and many words, but fear God.' Hezekiah immediately turned his face to the wall and prayed.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ḥanan teaches that even if a dream tells a person he will die tomorrow, he should not refrain from prayer, citing the verse 'For in many dreams and vanities and many words, but fear God.'
The Gemara notes that Hezekiah immediately turned his face to the wall and prayed, illustrating the principle.

items.text: Interpretations of 'wall' and Hezekiah's merit
items.text_en: Interpretations of 'wall' and Hezekiah's merit
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish interprets 'wall' as the walls of his heart. Rabbi Levi says Hezekiah prayed about the wall of the Shunammite woman, arguing that if God revived her son for a small wall, He should surely save him for his father's great deeds. Rav Yehuda and Rabbi Levi explain 'I have done what is good in Your eyes' as connecting redemption to prayer or hiding the book of remedies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'wall' refers to in the verse.
Reish Lakish interprets 'wall' as the walls of Hezekiah's heart, citing a verse.
Rabbi Levi says Hezekiah prayed about the wall of the Shunammite woman, arguing from minor to major.
The Gemara asks what 'I have done what is good in Your eyes' means.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains that Hezekiah connected redemption to prayer.
Rabbi Levi says Hezekiah hid the book of remedies.

items.text: Hezekiah's six actions: three approved, three disapproved
items.text_en: Hezekiah's six actions: three approved, three disapproved
items.desc_en: The Sages list six actions of Hezekiah: three were approved (hiding the book of remedies, crushing the copper serpent, dragging his father's bones on a rope bed) and three were not (stopping the Gihon spring, cutting the Temple doors for the Assyrian king, intercalating Nisan in Nisan). The Gemara explains the error regarding intercalation, citing Shmuel's rule.

sub.desc_en: The Sages introduce that King Hezekiah performed six actions, three approved and three disapproved.
The Sages list the three approved actions: hiding the book of remedies, crushing the copper serpent, and dragging his father's bones on a rope bed.
The Sages list the three disapproved actions: stopping the Gihon spring, cutting the Temple doors for the Assyrian king, and intercalating Nisan in Nisan.
The Gemara questions how Hezekiah could intercalate Nisan, given the verse that Nisan is the first month and no other month is Nisan.

The Gemara resolves that Hezekiah erred regarding Shmuel's rule that one does not intercalate the year on the thirtieth of Adar because it is fit to be established as Nisan; Hezekiah thought the principle 'since it is fit' is not applied.

items.text: Principle of relying on one's own merit vs. others' merit
items.text_en: Principle of relying on one's own merit vs. others' merit
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yoḥanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra states: One who relies on his own merit is judged by others' merit, and vice versa. Moses relied on others' merit (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob) and was judged by his own; Hezekiah relied on his own merit and was judged by others' (David). Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi adds that even when God sent peace to Hezekiah, it was bitter to him.

sub.text: Rabbi Yoḥanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yoḥanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yoḥanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra states the principle: one who relies on his own merit is judged by others' merit, and one who relies on others' merit is judged by his own.
Moses relied on others' merit (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob) and was judged by his own merit, as shown by verses.
Hezekiah relied on his own merit and was judged by others' merit (David), as shown by verses.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi adds that even when God sent peace to Hezekiah, it was bitter to him.

items.text: The Shunammite woman's upper chamber: dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.text_en: The Shunammite woman's upper chamber: dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the verse 'Let us make a small upper chamber with a wall.' Rav and Shmuel disagree: one says it was an open roof chamber that they walled in; the other says it was a large portico divided into two. The Gemara reconciles each opinion with the verse's wording.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse about the Shunammite woman's upper chamber.
Rav and Shmuel disagree: one says it was an open roof chamber that they walled in; the other says it was a large portico divided into two.
The Gemara asks: according to the opinion that it was a portico, the word 'wall' fits, but according to the opinion that it was a roof chamber, what does 'wall' mean?
The answer: they walled it in.
The Gemara asks: according to the opinion that it was a roof chamber, the word 'upper chamber' fits, but according to the opinion that it was a portico, what does 'upper chamber' mean?
The answer: it refers to the finest of the houses.

items.text: Hospitality and the Shunammite woman's recognition of Elisha's holiness
items.text_en: Hospitality and the Shunammite woman's recognition of Elisha's holiness
items.desc_en: Abaye or Rabbi Yitzḥak teaches: One who wishes to benefit may do so like Elisha; one who does not wish to benefit may refrain like Samuel the Ramathite. Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina says a woman recognizes guests more than a man. Rav and Shmuel debate how she knew Elisha was holy: either no fly on his table or no seminal emission on his sheet. Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina adds that Elisha was holy but Gehazi was not. Finally, hosting a Torah scholar is like offering the daily offerings.

sub.desc_en: Abaye or Rabbi Yitzḥak teaches that one who wishes to benefit from guests may do so like Elisha, and one who does not wish to benefit may refrain like Samuel the Ramathite, citing a verse about Samuel's home always being with him.
Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina derives from the Shunammite woman's statement that a woman recognizes guests more than a man.

sub.text: Gemara's question with Rav and Shmuel's answers
sub.text_en: Gemara's question with Rav and Shmuel's answers
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the Shunammite woman knew Elisha was holy, and presents a debate between Rav and Shmuel: one says she never saw a fly on his table, the other says she never saw seminal emission on his sheet.

Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina adds that Elisha was holy but his servant Gehazi was not, citing the verse where Gehazi pushed the Shunammite woman away, which he interprets as Gehazi grabbing her by her beauty.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina citing Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina citing Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov concludes that hosting a Torah scholar and benefiting him is considered by Scripture as if one offers the daily offerings.

items.text: Laws of prayer: low place, intention, and eating before prayer
items.text_en: Laws of prayer: low place, intention, and eating before prayer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov teaches: One should pray in a low place, not a high one, citing 'From the depths I called You.' A baraita supports this. He also says one must align one's feet during prayer. Another teaching: 'Do not eat upon the blood' means do not eat before praying for your blood. A variant says eating and drinking before prayer is like throwing God behind one's back.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov teaches that one should pray in a low place, not a high one, citing the verse 'From the depths I called You.'
A baraita supports the teaching, stating one should not pray on a high place, citing the same verse and another: 'A prayer of the afflicted when he faints.'

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov teaches that one praying must align one's feet, citing the verse 'And their feet were a straight foot.'

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzḥak in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan, quoting Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzḥak in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan, quoting Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzḥak in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan, quoting Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, interprets the verse 'Do not eat upon the blood' as a prohibition against eating before praying for one's blood (life).

sub.text: Alternative version: Rabbi Yitzḥak in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan, quoting Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.text_en: Alternative version: Rabbi Yitzḥak in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan, quoting Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that one who eats and drinks before praying is described by the verse 'And Me you have cast behind your back,' interpreted as 'behind your pride,' meaning after being haughty one accepts the yoke of heaven.

items.text: Time for Shema and the blessing of Yotzer Or
items.text_en: Time for Shema and the blessing of Yotzer Or
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua says Shema can be recited until the third hour; Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules accordingly. Rav Ḥisda in the name of Mar Ukva says one who reads after that time should not say Yotzer Or, but a baraita contradicts this. An alternative version explains 'did not lose' means did not lose the blessings. Rabbi Mani concludes that reading Shema at its proper time is greater than engaging in Torah study.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua states that the Shema may be recited until the third hour.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shmuel that the binding law (הלכה) follows Rabbi Yehoshua.
An anonymous statement says that one who reads the Shema after the third hour has not lost out.

sub.text: Rav Ḥisda in the name of Mar Ukva
sub.text_en: Rav Ḥisda in the name of Mar Ukva
sub.desc_en: Rav Ḥisda in the name of Mar Ukva qualifies that such a person should not recite the blessing of Yotzer Or (יוצר אור).
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that states one who reads after the third hour may still recite the blessings before and after the Shema, contradicting Rav Ḥisda's ruling.
The Gemara declares that this is a conclusive refutation (תיוּבתּא) of Rav Ḥisda's position.
An alternative version reinterprets Rav Ḥisda's statement: 'did not lose' means he did not lose the blessings.
A baraita supports this interpretation, stating that one who reads after the third hour recites the blessings before and after the Shema.
Rabbi Mani concludes that reading the Shema at its proper time is greater than engaging in Torah study, as implied by the baraita.

items.text: Mishnah: Posture for Shema – Beit Shammai vs. Beit Hillel
items.text_en: Mishnah: Posture for Shema – Beit Shammai vs. Beit Hillel
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: Beit Shammai say in the evening one should recline and read, in the morning stand, citing 'when you lie down and when you rise.' Beit Hillel say everyone reads in their usual manner, citing 'when you walk on the way.' The verse 'when you lie down and when you rise' refers to the times people lie down and rise. Rabbi Tarfon recounts that he followed Beit Shammai and endangered himself from bandits; the Sages said he deserved to be liable for violating Beit Hillel's ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with Beit Shammai's position: in the evening one must recline to read Shema, and in the morning stand, citing the verse 'when you lie down and when you rise.'
Beit Hillel counters that everyone reads in their usual manner, citing the verse 'when you walk on the way.'
The Mishnah resolves the dispute: the verse 'when you lie down and when you rise' refers to the times when people lie down and rise, not the posture.
Rabbi Tarfon recounts that he followed Beit Shammai's ruling while traveling and endangered himself from bandits.
The Sages rebuke Rabbi Tarfon, saying he deserved to be liable for violating Beit Hillel's ruling.

items.text: Gemara's opening question on Beit Shammai's reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara's opening question on Beit Shammai's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Beit Shammai do not adopt Beit Hillel's interpretation of the verses for Shema times, since Beit Hillel explain both their own and Beit Shammai's positions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Beit Shammai do not adopt Beit Hillel's interpretation of the verses for Shema times, since Beit Hillel explain both their own and Beit Shammai's positions.

items.text: Beit Shammai's answer and the derivation for a bridegroom
items.text_en: Beit Shammai's answer and the derivation for a bridegroom
items.desc_en: Beit Shammai explain that the verse 'when you lie down and when you rise' implies literal times of lying down and rising. The Gemara then cites a baraita that derives from 'when you sit in your house' and 'when you walk on the road' exemptions for one engaged in a mitzvah and for a bridegroom.

sub.desc_en: Beit Shammai answer that the verse uses 'בשכבך ובקומך' (when you lie down and when you rise) to indicate literal times of lying down and rising, rather than general morning and evening.
The Gemara asks how Beit Shammai interpret the phrase 'ובלכתך בדרך' (and when you walk on the road), since they already used 'בשכבך ובקומך' for the literal times.

The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from 'בשבתך בביתך' (when you sit in your house) an exemption for one engaged in a mitzvah, and from 'ובלכתך בדרך' (when you walk on the road) an exemption for a bridegroom, establishing that a bridegroom who marries a virgin is exempt from Shema, while one who marries a widow is obligated.

items.text: Rav Pappa's explanation of the derivation
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's explanation of the derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the verse implies an exemption, and Rav Pappa answers that 'way' (derekh) implies a permitted activity, so any permitted activity is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the verse implies an exemption for a bridegroom.
Rav Pappa explains that 'way' (דֶרֶךְ) implies a permitted activity, so any permitted activity is exempt.

items.text: Refining the exemption: mitzvah vs. personal distress
items.text_en: Refining the exemption: mitzvah vs. personal distress
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the exemption applies only to one's own activities, not to a mitzvah. It then distinguishes between distress from a mitzvah (exempt) and personal distress (obligated), citing Rabbi Abba bar Zavda's statement about a mourner.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the exemption for a bridegroom applies even when he is going to perform a mitzvah, since the verse still requires reading.
The Gemara answers that the verse's wording 'בשבתך' (your sitting) and 'בלכתך' (your going) teaches that only one's own activities obligate, but a mitzvah exempts.
An objection is raised: if the exemption is based on being busy with a mitzvah, then one marrying a widow (who is obligated) should also be exempt.
The Gemara answers that the bridegroom with a virgin is distressed (טריד) and therefore exempt, while one marrying a widow is not distressed and thus obligated.
An objection is raised: if distress exempts, then even one whose ship sank at sea should be exempt from Shema.

sub.text: Supporting baraita via Rabbi Abba bar Zavda
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita via Rabbi Abba bar Zavda
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Abba bar Zavda's statement that a mourner is obligated in all mitzvot except tefillin, implying that personal distress does not exempt.
The Gemara resolves that a mourner's distress is from a mitzvah (טירדא דמצוה) and does not exempt, while a bridegroom's distress is personal (טירדא דרשות) and does exempt.

items.text: Beit Shammai's alternative derivation and Beit Hillel's response
items.text_en: Beit Shammai's alternative derivation and Beit Hillel's response
items.desc_en: Beit Shammai use the verse to exempt agents of a mitzvah, while Beit Hillel infer from the same verse that one may recite even while walking.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Beit Shammai interpret the verse 'וּבְלֶכְתְּךָ בַדֶּרֶךְ' (and when you walk on the way) since they already used it for the exemption of a groom.

sub.text: Gemara's answer on behalf of Beit Shammai
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer on behalf of Beit Shammai
sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that Beit Shammai derive from the verse a פרט (exclusion) for agents of a mitzvah (commandment), exempting them from reciting the Shema.
Beit Hillel respond that from the same verse one learns ממילא (by inference) that one may recite the Shema even while walking on the way.

items.text: Baraita on posture and the story of Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah
items.text_en: Baraita on posture and the story of Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah
items.desc_en: A baraita lists various permissible postures for Shema, followed by a story where Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah adjust their positions. The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yishmael's change might lead students to think he follows Beit Shammai.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists the permissible postures for reciting Shema according to Beit Hillel.

The baraita recounts a story where Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah were reclining, and when the time for Shema arrived, each changed their posture, prompting Rabbi Elazar's parable about a man with a long beard.
Rabbi Yishmael explains that he acted according to Beit Hillel and Rabbi Elazar according to Beit Shammai, and warns that students might see and establish the halacha for generations.
The Gemara asks what is meant by the phrase 'and moreover' in Rabbi Yishmael's statement.
The Gemara explains that although Beit Hillel permits reclining, Rabbi Yishmael's change from upright to reclining might lead students to think he follows Beit Shammai, hence the warning.

items.text: Dispute on following Beit Shammai's ruling
items.text_en: Dispute on following Beit Shammai's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Yechezkel, Rav Yosef, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak debate whether one who acts like Beit Shammai has fulfilled the obligation, with Rav Nachman citing a story where Rabbi Tarfon endangered himself and was rebuked.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'and moreover' adds in the story of Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, and explains that it precludes the concern that students might see a change in posture and mistakenly fix the halacha like Beit Shammai.

The Gemara explains that the phrase 'and moreover' addresses a potential objection: although Beit Hillel permits reclining, the concern is that a sudden change from upright to reclining might lead students to think the rabbi follows Beit Shammai.
Rav Yechezkel teaches a baraita stating that one who acts according to Beit Shammai has fulfilled the obligation, and one who acts according to Beit Hillel has also fulfilled the obligation.
Rav Yosef objects, citing a Mishnah about sukkah where Beit Shammai invalidate and Beit Hillel validate, arguing that acting like Beit Shammai is ineffective.

sub.text: Story about Rabbi Yochanan ben Hachoranit
sub.text_en: Story about Rabbi Yochanan ben Hachoranit
sub.desc_en: Beit Hillel brings a story where elders of both houses visited Rabbi Yochanan ben Hachoranit who was sitting with his head and most of his body in the sukkah but his table inside the house, and they said nothing to him.
Beit Shammai rejects the proof, arguing that the elders actually rebuked Rabbi Yochanan ben Hachoranit, saying that if he had always acted that way he never fulfilled the mitzvah of sukkah.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak rules that one who acts like Beit Shammai is liable for death, citing the story of Rabbi Tarfon who endangered himself by following Beit Shammai and was rebuked by the Sages for transgressing Beit Hillel's words.

items.text: Mishnah on blessings for Shema and Gemara's question
items.text_en: Mishnah on blessings for Shema and Gemara's question
items.desc_en: The Mishnah specifies the number of blessings before and after Shema in the morning and evening, and rules on varying length. The Gemara asks what blessings are recited, and Rabbi Yaakov cites Rabbi Oshaya.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the number of blessings before and after Shema in the morning and evening, and rules on varying length and concluding formulas.
The Gemara asks what specific blessings are recited.
Rabbi Yaakov begins to cite Rabbi Oshaya's answer regarding the blessings.

items.text: Why the evening blessing says 'borei choshekh' instead of 'nogah'
items.text_en: Why the evening blessing says 'borei choshekh' instead of 'nogah'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the evening blessing uses 'borei choshekh' (creates darkness) rather than the more positive 'nogah' (light). It first suggests it follows the biblical verse, but then objects that the blessing for evil is also euphemized. Rava explains that the wording is to mention the attribute of day at night and night at day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the evening blessing says 'borei choshekh' (creates darkness) rather than the more positive 'nogah' (light). It first suggests it follows the biblical verse, but then objects that the blessing for evil is also euphemized. Rava explains that the wording is to mention the attribute of day at night and night at day.

items.text: How day is mentioned at night
items.text_en: How day is mentioned at night
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the attribute of day is mentioned at night, since the blessing only mentions darkness. Abaye answers that the phrase 'golel or mipnei choshekh' (rolling away light before darkness) implies the day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the attribute of day is mentioned at night, since the blessing only mentions darkness.
Abaye answers that the phrase 'גולל אור מפני חשך' (rolling away light before darkness) implies the day.

items.text: The blessing before Shema: 'Ahavah Rabbah' vs 'Ahavat Olam'
items.text_en: The blessing before Shema: 'Ahavah Rabbah' vs 'Ahavat Olam'
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the second blessing before Shema as 'Ahavah Rabbah' (great love), citing Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel and Rabbi Elazar. A baraita supports this, stating that one says 'Ahavah Rabbah' and not 'Ahavat Olam', though the Rabbis say 'Ahavat Olam' with a supporting verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the second blessing before Shema.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel answers that the blessing is 'Ahavah Rabbah'.
Rabbi Elazar similarly instructed his son Rabbi Pedat to say 'Ahavah Rabbah'.
A baraita supports that one says 'Ahavah Rabbah' and not 'Ahavat Olam'.
The Rabbis say 'Ahavat Olam' and cite the verse 'וְאַהֲבַת עוֹלָם אֲהַבְתִּיךְ' (Jeremiah 31:3) as support.

items.text: Blessing for Torah study: when and for what
items.text_en: Blessing for Torah study: when and for what
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules that if one studied before Shema, a blessing is needed; after Shema, the 'Ahavah Rabbah' suffices. Then a dispute unfolds: Rav Huna says a blessing is needed for Mikra but not Midrash; Rabbi Elazar adds Midrash but not Mishnah; Rabbi Yochanan adds Mishnah but not Talmud; Rava adds even Talmud.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules that if one studied before Shema a blessing is needed, but after Shema the blessing 'Ahavah Rabbah' suffices.
Rav Huna says a blessing is needed for Mikra (Scripture) but not for Midrash (homiletical interpretation).
Rabbi Elazar adds that a blessing is needed for Mikra and Midrash but not for Mishnah.
Rabbi Yochanan says a blessing is needed even for Mishnah but not for Talmud.
Rava says a blessing is needed even for Talmud.

items.text: The text of the Torah study blessing
items.text_en: The text of the Torah study blessing
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a story of Rav who would wash his hands and bless before teaching. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel gives the blessing 'asher kiddeshanu... la'asok bedivrei Torah'. Rabbi Yochanan adds a longer conclusion. Rav Hamnuna offers a different blessing and declares it superior. The Gemara concludes that one should say all of them.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi testifies that Rav would wash his hands and bless before teaching Torah.
The Gemara asks what blessing Rav recited.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel states the blessing: 'אשר קדשנו במצותיו וצונו לעסוק בדברי תורה'.
Rabbi Yochanan adds a longer conclusion to the blessing, including 'הערב נא' and the closing 'המלמד תורה לעמו ישראל'.
Rav Hamnuna offers a different blessing: 'אשר בחר בנו מכל העמים ונתן לנו את תורתו... נותן התורה'.
Rav Hamnuna declares his blessing the most excellent of the blessings.
The Gemara concludes that one should recite all of these blessings.

items.text: The single blessing in the Temple: 'Ahavah Rabbah' or 'Yotzer Or'
items.text_en: The single blessing in the Temple: 'Ahavah Rabbah' or 'Yotzer Or'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the Temple procedure where the officer says 'bless one blessing'. The Gemara identifies it as 'Ahavah Rabbah' based on Shmuel. Rabbi Zerika reports Resh Lakish says it is 'Yotzer Or', but this is clarified as a deduction from a principle that blessings do not impede each other, not a direct statement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah describing the Temple procedure: the officer says 'bless one blessing', they recite the Ten Commandments and Shema, and then bless the people with three blessings.
The Gemara asks what is the 'one blessing' mentioned in the Mishnah, and notes that Rabbi Abba and Rabbi Yosei bar Abba were asked this and did not know.
Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shmuel that the one blessing is 'Ahavah Rabbah'.

sub.text: Resh Lakish's answer via Rabbi Zerika
sub.text_en: Resh Lakish's answer via Rabbi Zerika
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zerika reports in the name of Rabbi Ami citing Resh Lakish that the one blessing is 'Yotzer Or'.
Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef clarifies that Resh Lakish's statement was not explicit but inferred from the principle that blessings do not impede each other.
The Gemara explains that if they said 'Yotzer Or' and omitted 'Ahavah Rabbah', this demonstrates that blessings do not impede each other.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's statement about blessings not impeding each other
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's statement about blessings not impeding each other
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement that blessings do not impede each other, suggesting that if the Sages originally said 'Ahavah Rabbah' and not 'Yotzer Or', it might be because the time for 'Yotzer Or' had not yet arrived. It then proposes an alternative interpretation that the Mishnah refers to the order of blessings, not their content.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement that blessings do not impede each other, suggesting that if the Sages originally said 'Ahavah Rabbah' and not 'Yotzer Or', it might be because the time for 'Yotzer Or' had not yet arrived.
The Gemara proposes an alternative interpretation that the Mishnah refers to the order of blessings, not their content.

The Gemara explains that if the Mishnah means the order of blessings, then they always said 'Ahavah Rabbah' and when the time for 'Yotzer Or' came they said it, and the Mishnah's statement means that the order of blessings does not impede.

items.text: The recitation of the Ten Commandments and its cancellation
items.text_en: The recitation of the Ten Commandments and its cancellation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the order of recitation including the Ten Commandments. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel reports that even outside the Temple they sought to recite them, but they were cancelled due to the insinuation of the heretics. A baraita supports this, and later attempts by Rabbah bar bar Chanah and Ameimar to reinstate them were rejected.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the order of recitation in the Temple, including the Ten Commandments, Shema, and other sections.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shmuel that even outside the Temple they sought to recite the Ten Commandments, but they were abolished due to the grievance of the heretics.
A baraita supports this, with Rabbi Natan stating the same tradition about the cancellation due to heretics.

sub.text: Story about Rabbah bar bar Chanah
sub.text_en: Story about Rabbah bar bar Chanah
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah thought to reinstitute the recitation in Sura, but Rav Chisda told him it was already abolished due to the heretics.
Ameimar thought to reinstitute the recitation in Neharde'a, but Rav Ashi told him it was already abolished due to the heretics.

items.text: Additional blessing for the outgoing watch on Shabbat
items.text_en: Additional blessing for the outgoing watch on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that on Shabbat an additional blessing is added for the outgoing watch. Rabbi Chelbo explains that the outgoing watch says to the incoming watch a blessing invoking peace and brotherhood.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that on Shabbat an additional blessing is added for the outgoing watch.
The Gemara asks what is that single blessing.
Rabbi Chelbo explains that the outgoing watch says to the incoming watch a blessing invoking peace and brotherhood.

items.text: The principle of following the conclusion of a blessing
items.text_en: The principle of following the conclusion of a blessing
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a case where one holds a cup of wine but thinks it is beer, and opens with a blessing for beer but concludes for wine—he has fulfilled his obligation. It then raises a question: if one holds beer but thinks it is wine, and opens for wine but concludes for beer, do we follow the main blessing or the conclusion?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states a clear case: if one holds a cup of wine but thinks it is beer, and opens the blessing for beer but concludes for wine, he has fulfilled his obligation, citing the Mishnah that 'shehakol' covers all.
The Gemara raises a question: if one holds beer but thinks it is wine, and opens for wine but concludes for beer, do we follow the main blessing or the conclusion?

items.text: Proof from the morning and evening blessings
items.text_en: Proof from the morning and evening blessings
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a proof from the morning and evening blessings: if one opened with 'Yotzer Or' and concluded with 'Ma'ariv Aravim', he did not fulfill his obligation; but if he opened with 'Ma'ariv Aravim' and concluded with 'Yotzer Or', he did. The rule is that everything follows the conclusion. The Gemara then addresses an objection based on the requirement for mentioning God's name and kingship, resolving it with the principle of mentioning the attribute of day at night and night at day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita as proof that the conclusion of a blessing determines its validity, showing that if one opened with 'יוצר אור' and concluded with 'מעריב ערבים' he did not fulfill his obligation, and vice versa, with the rule that everything follows the conclusion.

The Gemara objects that the case is different because the blessing includes 'ברוך יוצר המאורות' (mention of God's name), but for Rabbi Yochanan who requires kingship (מלכות) in every blessing, the proof is insufficient.
Rabbah bar Ulla resolves the objection by explaining that the blessing mentions both the attribute of day at night and night at day, so it includes both God's name and kingship from the outset.

items.text: Clarification of the rule 'everything follows the conclusion'
items.text_en: Clarification of the rule 'everything follows the conclusion'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the general rule 'everything follows the conclusion' includes the case discussed. It explains that the rule actually comes to include a case of bread and dates: if one ate dates but thought they were bread, and opened with the blessing for bread but concluded for dates, he has fulfilled his obligation, because dates also sustain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the general rule 'everything follows the conclusion' in the baraita comes to include the case of bread and dates that was just discussed.

The Gemara rejects the suggestion and explains that the rule comes to include a case of bread and dates, but the straightforward scenario (ate bread, thought it was dates) is exactly the unresolved question.

The Gemara resolves that the rule applies to a case where one ate dates thinking they were bread, opened with the blessing for bread, and concluded for dates — he has fulfilled his obligation because dates also sustain (מזון).

items.text: The necessity of 'Emet VeYatziv' and the proper posture for bowing
items.text_en: The necessity of 'Emet VeYatziv' and the proper posture for bowing
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Chinana Saba in the name of Rav states that one who does not say 'Emet VeYatziv' in the morning and 'Emet VeEmunah' in the evening has not fulfilled his obligation. Additionally, Rav teaches that when bowing in prayer, one should bow at 'Baruch' and straighten at God's name. Shmuel explains the reason from a verse, and an objection is raised and resolved.

sub.text: Rabbah bar Chinana Saba in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar Chinana Saba in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Chinana Saba states in Rav's name that one who does not say 'Emet VeYatziv' in the morning and 'Emet VeEmunah' in the evening has not fulfilled his obligation, citing a verse.

sub.text: Rabbah bar Chinana Saba in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar Chinana Saba in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Chinana Saba further states in Rav's name that when bowing in prayer, one should bow at 'Baruch' and straighten at God's name.
Shmuel explains Rav's reason for bowing at 'Baruch' and straightening at God's name, citing the verse 'ה׳ זוֹקֵף כְּפוּפִים' (the Lord straightens the bowed).
An objection is raised from a verse that says 'מִפְּנֵי שְׁמִי נִחַת הוּא' (because of My name he is subdued), implying bowing at God's name, not straightening.
The gemara rejects the objection by noting that the verse says 'מִפְּנֵי שְׁמִי' (because of My name), not 'בִּשְׁמִי' (in My name), so it does not require bowing at the name itself.
Shmuel tells Chiyya bar Rav a fine teaching from his father (Rav): when bowing, bow at 'Baruch'; when straightening, straighten at God's name.

items.text: Dispute over prayer formulations during the Ten Days of Repentance
items.text_en: Dispute over prayer formulations during the Ten Days of Repentance
items.desc_en: Rav Shešet's posture during prayer is described. Rav's teaching distinguishes between the standard year and the Ten Days of Repentance regarding the use of 'האל הקדוש' vs 'המלך הקדוש' and 'מלך אוהב צדקה ומשפט' vs 'המלך המשפט'. Rabbi Elazar argues that even saying 'האל הקדוש' fulfills the obligation, citing a verse. The Gemara asks for the conclusion, and Rav Yosef and Rabbah rule in favor of Rabbah's opinion.

sub.desc_en: Describes Rav Shešet's distinctive posture when bowing and straightening during prayer.

sub.text: Rabbah bar Chinana Saba in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar Chinana Saba in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav teaches that throughout the year one prays 'האל הקדוש' and 'מלך אוהב צדקה ומשפט', except during the Ten Days of Repentance when one says 'המלך הקדוש' and 'המלך המשפט'.
Rabbi Elazar argues that even saying 'האל הקדוש' fulfills the obligation, citing a verse that associates 'האל הקדוש' with the Ten Days of Repentance.
The Gemara asks what the conclusion is regarding the dispute.
Rav Yosef and Rabbah state their opinions, and the halacha is ruled in accordance with Rabbah.

items.text: Obligation to pray for others
items.text_en: Obligation to pray for others
items.desc_en: Rav teaches that one who can pray for another and does not is called a sinner, citing Samuel's words. Rava adds that if the other is a Torah scholar, one must exert oneself for him. The Gemara questions the source, initially considering a verse about a king, but ultimately derives it from David's conduct.

sub.text: Rav via Rabba bar Chinana Saba
sub.text_en: Rav via Rabba bar Chinana Saba
sub.desc_en: Rav states that one who can pray for another and does not is called a sinner, citing Samuel's words.
Rava adds that if the other is a Torah scholar, one must exert oneself for him.
The Gemara asks for the source of Rava's statement.
The Gemara initially suggests a verse about a king but rejects it as a king is different.
The Gemara derives the obligation from David's conduct in Psalms.

items.text: Forgiveness for one who is ashamed of his sin
items.text_en: Forgiveness for one who is ashamed of his sin
items.desc_en: Rav teaches that one who commits a transgression and is ashamed of it is forgiven all his sins, citing a verse. The Gemara questions whether this applies to the community, but derives it from Saul's shame for killing the priests of Nov. Proof that Saul was forgiven comes from Samuel's statement and a Bat Kol.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that one who commits a transgression and is ashamed of it is forgiven all his sins, citing the verse from Ezekiel.
The Gemara objects that the verse may refer specifically to the community, not an individual.
The Gemara derives the principle from Saul, who was ashamed to mention consulting the Urim and Tumim because he killed the priests of Nov.
The Gemara explains that Saul omitted the Urim and Tumim because he was ashamed of killing the priests of Nov.
Rabbi Yochanan proves that Saul was forgiven from heaven, as Samuel said 'with me' meaning in his compartment in the Garden of Eden.
Rabbannan derive forgiveness from the Bat Kol that called Saul 'the chosen of the Lord' after his death.

items.text: Why Balaam's section was not included in Shema
items.text_en: Why Balaam's section was not included in Shema
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu reports that the Sages considered including Balaam's section in Shema but refrained due to communal burden. The Gemara questions why, noting that other sections mention the Exodus. Rabbi Yosi bar Avin explains it is because of the verse 'כרע שכב כארי וכלביא מי יקימנו'. The Gemara then asks why not just that verse, and answers that we do not break up sections that Moses did not break. Finally, the Gemara explains why the section of Tzitzit was included, listing five matters it contains, and derives the last three from a baraita.

sub.text: Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Yehuda bar Zevida
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Yehuda bar Zevida
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu reports that the Sages considered including Balaam's section in Shema but refrained due to communal burden.
The Gemara questions why the reason cannot be the mention of the Exodus, noting that other sections also mention it.
Rabbi Yosi bar Avin explains that the reason is the verse 'כרע שכב כארי וכלביא מי יקימנו' (he crouched, lay down like a lion, and like a lioness, who will rouse him).
The Gemara asks why not just include that verse alone.
The Gemara answers that we do not break up sections that Moses did not break.
The Gemara asks why the section of Tzitzit was included in Shema.
Rabbi Yehuda bar Chaviva explains that the section contains five matters: the mitzvah of tzitzit, the Exodus, the yoke of commandments, awareness of heresy, sinful thoughts, and idolatrous thoughts.
The Gemara notes that three matters are explicit in the text, and asks: from where do we derive the other three (awareness of heresy, sinful thoughts, idolatrous thoughts)?

A baraita derives the three matters from the verse 'אחרי לבבכם' (after your hearts) for heresy, 'אחרי עיניכם' (after your eyes) for sinful thoughts, and 'אתם זונים' (you go astray) for idolatrous thoughts.

items.text: Mentioning the Exodus at night and in the Messianic era
items.text_en: Mentioning the Exodus at night and in the Messianic era
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the Exodus is mentioned at night. Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya says he did not merit this until Ben Zoma expounded it from the verse 'כל ימי חייך'. The Sages argue that 'ימי חייך' refers to this world, and 'כל' includes the days of the Messiah. The Gemara cites a baraita where Ben Zoma questions the Sages about mentioning the Exodus in the Messianic era, citing a verse that the redemption from Egypt will be superseded. The Sages respond that the Exodus will not be uprooted but will become secondary to the redemption from other lands, analogous to Jacob's name change.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the Exodus is mentioned at night, and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya notes that he did not merit this until Ben Zoma expounded it.
Ben Zoma expounds the verse 'כל ימי חייך' (all the days of your life) to include nights.
The Sages argue that 'ימי חייך' refers to this world, and 'כל' includes the days of the Messiah.

sub.text: Ben Zoma's question to the Sages
sub.text_en: Ben Zoma's question to the Sages
sub.desc_en: Ben Zoma questions the Sages about mentioning the Exodus in the Messianic era, citing a verse that the redemption from Egypt will be superseded.
The Sages respond that the Exodus will not be uprooted but will become secondary to the redemption from other lands.
The Gemara provides an analogy: just as Jacob's name change did not uproot the original name, so too the Exodus will not be uprooted.

items.text: The name 'Israel' is primary, 'Jacob' secondary, with a mashal about forgetting earlier troubles
items.text_en: The name 'Israel' is primary, 'Jacob' secondary, with a mashal about forgetting earlier troubles
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'Israel' is the primary name and 'Jacob' is secondary, citing a verse. A mashal of a man saved from a wolf, lion, and snake illustrates that later troubles cause earlier ones to be forgotten, applied to Israel's history.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the name 'Jacob' is not uprooted, but 'Israel' is primary and 'Jacob' secondary.
The Gemara cites a verse from Isaiah and interprets 'first things' as subjugation to kingdoms and 'former things' as the Exodus.
Rav Yosef teaches that the 'new thing' in the verse refers to the war of Gog and Magog.
A mashal of a man saved from a wolf, lion, and snake illustrates that later troubles cause earlier ones to be forgotten, applied to Israel's history.

items.text: Abraham and Sarah's name changes: from specific to universal
items.text_en: Abraham and Sarah's name changes: from specific to universal
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Abraham was initially father to Aram but later to the entire world, and similarly Sarah was initially princess to her nation but later to the entire world.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the topic of Abram's name change to Abraham by citing the verse 'Abram is Abraham'.
The Gemara explains that initially Abram was father to Aram, but ultimately became father to the entire world.
The Gemara shifts to the parallel case of Sarai's name change to Sarah, citing the verse 'Sarai is Sarah'.
The Gemara explains that initially Sarai was princess only to her nation, but ultimately became princess to the entire world.

items.text: Calling Abraham 'Abram' is prohibited; Jacob's name is different
items.text_en: Calling Abraham 'Abram' is prohibited; Jacob's name is different
items.desc_en: Bar Kappara teaches that calling Abraham 'Abram' violates a positive commandment, and Rabbi Eliezer says it violates a negative commandment. The Gemara questions whether the same applies to Sarah and Jacob, and distinguishes Jacob because Scripture later uses his former name. A challenge from Nehemiah 9:7 is answered by saying the prophet was describing the past.

sub.desc_en: Bar Kappara teaches that calling Abraham 'Abram' violates a positive commandment, and Rabbi Eliezer adds that it also violates a negative commandment.
The Gemara asks whether calling Sarah 'Sarai' similarly violates a commandment.
The Gemara answers that the prohibition regarding Sarah was only addressed to Abraham, not to everyone.
The Gemara asks whether calling Jacob 'Jacob' also violates a commandment.
The Gemara answers that Jacob's case is different because Scripture itself later refers to him as Jacob.
Rabbi Yosei bar Avin objects by citing Nehemiah 9:7, which refers to Abraham as 'Abram'.
The Gemara resolves that the prophet was recounting God's praise for what was originally the case, before the name change.

items.text: Mishnah: Interruptions during Shema and the order of paragraphs
items.text_en: Mishnah: Interruptions during Shema and the order of paragraphs
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one was reading Torah and the time for Shema arrived, if they intended to fulfill the obligation, they have fulfilled it. It details when one may interrupt between paragraphs and in the middle, according to Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda. The paragraphs of Shema are listed, and Rabbi Yehuda prohibits interrupting between 'Vayomer' and 'Emet Veyatziv'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with a transitional phrase marking the end of the previous chapter.
The Mishnah states that if one was reading Torah and the time for Shema arrived, if they intended to fulfill the obligation, they have fulfilled it.
Rabbi Meir rules that between paragraphs one may greet out of respect and respond, but in the middle one may only greet out of fear and respond.
Rabbi Yehuda rules that in the middle one may greet out of fear and respond out of respect, and between paragraphs one may greet out of respect and respond with a greeting to anyone.

The Mishnah lists the breaks between paragraphs of Shema: between the first blessing and the second, between the second and Shema, between Shema and Vehaya Im Shamoa, between Vehaya Im Shamoa and Vayomer, and between Vayomer and Emet Veyatziv.
Rabbi Yehuda rules that one may not interrupt between Vayomer and Emet Veyatziv.

items.text: Reason for the order of Shema paragraphs
items.text_en: Reason for the order of Shema paragraphs
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha explains that 'Shema' precedes 'VeHaya Im Shamoa' to first accept the yoke of heaven, then the yoke of commandments. 'VeHaya Im Shamoa' precedes 'Vayomer' because it applies both day and night, while 'Vayomer' applies only by day.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha explains that the paragraph 'Shema' precedes 'VeHaya Im Shamoa' so that one first accepts the yoke of heaven and then the yoke of commandments.
He further explains that 'VeHaya Im Shamoa' precedes 'Vayomer' because the former applies both day and night, while the latter applies only by day.

items.text: Gemara: Mitzvot require intention; clarifying the Mishnah's case
items.text_en: Gemara: Mitzvot require intention; clarifying the Mishnah's case
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that mitzvot require intention. It clarifies that 'if he intended his heart' refers to intention to read, but since he is already reading, it must be a case where he was reading for correction (not for obligation).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that mitzvot require intention.
The Gemara asks: what does 'if he intended his heart' mean — intention to read? But he is already reading!
The Gemara answers: it refers to one who is reading for correction (not for obligation).

items.text: Debate: Shema in any language or only in Hebrew
items.text_en: Debate: Shema in any language or only in Hebrew
items.desc_en: Rabbi holds that Shema must be recited in Hebrew (as written), while the Sages permit any language. Each side derives their position from the verses 'VeHayu' and 'Shema'. The Gemara explains how each interprets the other's verse and concludes that Rabbi believes the entire Torah was said in any language, while the Sages believe it was said in Hebrew, but each verse is needed for a specific derivation.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the dispute: Rabbi requires Shema in Hebrew (as written), while the Sages permit any language.
The Gemara explains Rabbi's reasoning: the verse 'והיו' (and they shall be) implies they must remain as they are, i.e., in Hebrew.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the Sages' position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Sages' position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Sages' reasoning: the verse 'שמע' (hear) implies in any language you understand.
The Gemara objects: for Rabbi, what does the verse 'שמע' teach? It answers: it requires one to hear what he says with his own ears.

sub.text: Gemara's note on the Sages' view
sub.text_en: Gemara's note on the Sages' view
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Sages follow the opinion that one who did not hear his own recitation has fulfilled the obligation.
The Gemara objects: for the Sages, what does the verse 'והיו' teach? It answers: it prohibits reciting the Shema out of order.
The Gemara asks: from where does Rabbi derive the prohibition against reciting out of order? It answers: from the words 'דברים' and 'הדברים', which the Sages do not expound.
The Gemara infers that Rabbi holds the entire Torah was said in any language, otherwise the verse 'והיו' would be superfluous.
The Gemara rejects the inference: 'והיו' is still needed because of the verse 'שמע' (which might otherwise imply any language).
The Gemara infers that the Sages hold the entire Torah was said in Hebrew, otherwise the verse 'שמע' would be superfluous.
The Gemara rejects the inference: 'שמע' is still needed because of the verse 'והיו' (which might otherwise require Hebrew).

items.text: Baraita: Intention required only for the first verse of Shema
items.text_en: Baraita: Intention required only for the first verse of Shema
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that 'VeHayu' teaches not to read backwards, and 'Hadevarim... al levavecha' might imply the whole paragraph needs intention, but 'Haeleh' limits it to only these words (the first verse). Rabbi Akiva challenges this with a verse.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by citing the verse 'והיו' (and they shall be) to teach that one must not read the Shema backwards.
The baraita raises the possibility that the verse 'הדברים... על לבבך' (these words... upon your heart) might imply that the entire paragraph requires intention.
The baraita answers that the word 'האלה' (these) limits the requirement for intention to only these words (the first verse), and from that point onward intention is not required.
The baraita attributes this ruling to Rabbi Eliezer.
Rabbi Akiva challenges Rabbi Eliezer's position by citing a verse, setting up a counter-argument.

items.text: Opening: Requirement of intention for the entire first paragraph
items.text_en: Opening: Requirement of intention for the entire first paragraph
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse 'על לבבך' that the entire first paragraph of Shema requires intention. Rabba bar bar Chana cites Rabbi Yochanan that the halakha follows Rabbi Akiva (who presumably holds this view).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse 'על לבבך' that the entire first paragraph of Shema requires intention.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the halakha follows Rabbi Akiva (who presumably holds this view).

items.text: Alternative version: Intention only for first chapter
items.text_en: Alternative version: Intention only for first chapter
items.desc_en: An alternative tradition cites a baraitha where Rabbi Acha in the name of Rabbi Yehuda says that once one has intention in the first chapter, no further intention is needed. Rabba bar bar Chana again cites Rabbi Yochanan that the halakha follows this view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative version of the tradition, citing a baraitha that one who recites Shema must have intention.

sub.text: Rabbi Acha in the name of Rabbi Yehuda
sub.text_en: Rabbi Acha in the name of Rabbi Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Acha, citing Rabbi Yehuda, states that once one has intention in the first chapter, no further intention is required.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana reports that Rabbi Yochanan ruled the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Acha's statement in the name of Rabbi Yehuda.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Zutra and Rabbi Yoshiya on intention vs. reading
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Zutra and Rabbi Yoshiya on intention vs. reading
items.desc_en: A baraitha presents a dispute: Rav Zutra says that up to 'על לבבך' requires intention, thereafter only reading; Rabbi Yoshiya reverses this. The Gemara challenges both views with scriptural verses and resolves them by reinterpreting each position: Rav Zutra means intention and reading up to that point, then reading without intention; Rabbi Yoshiya means reading and intention up to that point, then intention without reading. The Gemara distinguishes between the verses for Shema and those for Torah study.

sub.desc_en: A baraitha is cited, presenting the dispute between Rav Zutra and Rabbi Yoshiya regarding the point in Shema up to which intention is required versus mere reading.
The Gemara objects to Rav Zutra's view: why should the later part require only reading, given that the verse 'ודברת בם' (and you shall speak of them) applies to the entire passage?
The Gemara reinterprets Rav Zutra: up to that point requires both intention and reading, thereafter reading without intention.
The Gemara objects: why should the earlier part require both intention and reading, since the same verse 'על לבבכם...לדבר בם' (upon your heart...to speak of them) appears in the second paragraph?
The Gemara resolves: that verse is needed for Rabbi Yitzchak's teaching that 'ושמתם את דברי אלה' (and you shall place these words of mine) requires placing the words opposite the heart.
The Gemara objects to Rabbi Yoshiya's view: why should the later part require only intention, given that the verse 'על לבבך' (upon your heart) appears in the first paragraph as well?
The Gemara reinterprets Rabbi Yoshiya: up to that point requires both reading and intention, thereafter intention without reading.
The Gemara objects: why should the earlier part require both reading and intention, since the same verse 'על לבבכם...לדבר בם' (upon your heart...to speak of them) appears in the second paragraph?
The Gemara resolves: that verse refers to words of Torah, meaning one should teach Torah to one's children so they will be engaged in it.

items.text: Intention required only for the first verse according to Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Intention required only for the first verse according to Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: A baraitha states that according to Rabbi Meir, intention is required only for the first verse of Shema ('שמע ישראל...'). Rava rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Meir.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that according to Rabbi Meir, intention is required only for the first verse of Shema.
Rava rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Meir.

items.text: Lengthening the word 'Echad' and its limits
items.text_en: Lengthening the word 'Echad' and its limits
items.desc_en: Somchus says that one who lengthens the word 'אחד' will have his days and years lengthened. Rav Acha bar Yaakov adds that this applies specifically to the letter dalet, and Rav Ashi says provided one does not slur the chet. Rabbi Yirmiya saw Rabbi Chiya bar Abba lengthening excessively and told him that once one has acknowledged God's sovereignty in all directions, no further lengthening is needed.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited in which Somchus states that one who lengthens the word 'אחד' will have his days and years lengthened.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov specifies that the lengthening applies specifically to the letter dalet.
Rav Ashi adds that the lengthening is valid provided one does not slur the letter chet.

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmiya to Rabbi Chiya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmiya to Rabbi Chiya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmiya sees Rabbi Chiya bar Abba lengthening excessively and tells him that once one has acknowledged God's sovereignty in all directions, no further lengthening is needed.

items.text: Posture for reciting Shema: standing or not
items.text_en: Posture for reciting Shema: standing or not
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says that up to 'על לבבך' must be recited standing, but thereafter not. Rabbi Yochanan says the entire paragraph must be recited standing, consistent with his earlier ruling that the halakha follows Rabbi Acha in the name of Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.text: Rav Nathan bar Mar Ukva citing Rav Yehuda
sub.text_en: Rav Nathan bar Mar Ukva citing Rav Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Rav Nathan bar Mar Ukva reports Rav Yehuda's ruling that the Shema must be recited standing only up to 'על לבבך' (upon your heart), but not thereafter.
Rabbi Yochanan states that the entire paragraph must be recited standing, contradicting Rav Yehuda's limitation.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation citing Rabba bar bar Chana
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation citing Rabba bar bar Chana
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yochanan's ruling is consistent with his earlier position, as reported by Rabba bar bar Chana, that the halakha follows Rabbi Acha who said in the name of Rabbi Yehuda.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's practice and the dispute about repeating Shema
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's practice and the dispute about repeating Shema
items.desc_en: A baraitha identifies 'שמע ישראל' as the Shema of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. Rav asked Rabbi Chiya why he never saw Rabbi accept the yoke of heaven; Rabbi Chiya explained that he does so while passing his hands over his face. A dispute arises: Bar Kappara says Rabbi does not repeat the entire Shema, while Rabbi Shimon ben Rabbi says he does. Bar Kappara argues that if he repeats it, why does he go back to the section about yetziat Mitzrayim? The answer is to mention the Exodus at its proper time.

sub.desc_en: A baraitha is cited, identifying the verse 'שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל' as the Shema of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
Rav asks Rabbi Chiya why he never saw Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi accept the yoke of heaven.
Rabbi Chiya answers that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi accepts the yoke of heaven while passing his hands over his face.
The Gemara raises a dispute: does Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi repeat the entire Shema after his brief acceptance, or not?
Bar Kappara states that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi does not repeat the entire Shema.
Rabbi Shimon ben Rabbi argues that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi does repeat the entire Shema.
Bar Kappara objects to Rabbi Shimon ben Rabbi: if Rabbi repeats the entire Shema, why does he go back to the section about yetziat Mitzrayim?
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi goes back to mention the Exodus at its proper time.

items.text: One who falls asleep during Shema and the case of a prone sleeper
items.text_en: One who falls asleep during Shema and the case of a prone sleeper
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ila in the name of Rav says that if one said the first verse and then was overcome by sleep, he has fulfilled his obligation. Rav Nachman instructs his servant to trouble him only for the first verse. Rav Yosef asks about his father's practice, and is told similarly. Rav Yosef then rules that a prone sleeper (פרקדן) should not recite Shema, but the Gemara questions this based on Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's curse on one who sleeps prone. The Gemara distinguishes between sleeping while praying (permitted) and reciting Shema (forbidden), and notes that Rabbi Yochanan was an exception due to his corpulence.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ila in the name of Rav rules that if one recited the first verse of Shema and was overcome by sleep, he has fulfilled his obligation.
Rav Nachman instructs his servant Daru to trouble him only for the first verse of Shema, supporting the previous ruling.
Rav Yosef asks his son about his father's practice and is told that he troubled himself only for the first verse, further corroborating the ruling.
Rav Yosef rules that a prone sleeper (פרקדן) should not recite Shema, but the Gemara questions this based on Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's curse on one who sleeps prone.
The Gemara answers that sleeping while praying is permitted, but reciting Shema while prone is forbidden.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yochanan would pray and recite Shema while prone.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yochanan was an exception due to his corpulence, which made lying prone comfortable.

items.text: Interruptions between paragraphs of Shema
items.text_en: Interruptions between paragraphs of Shema
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that between paragraphs one may greet out of respect and respond. The Gemara clarifies the reasons: greeting out of respect and responding to any person. It then addresses the middle of a paragraph, where one may greet out of fear and respond out of respect according to Rabbi Yehuda. The Gemara resolves a contradiction by explaining that the Mishnah is missing a clause: Rabbi Meir says that in the middle one may greet out of fear and certainly respond, while Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between greeting (out of fear) and responding (out of respect).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's rule about greeting and responding between paragraphs of Shema.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies that one may respond due to respect, since if greeting is permitted, responding is obviously also permitted.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah means one may greet due to respect and respond to any person.
The Gemara cites the latter clause of the Mishnah about the middle of a paragraph and asks what reason applies to responding there.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies that one may respond due to fear, since if greeting is permitted, responding is obviously also permitted.
The Gemara suggests that in the middle one responds due to respect, which would match Rabbi Yehuda's position, and asks if this is identical to his explicit ruling.

The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah is missing a clause: Rabbi Meir says that in the middle one may greet due to fear and certainly respond, while Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between greeting due to fear and responding due to respect.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Baraita on Interruptions during Shema
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Baraita on Interruptions during Shema
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that during the breaks between paragraphs of Shema one may greet out of respect and return greetings to anyone. A Baraita elaborates: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda dispute whether in the middle of a paragraph one may greet out of fear and return greetings out of respect, or only greet out of fear and return greetings out of respect during breaks.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that during the breaks between paragraphs of Shema one may greet out of respect and return greetings to anyone.

A Baraita elaborates: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda dispute whether in the middle of a paragraph one may greet out of fear and return greetings out of respect, or only greet out of fear and return greetings out of respect during breaks.

items.text: Interruptions during Hallel and Megillah
items.text_en: Interruptions during Hallel and Megillah
items.desc_en: A question is raised whether one may interrupt Hallel and Megillah reading. A kal vachomer suggests that since one interrupts for Shema (Torah law), one should certainly interrupt for rabbinic Hallel, but perhaps publicizing the miracle takes precedence. Rabbi Chiyya rules that one may interrupt. Rabba distinguishes between days when the individual completes Hallel and days when not. A challenge from Rav bar Sheva's practice is deflected because he was not important to Ravina.

sub.text: Achai Tanna of Bei Rabbi Chiyya
sub.text_en: Achai Tanna of Bei Rabbi Chiyya
sub.desc_en: Achai asks Rabbi Chiyya whether one may interrupt Hallel and Megillah reading, considering a kal vachomer from Shema versus the priority of publicizing the miracle.
Rabbi Chiyya rules that one may interrupt and it is of no concern.
Rabba distinguishes between days when the individual completes Hallel (interrupt only between paragraphs) and days when not (interrupt even in the middle).
The Gemara objects from Rav bar Shaba's visit to Ravina on a non-completion day, where Ravina did not interrupt.
The Gemara resolves that Rav bar Shaba was not considered important to Ravina, so he did not interrupt.

items.text: Tasting Food While Fasting
items.text_en: Tasting Food While Fasting
items.desc_en: A question is asked whether one who is fasting may taste food. The dilemma is whether the fast is only about eating and drinking (so tasting is permitted) or about any enjoyment (so tasting is forbidden). Rabbi Ammi rules that one may taste without concern. A baraita supports this. The measure for tasting is discussed: up to a revi'it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: One who is in a fast — what is the rule about tasting?

items.text: Greeting Others Before Prayer
items.text_en: Greeting Others Before Prayer
items.desc_en: Rav states that greeting a friend before prayer is like making a high place (bamah) for idolatry, based on a verse. Shmuel interprets the verse differently. Rav Sheshet challenges from the Mishnah that one may return greetings during breaks. Rabbi Abba resolves that this refers to greeting at one's door (before entering the synagogue).

sub.desc_en: Rav states that greeting a friend before prayer is like making a high place (בָּמָה) for idolatry, based on a verse.
Shmuel interprets the same verse differently, as a rhetorical question about prioritizing human over God.
Rav Sheshet challenges from the Mishnah that one may return greetings during breaks in the Shema, implying greeting before prayer is permitted.
Rabbi Abba resolves that Rav's statement refers to greeting at one's door before entering the synagogue, not during the prayer service itself.

items.text: Attending to Personal Needs Before Prayer
items.text_en: Attending to Personal Needs Before Prayer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yona in the name of Rabbi Zeira says that one who attends to his needs before prayer is like building a high place. When challenged, he clarifies that it is merely forbidden. Rav Idi bar Avin cites a verse to support that one must not do personal business before prayer, and that one who prays first will have God attend to his needs.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yona in the name of Rabbi Zeira states that one who attends to his personal needs before prayer is like one who built a high place (במה) for idol worship.
The listeners challenge Rabbi Yona, asking if he really said that it is like building a high place (במה).
Rabbi Yona clarifies that he did not say 'high place' but rather that it is merely 'forbidden' (אסור).

sub.text: Rav Idi bar Avin citing Rav Yitzchak bar Ashyan
sub.text_en: Rav Idi bar Avin citing Rav Yitzchak bar Ashyan
sub.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin in the name of Rav Yitzchak bar Ashyan cites the verse 'צֶדֶק לְפָנָיו יְהַלֵּךְ' (Psalms 85:14) to support that a person is forbidden to attend to his own affairs before prayer.

sub.text: Rav Idi bar Avin citing Rav Yitzchak bar Ashyan
sub.text_en: Rav Idi bar Avin citing Rav Yitzchak bar Ashyan
sub.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin further states in the name of Rav Yitzchak bar Ashyan that one who prays first and then goes out on his way will have the Holy One, Blessed be He, attend to his affairs, citing the same verse.

items.text: Sleeping Without a Dream and Being Sated with Torah
items.text_en: Sleeping Without a Dream and Being Sated with Torah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yona in the name of Rabbi Zeira says that one who sleeps seven days without a dream is called 'evil', based on a verse. Rabbi Acha bar Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan says that one who satiates himself with words of Torah and sleeps will not be informed of bad tidings.

sub.desc_en: רבי יונה (Rabbi Yona) in the name of רבי זירא (Rabbi Zeira) states that one who sleeps seven nights without a dream is called 'evil', based on a homiletic reading of the verse 'ושבע ילין בל יפקד רע' (and satisfied he shall lie down, no evil shall befall him).

sub.text: Rabbi Acha bar Chiyya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Acha bar Chiyya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: רב אחא בריה דרבי חייא בר אבא (Rabbi Acha bar Chiyya bar Abba) reports in the name of רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) that one who satiates himself with words of Torah and sleeps will not be informed of bad tidings, citing the same verse.

items.text: Halacha like Rabbi Yehuda Regarding Interruptions
items.text_en: Halacha like Rabbi Yehuda Regarding Interruptions
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the breaks between paragraphs of Shema. Rabbi Avahu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan rules that the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda, who says that between 'Elocheichem' and 'Emet Veyatziv' one may not interrupt, citing a verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the mishna's list of breaks between paragraphs of Shema.
Rabbi Avahu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda, who forbids interrupting between 'אלוהיכם' (your God) and 'אמת ויציב' (true and established).
Rabbi Avahu again in the name of Rabbi Yochanan asks for the reason behind Rabbi Yehuda's opinion, and begins to cite a verse.

items.text: Opening citation
items.text_en: Opening citation
items.desc_en: The daf opens with a citation from the Shema: 'And the Lord God is truth'.

sub.desc_en: The daf opens with a citation from the Shema: 'And the Lord God is truth'.

items.text: Dispute about repeating 'Emet'
items.text_en: Dispute about repeating 'Emet'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether one must repeat the word 'Emet' after the Shema. Rabbi Avahu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan says yes, Rabbah says no. Rav Yosef praises a tradition from the West that includes 'Ani Hashem Eloheichem Emet'. Abaye objects based on Rav's ruling that one should not begin but if one begins, one finishes. Rav Pappa explains the Western view that 'Ve'amarta aleihem' is not a beginning until 'Ve'asu lahem tzitzit'. Abaye concludes that since the West begins, we also begin and finish.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether one repeats the word 'Emet' after the Shema or not.
Rabbi Avahu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan rules that one does repeat 'Emet'.
Rabbah rules that one does not repeat 'Emet'.
A story is told of a prayer leader who said 'Emet' twice before Rabbah, and Rabbah mocked him.
Rav Yosef praises a tradition from the West that includes 'Ani Hashem Eloheichem Emet' in the evening prayer.
Abaye objects that according to Rav, one should not begin the portion of tzitzit at night, and 'Ve'amarta aleihem' is considered a beginning.
Rav Pappa explains that in the West, 'Ve'amarta aleihem' is not considered a beginning until one says 'Ve'asu lahem tzitzit'.
Abaye concludes that since the West begins the portion, we also begin and then complete it, following Rav's rule.

items.text: Chiya bar Rav's ruling on 'Emet'
items.text_en: Chiya bar Rav's ruling on 'Emet'
items.desc_en: Chiya bar Rav rules that if one said 'Ani Hashem Eloheichem', one must say 'Emet'; otherwise not. The Gemara questions how one can mention the Exodus without saying 'Emet', and suggests a formula that includes the Exodus.

sub.desc_en: Chiya bar Rav rules that if one recited 'Ani Hashem Eloheichem' in the evening, he must say 'Emet'; otherwise, he need not.
The Gemara objects: Isn't one required to mention the Exodus from Egypt at night as well, which is normally done in the blessing of 'Emet ve'Emuna'?
The Gemara answers that one can recite a shorter formula that includes the Exodus, instead of the full 'Emet ve'Emuna' blessing.

items.text: Order of Shema paragraphs
items.text_en: Order of Shema paragraphs
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha asks why 'Shema' precedes 'Vehaya im shamoa'. A baraita cites Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's explanation: 'Shema' includes learning, teaching, and doing, while 'Vehaya' includes teaching and doing, and 'Vayomer' only doing. The Gemara refines this: 'Shema' precedes 'Vehaya' because it includes all three, and 'Vehaya' precedes 'Vayomer' because it includes teaching and doing. The Gemara adds that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's reason is to first accept the yoke of heaven, then the yoke of commandments.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha asks why the paragraph of 'Shema' precedes 'Vehaya im shamoa' in the order of the Shema.

sub.text: Supporting baraita citing Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita citing Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's explanation: 'Shema' should precede 'Vehaya' because it includes learning, while 'Vehaya' includes teaching, and 'Vehaya' precedes 'Vayomer' because it includes learning while 'Vayomer' only includes doing.
The Gemara objects that 'Shema' also includes teaching and doing, as it says 'ושננתם' (teach) and 'וקשרתם' (do), and 'Vehaya' also includes doing, as it says 'וקשרתם' and 'וכתבתם'.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai meant: 'Shema' includes learning, teaching, and doing; 'Vehaya' includes teaching and doing; 'Vayomer' includes only doing.
The Gemara adds that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's reason is twofold: first, to accept the yoke of heaven before the yoke of commandments, and second, because 'Shema' contains additional matters.

items.text: Rav's practice and the order of mitzvot
items.text_en: Rav's practice and the order of mitzvot
items.desc_en: Rav washes his hands, recites Shema, puts on tefillin, and prays. The Gemara questions this based on a baraita about a grave-digger who is exempt from Shema, tefillin, and prayer, but when the time comes, he ascends, washes, puts on tefillin, recites Shema, and prays. The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between one person and two. It then questions Rav's practice against Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's principle that the yoke of heaven precedes the yoke of commandments. Rav Chiya bar Ashi testifies that Rav would wash, bless, teach, put on tefillin, and then recite Shema. The Gemara concludes that the messenger erred in reporting Rav's practice.

sub.desc_en: Describes Rav's practice: he washes his hands, recites Shema, puts on tefillin, and prays.

The Gemara questions Rav's practice by citing a baraita about a grave-digger who is exempt from Shema, tefillin, and prayer, but when the time comes, he ascends, washes, puts on tefillin, recites Shema, and prays.
The Gemara objects that the baraita itself is contradictory: the beginning says exempt, the end says obligated.
Resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between one person (exempt) and two people (obligated).
The Gemara questions Rav's practice against Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's principle that the yoke of heaven precedes the yoke of commandments.
Objects that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha only said to prioritize one recitation over another, not recitation over action.
Questions whether Rav actually holds like Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, citing Rav Chiya bar Ashi's testimony that Rav would wash, bless, teach, put on tefillin, and then recite Shema.
