Resolves that Rav Chiya bar Ashi's testimony was to refute the claim that one need not bless before teaching mishna.
Concludes that the contradiction with Rav's practice remains, and the messenger erred in reporting Rav's practice.

items.text: The importance of tefillin with Shema
items.text_en: The importance of tefillin with Shema
items.desc_en: Ulla says that reciting Shema without tefillin is like bearing false witness. Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan says it is like offering an olah without a minchah or a shelamim without nesachim. Rabbi Yochanan adds that one who wants to accept the complete yoke of heaven should recite Shema with tefillin.

sub.desc_en: Ulla states that reciting Shema without tefillin is like bearing false witness against oneself.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan compares reciting Shema without tefillin to offering an olah without a minchah or a shelamim without nesachim.
Rabbi Yochanan adds that one who wishes to accept the complete yoke of heaven should recite Shema with tefillin.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Order of mitzvot for accepting the yoke of heaven
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Order of mitzvot for accepting the yoke of heaven
items.desc_en: The Mishnah prescribes the sequence: relieve oneself, wash hands, don tefillin, recite Shema, and pray, calling this the complete acceptance of the yoke of heaven.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah prescribes the sequence of actions for accepting the yoke of heaven: relieve oneself, wash hands, don tefillin, recite Shema, and pray.

items.text: Gemara: Washing hands with non-water substances and the distance to seek water
items.text_en: Gemara: Washing hands with non-water substances and the distance to seek water
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan praises one who follows the Mishnah's order, comparing it to building an altar. Rava objects that the verse implies immersion, not just hand-washing. Ravina reports a teaching from the West that one without water may use earth or a pebble; Rava supports this, citing Rav Chisda's curse on those who seek water during prayer. The Gemara then limits this leniency to Shema, but for prayer one must seek water up to a parasang forward, but not even a mil backward.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan (via Rabbi Chiya bar Abba)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan (via Rabbi Chiya bar Abba)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan praises one who follows the Mishnah's order of washing hands, donning tefillin, reciting Shema, and praying, comparing it to building an altar.
Rava objects that the verse implies immersion, not just hand-washing, since it says 'אֶרְחַץ' (I will bathe) rather than 'אַרְחִיץ' (I will wash).

sub.text: Ravina's report of a Western teaching
sub.text_en: Ravina's report of a Western teaching
sub.desc_en: Ravina reports a teaching from the West that one without water may wipe hands with earth, a pebble, or a chip.

sub.text: Rava's support and citation of Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Rava's support and citation of Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rava supports the teaching, noting that the verse says 'בְּנִקָּיוֹן' (in cleanliness), not specifically water, and cites Rav Chisda's curse on those who seek water during prayer.
The Gemara limits the leniency to Shema, but for prayer one must seek water up to a parasang forward, though not even a mil backward; less than a mil backward, one must return.

items.text: Mishnah: Disputes about Shema recitation
items.text_en: Mishnah: Disputes about Shema recitation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents disputes: whether one who recites Shema without hearing it fulfills the obligation (Rabbi Yosei says no, the first Tanna says yes); whether one who does not enunciate letters properly fulfills it (Rabbi Yosei says yes, Rabbi Yehuda says no); and the rule that reading backwards is invalid, but if one errs they return to the point of error.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the ruling of the first Tanna (תנא קמא) that one who recites Shema without hearing it fulfills the obligation.
Rabbi Yosei (רבי יוסי) objects, ruling that one who does not hear the recitation does not fulfill the obligation.
The Mishnah shifts to a second dispute: Rabbi Yosei (רבי יוסי) rules that one who recites without enunciating letters properly fulfills the obligation.
Rabbi Yehuda (רבי יהודה) objects, ruling that one who does not enunciate properly does not fulfill the obligation.
The Mishnah concludes with a resolution: reading backwards is invalid, but if one errs they return to the point of error.

items.text: Gemara: Reason for Rabbi Yosei's position on hearing Shema
items.text_en: Gemara: Reason for Rabbi Yosei's position on hearing Shema
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Yosei's reasoning: the verse 'Shema' implies 'make your ears hear what your mouth utters.' The first Tanna interprets 'Shema' as 'in any language you understand.' Rabbi Yosei derives two lessons from the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the reason for Rabbi Yosei's position regarding hearing the Shema.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yosei derives from the verse 'שְׁמַע' (Shema) that one must make one's ears hear what one's mouth utters.
The Gemara notes that the first Tanna interprets 'שְׁמַע' (Shema) as meaning 'in any language that you understand.'
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yosei derives two lessons from the verse 'שְׁמַע' (Shema).

items.text: Gemara: Comparing the Shema dispute to terumah and Birkat HaMazon
items.text_en: Gemara: Comparing the Shema dispute to terumah and Birkat HaMazon
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a deaf person who can speak but not hear: he may not separate terumah ab initio, but if he did it is valid. Rav Chisda attributes this to Rabbi Yosei, but the Gemara challenges this, suggesting it could be Rabbi Yehuda. It then brings a baraita about Birkat HaMazon recited silently, and a baraita from Rabbi Yehuda ben Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi that a deaf person may separate terumah ab initio. After analysis, the Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yehuda follows his teacher Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya (who requires hearing), while Rabbi Meir holds that intention of the heart suffices.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a deaf person who can speak but not hear: he may not separate תרומה (priestly portion) לכתחילה (the ideal standard), but if he did it is valid.
The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of this baraita that distinguishes between בדיעבד (after the fact) and לכתחילה (the ideal standard).
Rav Chisda answers that it is Rabbi Yosei, citing a Mishnah where Rabbi Yosei says one who recites Shema without hearing it has not fulfilled the obligation, while Rabbi Yehuda says he has.

The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yosei's strict position applies only to Shema which is Torah law, but regarding תרומה (priestly portion) the issue is the blessing, which is rabbinic, so the comparison is not straightforward.
The Gemara questions why it must be Rabbi Yosei; perhaps it is Rabbi Yehuda, who might also hold that regarding Shema, only בדיעבד (after the fact) it is valid, not לכתחילה (the ideal standard).

The Gemara rejects the alternative, explaining that the Mishnah's phrasing 'one who recites' (בדיעבד) is meant to highlight Rabbi Yosei's stringency that even בדיעבד (after the fact) it is invalid, whereas Rabbi Yehuda would permit it even לכתחילה (the ideal standard).
The Gemara questions the attribution to Rabbi Yosei by citing a baraita that one should not recite Birkat HaMazon silently, but if he did he has fulfilled the obligation.

The Gemara objects that this baraita fits neither Rabbi Yosei nor Rabbi Yehuda, since Rabbi Yehuda would permit it לכתחילה (the ideal standard) and Rabbi Yosei would invalidate it even בדיעבד (after the fact).
The Gemara resolves that the baraita about Birkat HaMazon is actually Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that silent recitation is valid only בדיעבד (after the fact), not לכתחילה (the ideal standard).

The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of the baraita cited by Rabbi Yehuda ben Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi, which permits a deaf person who can speak to separate תרומה (priestly portion) לכתחילה (the ideal standard).
The Gemara objects that this baraita fits neither Rabbi Yehuda (who permits only בדיעבד) nor Rabbi Yosei (who invalidates even בדיעבד).

The Gemara resolves that it is indeed Rabbi Yehuda, who permits even לכתחילה (the ideal standard) according to his own opinion, but the earlier baraita reflects his teacher Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's view that one must hear the words, while Rabbi Meir holds that intention of the heart suffices.

The Gemara concludes that now that this has been established, the contradiction is resolved: one baraita follows Rabbi Meir (who requires only intention) and the other follows Rabbi Yehuda (who requires hearing).

items.text: Gemara: Comparing to Megillah reading
items.text_en: Gemara: Comparing to Megillah reading
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that all are fit to read the Megillah except a deaf person, a fool, and a minor; Rabbi Yehuda validates a minor. Rav Matna attributes the disqualification of a deaf person to Rabbi Yosei, based on the Shema dispute. The Gemara questions whether this proves Rabbi Yosei holds it invalid even after the fact.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishna from Megillah: all are fit to read the Megillah except a deaf person, a fool, and a minor; Rabbi Yehuda validates a minor.
The Gemara asks: who is the tanna who holds that even after the fact a deaf person's reading is invalid?
Rav Mattana answers: it is Rabbi Yosei, citing the Shema dispute where Rabbi Yosei says one who does not hear his recitation did not fulfill his obligation.
The Gemara questions: from where do we know that this mishna is according to Rabbi Yosei and that even after the fact it is invalid?

items.text: Opening: Deaf person's validity in mitzvot
items.text_en: Opening: Deaf person's validity in mitzvot
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by questioning whether a deaf person (cheresh) can perform mitzvot, comparing them to a shoteh (imbecile) and katan (minor) who cannot. It suggests maybe Rabbi Yehuda's view applies, but then notes a contradiction with his ruling on a minor who has reached age of chinuch.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the mishna might follow Rabbi Yehuda, who permits a deaf-mute's reading after the fact but not ab initio.
The Gemara rejects this, arguing that the mishna groups deaf-mute with imbecile and minor, implying even after the fact it is invalid.
The Gemara objects that the cases might be different despite being listed together, so no proof can be drawn.
The Gemara objects further: since the latter clause says Rabbi Yehuda validates a minor, the first clause cannot be his view.
The Gemara answers that the entire mishna is Rabbi Yehuda's, distinguishing between a minor who has not reached the age of training (invalid) and one who has (valid ab initio).

The Gemara questions: if the mishna is Rabbi Yehuda (after the fact valid, ab initio not), how does the baraita of Rabbi Yehuda ben Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi permit a deaf person to separate teruma ab initio?

items.text: Gemara's first question: Who holds the ruling?
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: Who holds the ruling?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who holds the ruling that a deaf person cannot perform mitzvot initially but can post-facto. It considers Rabbi Yehuda vs. Rabbi Yosei, concluding it must be Rabbi Yehuda because Rabbi Yosei would forbid even post-facto.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who holds the ruling that a deaf person cannot perform mitzvot initially but can post-facto, and rejects both Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei.
The Gemara objects that perhaps Rabbi Yehuda permits even initially, and then questions the baraita about Grace after Meals.
The Gemara rejects both Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei as the author of the baraita about Grace after Meals.

items.text: Clarification: Rabbi Yehuda's position on blessing
items.text_en: Clarification: Rabbi Yehuda's position on blessing
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Yehuda allows blessing even initially, citing a baraita where he permits a deaf person to recite the blessing of the meal (birkat hamazon) initially, contradicting the earlier assumption.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the baraita permitting a deaf person to separate תרומה (priestly portion) even לכתחילה (the ideal standard) is indeed in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda, who allows it even initially.

The Gemara explains that there is no contradiction: the baraita that prohibits reciting Grace after Meals inaudibly is Rabbi Yehuda's own opinion, while the baraita permitting a deaf person to separate תרומה (priestly portion) is his teacher's opinion.

A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yehuda said in the name of רבי אלעזר בן עזריה (Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya) that one who recites קריאת שמע (Shema) must make it audible to his ears, based on the verse 'שמע ישראל' (Hear, Israel); Rabbi Meir objects, citing the verse 'על לבבך' (upon your heart), arguing that intention of the heart suffices.

The Gemara concludes that even if Rabbi Yehuda holds like his teacher, there is no difficulty: the baraita prohibiting inaudible Grace after Meals is Rabbi Yehuda's own opinion, while the baraita permitting a deaf person to separate תרומה (priestly portion) is the opinion of רבי מאיר (Rabbi Meir).

items.text: Halakhic ruling: Rabbi Yehuda vs. Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Halakhic ruling: Rabbi Yehuda vs. Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda and Rav Sheila state the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda (who requires audible hearing for Shema) and also follows Rabbi Yehuda's view on writing commands. The Gemara explains why both rulings are needed to avoid misinterpretation.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda citing Rav Sheila rules that the halakha follows both Rabbi Yehuda's statement in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya (requiring audible Shema) and Rabbi Yehuda's own opinion (that after the fact it is valid).

The Gemara explains that both rulings are necessary: if only the first were stated, one might mistakenly think Rabbi Yehuda permits even לכתחילה (the ideal standard); therefore the second ruling clarifies that one must recite Shema audibly.

The Gemara adds that if only the second ruling were stated, one might think that failure to recite audibly has no remedy; therefore the first ruling teaches that בדיעבד (after the fact) the recitation is valid.

items.text: Rav Yosef's distinction: Shema vs. other mitzvot
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's distinction: Shema vs. other mitzvot
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef argues that the dispute about audible hearing applies only to Shema (because of the verse 'Hasket uShema'), but for other mitzvot, all agree one fulfills even without hearing, as per the verse 'Ukhtavtam' (writing commands).

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef states that the dispute about audible recitation applies only to Shema, but for other mitzvot all agree one does not fulfill the obligation without hearing, citing the verse 'הסכת ושמע ישראל' (Pay attention and hear, Israel).

The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about Grace after Meals, which states that if one recited inaudibly he fulfilled his obligation, contradicting Rav Yosef's claim that for other mitzvot one does not fulfill the obligation.
The Gemara emends Rav Yosef's statement: the dispute is only about Shema, but for other mitzvot all agree one fulfills the obligation even without hearing.

items.text: Proof from verses: Shema vs. Torah study
items.text_en: Proof from verses: Shema vs. Torah study
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites verses: 'Hasket uShema Yisrael' (for Shema) vs. 'Kara velo dikdek' (for Torah study) and Rabbi Tabi's ruling that both views are lenient. It also notes the verse 'Shalosh henah lo tisbahna' linking Sheol and womb to argue resurrection.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing the verse 'הַסְכֵּת וּשְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל' (Listen and hear, Israel), which seems to require audible hearing for Shema.
The Gemara answers that that verse refers to Torah study, not to the recitation of Shema.
A baraita is cited: 'He read but did not enunciate its letters precisely' — implying that for Torah study, precision is required, but for Shema it is not.
Rabbi Tabi in the name of Rabbi Yoshiya rules that the halacha follows both views leniently — one may read Shema without audible hearing, and one may read Torah without precise enunciation.

Rabbi Tabi in the name of Rabbi Yoshiya interprets the verse 'שָׁלוֹשׁ הֵנָּה לֹא תִשְׂבַּעְנָה' (Three things are never satisfied) to draw an analogy between the womb and Sheol — both take in and bring out.

The Gemara derives a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument): if the womb, which receives quietly, expels with great noise, then Sheol, which receives with great noise, should certainly expel with great noise — providing a proof for resurrection from the Torah.

items.text: Rabbi Oshaya's teaching: Writing includes commands
items.text_en: Rabbi Oshaya's teaching: Writing includes commands
items.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya teaches that 'Ukhtavtam' (and you shall write them) includes all commands, even tzavaot (instructions). Rabbi Yehuda disagrees, limiting to oaths (alot) only. The Gemara resolves by noting the verse 'Vekhatav et ha'alot ha'eleh' for sotah vs. 'Ukhtavtam' for general mitzvot.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya teaches before Rava that the verse 'וּכְתַבְתָּם' (and you shall write them) includes all commands, even instructions (צַוָּאוֹת).
Rava explains that Rabbi Oshaya's teaching aligns with Rabbi Yehuda, who limits writing to oaths (אָלוֹת) in the sotah case but extends to all commands here due to the broader term 'וּכְתַבְתָּם'.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning: Oaths vs. commands
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning: Oaths vs. commands
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda argues that 'Vekhatav et ha'alot' implies only oaths, not commands. The Gemara counters by learning 'ketivah' from sotah to general mitzvot, concluding that 'Ukhtavtam' includes commands too.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the assumption that Rabbi Yehuda's distinction between oaths and commands is based on the word 'וְכָתַב' (and he shall write), arguing it is actually based on the word 'אָלוֹת' (oaths).

The Gemara resolves that the verse 'וּכְתַבְתָּם' (and you shall write them) is necessary to teach that commands are included, countering a possible verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from the sotah passage that would exclude them.

items.text: Rava's teaching: Spacing in Shema letters
items.text_en: Rava's teaching: Spacing in Shema letters
items.desc_en: Rava teaches that 'Velimadtem' requires spacing between words in Shema, citing examples like 'al levavcha', 'al levavchem', 'bechol levavcha', etc. This ensures proper reading.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ovadyah taught before Rava that the verse 'וְלִמַּדְתֶּם' (and you shall teach them) implies that your study should be 'תָּם' (perfect), meaning one should leave space between words that are attached.

Rava provides examples of such attached words, including 'עַל לְבָבֶךָ', 'עַל לְבַבְכֶם', 'בְּכָל לְבָבְךָ', 'בְּכָל לְבַבְכֶם', 'עֵשֶׂב בְּשָׂדְךָ', 'וַאֲבַדְתֶּם מְהֵרָה', 'הַכָּנָף פְּתִיל', and 'אֶתְכֶם מֵאֶרֶץ'.

items.text: Rabbi Chama's teaching: Careful reading cools Gehinnom
items.text_en: Rabbi Chama's teaching: Careful reading cools Gehinnom
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina says that one who reads Shema carefully and diqduq (precise) in its letters is cooled from Gehinnom, based on the verse 'Befaresh Shaddai melachim bah tashleg beTzalmon' — read as 'Befaresh' (spread) and 'beTzalmavet' (shadow of death).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina states that one who reads the Shema precisely in its letters will have Gehinnom cooled for him, citing a verse with a wordplay.

items.text: Opening exposition on tents and merits
items.text_en: Opening exposition on tents and merits
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets a biblical verse comparing tents to streams, teaching that just as streams purify from impurity, tents (i.e., study halls) elevate a person from the scale of guilt to the scale of merit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse comparing tents to streams, teaching that just as streams purify from impurity, tents (study halls) elevate a person from guilt to merit.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi with Rabbi Elazar
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi with Rabbi Elazar
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi were building a canopy for Rabbi Elazar. He went to hear a teaching from Rabbi Yochanan about a reader who erred in the Shema, and upon returning, they praised the teaching.

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites the Mishnah's rule that one who reads the Shema out of order has not fulfilled the obligation.
Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi were building a canopy for Rabbi Elazar, who excused himself to hear a teaching from the study hall and report back.

A baraita taught before Rabbi Yochanan rules that if one erred in the Shema, he returns to the beginning of the paragraph, between paragraphs, or to the first section of the Shema, depending on where he erred.
Rabbi Yochanan qualifies that the baraita applies only if he had not yet begun the paragraph 'למען ירבו ימיכם' (so that your days may be multiplied), but if he had, he can continue from there.

sub.text: Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi's praise
sub.text_en: Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi's praise
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar returned and reported the teaching; Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi praised it, saying that hearing this alone was sufficient reward for their efforts.

items.text: Mishnah: Craftsmen and bridegroom
items.text_en: Mishnah: Craftsmen and bridegroom
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that craftsmen may recite the Shema while atop a tree or scaffolding, but may not pray there. A bridegroom is exempt from Shema on the first night until after Shabbat if he has not consummated, with a story about Rabban Gamliel who read despite his exemption.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that craftsmen may recite the Shema while atop a tree or scaffolding, but may not pray there.

The Mishnah states that a bridegroom is exempt from Shema on the first night, and recounts that Rabban Gamliel read despite his exemption, explaining that he would not forgo accepting the yoke of Heaven even for one hour.

items.text: Gemara: Contradiction on kavvanah resolved
items.text_en: Gemara: Contradiction on kavvanah resolved
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a baraita detailing where craftsmen may pray. Rav Mari raises a contradiction: the Mishnah implies no kavvanah is needed, but another source requires intention. Rav Sheshet resolves that the craftsmen must pause their work. A further contradiction with Beit Hillel is resolved by distinguishing between the first and second chapters of Shema.

items.text: Baraitot on workers' prayers and blessings
items.text_en: Baraitot on workers' prayers and blessings
items.desc_en: A baraita states that workers recite Shema and pray the full Amidah but do not lead the service. A contradiction arises with another baraita that mentions a shortened prayer. Rav Sheshet initially distinguishes between Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua, but the Gemara refines this by distinguishing between workers hired for wages and those eating with the homeowner.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that workers recite Shema, pray the full Amidah, and eat bread with blessings, but do not lead the service or perform the priestly blessing.
The Gemara raises a contradiction: another baraita mentions a shortened prayer (מעין שמונה עשרה) instead of the full Amidah.
Rav Sheshet initially resolves the contradiction by attributing the full prayer to Rabban Gamliel's view and the shortened prayer to Rabbi Yehoshua's view.
The Gemara objects: if the shortened prayer follows Rabbi Yehoshua, why mention workers specifically? Even all people would say it.
The Gemara refines the resolution: both baraitot follow Rabban Gamliel, but one refers to workers hired for wages (שכרן) and the other to those eating with the homeowner (סעודתן).
A third baraita is cited, detailing that workers hired for wages recite a shortened Grace after Meals, omitting the first blessing but including a combined second blessing.
The baraita concludes: the shortened Grace applies only to workers hired for wages, but those eating with the homeowner or when the homeowner dines with them recite the full Grace as prescribed.

items.text: Exemption of a bridegroom from Shema
items.text_en: Exemption of a bridegroom from Shema
items.desc_en: A baraita derives from the verse 'when you walk on the road' that a bridegroom is exempt, as his activity is like a permitted journey. The Gemara questions whether this applies even when going to perform a mitzvah, and concludes that the verse specifically exempts one's own journey, not a mitzvah journey.

sub.desc_en: A baraita exempts a bridegroom from Shema based on the verse 'וּבְלֶכְתְּךָ בַּדֶּרֶךְ' (and when you walk on the road), interpreting it as excluding one engaged in a mitzvah and a bridegroom.
The Gemara asks how the baraita derives the exemption from the verse.
Rav Pappa explains that the verse compares the bridegroom's activity to a permitted journey (דֶּרֶךְ רְשׁוּת), thus exempting him.
The Gemara objects: perhaps the verse refers to one going to perform a mitzvah, and even then the Torah obligates reading Shema.
The Gemara resolves that the verse's extra wording 'בְּלֶכְתְּךָ' (your walking) specifically exempts a mitzvah journey, not one's own journey.

items.text: Gemara's resolution of the groom's exemption
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of the groom's exemption
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifies a groom marrying a virgin, suggesting even a widower would be exempt. It distinguishes between distraction due to a mitzvah (groom) and distraction due to personal matters (mourner), and rejects a comparison to a shipwreck by noting that the groom's distraction is a mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah specifies a groom marrying a virgin, suggesting even a widower would be exempt.
The Gemara distinguishes between a groom who is distracted (טְרִיד) due to the mitzvah and a mourner who is not distracted.

The Gemara objects that if distraction were the reason, even a shipwreck victim should be exempt, citing Rabbi Abba bar Zavda's statement that a mourner is obligated in all commandments except tefillin.
The Gemara resolves that a shipwreck involves personal distraction (טִרְדָּא דִרְשׁוּת), while a groom's distraction is due to a mitzvah (טִרְדָּא דְמִצְוָה), justifying the exemption.

items.text: Stories of Rabban Gamliel's leniencies
items.text_en: Stories of Rabban Gamliel's leniencies
items.desc_en: Two stories are told: Rabban Gamliel bathed on the first night after his wife's death, claiming he was delicate, and accepted condolences for his slave Tabi, claiming Tabi was worthy. These illustrate exceptions to general mourning rules.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah recounts that Rabban Gamliel bathed on the first night after his wife's death, and when his students questioned him, he excused himself as being delicate (איסטניס).
The Mishnah further recounts that when Rabban Gamliel's slave Tabi died, he accepted condolences, explaining that Tabi was a worthy slave, unlike ordinary slaves.

items.text: Dispute about a groom reciting Shema on the first night
items.text_en: Dispute about a groom reciting Shema on the first night
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states a groom may recite Shema on the first night if he wishes, but Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says not everyone who wants to take the name may do so. The Gemara explains his reasoning: the prohibition of aninut at night is rabbinic, and for a delicate person the Sages did not decree.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a groom may recite the Shema on the first night if he wishes, but Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel objects that not everyone who wants to take the name may do so.

The Gemara explains Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's reasoning: the prohibition of אנינות (mourning before burial) at night is only rabbinic, and for a delicate person (איסטניס) the Sages did not impose their decree.

items.text: Baraitot on mourning for slaves
items.text_en: Baraitot on mourning for slaves
items.desc_en: A baraita states that for slaves one does not stand in a row or recite mourner's blessings. A story about Rabbi Eliezer's students trying to console him for his slave's death illustrates this, and he teaches them the proper consolation formula. Another baraita adds that one does not eulogize slaves, but Rabbi Yosei allows it for a worthy slave, though the Sages object.

items.text: Baraitot on calling slaves 'father' and 'mother'
items.text_en: Baraitot on calling slaves 'father' and 'mother'
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that slaves are not called 'Abba so-and-so' or 'Imma so-and-so', but Rabban Gamliel's slaves were called thus. The Gemara resolves the contradiction by noting that Rabban Gamliel's slaves were important. A related baraita limits the term 'Patriarchs' to three and 'Matriarchs' to four, with the Gemara explaining the reason.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the term 'Patriarchs' is only applied to three and 'Matriarchs' to four.
The Gemara questions why the Patriarchs are limited to three, initially suggesting it's due to uncertainty of lineage, but then rejects this by noting the same uncertainty applies to the Matriarchs.
The Gemara answers that the Patriarchs and Matriarchs are limited because only these are considered sufficiently important.
A related baraita teaches that slaves are not called 'Abba so-and-so' or 'Imma so-and-so'.
The Gemara notes a contradiction: Rabban Gamliel's slaves were called by these titles.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that Rabban Gamliel's slaves were important, so the rule did not apply to them.

items.text: Personal prayers of the sages after the Amidah
items.text_en: Personal prayers of the sages after the Amidah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar interprets a verse as referring to Shema and prayer, and promises reward. Then several sages (Rabbi Elazar, Rabbi Yochanan, Rabbi Zeira, Rabbi Chiyya, Rav, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, and Rav Safra) recite their personal supplications after the formal prayer, each with a unique focus.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar interprets the verse 'כֵּן אֲבָרֶכְךָ בְחַיָּי' (So I will bless You in my life) as referring to the Shema (קריאת שמע) and prayer (תפילה), and promises reward of both worlds.
Rabbi Elazar recites a personal supplication after the Amidah (תפילת העמידה), asking for love, peace, good students, a portion in the Garden of Eden, and a good heart.
Rabbi Yochanan recites a supplication asking God to look upon their shame, clothe Himself in mercy, and bring His attribute of goodness and humility before Him.
Rabbi Zeira prays that they not sin, nor be shamed or disgraced before their ancestors.
Rabbi Chiyya asks that Torah be their craft (אוּמָּנוּת), and that their heart not ache nor their eyes darken.
Rav asks for a long life of peace, goodness, blessing, sustenance, bone strength, fear of sin, no shame, wealth, honor, love of Torah, and fulfillment of heart's desires.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi prays for deliverance from insolent people, evil, bad inclination, bad company, harsh judgment, and the destroying angel, even though Roman oppressors (קצוצי) were over him.
Rav Safra prays for peace, concluding the series of personal supplications.

items.text: Opening prayer of the Sages
items.text_en: Opening prayer of the Sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a prayer recited by the Sages after the Amidah, asking that all who study Torah, whether for its own sake or not, may eventually study for its own sake.

sub.desc_en: The Sages recite a prayer after the Amidah, asking that all who study Torah, whether for its own sake or not, may eventually study for its own sake.

items.text: Rabbi Alexandri's and Rav Hamnuna's prayers
items.text_en: Rabbi Alexandri's and Rav Hamnuna's prayers
items.desc_en: Rabbi Alexandri recites a prayer for light and a clear heart, and another acknowledging the yetzer hara and subjugation to kingdoms as obstacles to fulfilling God's will. Some attribute the first prayer to Rav Hamnuna.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Alexandri recites a prayer asking God to place him in a lighted corner, not a darkened one, and that his heart not be faint nor his eyes dim.
Some say that the first prayer was actually recited by Rav Hamnuna, not Rabbi Alexandri.
Rabbi Alexandri recites a second prayer acknowledging that the yetzer hara and subjugation to kingdoms prevent fulfilling God's will, and asking for deliverance.

items.text: Rava's prayer and Rav Hamnuna Zuti's confession
items.text_en: Rava's prayer and Rav Hamnuna Zuti's confession
items.desc_en: Rava prays with humility, acknowledging his unworthiness and asking for forgiveness without suffering. This is identified as the confession of Rav Hamnuna Zuti on Yom Kippur.

sub.desc_en: Rava recites a prayer of humility, acknowledging his worthlessness and asking for forgiveness without suffering.
The Gemara identifies Rava's prayer as the confession of Rav Hamnuna Zuti on Yom Kippur.

items.text: Mar bar Ravina's prayer
items.text_en: Mar bar Ravina's prayer
items.desc_en: Mar bar Ravina concludes his prayer with a plea for protection from evil speech, the evil inclination, a bad wife, and all troubles, and for the nullification of his enemies' plans.

sub.desc_en: Mar bar Ravina concludes his prayer with a plea for protection from evil speech, the evil inclination, a bad wife, and all troubles, and for the nullification of his enemies' plans.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's prayer on a fast day
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's prayer on a fast day
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet, after fasting, prays that his diminished fat and blood be considered as if offered on the altar, since he cannot bring a sacrifice in the absence of the Temple.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet recites a prayer after fasting, asking that his diminished fat and blood be considered as a sacrifice on the altar, since he cannot bring a sacrifice in the absence of the Temple.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's reflection upon finishing Job
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's reflection upon finishing Job
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan reflects on the inevitability of death and praises one who grows in Torah, pleases his Creator, and departs with a good name, citing Solomon's verse.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan reflects on the inevitability of death and praises one who grows in Torah, pleases his Creator, and departs with a good name, citing Solomon's verse.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's maxim
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's maxim
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir's maxim urges wholehearted devotion to God's ways, guarding one's mouth from sin, and promises God's presence.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir's maxim urges wholehearted devotion to God's ways, guarding one's mouth from sin, and promises God's presence.

items.text: Maxim of the Sages of Yavneh
items.text_en: Maxim of the Sages of Yavneh
items.desc_en: The Sages of Yavneh teach humility: each person has their own role, and one should not boast over another, as the essential thing is sincerity of heart before Heaven.

sub.desc_en: The Sages of Yavneh open with a statement of mutual humility: each person is a creature with their own work, and no one should boast over another's role.
They anticipate an objection about differing amounts of Torah study and answer that the essential thing is sincerity of heart before Heaven, not the quantity.

items.text: Abaye's maxim and Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's practice
items.text_en: Abaye's maxim and Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's practice
items.desc_en: Abaye advises being cunning in fear of sin and increasing peace with everyone, even a gentile in the market. The Gemara notes that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai was never preceded by anyone in greeting, even a gentile.

sub.desc_en: Abaye teaches that one should always be cunning in fear of sin, respond gently to anger, and increase peace with everyone, even a gentile in the market, to be loved above and pleasant below.
The Gemara notes that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai was never preceded by anyone in greeting, not even a gentile in the market, illustrating Abaye's principle.

items.text: Rava's maxim on the purpose of wisdom
items.text_en: Rava's maxim on the purpose of wisdom
items.desc_en: Rava states that the purpose of wisdom is repentance and good deeds, and that one should not be arrogant toward parents or teachers. He interprets a verse to mean that wisdom is for those who act for its sake.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that the purpose of wisdom is repentance and good deeds, and that one should not be arrogant toward parents, teachers, or those greater in wisdom or age.
Rava cites the verse 'The beginning of wisdom is fear of the Lord, a good understanding have all who fulfill them' to support his point.
Rava interprets the verse to mean that wisdom is for those who act for its own sake, not for those who act not for its own sake.
Rava concludes that one who acts not for its own sake would have been better off not having been created.

items.text: Rav's maxim on the World to Come
items.text_en: Rav's maxim on the World to Come
items.desc_en: Rav describes the World to Come as having no physical pleasures, but the righteous sit with their crowns on their heads and enjoy the Divine Presence, citing a verse.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that the World to Come has no physical pleasures; the righteous sit with crowns on their heads and enjoy the Divine Presence, citing a verse.

items.text: Women's merit and Rav's explanation
items.text_en: Women's merit and Rav's explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that God's promise to women is greater than to men. Rav explains to Rabbi Chiyya that women merit through bringing their children to synagogue, sending their husbands to study, and waiting for them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that God's promise to women is greater than to men, citing a verse.

sub.text: Rav's question and answer to Rabbi Chiyya
sub.text_en: Rav's question and answer to Rabbi Chiyya
sub.desc_en: Rav asks Rabbi Chiyya by what merit women earn this reward, and answers that it is through bringing their children to synagogue, sending their husbands to study, and waiting for them.

items.text: Blessing when departing from Rabbi Ami or Rabbi Chanina
items.text_en: Blessing when departing from Rabbi Ami or Rabbi Chanina
items.desc_en: When scholars departed from Rabbi Ami (or Rabbi Chanina), they would bless him with a long life, a share in the World to Come, wisdom, and Torah study.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the custom: when scholars departed from the study hall of Rabbi Ami (or Rabbi Chanina), they would recite a blessing to him.
The scholars bless the departing teacher with a long life, a share in the World to Come, wisdom, Torah study, and the ability to hear the words of the Ancient of Days.

items.text: Blessing when departing from Rav Chisda and its interpretation
items.text_en: Blessing when departing from Rav Chisda and its interpretation
items.desc_en: When departing from Rav Chisda (or Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani), they would bless with the verse 'Alufeinu mesubalim'. Rav and Shmuel (or Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar) debate its meaning: one says it refers to Torah and mitzvot, the other to Torah and mitzvot along with suffering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that when the Sages departed from the study hall of רב חסדא (Rav Chisda) or from that of רבי שמואל בר נחמני (Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani), they would bless him with the verse 'אלופינו מסובלים' (Our leaders are laden).

sub.text: Rav and Shmuel (or Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar)
sub.text_en: Rav and Shmuel (or Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar)
sub.desc_en: One opinion (attributed to רב (Rav) and שמואל (Shmuel), or alternatively to רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) and רבי אלעזר (Rabbi Elazar)) explains that 'אלופינו' (our leaders) refers to Torah, and 'מסובלים' (laden) refers to mitzvot.
The other opinion holds that 'אלופינו' (our leaders) refers to both Torah and mitzvot, while 'מסובלים' (laden) refers to suffering.

items.text: Interpretation of the verse 'No breach'
items.text_en: Interpretation of the verse 'No breach'
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse 'No breach, no going out, no outcry in our streets' as referring to the avoidance of having in one's group individuals like Ahithophel, Doeg the Edomite, Gehazi, or a student who spoils his dish in public like Jesus the Nazarene.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets each phrase of the verse 'No breach, no going out, no outcry in our streets' as a prayer that one's group not produce wicked figures like Ahithophel, Doeg, Gehazi, or a student who spoils his dish in public like Jesus the Nazarene.

items.text: Dispute on 'strong-hearted' and sustenance
items.text_en: Dispute on 'strong-hearted' and sustenance
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel (or Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar) dispute the meaning of 'strong-hearted' in Isaiah. One says the entire world is sustained through charity, but they are sustained by force; the other says the world is sustained by their merit, but they are not even sustained by their own merit. This is supported by Rav Yehuda citing Rav that a heavenly voice declares the world is sustained for the sake of Chanina ben Dosa, yet he himself subsists on a small measure of carobs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse from Isaiah and introduces the dispute between Rav and Shmuel, or alternatively Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar.
One opinion holds that the entire world is sustained through charity, but the 'strong-hearted' are sustained by force (directly from God).
The other opinion holds that the entire world is sustained by their merit, but they are not even sustained by their own merit.

The Gemara supports the second opinion with Rav Yehuda's report that a heavenly voice declares the world is sustained for the sake of Chanina ben Dosa, yet he himself subsists on a small measure of carobs.

items.text: Alternative interpretation of 'strong-hearted'
items.text_en: Alternative interpretation of 'strong-hearted'
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda interprets 'strong-hearted' as referring to foolish tax collectors, and Rav Yosef supports this by noting that no convert has ever come from them. Rav Ashi adds that the people of his town, Machseya, are 'strong-hearted' because they see the honor of the Torah twice a year yet no convert comes from them.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda interprets 'אַבִּירֵי לֵב' (strong-hearted) as referring to foolish tax collectors.
Rav Yosef supports Rav Yehuda's interpretation by noting that no convert has ever come from these tax collectors.
Rav Ashi adds that the people of his town, Machseya, are 'strong-hearted' because they see the honor of the Torah twice a year yet no convert comes from them.

items.text: Return to Mishnah: Groom's reading
items.text_en: Return to Mishnah: Groom's reading
items.desc_en: The Gemara resumes the discussion of the Mishnah's ruling that a groom may read Shema if he wishes, and questions the positions of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Rabbis regarding the concern for arrogance.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's ruling that a groom may recite the Shema on his wedding night if he wishes.
The Gemara questions whether Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is concerned for arrogance (יוהרא) and the Rabbis are not, citing a contradictory baraita about work on Tisha b'Av.
The Gemara notes that both the Rabbis and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel appear inconsistent across the two contexts.
Rabbi Yochanan resolves the contradiction by stating that the positions are reversed between the two cases.

Rav Shisha argues that there is no reversal: regarding Shema, since everyone reads, the groom does not appear arrogant; regarding work on Tisha b'Av, since others work and he refrains, it appears arrogant.

Rav Shisha explains that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's own positions are consistent: regarding Shema, the concern is intention (כוונה), which the groom cannot achieve; regarding work, onlookers think he is merely idle, not a scholar.

items.text: Contradiction in positions on arrogance
items.text_en: Contradiction in positions on arrogance
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes an apparent contradiction: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is concerned about arrogance in the case of the groom, but in the Mishnah about work on Tisha B'Av he says one should always act like a Torah scholar. Similarly, the Rabbis seem unconcerned about arrogance in the groom's case but are concerned in the Tisha B'Av case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out an apparent contradiction: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is concerned about arrogance (יוהרא) regarding the groom, but in the Mishnah about Tisha B'Av he says one should always act like a Torah scholar; the Rabbis seem unconcerned about arrogance in the groom's case but are concerned in the Tisha B'Av case.
Rabbi Yochanan resolves the contradiction by stating that the positions are reversed (מוחלפת השיטה) — the attributions in the Mishnah are swapped.

Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi offers an alternative resolution without swapping attributions: regarding the groom, since everyone reads the Shema, the groom reading does not appear arrogant; regarding Tisha B'Av, since others work, the scholar refraining appears arrogant.

Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi further resolves the contradiction for Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: regarding the groom, the concern is about intention (כוונה) — we testify he cannot concentrate; regarding Tisha B'Av, an onlooker would say he merely has no work, as many idlers are in the market.

items.text: Resolution of contradictions
items.text_en: Resolution of contradictions
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says the positions are reversed (the attributions are mistaken). Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi says there is no reversal: the Rabbis' positions are consistent because reciting Shema is not seen as arrogant since everyone reads, but refraining from work on Tisha B'Av appears arrogant. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's positions are consistent because in the Tisha B'Av case the matter depends on intention, and we can testify that he cannot concentrate, whereas in the groom's case, refraining from work would appear as if he has no work.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan resolves the contradiction by asserting that the attributions in one of the sources are reversed.

Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi offers an alternative resolution: no reversal is needed, because reciting Shema on the wedding night is not seen as arrogant since everyone recites it, whereas refraining from work on Tisha B'Av appears arrogant.

Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi further resolves the contradiction in Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's positions: in the Tisha B'Av case, the matter depends on intention and we can testify he cannot concentrate, whereas in the groom's case, refraining from work would appear as if he has no work.
The Gemara marks the end of the chapter with the formula 'הדרן עלך (we return to you)'.

items.text: Mishnah: One whose deceased lies before him
items.text_en: Mishnah: One whose deceased lies before him
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one whose deceased relative lies before him is exempt from Shema, prayer, tefillin, and all mitzvot. It details the exemptions for pallbearers and those in the funeral procession, and the rules for those returning from burial. Women, slaves, and minors are exempt from Shema and tefillin but obligated in prayer, mezuzah, and Grace after Meals.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that one whose deceased relative lies before him is exempt from Shema, prayer, tefillin, and all Torah commandments.

The Mishnah details the exemptions for pallbearers and their replacements: those before the bier who are needed are exempt from Shema, those after the bier are obligated, but all are exempt from prayer.
The Mishnah rules that after burial, if there is time to begin and complete Shema before reaching the row of comforters, they should begin; otherwise, they should not.

The Mishnah concludes: those in the interior row of comforters are exempt from Shema, the exterior row is obligated; women, slaves, and minors are exempt from Shema and tefillin but obligated in prayer, mezuzah, and Grace after Meals.

items.text: Gemara's question from a baraita
items.text_en: Gemara's question from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that only if the deceased lies before him is he exempt, but if not, he is obligated. It raises a contradiction from a baraita that details the restrictions for one whose deceased lies before him, including eating in another room, making a partition, and not eating meat or drinking wine, implying he is still obligated in some matters.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that only if the deceased lies before him is he exempt, but if not, he is obligated.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that details restrictions for one whose deceased lies before him, implying he is still obligated in some matters.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Mourner's exemptions and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Mourner's exemptions and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that an avel (mourner) before burial is exempt from all positive commandments, but on Shabbat he is obligated. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says that because he is obligated in some (Shabbat), he is obligated in all.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that an avel (mourner) before burial is exempt from all positive commandments, but on Shabbat he is obligated. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says that because he is obligated in some (Shabbat), he is obligated in all.
Mishnah continuation: On Shabbat he sits, eats meat, drinks wine, blesses, is blessed, and is obligated in all Torah commandments.
Mishnah continuation: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: Since he is obligated in these, he is obligated in all.

items.text: Gemara's question: What is the practical difference between the Tanna Kamma and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: What is the practical difference between the Tanna Kamma and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel?
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that the difference between the Tanna Kamma and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is marital relations (תַּשְׁמִישׁ הַמִּטָּה).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What is the difference between the Tanna Kamma and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel? The answer: the use of the bed (for marital relations) is the difference.

items.text: Gemara's objection: The Mishnah says he is exempt from all mitzvot, even when not in the presence of the dead?
items.text_en: Gemara's objection: The Mishnah says he is exempt from all mitzvot, even when not in the presence of the dead?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah states the avel is exempt from all mitzvot, implying even when the dead is not before him. Rav Pappa answers that the Mishnah refers to one who turns his face away and eats. Rav Ashi answers that since he is obligated to bury the dead, it is considered as if the dead is before him, citing verses about Abraham.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: the mourner before burial is exempt from Shema, prayer, tefillin, and all Torah commandments. Rav Papa explains: this applies when he turns away his face and eats.
Rav Pappa answers that the Mishnah refers to one who turns his face away from the dead and eats.
Rav Ashi answers that since the avel is obligated to bury the dead, it is considered as if the dead is before him, citing verses about Abraham.

items.text: Gemara's inference: Only his own dead, but a watchman is not exempt? And a baraita contradicts this
items.text_en: Gemara's inference: Only his own dead, but a watchman is not exempt? And a baraita contradicts this
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that only one whose dead is before him is exempt, but a watchman of the dead is not. However, a baraita states that a watchman of the dead, even if not his own, is exempt from all mitzvot. The Gemara resolves: a watchman of the dead, even if not his own, is exempt; his own dead, even if he is not watching him, is exempt.

sub.desc_en: Gemara infers: Only his own dead exempts, but a watchman of the dead does not exempt.
Baraita contradicts: A watchman of the dead, even if not his own, is exempt from Shema, prayer, tefillin, and all Torah commandments. His own dead, even if he is not watching him, is exempt.
Gemara resolves: His own dead, even if not watching him, exempts; a watchman, even if not his own dead, exempts.

items.text: Gemara's inference: Only his own dead and watching, but walking in a cemetery is not exempt? And a baraita contradicts this
items.text_en: Gemara's inference: Only his own dead and watching, but walking in a cemetery is not exempt? And a baraita contradicts this
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that only one who is with his dead and watching is exempt, but one walking in a cemetery is not. However, a baraita forbids walking in a cemetery with tefillin. The Gemara resolves: there (in the baraita) it is forbidden only within four cubits of a grave, but outside four cubits one is obligated; here (the Mishnah) even outside four cubits one is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that only one who is with his dead and watching is exempt, but one walking in a cemetery is not exempt.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that forbids walking in a cemetery with tefillin, implying one is obligated in the מצוה (commandment) there.
The Gemara resolves: there (in the baraita) it is forbidden only within four cubits of a grave, but outside four cubits one is obligated; here (the Mishnah) even outside four cubits one is exempt.

items.text: Baraita on watchmen and the dispute between the first Tanna and Ben Azzai
items.text_en: Baraita on watchmen and the dispute between the first Tanna and Ben Azzai
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita: a watchman of the dead is exempt from mitzvot; if there are two, one watches and one reads. Ben Azzai says: if they are on a boat, they place the dead in one corner and both pray in another. Ravina explains the difference: the first Tanna is concerned about mice, Ben Azzai is not.

items.text: Baraita on transporting bones and the Gemara's clarification
items.text_en: Baraita on transporting bones and the Gemara's clarification
items.desc_en: The baraita states that one who transports bones should not place them in a sack and ride on them, unless he fears gentiles or bandits. The same applies to a Torah scroll. The Gemara asks: to which part of the baraita does this apply? It cannot be the first part (it is obvious), so it applies to the latter part (the exception).

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that one transporting bones may not place them in a sack and ride on them, unless fearing gentiles or bandits, and the same applies to a Torah scroll.
The Gemara asks to which part of the baraita the rule about a Torah scroll applies, rejecting the possibility that it applies to the first part as obvious.
The Gemara concludes that the rule applies to the latter part of the baraita, the exception for fear of gentiles or bandits.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's statement on accompanying the dead and its reward
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's statement on accompanying the dead and its reward
items.desc_en: Rachbah quoting Rav Yehuda says that one who sees a dead person and does not accompany him violates 'he who mocks the poor'. Rav Asi says the reward for accompanying is great, as per the verse 'he who lends to the Lord honors the poor'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Which part of the baraita is the point? If the beginning (the bones part), it is obvious — does a Torah scroll degrade more than bones? Rather, it is the end (the Torah scroll part).
The Gemara asks what reward one receives for accompanying the dead.
Rav Asi answers that the reward is great, as the verse says 'he who lends to the Lord honors the poor'.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Yonatan in a cemetery: Do the dead know?
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Yonatan in a cemetery: Do the dead know?
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Yonatan were walking in a cemetery. Rabbi Yonatan's techelet was dragging; Rabbi Chiyya told him to lift it so the dead would not say they are being mocked. Rabbi Yonatan asked: do the dead know? He cites 'the dead know nothing'. Rabbi Chiyya responds that if he read, he did not review; the verse refers to the wicked, but the righteous are called 'living' even in death, citing a verse about Benaiah.

sub.desc_en: The story opens with Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Yonatan walking in a cemetery; Rabbi Chiyya tells Rabbi Yonatan to lift his techelet so the dead will not say they are being mocked.
Rabbi Yonatan questions whether the dead know anything, citing the verse 'the dead know nothing'.

Rabbi Chiyya responds that if Rabbi Yonatan read the verse, he did not review it properly; the verse refers to the wicked, but the righteous are called 'living' even in death, citing a verse about Benaiah.

items.text: Exegesis of biblical verses about a righteous man
items.text_en: Exegesis of biblical verses about a righteous man
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets verses from Chronicles describing a man named 'Ben Ish Chai' and 'Rav Pe'alim Mikabtz'el', explaining that even in death he is called 'alive' and that he gathered workers for Torah. It also explains his feats of killing two 'Ariel of Moab' and a lion in a pit on a snowy day, with two interpretations of the latter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the phrase 'Ben Ish Chai' (son of a living man), asking whether all people are not sons of the dead.
The Gemara explains that the phrase means that even in death a righteous person is called 'alive'.
The Gemara interprets 'Rav Pe'alim Mikabtz'el' as referring to one who gathered workers for Torah.
The Gemara interprets the killing of two 'Ariel of Moab' as meaning there was no one like him in the First or Second Temple.
One opinion interprets the lion in a pit on a snowy day as breaking ice blocks and descending to immerse.
Another opinion interprets it as studying the Sifra of Rav's house on a snowy day.

items.text: Verse about the dead not knowing anything
items.text_en: Verse about the dead not knowing anything
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'The dead know nothing' and explains it refers to the wicked, who are called 'dead' even in life, as per Ezekiel. An alternative proof from Deuteronomy shows that the term 'the dead' refers to one who was dead from the start.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'The dead know nothing' and explains it refers to the wicked, who are called 'dead' even in life, as per Ezekiel.
An alternative proof from Deuteronomy shows that the term 'the dead' refers to one who was dead from the start.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Chiyya's sons and the dead's awareness
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Chiyya's sons and the dead's awareness
items.desc_en: The sons of Rabbi Chiyya went to a village and forgot their learning. They wondered if their father knew their distress, citing a verse that the dead do not know. Another son countered with a verse that the dead feel pain, citing Rabbi Yitzchak that a worm is as painful to the dead as a needle in living flesh. They concluded that the dead know their own pain but not that of others.

sub.desc_en: The sons of Rabbi Chiyya went to a village and forgot their learning, causing them distress.
One son asks whether their father knows of their suffering.
The other son answers that the dead do not know, citing the verse 'יִכְבְּדוּ בָנָיו וְלֹא יֵדָע'.
The first son objects, citing a verse that the dead feel pain.
Rabbi Yitzchak adds that a worm is as painful to the dead as a needle in living flesh.
The sons conclude that the dead know their own pain but not that of others.

items.text: Story of the pious man and the spirits
items.text_en: Story of the pious man and the spirits
items.desc_en: A pious man, after a quarrel with his wife, slept in a cemetery and overheard two spirits discussing future punishments. He acted on their information and prospered. Later, his wife revealed the secret, leading to a quarrel. The next year, one spirit said their conversation was already known among the living, proving the dead know.

sub.desc_en: The baraita tells the first part of the story: a pious man, after a quarrel with his wife, sleeps in a cemetery and overhears two spirits discussing that barley sown in the first quarter will be struck by hail; he acts on this and his crop is spared.
The baraita continues: the next year, the pious man again overhears the spirits, learning that barley sown in the second quarter will be blighted; he acts accordingly and his crop is again spared.
The baraita continues: the wife presses the pious man for the secret, he tells her, and she later reveals it during a quarrel, exposing the spirit buried in a reed mat.
The baraita concludes: the next year, one spirit tells the other that their conversation is already known among the living, proving that the dead know what happens among the living.

items.text: Rejection: Perhaps another dead person told them
items.text_en: Rejection: Perhaps another dead person told them
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof from the story, suggesting that perhaps another dead person who had heard the conversation told the living.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof from the story, suggesting that perhaps another dead person who had heard the conversation told the living.

items.text: Story of Ze'iri and the innkeeper
items.text_en: Story of Ze'iri and the innkeeper
items.desc_en: Ze'iri deposited money with an innkeeper who died. He went to the cemetery and asked her where the money was. She told him to take it from under the door hinge and to tell her mother to send her comb and eye-paint with a certain woman coming tomorrow. This shows the dead know.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the story of Ze'iri, who deposited money with an innkeeper who died; he went to the cemetery, asked her where the money was, and she replied, directing him to take it from under the door hinge and to tell her mother to send her comb and eye-paint with a certain woman coming tomorrow, proving that the dead know.

items.text: Rejection: Perhaps Dumah announced it
items.text_en: Rejection: Perhaps Dumah announced it
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects this proof, suggesting that perhaps the angel Dumah, who is in charge of the dead, announced the matter to them beforehand.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof from Ze'iri's story, suggesting that perhaps the angel Dumah (דומה), who is in charge of the dead, announced the matter to them beforehand.

items.text: Story of Shmuel's father and the orphans' money
items.text_en: Story of Shmuel's father and the orphans' money
items.desc_en: Shmuel's father had deposited orphans' money, and after his death, Shmuel was called 'eater of orphans' money'. He went to the cemetery and asked for his father. He saw Levi sitting outside the heavenly academy and learned why. Then his father appeared, crying and laughing, explaining why. He told Shmuel where the money was hidden. This proves the dead know.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces the story: Shmuel's father held orphans' money, and after his death, Shmuel was called 'eater of orphans' money', so he went to the cemetery to find his father.
Shmuel asks the dead for his father, specifying 'Abba bar Abba, father of Shmuel'.
The dead tell Shmuel that his father has ascended to the heavenly academy, and Shmuel sees Levi sitting outside, who explains why he is excluded.
Shmuel's father appears, crying and laughing, explaining that he cries because Shmuel will soon die and laughs because Shmuel is highly esteemed, and then Levi is admitted to the academy.

sub.text: Shmuel's father's instruction about the money
sub.text_en: Shmuel's father's instruction about the money
sub.desc_en: Shmuel asks about the orphans' money, and his father tells him where it is hidden and explains why he placed it among his own money.
The gemara concludes that this story proves the dead know what happens among the living.

items.text: Rejection: Shmuel was honored, and Rabbi Yonatan's retraction
items.text_en: Rejection: Shmuel was honored, and Rabbi Yonatan's retraction
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof from Shmuel's story, suggesting that because Shmuel was important, they announced his coming. It then notes that Rabbi Yonatan retracted his earlier view, citing a verse that the dead speak with each other, as God told Moses to tell the patriarchs that He had fulfilled His oath.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof from Shmuel's story, suggesting that because Shmuel was important, they announced his coming.

sub.text: Rabbi Yonatan via Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yonatan via Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yonatan retracted his earlier view, citing a verse that the dead speak with each other, as God told Moses to tell the patriarchs that He had fulfilled His oath.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rabbi Yitzchak's statement about speaking after the dead
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rabbi Yitzchak's statement about speaking after the dead
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the dead know of the honor done to them, concluding that they do not. Rabbi Yitzchak states that speaking after the dead is like speaking after a stone, with a dispute about whether the dead know or know but do not care.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the dead know of the honor done to them, presenting two opinions: that they do not know, or that they know but do not care.

items.text: Objection from Rav Papa's story and distinction for Torah scholars
items.text_en: Objection from Rav Papa's story and distinction for Torah scholars
items.desc_en: Rav Papa's story about a man who spoke after Mar Shmuel and was struck by a reed seems to contradict the idea that the dead do not care. The Gemara distinguishes: a Torah scholar is different, as God demands respect for him.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa objects with a story: someone spoke after Mar Shmuel and a cane fell from the ceiling, striking his brain.
The Gemara resolves: a Torah scholar (צורבא מרבנן) is different, because God demands respect for him.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: speaking after a Torah scholar's bier leads to Gehinnom
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: speaking after a Torah scholar's bier leads to Gehinnom
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that anyone who speaks after the bier of Torah scholars falls into Gehinnom, citing a verse that even when Israel has peace, evildoers are led away.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: a great rabbi (צורבא מרבנן) is different — God seeks his honor.

items.text: Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael: do not suspect a Torah scholar who sinned at night
items.text_en: Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael: do not suspect a Torah scholar who sinned at night
items.desc_en: The Tanna teaches that if you see a Torah scholar sin at night, do not suspect him by day, for he surely repented. This applies to bodily sins, but for monetary sins, he must return the money.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states: anyone who speaks after the death of Torah scholars falls into Gehinnom, as per the verse 'And the perverters of paths will He lead into peace on Israel' — even when peace is on Israel, the perverters go to Gehinnom.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: 24 places the court excommunicates for disrespect to a rabbi
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: 24 places the court excommunicates for disrespect to a rabbi
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states that in 24 places the court excommunicates for disrespect to a rabbi, all taught in the Mishnah. Rabbi Elazar asks where, and he says 'when you find'. He finds three: one who is disrespectful to hand-washing, one who speaks after a Torah scholar's bier, and one who is arrogant toward Heaven.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states that in 24 places the court excommunicates for disrespect to a rabbi, all taught in the Mishnah.
Rabbi Elazar asks where these places are, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi replies 'when you find'.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi (via the gemara's narrative)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi (via the gemara's narrative)
sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi examined and found three cases: one who is disrespectful to hand-washing, one who speaks after a Torah scholar's bier, and one who is arrogant toward Heaven.

items.text: Explanation of the three cases of excommunication
items.text_en: Explanation of the three cases of excommunication
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains each case: speaking after a Torah scholar's bier (from the story of the Sadducee who was excommunicated and his coffin stoned), disrespect to hand-washing (from the story of Elazar ben Chanokh), and arrogance toward Heaven (from the story of Choni HaMe'agel).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the case of 'one who speaks after the bier of Torah scholars'?
The Gemara cites a baraita about a Sadducee who was excommunicated for disputing the Sages on the law of the suspected adulteress, and whose coffin was stoned after his death.
The Gemara asks: what is the case of 'one who treats hand-washing disrespectfully'?
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda clarifies that it was Elazar ben Chanokh, not Akavya ben Mahalalel, who was excommunicated for disrespecting hand-washing, and his coffin was stoned.
The Gemara asks: what is the case of 'one who is arrogant toward Heaven'?

The Gemara cites a baraita about Choni HaMe'agel, whom Shimon ben Shetach threatened with excommunication for his presumptuous prayer, but refrained because Choni was like a son who cajoles his father.

items.text: Additional cases and the dispute about the 24 places
items.text_en: Additional cases and the dispute about the 24 places
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks if there are no more cases, citing the story of Todos of Rome. It notes that the case of the oven of Akhnai is in the Mishnah but not explicitly about excommunication. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi analogizes cases, while Rabbi Elazar does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether there are more cases of excommunication, citing the baraita about Todos of Rome who was threatened with excommunication by Shimon ben Shetach.
The Gemara objects that the case of Todos is a baraita, not a Mishnah, while Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi claimed all 24 cases are in the Mishnah.
The Gemara asks whether there is no Mishnah case, citing the oven of Akhnai, and explains the name 'Akhnai' via Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel.
A baraita describes that on that day they burned all pure items Rabbi Eliezer had declared pure, and ultimately blessed him.
The Gemara concludes that excommunication is not explicitly taught in the Mishnah for the oven of Akhnai, and explains that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi analogizes cases while Rabbi Elazar does not.

items.text: Laws of burial and Torah study: interruptions and eulogies
items.text_en: Laws of burial and Torah study: interruptions and eulogies
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses when one may interrupt Torah study for burial, the order of eulogies, and the rule that if one can begin and complete even one chapter or verse before reaching the row, they may start; otherwise not.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that one does not take out a dead person close to the time of Shema recitation, but if they already began, they do not interrupt.
The Gemara objects: But Rav Yosef was taken out close to Shema recitation, contradicting the baraita.
The Gemara resolves: An important person is different, so the baraita's rule does not apply to Rav Yosef.
A baraita details the conduct of those involved in eulogy: when the dead lies before them they slip away one by one to read Shema, and the mourner recites a prayer accepting divine judgment.
Abaye objects to the mourner's prayer, citing Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish that one should never open his mouth to the Satan (i.e., invite harm by mentioning sins).
Rav Yosef supports this with a verse: because Israel said 'we almost became like Sodom', the prophet rebuked them as 'rulers of Sodom', showing that mentioning sin invites harsh response.
The Gemara quotes the Mishnah that after burial, if they can begin and complete the entire Shema they may start, but not just a chapter or verse, and raises a contradiction.
The Gemara objects with a baraita that says they may begin even just a chapter or verse, contradicting the Mishnah.
The Gemara resolves: The Mishnah means the same as the baraita — if they can begin and complete even one chapter or verse before reaching the row, they may start; otherwise not.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Tosefta on mourners' rows
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Tosefta on mourners' rows
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses those standing in the mourners' row. The Tosefta adds that a row facing the inner row is exempt, and Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between those coming because of the mourner (exempt) and those coming for themselves (obligated).

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states the rule: a row that sees the inner area is exempt from reciting Shema, while one that does not see it is obligated.
Rabbi Yehuda adds a distinction: those coming because of the mourner are exempt, while those coming for their own sake are obligated.

items.text: Rav's principle: removing kilayim even in public
items.text_en: Rav's principle: removing kilayim even in public
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav states that one who finds forbidden mixtures (כלאים) in his garment must remove them even in the street, because the verse 'אין חכמה... לנגד ה'' teaches that where there is a desecration of God's name, we show no respect to a teacher.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav states that one who finds forbidden mixtures (כלאים) in his garment must remove them even in the street, because the verse 'אין חכמה... לנגד ה'' teaches that where there is a desecration of God's name, we show no respect to a teacher.

items.text: First challenge: returning from burial with impure path
items.text_en: First challenge: returning from burial with impure path
items.desc_en: A baraita describes mourners returning from burial who choose the impure path for the sake of the mourner's honor. The Gemara challenges: why not apply 'אין חכמה...'? Rabbi Abba resolves that it refers to a rabbinic בית הפרס, which is lenient, citing Rav Yehuda and Shmuel that one may sift a בית הפרס and proceed, and Rav Yehuda bar Ashe that a trodden בית הפרס is pure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: mourners returning from burial take the impure path for the mourner's honor, challenging why the principle 'אין חכמה...' does not apply.
Rabbi Abba resolves that the baraita refers to a rabbinic בית הפרס (field of uncertain grave), not a Torah-level impurity.

sub.text: Supporting evidence from Rav Yehuda and Shmuel
sub.text_en: Supporting evidence from Rav Yehuda and Shmuel
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel that one may sift a בית הפרס and proceed, and Rav Yehuda bar Ashe citing Rav that a trodden בית הפרס is pure, confirming its rabbinic leniency.

items.text: Second challenge: leaping over coffins for kings
items.text_en: Second challenge: leaping over coffins for kings
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok reports that they would leap over coffins to greet kings, even non-Jewish kings. The Gemara challenges: why not apply 'אין חכמה...'? Rava explains that by Torah law, a tent with a handbreadth of space interposes against impurity, and most coffins have such space; the Sages decreed impurity for all coffins but did not apply the decree for the honor of kings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok's report that priests would leap over coffins to greet kings, and challenges why the principle of 'אין חכמה...' (no wisdom against the Lord) does not forbid this.
Rava explains that by Torah law, a tent with a handbreadth of space interposes against impurity, so leaping over coffins is not a Torah violation.
The Gemara concludes that most coffins have a handbreadth of space, so the Sages decreed impurity for all coffins but did not apply the decree for the honor of kings.

items.text: Third challenge: human dignity overrides a Torah prohibition
items.text_en: Third challenge: human dignity overrides a Torah prohibition
items.desc_en: A baraita states that human dignity overrides a negative commandment. The Gemara challenges: why not apply 'אין חכמה...'? Rav bar Sheva explains before Rav Kahana that it refers to the prohibition of 'לא תסור' (do not deviate from rabbinic rulings). Rav Kahana defends this, noting that all rabbinic laws are linked to 'לא תסור', and the Sages permitted the violation for dignity.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that human dignity overrides a negative commandment in the Torah.
The Gemara questions why the principle of 'אין חכמה...' does not apply here to forbid overriding a Torah prohibition for human dignity.
Rav bar Sheva explains before Rav Kahana that the baraita refers to the prohibition of 'לא תסור' (do not deviate from rabbinic rulings).
The students laugh at Rav bar Sheva, objecting that 'לא תסור' is itself a Torah prohibition, so the difficulty remains.
Rav Kahana defends Rav bar Sheva, explaining that all rabbinic laws are linked to 'לא תסור', and the Sages permitted their violation for human dignity.

items.text: Fourth challenge: the verse 'והתעלמת' and priestly honor
items.text_en: Fourth challenge: the verse 'והתעלמת' and priestly honor
items.desc_en: The verse 'והתעלמת' implies that sometimes one may ignore a lost object, e.g., if the finder is a priest in a cemetery or an elder for whom it is undignified. The Gemara challenges: why not apply 'אין חכמה...'? It answers that the case is different because the Torah itself wrote 'והתעלמת'. The Gemara then asks why we cannot learn from this case to others, and answers that we do not derive monetary law from prohibition law.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that the verse 'והתעלמת' (and you shall ignore them) implies that sometimes one may ignore a lost object and sometimes not.

The Gemara explains the baraita: if the finder is a priest in a cemetery or an elder for whom it is undignified, the Torah permits ignoring the lost object. The Gemara then challenges: why not apply the principle of 'אין חכמה...' (no wisdom against the Lord) here as well?

The Gemara answers that the case is different because the Torah itself wrote 'והתעלמת' (and you shall ignore them), creating an explicit exception. The Gemara then asks why we cannot learn from this case to others, and answers that we do not derive monetary law from prohibition law.

items.text: Fifth challenge: a kohen going to slaughter his Paschal lamb
items.text_en: Fifth challenge: a kohen going to slaughter his Paschal lamb
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins another challenge (תא שמע) regarding a kohen who is on his way to slaughter his Paschal lamb or circumcise his son and hears of a death. The verse 'ולאחותו' teaches that he may not become impure for his sister, but for a מת מצוה he may. The section ends mid-argument.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a new challenge with the phrase 'תא שמע' (Come and hear).

The Tanna asks: regarding the verse 'ולאחותו' (and for his sister), what does it come to teach?
