It addresses a case where one is going to slaughter his Paschal lamb or circumcise his son and hears of a death — one might think he should return and become impure, but the answer is that he does not become impure.

The Tanna explains: one might think that just as he does not become impure for his relatives, so too he does not become impure for a מת מצוה (corpse with no one to bury it); therefore the verse says 'ולאחותו' — only for his sister he does not become impure, implying that for a מת מצוה he does become impure.

items.text: Exemption for a High Priest to become impure for a mitzvah corpse
items.text_en: Exemption for a High Priest to become impure for a mitzvah corpse
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a High Priest may become impure for a mitzvah corpse, given the verse that seems to forbid any impurity. It answers that the verse 'and to his sister' teaches that only impurity for a close relative is forbidden, but impurity for a mitzvah corpse is permitted. The Gemara then rejects a possible inference from this case, stating that the principle of 'sit and do not act' applies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a High Priest may become impure for a mitzvah corpse (מֵת מִצְוָה), given the verse that seems to forbid any impurity.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'וְלַאֲחוֹתוֹ' (and to his sister) teaches that only impurity for a close relative is forbidden, but impurity for a mitzvah corpse is permitted.
The Gemara rejects a possible inference from this case, stating that the principle of 'שב ואל תעשה' (sit and do not act) applies, so the leniency is limited.

items.text: Why miracles no longer occur: the piety of earlier generations
items.text_en: Why miracles no longer occur: the piety of earlier generations
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye why earlier generations experienced miracles while the current generation does not, despite their greater Torah study. Abaye answers that earlier generations were willing to sacrifice themselves for the sanctification of God's name, unlike the current generation. He illustrates this with a story about Rav Adda bar Ahava, who tore a garment from a woman he thought was Jewish but was actually a Samaritan, and then paid her a large sum.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye why earlier generations experienced miracles while the current generation does not, despite their greater Torah study.

Abaye answers that earlier generations were willing to sacrifice themselves for קידוש השם (sanctification of God's name), unlike the current generation, and illustrates with the story of Rav Adda bar Ahava.

sub.text: Story about Rav Adda bar Ahava
sub.text_en: Story about Rav Adda bar Ahava
sub.desc_en: Abaye illustrates his point with a story about Rav Adda bar Ahava, who tore a garment from a woman he thought was Jewish but was actually a Samaritan, and then paid her a large sum.

items.text: Rav Giddel sits at the entrance to the immersion pool
items.text_en: Rav Giddel sits at the entrance to the immersion pool
items.desc_en: Rav Giddel would sit at the entrance to the immersion pool to instruct women on the proper method of immersion. When the rabbis expressed concern about his exposure to the evil inclination, he replied that the women appeared to him like white geese, indicating his lack of lustful thoughts.

sub.desc_en: Rav Giddel would sit at the entrance to the immersion pool to instruct women on proper immersion, and when questioned about the evil inclination, he replied that the women appeared to him like white geese.
The rabbis asked Rav Giddel whether he was not afraid of the evil inclination (יֵצֶר הָרָע) by sitting there.
Rav Giddel replied that the women appeared to him like white geese, indicating his complete lack of lustful thoughts.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan sits at the immersion pool and the protection of Joseph's descendants from the evil eye
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan sits at the immersion pool and the protection of Joseph's descendants from the evil eye
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan would sit at the entrance to the immersion pool so that the women would see him and bear children as handsome as he. When questioned about the evil eye, he explained that he is a descendant of Joseph, who is immune to the evil eye, as derived from the verse 'ben porat Yosef' and the interpretation of Rabbi Abahu. Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina adds a proof from the verse 'vayidgu larov' that just as fish are covered by water and immune to the evil eye, so too are Joseph's descendants. An alternative explanation is given: the eye that did not desire to benefit from what was not its own is not subject to the evil eye.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan would sit at the entrance to the immersion pool so that the women would see him and bear children as handsome as he.
The rabbis ask Rabbi Yochanan whether he is not afraid of the evil eye.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that he is a descendant of Joseph, who is immune to the evil eye, as derived from the verse 'בן פורת יוסף' and Rabbi Abahu's interpretation.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina adds a proof from the verse 'וידגו לרב' that just as fish are covered by water and immune to the evil eye, so too are Joseph's descendants.
An alternative explanation is given: the eye that did not desire to benefit from what was not its own is not subject to the evil eye.

items.text: Mishnah: Women, slaves, and minors are exempt from Shema
items.text_en: Mishnah: Women, slaves, and minors are exempt from Shema
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that women, slaves, and minors are exempt from the recitation of the Shema, introducing the next topic of discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that women, slaves, and minors are exempt from the recitation of the Shema (קריאת שמע).

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that women are exempt from Shema and tefillin but obligated in prayer, mezuzah, and Grace after Meals.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's list
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's list
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why each item in the Mishnah needed to be stated, as women are generally exempt from time-bound positive commandments. It explains that for Shema, tefillin, prayer, mezuzah, and Grace after Meals, there were potential reasons to think women might be obligated, so the Mishnah teaches they are not.

items.text: Women's obligation in Kiddush HaYom
items.text_en: Women's obligation in Kiddush HaYom
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava states women are biblically obligated in Kiddush HaYom. Abaye says it's rabbinic. Rava objects and derives the obligation from the juxtaposition of 'zachor' and 'shamor' — those included in 'shamor' (negative commandments) are included in 'zachor' (positive).

items.text: Women's obligation in Grace after Meals: biblical or rabbinic?
items.text_en: Women's obligation in Grace after Meals: biblical or rabbinic?
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rava whether women's obligation in Grace after Meals is biblical or rabbinic. The practical difference is whether a woman can exempt others. A baraita is cited where a woman blesses for her husband, suggesting it is biblical. The Gemara resolves that the case involves a rabbinic measure of food, so a rabbinically obligated person can exempt another rabbinically obligated person.

items.text: Aggadic teaching: God's favor for Israel
items.text_en: Aggadic teaching: God's favor for Israel
items.desc_en: Rav Avira teaches in the name of R. Ammi and R. Assi that the ministering angels questioned God's favoritism toward Israel, citing 'He does not lift up faces'. God responds that He lifts His face because Israel is meticulous in blessing Him even for small amounts like a kezayit or kabeitza.

items.text: Mishnah: Ba'al Keri
items.text_en: Mishnah: Ba'al Keri
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a ba'al keri (one who had a seminal emission) may mentally recite Shema but not recite the blessings before or after it. For Grace after Meals, he recites the after-blessing but not the before-blessing. Rabbi Yehuda says he recites both before and after blessings.

items.text: Gemara: Is hirhur (mental recitation) like speech?
items.text_en: Gemara: Is hirhur (mental recitation) like speech?
items.desc_en: Ravina infers from the Mishnah that mental recitation is considered like speech, otherwise why require it? The Gemara objects that if so, he should recite aloud. Rav Chisda argues mental recitation is not like speech, and R. Elazar explains the purpose is to keep him engaged. Rav Adda bar Ahava adds that one should study a topic the public is engaged in.

items.text: Gemara's challenge from prayer to the Mishnah's rule
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge from prayer to the Mishnah's rule
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah's distinction between Shema and prayer by noting that prayer, which the community is engaged in, also has a rule that one who began does not stop but shortens, implying one who did not begin does not start. The Gemara answers that prayer lacks the element of accepting the yoke of heaven, unlike Shema and Grace after Meals.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah's rule by citing a baraita about prayer: one who began praying and remembered he is a בעל קרי (one who had a seminal emission) shortens but does not stop, implying one who did not begin does not start at all.

The Gemara answers that prayer is different because it lacks the element of accepting the yoke of heaven (מלכות שמים), unlike Shema and Grace after Meals; the latter are Torah law, while prayer is rabbinic.

items.text: Derivations for blessings after food and before Torah
items.text_en: Derivations for blessings after food and before Torah
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda derives the obligation of Grace after Meals from the Torah verse 'And you shall eat and be satisfied and bless'. The Gemara then cites Rabbi Yochanan who derives the blessing after Torah from Grace after Meals via a kal vachomer, and the blessing before food from the blessing before Torah via another kal vachomer.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda derives the obligation of Grace after Meals (ברכת המזון) from the Torah verse 'וְאָכַלְתָּ וְשָׂבָעְתָּ וּבֵרַכְתָּ' (and you shall eat and be satisfied and bless).
Rav Yehuda derives the blessing before Torah study from the verse 'כִּי שֵׁם ה׳ אֶקְרָא הָבוּ גֹדֶל לֵאלֹהֵינוּ' (when I call the name of the Lord, ascribe greatness to our God).

Rabbi Yochanan derives the blessing after Torah from Grace after Meals via a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument): if food, which requires no blessing before it, requires a blessing after it, then Torah, which requires a blessing before it, certainly requires a blessing after it.

Rabbi Yochanan derives the blessing before food from the blessing before Torah via a kal vachomer: if Torah, which requires no blessing after it, requires a blessing before it, then food, which requires a blessing after it, certainly requires a blessing before it.

items.text: Refutation of the kal vachomer
items.text_en: Refutation of the kal vachomer
items.desc_en: The Gemara refutes Rabbi Yochanan's kal vachomer by pointing out that food has the unique aspect of enjoyment, and Torah has the unique aspect of eternal life. Additionally, the Mishnah explicitly states that one blesses after food but not before, which contradicts the kal vachomer's conclusion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a refutation against Rabbi Yochanan's kal vachomer: food has the unique aspect of enjoyment, while Torah has the unique aspect of eternal life, so the comparison is invalid.
The Gemara cites the Mishnah which explicitly states that one blesses after food but not before, contradicting the kal vachomer's conclusion.
The Gemara concludes that the kal vachomer is conclusively refuted (תְּיוּבְתָּא).

items.text: Rav Yehuda's ruling on doubt regarding Shema and Emet VeYatziv
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's ruling on doubt regarding Shema and Emet VeYatziv
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that if one is unsure whether he recited Shema, he does not repeat it because Shema is rabbinic. But if unsure whether he recited Emet VeYatziv, he repeats it because it is Torah. Rav Yosef challenges this from the verse 'when you lie down and when you rise up', and Abaye deflects by saying that verse refers to words of Torah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that doubt about reciting Shema does not require repetition because it is rabbinic, but doubt about Emet VeYatziv requires repetition because it is Torah.
Rav Yosef objects by citing the verse 'when you lie down and when you rise up', which implies that Shema is Torah law.
Abaye deflects the objection by explaining that the verse refers to words of Torah study, not to the recitation of Shema.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah of a zav
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah of a zav
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Yehuda's view from the Mishnah that a zav recites Shema in his heart but does not bless before or after it, and blesses after food but not before. If Emet VeYatziv were Torah, he should bless after Shema. The Gemara answers that the blessing after Shema is for the Exodus, which is already mentioned in Shema, and Shema is preferable because it contains both acceptance of the yoke and the Exodus.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah that a zav (one with a seminal emission) recites Shema in his heart but does not recite blessings before or after it, and blesses after food but not before.
The Gemara challenges: if Emet VeYatziv were Torah law, the zav should be required to bless after Shema, but the Mishnah says he does not.
The Gemara answers: the blessing after Shema is for the Exodus, which is already mentioned in Shema itself.
The Gemara resolves: Shema is preferable because it contains both acceptance of the yoke of Heaven and the Exodus.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan on doubt in prayer
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan on doubt in prayer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar rules that if one is unsure whether he recited Shema, he repeats it, but if unsure whether he prayed, he does not repeat. Rabbi Yochanan says that one should pray all day long.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar rules that one who is unsure whether he recited Shema repeats it, but if unsure whether he prayed the Amidah, he does not repeat.
Rabbi Yochanan says that one should pray all day long, implying that repeating the Amidah in doubt is desirable.

items.text: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel on stopping prayer
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel on stopping prayer
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel rules that if one is standing in prayer and remembers he already prayed, he stops even in the middle of a blessing. The Gemara questions this from Rav Nachman's report that students who mistakenly recited a weekday prayer on Shabbat were told to complete the blessing. The Gemara distinguishes: there the person is obligated, but the Sages did not burden him due to Shabbat honor; here he already prayed.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel's ruling that if one remembers during prayer that he already prayed, he stops, even in the middle of a blessing.
The Gemara objects from Rav Nachman's report, where students who mistakenly recited a weekday prayer on Shabbat were told to complete the blessing, implying a contradiction.
The Gemara resolves the objection by distinguishing: in the Shabbat case, one is still obligated but the Sages did not burden him due to Shabbat honor; here, the person already prayed.

items.text: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel on repeating prayer with the congregation
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel on repeating prayer with the congregation
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel rules that if one prayed and then entered a synagogue and found the congregation praying, if he can add something new, he should pray again; otherwise not. The Gemara notes that this ruling is necessary because the first case involved an individual versus an individual.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel rules that if one prayed and then entered a synagogue and found the congregation praying, if he can add something new, he should pray again; otherwise not.
The Gemara notes that this ruling is necessary because the first case involved an individual versus an individual.

items.text: Gemara's conclusion on the necessity of the two teachings
items.text_en: Gemara's conclusion on the necessity of the two teachings
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why both the earlier Mishnah and the Baraita were necessary: one teaches about an individual who began praying, the other about one who did not. Without both, one might have thought the law differs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves why both the Mishnah and Baraita were necessary: each teaches a different case (individual vs. community), and without both one might mistakenly think the law differs.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi regarding when an individual may pray with the congregation
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi regarding when an individual may pray with the congregation
items.desc_en: Rav Huna and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi disagree about the latest point at which an individual may begin the Amidah to join the congregation. The Gemara explains their dispute hinges on whether an individual may recite Kedushah alone.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states that an individual entering the synagogue who finds the congregation praying may begin the Amidah only if he can finish before the prayer leader reaches Modim.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi gives a different deadline: the individual may begin only if he can finish before the prayer leader reaches Kedushah.
The Gemara explains that the dispute hinges on whether an individual may recite Kedushah alone: Rav Huna holds he may, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi holds he may not.

items.text: Proof that an individual does not recite Kedushah
items.text_en: Proof that an individual does not recite Kedushah
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah cites a verse to prove that Kedushah requires a minyan of ten. The Gemara then derives this through a verbal analogy (gezerah shavah) between the word "within" in two verses.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah cites a verse to prove that an individual does not recite Kedushah, requiring a minyan of ten.
The Gemara explains the derivation through a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) on the word 'תּוֹךְ' (within), linking the verse about sanctification to the verse about the ten spies.

items.text: Inquiry about interrupting for 'Y'hei Shmei Rabbah'
items.text_en: Inquiry about interrupting for 'Y'hei Shmei Rabbah'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether one may interrupt prayer to respond to 'Y'hei Shmei Rabbah'. Rav Dimi reports that Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Shimon taught that one interrupts for nothing except this, but the halakhah does not follow them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that everyone agrees one does not interrupt prayer for the קדושה (sanctification) or מודים (thanksgiving).
The Gemara asks whether one may interrupt prayer to respond to 'Y'hei Shmei Rabbah'.
Rav Dimi reports that Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Shimon taught that one interrupts for nothing except 'Y'hei Shmei Rabbah', even if engaged in the מעשה מרכבה (work of the chariot).
The Gemara rules that the halakhah does not follow their opinion.

items.text: Debate on whether a ba'al keri is permitted to study Torah
items.text_en: Debate on whether a ba'al keri is permitted to study Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yehudah's view that a ba'al keri may recite blessings before and after Torah study, citing a verse that seems to prohibit it. It then discusses whether Rabbi Yehudah expounds 'semuchin' (adjacent verses), concluding that he does not in the rest of the Torah but does in Mishneh Torah, and resolves the contradiction by reinterpreting the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Rabbi Yehudah permits a ba'al keri to recite blessings before and after Torah study.
The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehudah holds that a ba'al keri is permitted to engage in Torah study.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi cites a verse to prove that a ba'al keri is forbidden to study Torah, contradicting Rabbi Yehudah's leniency.
The Gemara suggests that Rabbi Yehudah does not expound 'semuchin' (adjacent verses) in the rest of the Torah, but does so in Mishneh Torah, which might resolve the contradiction.
A baraita demonstrates that Rabbi Yehudah does not expound 'semuchin' in the rest of the Torah, as he rejects Ben Azzai's derivation of stoning for a sorceress from adjacent verses.
A baraita shows that Rabbi Yehudah does expound 'semuchin' in Mishneh Torah, as he derives a prohibition from adjacent verses regarding a father's violated woman.

The Gemara resolves that the adjacent verses cited by Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi are needed for a different teaching—that teaching Torah to one's son is like receiving it at Sinai—so they do not prohibit a ba'al keri.

items.text: Proof from a Mishnah that Rabbi Yehudah requires a ba'al keri to immerse
items.text_en: Proof from a Mishnah that Rabbi Yehudah requires a ba'al keri to immerse
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Yehudah exempts a zav who had a seminal emission from immersion, implying that a regular ba'al keri is obligated. It then refutes the possibility that Rabbi Yehudah exempts even a regular ba'al keri, by analyzing the case of a woman who served and saw blood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Yehudah exempts a zav who had a seminal emission from immersion, implying that a regular ba'al keri is obligated.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehudah only exempts a zav who saw a keri, not a regular ba'al keri.
The Gemara raises the possibility that Rabbi Yehudah exempts even a regular ba'al keri, and the Mishnah only mentions the zav to show the strength of the Sages' position.

The Gemara refutes the objection by analyzing the case of a woman who served and saw blood, concluding that the Mishnah must be Rabbi Yehudah's view and that he specifically obligates her, proving he obligates a regular ba'al keri.

items.text: Opening statement: distinction between a menstruant and a ba'al keri
items.text_en: Opening statement: distinction between a menstruant and a ba'al keri
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that a woman who served her husband and saw menstrual blood does not require immersion, but a ba'al keri is obligated. It clarifies that this obligation is not for blessing but for mental recitation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that a woman who served her husband and saw menstrual blood does not require immersion, but a ba'al keri is obligated, clarifying that the obligation is for mental recitation, not blessing.

items.text: Gemara's question on Rabbi Yehuda's view of hirhur
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Rabbi Yehuda's view of hirhur
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda allows hirhur (mental recitation) for a ba'al keri, citing a baraita where Rabbi Meir permits hirhur but Rabbi Yehuda requires verbal recitation. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that Rabbi Yehuda treats this as hilkhot derekh eretz.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda allows hirhur (mental recitation) for a ba'al keri, citing a baraita where Rabbi Meir permits hirhur but Rabbi Yehuda requires verbal recitation.
The baraita presents the dispute: Rabbi Meir permits hirhur (mental recitation) without moving lips, while Rabbi Yehuda requires verbal recitation in all cases.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that Rabbi Yehuda treats this case as hilkhot derekh eretz (rules of proper conduct), not as a binding halachic obligation.

items.text: Baraita on Torah study with reverence and the dispute about ba'alei kerayin
items.text_en: Baraita on Torah study with reverence and the dispute about ba'alei kerayin
items.desc_en: A baraita derives from a verse that Torah must be studied with awe and trembling. It then rules that zavim, metzoraim, and those who have intercourse with niddot may read Torah, but ba'alei kerayin are forbidden. A dispute follows among Tannaim about how much a ba'al keri may study, with opinions ranging from teaching mishnah to not entering the study hall at all.

sub.desc_en: The baraita derives from a verse that Torah study requires awe and trembling, just as at Sinai.
The baraita rules that zavim, metzoraim, and those who have intercourse with niddot may read Torah, but ba'alei kerayin are forbidden.
Rabbi Yosei permits a ba'al keri to review familiar material but not to teach mishnah.
Rabbi Yonatan ben Yosef permits teaching mishnah but not gemara.
Rabbi Natan ben Avishalom permits teaching gemara as long as one does not utter the divine names in it.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar in the name of Rabbi Akiva
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar in the name of Rabbi Akiva
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar, citing Rabbi Akiva, forbids a ba'al keri from entering the study hall at all.
Rabbi Yehuda permits a ba'al keri to study only practical ethical conduct (הלכות דרך ארץ).

items.text: Story of Rabbi Yehuda's stringency for himself
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Yehuda's stringency for himself
items.desc_en: A story is told: Rabbi Yehuda had a seminal emission and his students asked him to teach a chapter of hilkhot derekh eretz. He immersed and taught them, explaining that although he is lenient for others, he is stringent for himself.

sub.desc_en: The story opens: Rabbi Yehuda had a seminal emission, walked by a river, and when his students asked him to teach a chapter of hilkhot derekh eretz, he immersed and taught them.
The students challenge Rabbi Yehuda: did he not teach them that one who has a seminal emission may still teach hilkhot derekh eretz without immersion?
Rabbi Yehuda explains that although he is lenient for others, he is stringent for himself.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira: Torah words do not receive impurity
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira: Torah words do not receive impurity
items.desc_en: A baraita states Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's opinion that words of Torah do not become impure, based on a verse comparing Torah to fire. A story illustrates this: a student stuttering above him was told to open his mouth and let his words shine.

sub.desc_en: A baraita introduces Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's ruling that words of Torah do not receive impurity.

sub.text: Story about Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
sub.text_en: Story about Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
sub.desc_en: A story is told about a student stuttering above Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, who was told to open his mouth and let his words shine.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira supports his ruling with a verse comparing Torah to fire, arguing that just as fire does not receive impurity, so too words of Torah do not receive impurity.

items.text: Support for Rabbi Il'ai and dispute about teaching mishnah vs. gemara
items.text_en: Support for Rabbi Il'ai and dispute about teaching mishnah vs. gemara
items.desc_en: The Gemara supports Rabbi Il'ai's ruling that one may teach mishnah but not gemara, citing a baraita with a dispute between Rabbi Meir (permits mishnah) and Rabbi Yehuda ben Gamliel (both forbidden or both permitted). The Gemara aligns these views with earlier Tannaim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Mar's statement that one may teach mishnah but not gemara.

sub.text: Supporting citation of Rabbi Il'ai's ruling
sub.text_en: Supporting citation of Rabbi Il'ai's ruling
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this supports Rabbi Il'ai's ruling, transmitted by Rabbi Acha bar Yaakov in the name of Rabbeinu, that the הלכה (binding law) permits teaching mishnah but not gemara.

The Gemara cites a baraita presenting a dispute: Rabbi Meir permits teaching mishnah but not gemara; Rabbi Yehuda ben Gamliel says in the name of Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel that both are forbidden, and some say both are permitted.
The Gemara aligns the positions: the one who says both are forbidden follows Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar, and the one who says both are permitted follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: The world follows three elders
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: The world follows three elders
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak states that the world follows three elders: Rabbi Il'ai regarding reishit ha'gez, Rabbi Yoshiya regarding kilayim, and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira regarding words of Torah. Each opinion is briefly explained.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak declares that the world follows three elders: Rabbi Il'ai regarding reishit ha'gez, Rabbi Yoshiya regarding kilayim, and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira regarding words of Torah.
A baraita cites Rabbi Il'ai stating that reishit ha'gez applies only in the Land of Israel.
Rabbi Yoshiya explains that one is liable for kilayim only when sowing wheat, barley, and a grape pit in a single hand-throw.

sub.text: Supporting baraita for Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita for Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira stating that words of Torah do not become ritually impure.

items.text: Ze'iri's report: Abolition of immersion or netilat yadayim
items.text_en: Ze'iri's report: Abolition of immersion or netilat yadayim
items.desc_en: Ze'iri reports that immersion (for ba'al keri) was abolished, or alternatively, netilat yadayim (hand-washing) was abolished. The Gemara explains each view: the first aligns with Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, the second with Rav Chisda's curse on those who seek water during prayer.

sub.desc_en: Ze'iri reports that immersion (for ba'al keri) was abolished.
An alternative version states that netilat yadayim (hand-washing) was abolished instead.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the first version
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the first version
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the version abolishing immersion aligns with Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's view.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the second version
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the second version
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the version abolishing netilat yadayim aligns with Rav Chisda's curse on those who seek water during prayer.

items.text: Baraita on nine kav for a ba'al keri and the dispute about teaching it
items.text_en: Baraita on nine kav for a ba'al keri and the dispute about teaching it
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a ba'al keri who has nine kav of water poured on him becomes pure. Nachum Ish Gam Zu whispered this to Rabbi Akiva, who whispered to Ben Azzai, who either taught it publicly or whispered it. The Gemara explains the reasons: one view is due to bitul Torah and bitul p'riya u'r'viya, the other to prevent scholars from being with their wives like roosters.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that a ba'al keri who has nine kav of water poured on him becomes pure, and recounts the transmission chain from Nachum Ish Gam Zu to Ben Azzai, who taught it to his students in the market.
The Gemara notes that two Amoraim in the West disagree about whether Ben Azzai taught it publicly or whispered it.
The Gemara explains that the one who says he taught it did so to prevent bitul Torah and bitul p'riya u'r'viya (neglect of Torah study and procreation).
The Gemara explains that the one who says he whispered it did so to prevent scholars from being with their wives as frequently as roosters.

items.text: Rabbi Yannai: I have heard lenient and stringent views
items.text_en: Rabbi Yannai: I have heard lenient and stringent views
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai says he has heard both lenient and stringent views on this matter, and whoever is stringent on himself will have his days and years prolonged.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai states that he has heard both lenient and stringent views on this matter, and whoever is stringent on himself will have his days and years prolonged.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: What is the nature of morning bathers?
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: What is the nature of morning bathers?
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi questions the practice of those who bathe in the morning, clarifying that the issue is not about the obligation but about the method: why use forty se'ah when nine kav suffice, or why immersion when pouring suffices.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's initial question
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's initial question
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi asks: what is the nature of those who bathe in the morning?
The Gemara objects: why ask about their nature? He himself said that a ba'al keri (one who had a seminal emission) is forbidden in matters of Torah.
The Gemara resolves: he meant to ask why they use forty se'ah when nine kav would suffice.
The Gemara adds: he also meant to ask why they immerse when pouring water over themselves would suffice.

items.text: Rabbi Chanina: A great fence was erected with this immersion
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina: A great fence was erected with this immersion
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina explains that the requirement of forty se'ah for immersion was a great fence, as illustrated by a story where a woman deterred a potential sinner by asking if he had forty se'ah to immerse.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina declares that the requirement of forty se'ah for immersion was a great fence (deterrent).
A baraita is cited, recounting a story where a woman deterred a potential sinner by asking if he had forty se'ah to immerse, and he immediately desisted.

items.text: Rav Huna and Rav Chisda debate immersion in hot water
items.text_en: Rav Huna and Rav Chisda debate immersion in hot water
items.desc_en: Rav Huna asks the rabbis why they neglect this immersion, suggesting it could be done in bathhouses. Rav Chisda objects that there is no immersion in hot water, and Rav Huna responds that Rav Adda bar Ahava agrees with him.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna asks the rabbis why they neglect this immersion and suggests it could be done in bathhouses.
Rav Chisda objects that there is no immersion in hot water.
Rav Huna responds that Rav Adda bar Ahava agrees with Rav Chisda's objection.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's practice: nine kav by pouring, not immersion
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's practice: nine kav by pouring, not immersion
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira sat in a basin of water in the bathhouse and asked his attendant to pour nine kav over him. Rabbi Chiya bar Abba questioned why, since he was already in water. Rabbi Zeira explained that just as forty se'ah require immersion and not pouring, nine kav require pouring and not immersion.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira sits in a basin of water in the bathhouse and instructs his attendant to bring nine kav of water and pour it over him.
Rabbi Chiya bar Abba questions why Rabbi Zeira needs this, since he is already sitting in the water.
Rabbi Zeira explains by analogy: just as forty se'ah require immersion and not pouring, so nine kav require pouring and not immersion.

items.text: Rav Nachman's vessel and the distinction between one who is ill and one who is accustomed
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's vessel and the distinction between one who is ill and one who is accustomed
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman instituted a vessel of nine kav. Rav Dimi reported in the name of Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehuda Glostra that this was only for one who is ill due to circumstances, but for one who is accustomed, forty se'ah are required. Rav Yosef comments that Rav Nachman's vessel was broken, and Ravin reports a similar incident in Usha.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman instituted a vessel of nine kav for immersion.

sub.text: Rav Dimi citing Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehuda Glostra
sub.text_en: Rav Dimi citing Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehuda Glostra
sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports in the name of Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehuda Glostra that the nine-kav measure applies only to one who is ill due to circumstances, but for one who is accustomed, forty se'ah are required.
Rav Yosef comments that Rav Nachman's vessel was broken.
Ravin reports that a similar incident occurred in Usha.

items.text: The case of the kil'a of Rav Oshaya and Rav Asi's ruling
items.text_en: The case of the kil'a of Rav Oshaya and Rav Asi's ruling
items.desc_en: A story is told about a question brought to Rav Asi regarding a sick person who had a seminal emission. Rav Asi rules that the distinction between a regular occurrence and an accidental one applies only to a sick person who regularly experiences emissions, but a sick person who experiences it accidentally is exempt from any immersion requirement.

items.text: Abaye's explanation of the dispute among Amoraim
items.text_en: Abaye's explanation of the dispute among Amoraim
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the dispute among the Amoraim is based on Ezra's original enactments. Ezra instituted 40 se'ah for a healthy person who regularly experiences emissions and 9 kav for a healthy person who experiences it accidentally. The Amoraim then disagree about the sick person: one opinion equates a sick person who regularly experiences emissions to a healthy person who regularly experiences emissions, and a sick person who experiences it accidentally to a healthy person who experiences it accidentally; the other opinion equates a sick person who regularly experiences emissions to a healthy person who experiences it accidentally, and exempts a sick person who experiences it accidentally entirely.

items.text: Rava's alternative explanation of the dispute
items.text_en: Rava's alternative explanation of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rava objects to Abaye's explanation, arguing that Ezra only instituted immersion for ba'alei keri, not the pouring of 9 kav. Rava instead explains that Ezra instituted 40 se'ah for a healthy person who regularly experiences emissions, and the Rabbis later instituted 9 kav for a healthy person who experiences it accidentally. The Amoraim then disagree about the sick person, with the same two opinions as before.

items.text: Rava's final halakhic ruling
items.text_en: Rava's final halakhic ruling
items.desc_en: Rava concludes the halakha: a healthy person who regularly experiences emissions and a sick person who regularly experiences emissions require 40 se'ah; a healthy person who experiences it accidentally requires 9 kav; but a sick person who experiences it accidentally is exempt from any immersion.

items.text: Baraita on 9 kav for oneself vs. 40 se'ah for others, and dispute about Rabbi Yehuda's opinion
items.text_en: Baraita on 9 kav for oneself vs. 40 se'ah for others, and dispute about Rabbi Yehuda's opinion
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a ba'al keri who has 9 kav of water poured on him becomes pure, but this applies only for himself; for others, 40 se'ah is required. Rabbi Yehuda says 40 se'ah is required in all cases. A dispute among Amoraim arises: one says that the distinction between oneself and others applies only to a sick person who regularly experiences emissions, but for a sick person who experiences it accidentally, 9 kav suffices even for others; another says that for others, even a sick person who experiences it accidentally requires 40 se'ah. Another dispute concerns Rabbi Yehuda's statement: one says it applies only on the ground, not in vessels; another says it applies even in vessels. The Gemara explains that the phrase "in all cases" in Rabbi Yehuda's statement includes drawn water.

items.text: Story of Rav Pappa, Rav Huna, and Rava bar bar Shmuel regarding who should lead the blessing
items.text_en: Story of Rav Pappa, Rav Huna, and Rava bar bar Shmuel regarding who should lead the blessing
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa, Rav Huna, and Rava bar bar Shmuel were eating together. Rav Pappa asked to lead the blessing because 9 kav had been poured on him. Rava bar bar Shmuel objected, citing the baraita that for others, 40 se'ah is required, and asked to lead because 40 se'ah had been poured on him. Rav Huna then asked to lead because neither had been poured on him.

items.text: Rav Chama's practice and the rejection of his ruling
items.text_en: Rav Chama's practice and the rejection of his ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Chama would immerse on the eve of Passover to fulfill the obligation for the many, but the Gemara states that the halakha is not like him.

items.text: Mishnah: One who remembers he is a ba'al keri while praying
items.text_en: Mishnah: One who remembers he is a ba'al keri while praying
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that if one is standing in prayer and remembers he is a ba'al keri, he should not interrupt but shorten the prayer. If he went down to immerse, if he can come up, cover himself, and read the Shema before sunrise, he should do so; otherwise, he should cover himself in water and read. He should not cover himself in foul water or soaking water until he adds water to them. He must distance himself four cubits from these and from excrement.

items.text: Baraita on one who remembers while praying or reading Torah
items.text_en: Baraita on one who remembers while praying or reading Torah
items.desc_en: A baraita elaborates: if one is standing in prayer and remembers he is a ba'al keri, he should not interrupt but shorten. If he is reading Torah and remembers, he does not stop but mumbles and reads. Rabbi Meir says a ba'al keri may not read more than three verses.

items.text: Baraita on seeing excrement while praying
items.text_en: Baraita on seeing excrement while praying
items.desc_en: Another baraita: if one is standing in prayer and sees excrement in front of him, he should walk forward until he can cast it four cubits behind him. Another baraita says to the side. The Gemara resolves the contradiction: one is when possible, the other when not possible.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbah and Rava about one who prayed in a place with excrement
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbah and Rava about one who prayed in a place with excrement
items.desc_en: If one prayed and found excrement in his place, Rabbah says that although he sinned, his prayer is valid. Rava objects, citing the verse "The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination," and concludes that since he sinned, even though he prayed, his prayer is an abomination.

items.text: Baraita on one whose urine flows while praying, and dispute about where he resumes
items.text_en: Baraita on one whose urine flows while praying, and dispute about where he resumes
items.desc_en: A baraita: if one is standing in prayer and urine flows on his knees, he stops until the water ceases and then prays again. A dispute between Rav Chisda and Rav Hamnuna: one says he returns to the beginning, the other says he resumes from where he stopped. The Gemara suggests they disagree about this point.

items.text: Dispute about delaying prayer and returning to the beginning
items.text_en: Dispute about delaying prayer and returning to the beginning
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute between two authorities (Mar) about whether one who delays prayer must return to the beginning or to where he stopped. Rav Ashi clarifies that the dispute is actually about whether the person is considered unfit (דחויא) or fit (חזיא) for prayer, not about the delay itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute: one authority holds that if one delayed enough to finish the entire prayer, he returns to the beginning; another holds he returns only to where he stopped.
Rav Ashi clarifies that the dispute is not about the delay itself but about whether one who did not delay is considered unfit (דחויא) or fit (חזיא) for prayer.

items.text: One who needs to relieve himself and prays
items.text_en: One who needs to relieve himself and prays
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one who needs to relieve himself should not pray, and if he does, his prayer is an abomination. Rav Zevid (or Rav Yehuda) limits this to one who cannot hold himself, but if he can, his prayer is valid. Rav Sheshet defines the limit as a parasang.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that one who needs to relieve himself should not pray, and if he does, his prayer is an abomination.
Rav Zevid (or Rav Yehuda) limits the baraita to one who cannot hold himself, but if he can, his prayer is valid.
Rav Sheshet defines the limit of being able to hold oneself as a parasang (approximately 4 km).

items.text: Scriptural support for not praying when needing to relieve oneself
items.text_en: Scriptural support for not praying when needing to relieve oneself
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan derives from the verse 'Prepare to meet your God, O Israel' that one should not pray when needing to relieve himself, as one must be prepared and clean.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan derives from the verse 'Prepare to meet your God, O Israel' that one should not pray when needing to relieve himself, as one must be prepared and clean.

items.text: Exegesis of 'Guard your foot' and the foolishness of unrepentant sacrifices
items.text_en: Exegesis of 'Guard your foot' and the foolishness of unrepentant sacrifices
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani and Rabbi Yonatan interpret the verse 'Guard your foot when you go to the house of God' as a warning against sin and a call to bring a sacrifice if one sins. Rava adds that one should be close to the sages who bring sacrifices and repent. The Gemara questions the verse 'for they do not know to do evil' and explains that the foolish bring sacrifices without knowing whether they are for good or evil, which God rejects.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan interprets the verse 'Guard your foot' as a warning against sin and a call to bring a sacrifice if one sins, with Rava adding that one should be close to sages who bring sacrifices and repent.
The Gemara questions the verse 'for they do not know to do evil', asking whether this would make them righteous.
The Gemara explains that the verse refers to fools who bring sacrifices without knowing whether they are for good or evil.
The Holy One, Blessed be He, declares that since they cannot distinguish between good and evil, He rejects their sacrifices.

items.text: Alternative interpretation: Guard your orifices during prayer
items.text_en: Alternative interpretation: Guard your orifices during prayer
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi (or Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa) interprets the verse 'Guard your foot' as a directive to guard one's orifices (נקביך) while standing in prayer before God.

sub.text: Rav Ashi (or Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa)
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi (or Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa)
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi (or Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa) interprets the verse 'Guard your foot' as a directive to guard one's orifices (נקביך) while standing in prayer before God.

items.text: Entering a permanent lavatory with tefillin
items.text_en: Entering a permanent lavatory with tefillin
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one who enters a permanent lavatory removes his tefillin four cubits away and enters. Rav Acha bar Rav Huna in the name of Rav Sheshet distinguishes between a permanent and temporary lavatory. A dilemma is raised about entering a permanent lavatory to urinate with tefillin: Ravina permits, Rav Adda bar Matna prohibits, and Rava prohibits due to concern that one might defecate or pass gas in them.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that one entering a permanent lavatory removes his tefillin four cubits away before entering.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Huna in the name of Rav Sheshet
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Huna in the name of Rav Sheshet
sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet distinguishes the baraita as applying only to a permanent lavatory, not a temporary one.
A dilemma is raised whether one may enter a permanent lavatory with tefillin to urinate.
Ravina permits entering a permanent lavatory with tefillin to urinate.
Rav Adda bar Matna prohibits entering a permanent lavatory with tefillin to urinate.
Rava prohibits entering a permanent lavatory with tefillin even to urinate, due to concern that one might defecate or pass gas in them.

items.text: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on handling tefillin near a lavatory
items.text_en: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on handling tefillin near a lavatory
items.desc_en: Another baraita records a dispute: Beit Shammai says one places tefillin in a window near the public domain, while Beit Hillel says one holds them in hand. Rabbi Akiva says one holds them in his garment. The Gemara objects that holding them in the garment alone might cause them to fall, so it amends to holding them in both garment and hand. A story is told of a student who left his tefillin in a hole near the public domain, a prostitute took them and claimed they were payment, leading the student to commit suicide, prompting the enactment to hold tefillin in garment and hand.

sub.desc_en: A baraita records Beit Shammai's ruling that one removes tefillin four cubits from a permanent lavatory and places them in a window near the public domain.
Beit Hillel holds that one holds the tefillin in hand when entering a permanent lavatory.
Rabbi Akiva rules that one holds the tefillin in his garment when entering.
The Gemara objects that holding tefillin only in the garment might cause them to slip and fall.
The Gemara amends Rabbi Akiva's statement to read that one holds the tefillin in both garment and hand.
The baraita adds that one should place tefillin in holes near the lavatory, not near the public domain, to avoid theft and suspicion.
A story is told of a student who left tefillin in a hole near the public domain; a prostitute took them and claimed they were payment, leading the student to commit suicide.
At that time, the Sages enacted that one should hold tefillin in both garment and hand when entering a lavatory.

items.text: Historical development of the practice of handling tefillin near a lavatory
items.text_en: Historical development of the practice of handling tefillin near a lavatory
items.desc_en: A baraita recounts that initially tefillin were left in holes near the lavatory, but mice took them; then they were left in windows near the public domain, but passersby took them; so it was enacted that one should hold them in hand when entering.

sub.desc_en: A baraita recounts the historical development of the practice of handling tefillin near a lavatory, from leaving them in holes near the lavatory to holding them in hand.

items.text: How to hold tefillin when entering a lavatory
items.text_en: How to hold tefillin when entering a lavatory
items.desc_en: Rabbi Myasha bar Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules that one rolls tefillin like a scroll and holds them in the right hand against the heart. Rav Yosef bar Minyomi in the name of Rav Nachman adds that the strap should not protrude a handbreadth. Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha in the name of Rabbi Zeira distinguishes between day (when there is time to put them on) and night (when one makes a bag of a handbreadth). Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan rules similarly. Abaye limits the handbreadth requirement to a vessel that is a receptacle (כליין), but if not, even less. Mar Zutra (or Rav Ashi) supports this from the law of small jugs in a tent of a corpse. Rabba bar bar Chana relates that Rabbi Yochanan would give them his aggadah scroll but not his tefillin when entering the lavatory, since the sages permitted it.

sub.text: Rabbi Myasha bar Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Myasha bar Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Myasha bar Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules that one rolls tefillin like a scroll and holds them in the right hand against the heart.

sub.text: Rav Yosef bar Minyomi in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Minyomi in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Minyomi in the name of Rav Nachman adds that the strap should not protrude a handbreadth from under his hand.

sub.text: Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha in the name of Rabbi Zeira
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha in the name of Rabbi Zeira
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha in the name of Rabbi Zeira distinguishes between day (when there is time to put them on) and night (when one makes a bag of a handbreadth).

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan rules similarly, distinguishing between day and night.
Abaye limits the handbreadth requirement to a vessel that is a receptacle (כליין), but if not, even less is permitted.
Mar Zutra (or Rav Ashi) supports Abaye's distinction from the law of small jugs in a tent of a corpse.
Rabba bar bar Chana relates that Rabbi Yochanan would give them his aggadah scroll but not his tefillin when entering the lavatory, since the sages permitted it.

items.text: Rava's report on Rav Nachman's practice
items.text_en: Rava's report on Rav Nachman's practice
items.desc_en: Rava reports that when they followed Rav Nachman, he would hand them an aggadah scroll but not tefillin, saying that since the Sages permitted it, they should be guarded.

sub.desc_en: Rava reports that when they followed Rav Nachman, he would hand them an aggadah scroll but not tefillin, saying that since the Sages permitted it, they should be guarded.

items.text: Baraita on not holding tefillin while praying
items.text_en: Baraita on not holding tefillin while praying
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one should not hold tefillin in hand or a Torah scroll in arm while praying, nor urinate or sleep with them. Shmuel adds that a knife, money, bowl, and loaf are similar.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that one should not hold tefillin in hand or a Torah scroll in arm while praying, nor urinate or sleep with them in any manner.
Shmuel adds that a knife, money, bowl, and loaf are similarly forbidden to hold while praying.

items.text: Rava citing Rav Sheshet: the baraita is Beit Shammai
items.text_en: Rava citing Rav Sheshet: the baraita is Beit Shammai
items.desc_en: Rava says in the name of Rav Sheshet that the halakha is not like that baraita, as it follows Beit Shammai. According to Beit Hillel, if a permanent bathroom is permitted, a temporary one certainly should be.

sub.desc_en: Rava states in the name of Rav Sheshet that the halakha does not follow the baraita, as it reflects Beit Shammai's view, since Beit Hillel would certainly permit a temporary bathroom if a permanent one is permitted.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding the baraita
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding the baraita
items.desc_en: An objection is raised from a baraita about 'things I permitted here, I prohibited there.' The Gemara initially assumes it refers to tefillin, but then resolves that it deals with the laws of covering for bathroom privacy (tefach and tefachayim). The objection is refuted, but Rava's position is ultimately rejected.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about 'things I permitted here, I prohibited there,' and initially assumes it refers to tefillin.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita actually deals with the laws of covering for bathroom privacy (a tefach and tefachayim), not tefillin.
The Gemara questions whether the two baraitot can be reconciled by distinguishing between adults and children.
The Gemara rejects the adult-child distinction and instead distinguishes between a man and a woman.
The Gemara questions the meaning of the phrase 'this is a kal vachomer that has no refutation' in the baraita.
The Gemara concludes that the baraita indeed refers to tefillin, and Rava's position (citing Rav Sheshet) is refuted.

items.text: Reconsideration: the kal vachomer argument
items.text_en: Reconsideration: the kal vachomer argument
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the logic: if a permanent bathroom is permitted, a temporary one should certainly be. The answer distinguishes between bathrooms with and without sparks (nitzotzot). The phrase 'no refutation' is explained as meaning the kal vachomer cannot be applied due to a hidden reason.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: if a permanent bathroom is permitted, a temporary one should certainly be permitted by קל וחומר (a fortiori reasoning).
The Gemara answers: a permanent bathroom lacks sparks (ניצוצות) and is permitted, while a temporary one has sparks and is forbidden.
The Gemara objects: if so, why does the baraita call it 'a קל וחומר that has no refutation'? This is actually a good refutation.

The Gemara resolves: the phrase means that this matter should be understood through its hidden reason (טעמא), not through קל וחומר; if one tried to apply קל וחומר, it would be a קל וחומר that has no refutation.

items.text: Rulings on entering a fixed meal and tefillin
items.text_en: Rulings on entering a fixed meal and tefillin
items.desc_en: A baraita advises walking ten times four cubits or four times ten cubits before a fixed meal. Rabbi Yitzchak says one must remove tefillin before entering, while Rabbi Chiya says to place them on the table. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak limits this until the time of the blessing.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that one who wishes to enter a fixed meal should walk ten times four cubits or four times ten cubits, relieve himself, and then enter.
Rabbi Yitzchak states that one who enters a fixed meal must remove his tefillin before entering.
Rabbi Chiya disagrees, saying one should place the tefillin on the table, and that is the proper conduct.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak limits the practice of placing tefillin on the table until the time of the blessing.

items.text: Dispute about tying tefillin with money
items.text_en: Dispute about tying tefillin with money
items.desc_en: Two baraitot conflict: one permits tying tefillin with money in one's purse, the other forbids. The resolution distinguishes between designated and non-designated cloths, citing Rav Chisda and Abaye's views on designation (hazmanah).

sub.desc_en: Two conflicting baraitot are cited: one permits tying tefillin with money in one's purse, the other forbids it.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a cloth designated (הזמנה) for tefillin and one not designated, citing Rav Chisda's ruling that designation with actual use renders the cloth forbidden for money, but designation alone or use alone does not.
Abaye objects that according to his view, designation (הזמנה) alone is significant, so even designation without use renders the cloth forbidden for money.

items.text: Placing tefillin under one's pillow
items.text_en: Placing tefillin under one's pillow
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef asks Rav Yehuda whether one may place tefillin under his head. Shmuel permits it even with his wife. A baraita contradicts Shmuel, prohibiting it if his wife is with him unless the place is elevated or lowered three handbreadths. Rava rules like Shmuel despite the refutation.

sub.text: Rav Yosef's question to Rav Yehuda
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef's question to Rav Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef asks Rav Yehuda whether one may place tefillin under his pillow, distinguishing between under the feet (disrespectful) and under the head.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda's answer in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda's answer in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda answers that Shmuel permits placing tefillin under the pillow, even when his wife is with him.
A baraita is cited that prohibits placing tefillin under the pillow when one's wife is with him, unless the place is elevated or lowered three handbreadths, contradicting Shmuel's leniency.
The gemara declares that Shmuel's position is refuted by the baraita.
Rava rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows Shmuel despite the refutation, and the gemara asks for the reason.

items.text: Placement of tefillin while sleeping
items.text_en: Placement of tefillin while sleeping
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses where one should place tefillin when sleeping. Rabbi Yirmeyah says between the pillow and the mattress, not opposite the head. A baraita of Rabbi Chiyya says in a hat, and Bar Kappara ties them in a cloth. Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi places them on a bench and covers them with a cloth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Where should one place tefillin when sleeping? Rabbi Yirmeyah says between the pillow and the mattress, not opposite the head. A baraita of Rabbi Chiyya says in a hat, and Bar Kappara ties them in a cloth. Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi places them on a bench and covers them with a cloth.

items.text: Rav Hamnuna's testimony about Rava
items.text_en: Rav Hamnuna's testimony about Rava
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna bar Rav Yosef testifies that he once found Rava's tefillin between the pillow and mattress, not opposite the head, and that it was a day of immersion, so Rava was teaching halakhah le-ma'aseh.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Hamnuna bar Rabbi Yosef recounts a story: He stood before Rava, who told him to bring tefillin. He found them between the pillow and the mattress, not opposite the head. He knew it was a day of immersion, and he concluded that the halacha follows the practice.

items.text: Two people sleeping in one bed and reciting Shema
items.text_en: Two people sleeping in one bed and reciting Shema
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Rav Nechunya asks Rav Yehuda whether two people sleeping in one bed can each turn their faces away and recite Shema. Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel that even with his wife it is permitted. Rav Yosef objects that his wife is like himself, but another is not. A baraita supports Shmuel, but another baraita requires a separating garment. Shmuel resolves the contradiction by saying that the dispute is between Tannaim.

sub.text: Rav Yosef bar Rav Nechunya's question
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Rav Nechunya's question
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Rav Nechunya asks Rav Yehuda whether two people sleeping in one bed may each turn their faces away and recite Shema.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda's answer in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda's answer in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda answers in the name of Shmuel that it is permitted even if his wife is with him in the bed.
Rav Yosef objects that his wife is like his own body, so another person is not comparable and should require a separation.
A baraita is cited that permits two people in one bed to recite Shema, but another baraita requires a separating garment unless the children are small.
Shmuel resolves the contradiction by stating that the dispute is between Tannaim, just as Rav Yosef's own position is also a Tannaic dispute.

items.text: Discussion of 'agavot' (erotic thoughts) and Rav Huna
items.text_en: Discussion of 'agavot' (erotic thoughts) and Rav Huna
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how one can recite Shema while turning away, since there are 'agavot' (erotic thoughts). It cites Rav Huna that 'agavot' are not considered ervah. A baraita about a woman kneading dough naked is cited, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that her face was covered in the ground.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the earlier statement allowing one to turn away and recite Shema is possible, given the presence of erotic thoughts (עֲגָבוֹת).
The Gemara cites Rav Huna's ruling that erotic thoughts (עֲגָבוֹת) are not considered ervah (עֶרְוָה) for the purpose of reciting Shema.
A baraita is cited as supporting evidence: a woman may knead dough for חלה (challah) while naked because she can cover her face in the ground, but a man may not.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the baraita refers to a case where the woman's face was smeared in the ground, thus covering her face and preventing erotic thoughts.

items.text: Age limit for children in bed
items.text_en: Age limit for children in bed
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the age at which children are considered too old to be in bed without a separation. Rav Chisda says a girl of three years and one day, a boy of nine years and one day. Others say a girl of eleven years and one day, a boy of twelve years and one day, citing the verse 'Shadayim nakhonu u-s'arekh tzime'ach'.

sub.desc_en: Mar says: If his sons and household members are small, it is permitted. Up to what age? Rav Chisda says: A girl of three years and one day, a boy of nine years and one day. Some say: A girl of eleven years and one day, a boy of twelve years and one day — until the signs of maturity appear.
Rav Chisda rules that a girl up to three years and one day and a boy up to nine years and one day are considered קטנים (minors) for this purpose.
Others say a girl up to eleven years and one day and a boy up to twelve years and one day are considered קטנים (minors).
The Gemara notes that both opinions derive their age limits from the verse 'שָׁדַיִם נָכֹנוּ וּשְׂעָרֵךְ צִמֵּחַ' (Your breasts were formed and your hair grew), indicating the onset of puberty.

items.text: Halakhic ruling regarding Shmuel's opinion
items.text_en: Halakhic ruling regarding Shmuel's opinion
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana asks Rav Ashi whether the halakhah follows Shmuel's opinion, as Rava said elsewhere. Rav Ashi responds that the ruling was stated only in that specific context.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana asks Rav Asi: There, Rava said that despite Shmuel's objection, the halacha follows Shmuel. Here, what? Rav Asi answers: They are all in one stroke — where it was stated, it was stated; where it was not stated, it was not stated.
Rav Ashi responds that the ruling was stated only in that specific context and does not apply here.

items.text: Definitions of ervah (nakedness) for Shema
items.text_en: Definitions of ervah (nakedness) for Shema
items.desc_en: Rav Mari asks Rav Papa about hair protruding from clothing. Rabbi Yitzchak says a tefach of a woman is ervah, but only for his wife regarding Shema. Rav Chisda says the thigh is ervah, Shmuel says the voice is ervah, and Rav Sheshet says hair is ervah, each citing verses.

sub.text: Rav Mari's question to Rav Papa
sub.text_en: Rav Mari's question to Rav Papa
sub.desc_en: Rav Mari asks Rav Papa whether hair protruding from one's garment is considered ervah (nakedness) for the purpose of reciting Shema.
Rabbi Yitzchak states that a tefach (handbreadth) of a woman is ervah, and clarifies that this applies only to one's own wife regarding Shema recitation.
Rav Chisda says the thigh (שוק) of a woman is ervah, citing the verse 'גַּלִּי שׁוֹק עִבְרִי נְהָרוֹת' and its connection to nakedness.
Shmuel says the voice of a woman is ervah, citing the verse 'כִּי קוֹלֵךְ עָרֵב וּמַרְאֵךְ נָאוֶה'.
Rav Sheshet says hair of a woman is ervah, citing the verse 'שַׂעֲרֵךְ כְּעֵדֶר הָעִזִּים'.

items.text: Hanging tefillin and Rabbi's practice
items.text_en: Hanging tefillin and Rabbi's practice
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina says he saw Rabbi hanging his tefillin. A baraita condemns hanging tefillin. The Gemara distinguishes between hanging by the strap (permitted) and by the knot (forbidden). Alternatively, both are forbidden, but Rabbi hung them in a bag. This teaches that tefillin require placement like a Torah scroll.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina reports that he saw Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) hanging his tefillin.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that condemns hanging tefillin, saying such a person's life will be hung.
The Dorshei Chamurot (stringent interpreters) cite the verse 'Your life will be hung before you' as applying to one who hangs tefillin.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: hanging by the strap (רצועה) is permitted, but hanging by the knot (קציצה) is forbidden.
Alternatively, both hanging by the strap and by the knot are forbidden, but Rabbi hung them in a bag (כיסתא).
The Gemara explains the purpose of Rabbi's action: to teach that tefillin require placement (הנחה) like a Torah scroll, not merely hanging.

items.text: Rabbi's actions of yawning, sneezing, and spitting
items.text_en: Rabbi's actions of yawning, sneezing, and spitting
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina reports that he saw Rabbi yawn, sneeze, and spit. The text is cut off, but it likely relates to proper conduct during prayer.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina reports that he saw Rabbi yawn, sneeze, and spit, likely relating to proper conduct during prayer.

items.text: Opening description of Rabbi's prayer conduct
items.text_en: Opening description of Rabbi's prayer conduct
items.desc_en: Describes how a certain rabbi would feel his garment but not wrap himself, and when yawning would place his hand on his chin, setting the stage for the Gemara's discussion.

sub.desc_en: Describes the rabbi's modest conduct during prayer: he would feel his garment but not wrap himself, and when yawning would place his hand on his chin.

items.text: Baraita on improper prayer conduct
items.text_en: Baraita on improper prayer conduct
items.desc_en: A baraita lists behaviors that are improper during prayer: raising one's voice, yawning, sneezing, and spitting, each with a negative characterization.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by condemning one who sounds or raises his voice during prayer as being of little faith or among the false prophets.
The baraita continues listing improper behaviors: belching and yawning mark one as uncouth, sneezing is a bad omen (or shows repulsiveness), and spitting is like spitting in the king's face.

items.text: Resolution of contradiction about sneezing
items.text_en: Resolution of contradiction about sneezing
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves an apparent contradiction between the baraita's negative view of sneezing and a positive view attributed to Rav Zeira, distinguishing between sneezing from below (good sign) and from above (bad sign).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: while the contradiction about belching and yawning is resolved by distinguishing voluntary from involuntary, the contradiction about sneezing remains.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between sneezing from above (nose) and sneezing from below (flatulence).
Rav Zeira cites a tradition from the school of Rav Hamnuna that sneezing in prayer is a good omen, as it indicates pleasure both below and above.

items.text: Resolution of contradiction about spitting
items.text_en: Resolution of contradiction about spitting
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction about spitting during prayer by citing Rav Yehuda's ruling that one should swallow the spit in his garment or cloak, and relates an incident with Ravina and Rav Ashi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction about spitting during prayer, noting that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's action seems to conflict with the baraita that equates spitting to spitting in the king's face.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by suggesting it is possible to follow Rav Yehuda's ruling, which permits spitting by absorbing it in one's garment.
Rav Yehuda rules that one standing in prayer who has saliva should absorb it in his garment, or in his head covering if the garment is fine.
An incident is related where Ravina, standing behind Rav Ashi, spits behind him instead of absorbing it, and explains that he is delicate and the spit would disturb his concentration.

items.text: Rav Huna on raising one's voice in prayer
items.text_en: Rav Huna on raising one's voice in prayer
items.desc_en: Rav Huna qualifies the baraita about raising one's voice: it applies only if one can concentrate silently, but if not, it is permitted; and for an individual, but in public it may disturb the congregation.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that one who sounds his voice during prayer is among those of little faith.
Rav Huna qualifies the baraita: it applies only when one can concentrate silently; if unable to concentrate, raising the voice is permitted.
Rav Huna adds that this leniency applies only to an individual; in a congregation, raising one's voice may disturb others and is prohibited.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Abba and Rav Yehuda about sneezing in prayer
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Abba and Rav Yehuda about sneezing in prayer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba avoids Rav Yehuda to hear a teaching about sneezing during prayer, and learns that one should wait for the wind to pass and then resume, with a special prayer.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba avoids Rav Yehuda because he wants to ascend to Eretz Yisrael, which Rav Yehuda forbids, and plans to hear a teaching from him before leaving.

The tanna recites a baraita: one who sneezes during prayer waits for the wind to pass and resumes; some say he retreats four cubits, sneezes, waits, recites a prayer about human frailty, and resumes from where he stopped.
Rabbi Abba says that hearing this teaching alone was sufficient reason for his visit.

items.text: Baraita on sleeping in a tallit and reciting Shema
items.text_en: Baraita on sleeping in a tallit and reciting Shema
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses one who is sleeping in his tallit and cannot remove his head due to cold: he may place the tallit on his neck or heart and recite Shema, with a dispute about the heart seeing erva.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that one sleeping in his tallit who cannot expose his head due to cold may place the tallit on his neck and recite Shema.
Some say the barrier must be placed on the heart, not just the neck.
The Gemara asks: According to the first tanna, does the heart not see the erva (nakedness), which should be prohibited?
The Gemara answers: The first tanna holds that when the heart sees the erva, it is permitted to recite Shema.

items.text: Dispute about reciting Shema in filthy alleyways
items.text_en: Dispute about reciting Shema in filthy alleyways
items.desc_en: Rav Huna in the name of Rabbi Yochanan permits covering one's mouth and reciting Shema in filthy alleyways, but Rav Chisda strongly objects. A story with Rabbi Avahu and Rabbi Yochanan illustrates the practice, and the Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between standing and walking.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna in the name of Rabbi Yochanan rules that one walking in filthy alleyways may place his hand over his mouth and recite Shema.
Rav Chisda objects vehemently, swearing he would not obey even if Rabbi Yochanan said it directly.

sub.text: Alternative tradition citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Alternative tradition citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: An alternative tradition reports that Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi gives the same lenient ruling.
Rav Chisda again objects, saying he would not obey even if Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said it directly.
The Gemara questions Rav Huna's lenient ruling, citing his own earlier statement that a Torah scholar may not stand in a place of filth.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between standing (prohibited) and walking (permitted).
The Gemara questions Rabbi Yochanan's lenient ruling, citing his own statement that one may contemplate Torah everywhere except the bathhouse and bathroom.

The Gemara objects that the standing/walking distinction fails, citing a story where Rabbi Avahu stopped reciting Shema in a filthy alleyway and Rabbi Yochanan did not admonish him, implying prohibition.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yochanan was not stating his own view but instructing Rabbi Avahu according to his own stringent practice.

items.text: Supporting baraitot and consequences
items.text_en: Supporting baraitot and consequences
items.desc_en: Two baraitot support both Rav Huna and Rav Chisda, and the Gemara discusses the punishment for not stopping and the reward for stopping, citing various verses.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited in support of Rav Huna's lenient position: one walking in filthy alleyways places his hand over his mouth and recites Shema.
A baraita is cited in support of Rav Chisda's stringent position: one walking in filthy alleyways may not recite Shema, and if already reciting, must stop.
The Gemara asks: If one did not stop reciting Shema in a filthy alleyway, what is his status?
Rabbi Me'asha bar breih deRabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says that of him the verse states: 'Moreover, I gave them statutes that were not good and laws by which they could not live' (Ezekiel 20:25).
Rav Asi says that of him the verse states: 'Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of vanity' (Isaiah 5:18).
Rav Adda bar Ahava says that of him the verse states: 'For he has shown contempt for the word of the Lord' (Numbers 15:31).
The Gemara asks: And if one did stop, what is his reward?
Rabbi Avahu says that of him the verse states: 'And it is through this matter that you will prolong your days' (Deuteronomy 32:47).

items.text: Rav Huna on wearing a tallit as a belt for Shema
items.text_en: Rav Huna on wearing a tallit as a belt for Shema
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that if one's tallit is tied around his waist, he may recite Shema, and a baraita supports this.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that if one's tallit is tied around his waist, he may recite Shema.
A baraita supports Rav Huna's ruling, stating that a garment of cloth, leather, or sack tied around the waist permits reciting Shema.

items.text: Opening statement on prayer and covering the heart
items.text_en: Opening statement on prayer and covering the heart
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a ruling that for prayer, one must cover his heart (i.e., the area of the heart) before reciting. This sets the stage for the discussion of bodily exposure and recitation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that for prayer, one must cover his heart (the area of the heart) before reciting.

items.text: Rav Huna on entering a bathroom with tefillin
items.text_en: Rav Huna on entering a bathroom with tefillin
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that if one forgot and entered a bathroom with tefillin, he should place his hand over them until he finishes. The Gemara clarifies that this means only until he finishes the first column, citing a concern from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel about the danger of holding back waste.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that if one forgot and entered a bathroom with tefillin, he should place his hand over them until he finishes.
The Gemara objects: 'Until he finishes' — could it enter your mind that he must wait until he fully finishes?
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak clarifies that 'until he finishes' means only until he finishes the first column of waste.
The Gemara asks: Why not stop immediately and stand up?

sub.text: Gemara's answer citing Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer citing Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that one may not stop abruptly due to the danger cited in a baraita of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: holding back waste can cause serious illness.

items.text: Dispute: excrement on the body or hand in bathroom
items.text_en: Dispute: excrement on the body or hand in bathroom
items.desc_en: Rav Huna and Rav Chisda dispute whether one may recite Shema when there is excrement on his body or his hand is in the bathroom. Rav Huna permits it, citing the verse 'All souls praise God', while Rav Chisda forbids it, citing 'All my bones shall say, God, who is like You'.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Chisda regarding reciting Shema when there is excrement on one's body or one's hand is in the bathroom.
Rav Huna permits reciting Shema, citing the verse 'כל הנשמה תהלל יה' (All souls praise God), implying that the soul's praise is not hindered by bodily impurity.
Rav Chisda forbids reciting Shema, citing the verse 'כל עצמותי תאמרנה ה' מי כמוך' (All my bones shall say, God, who is like You), implying that the body must be pure for prayer.
