Abaye bar Avin and Rabbi Chanina bar Avin define it as prayer not recited at twilight, citing Rabbi Yochanan's teaching about praying at twilight, though in the West they curse those who do so due to time concerns.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by 'fixed prayer' (קבע).

sub.text: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi in the name of Rabbi Oshaya
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi in the name of Rabbi Oshaya
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi in the name of Rabbi Oshaya defines fixed prayer as prayer that feels like a burden (משאוי).
The Rabbis define fixed prayer as prayer not said with supplication (תחנונים).
Rabbah and Rav Yosef define fixed prayer as prayer without innovation (חידוש).
Rabbi Zeira says he can innovate in prayer but fears distraction (טירדא).

sub.text: Abaye bar Avin and Rabbi Chanina bar Avin
sub.text_en: Abaye bar Avin and Rabbi Chanina bar Avin
sub.desc_en: Abaye bar Avin and Rabbi Chanina bar Avin define fixed prayer as prayer not recited at twilight (דמדומי חמה).

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan teaches that it is a מצוה (commandment) to pray at twilight, supporting the definition.
Rabbi Zeira cites the verse 'יִירָאוּךָ עִם שָׁמֶשׁ' (they shall fear You with the sun) as a scriptural basis for praying at twilight.
In the West (ארץ ישראל) they curse one who prays at twilight, contradicting the earlier praise.
The Gemara explains the curse is due to concern that the time might become confused (טירוף שעה), resolving the contradiction.

items.text: Explanation of 'Parashat Ha'Ibbur' in Rabbi Yehoshua's statement
items.text_en: Explanation of 'Parashat Ha'Ibbur' in Rabbi Yehoshua's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the phrase 'Parashat Ha'Ibbur' from the Mishnah. Rav Chisda in the name of Mar Ukva gives two interpretations: even when you are filled with anger like a pregnant woman, or even when they transgress Torah, may all their needs be before You.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the meaning of 'פרשת העיבור' (the passage of intercalation) in the Mishnah?
Mar Ukva explains: even when you are filled with anger against them like a pregnant woman, may all their needs be before You.

sub.text: Alternate version of Rav Chisda quoting Mar Ukva
sub.text_en: Alternate version of Rav Chisda quoting Mar Ukva
sub.desc_en: An alternate version: even when they transgress the words of Torah, may all their needs be before You.

items.text: Texts of the short prayer (תפילה קצרה) and ruling
items.text_en: Texts of the short prayer (תפילה קצרה) and ruling
items.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma teaches that one traveling in a dangerous place recites a short prayer. Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok, and Acheirim each propose a different text. Rav Huna rules the halakha follows Acheirim.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that one traveling in a dangerous place recites a short prayer (תפילה קצרה), and then asks what that short prayer is.
Rabbi Eliezer proposes a text for the short prayer, asking God to do His will in heaven and grant peace to the righteous.
Rabbi Yehoshua proposes a different text, asking God to hear the cry of His people and fulfill their request quickly.
Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok proposes a text similar to Rabbi Yehoshua's but with 'צעקת' (cry) instead of 'שועת' (cry for help).
Acheirim proposes a text acknowledging the many needs of Israel and their limited understanding, asking God to provide for each individual.
Rav Huna rules that the halakha (הלכה) follows the opinion of Acheirim.

items.text: Elijah's advice and the prayer for a journey (תפילת הדרך)
items.text_en: Elijah's advice and the prayer for a journey (תפילת הדרך)
items.desc_en: Elijah tells Rav Yehuda not to get angry or drunk to avoid sin, and when going on a journey, to consult his Creator and go. Rabbi Yaakov in the name of Rav Chisda explains this as the prayer for a journey (תפילת הדרך), and states that anyone going on a journey must recite it. The text of the prayer is then given.

sub.desc_en: Elijah instructs Rav Yehuda not to get angry or drunk to avoid sin, and when going on a journey to consult his Creator and go.
The Gemara asks what it means to 'consult one's Creator and go.'

sub.text: Rabbi Yaakov in the name of Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov in the name of Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov in the name of Rav Chisda explains that this refers to the prayer for a journey (תפילת הדרך), and states that anyone going on a journey must recite it.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of the prayer text
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of the prayer text
sub.desc_en: The Gemara provides the full text of the prayer for a journey (תפילת הדרך).

items.text: Abaye's statement (incomplete)
items.text_en: Abaye's statement (incomplete)
items.desc_en: Abaye begins a statement with 'לעולם' (always), but the text is cut off, likely continuing to the next amud.

sub.desc_en: Abaye begins a statement with 'לעולם' (always), but the text is cut off.

items.text: Opening: The traveler's prayer
items.text_en: Opening: The traveler's prayer
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the concept that a person should join with the community in prayer, and presents the text of the traveler's prayer: 'May it be Your will, Lord our God, that You lead us in peace' etc.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the principle of joining the community in prayer and presents the traveler's prayer text.

items.text: When and how to recite the traveler's prayer
items.text_en: When and how to recite the traveler's prayer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov in the name of Rav Chisda states that the traveler's prayer is recited from the time one sets out on the road, and up to a parasang. There is a dispute between Rav Chisda and Rav Sheshet whether it must be recited standing or even while walking.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks when one should recite this prayer, and Rabbi Yaakov citing Rav Chisda answers: from the time one sets out on the road, and up to one parasang.
The Gemara asks how one should recite it, and Rav Chisda and Rav Sheshet disagree: Rav Chisda says standing, Rav Sheshet says even while walking.
The Gemara asks how the traveler's prayer is recited.
Rav Chisda answers that the traveler's prayer must be recited standing (מעומד).
Rav Sheshet answers that the traveler's prayer may be recited even while walking (אפילו מהלך).

items.text: Anecdote: Rav Chisda and Rav Sheshet on the road
items.text_en: Anecdote: Rav Chisda and Rav Sheshet on the road
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda and Rav Sheshet were traveling; Rav Chisda stopped and prayed standing. Rav Sheshet told his attendant to also stop him so he could pray, citing the verse 'Do not call evil what is good'.

sub.desc_en: A story illustrates the dispute: Rav Chisda stands to pray, and Rav Sheshet, citing the proverb 'Do not call evil what is good,' also stands to pray.
Rav Sheshet asks his attendant what Rav Chisda is doing.
The attendant answers that Rav Chisda is standing and praying.
Rav Sheshet instructs his attendant to stop him as well so he can pray, citing the verse 'Do not call evil what is good'.

items.text: Difference between Havinenu and a short prayer
items.text_en: Difference between Havinenu and a short prayer
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the difference between the 'Havinenu' prayer and a short prayer: Havinenu requires the first three and last three blessings and one need not repeat the prayer upon arriving home, while a short prayer requires no blessings but one must repeat the full prayer upon arriving home. The halakha is that Havinenu is recited standing, while a short prayer may be recited either standing or walking.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the difference between the Havinenu prayer and a short prayer.

The Gemara explains that Havinenu requires the first three and last three blessings and one need not repeat the prayer upon arriving home, while a short prayer requires no such blessings but one must repeat the full prayer upon arriving home.
The Gemara rules that Havinenu is recited standing, while a short prayer may be recited either standing or walking.

items.text: One riding a donkey at prayer time
items.text_en: One riding a donkey at prayer time
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses whether one riding a donkey should dismount to pray if someone can hold the animal, or remain seated. Rabbi says in either case he should remain seated because his mind is not settled. Rava (or Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi) rules the halakha follows Rabbi.

sub.desc_en: Rava (or Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi) rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi's position.

items.text: Direction of prayer: directing the heart
items.text_en: Direction of prayer: directing the heart
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that a blind person or one who cannot orient to the directions should direct their heart toward their Father in Heaven. One outside the Land of Israel should direct toward the Land; in the Land, toward Jerusalem; in Jerusalem, toward the Temple; in the Temple, toward the Holy of Holies. Rabbi Avin explains the verse 'like the tower of David, built for Talpiyot' — a mound toward which all mouths turn.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with a rule: a blind person or one who cannot orient to the directions should direct their heart toward their Father in Heaven, citing a verse.

The baraita elaborates a graduated system of directional intent: one outside the Land directs toward the Land; in the Land, toward Jerusalem; in Jerusalem, toward the Temple; in the Temple, toward the Holy of Holies; behind the Holy of Holies, one imagines being before it; all Israel thus direct their hearts to one place.

Rabbi Avin (or Rabbi Avina) provides a biblical support for the baraita's system, interpreting the verse 'like the tower of David, built for Talpiyot' as a mound (תל) toward which all mouths (פיות) turn.

items.text: Praying before the journey vs. at the proper time
items.text_en: Praying before the journey vs. at the proper time
items.desc_en: The father of Shmuel and Levi would pray before setting out on a journey, and recite Shema at its proper time. A baraita supports this practice. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says one should recite Shema and pray at the proper time to juxtapose redemption to prayer. The dispute is whether standing for prayer is more important or juxtaposing redemption to prayer is more important.

sub.text: Baraita (practice of the father of Shmuel and Levi)
sub.text_en: Baraita (practice of the father of Shmuel and Levi)
sub.desc_en: The father of Shmuel and Levi would pray before setting out on a journey, and recite Shema at its proper time.
The gemara identifies the practice with a specific Tanna, citing a baraita that permits performing other mitzvot early and reciting Shema at its proper time.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar objects, arguing that one should recite Shema and pray at their proper times to juxtapose redemption to prayer.
The gemara resolves the dispute: one side prioritizes standing for prayer (תפילה מעומד), the other prioritizes juxtaposing redemption to prayer (סמיכת גאולה לתפילה).

items.text: Practices of later Amoraim regarding prayer on the road
items.text_en: Practices of later Amoraim regarding prayer on the road
items.desc_en: Marimar and Mar Zutra would gather a minyan on the festival Sabbath and pray, then go to the lecture. Rav Ashi would pray with the congregation as an individual while seated, and when he came home he would pray again standing. The rabbis questioned his practice, and he explained that the earlier sages did so.

sub.desc_en: Marimar and Mar Zutra would gather a minyan on the festival Sabbath and pray, then go to the lecture.
Rav Ashi would pray with the congregation as an individual while seated, and when he came home he would pray again standing.
The rabbis questioned Rav Ashi why he did not follow the practice of Marimar and Mar Zutra or of the father of Shmuel and Levi.
Rav Ashi explained that gathering a minyan was burdensome for him, and he had not seen the earlier sages acting like the father of Shmuel and Levi.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: Musaf prayer in a settled town
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: Musaf prayer in a settled town
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya says Musaf prayer is only recited in a settled town (with a quorum). The Sages say both in a settled town and not. Rabbi Yehuda says in his name that wherever there is a settled town, an individual is exempt from Musaf. The Gemara clarifies the difference between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehuda regarding an individual outside a settled town. Rav Huna bar Chinana in the name of Rav Chiya bar Rav rules the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda, and Rav Chiya bar Avin supports this with Shmuel's statement that he never prayed Musaf as an individual.

items.text: Opening narrative: Rabbi Chanina's ruling on prayer during crisis
items.text_en: Opening narrative: Rabbi Chanina's ruling on prayer during crisis
items.desc_en: In Nehardea, during a royal military campaign that distracted the rabbis from praying, Rabbi Chanina prayed alone as an individual without a congregation, establishing that individual prayer is valid when the community cannot gather.

sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts that in Nehardea, during a royal military campaign that distracted the rabbis from praying, Rabbi Chanina prayed alone as an individual without a congregation, establishing that individual prayer is valid when the community cannot gather.

items.text: Gemara's question: Is individual prayer valid when community is unable?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Is individual prayer valid when community is unable?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Chanina's individual prayer is valid, given that the community was unable to pray due to the military distraction, and seeks to clarify the halacha.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina, sitting before Rabbi Yannai, states that the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya.
Rabbi Yannai dismisses Rabbi Chanina's ruling, telling him to go read his verses outside, as the halacha does not follow Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya.

items.text: First answer: Rabbi Yannai rejects Rabbi Chanina's ruling
items.text_en: First answer: Rabbi Yannai rejects Rabbi Chanina's ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai tells Rabbi Chanina to go outside and read his own statement, implying that the halacha does not follow Rabbi Yehuda's opinion cited by Rabbi Chanina, thus rejecting the validity of individual prayer in that context.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai tells Rabbi Chanina to go outside and read his own statement, rejecting the halacha as following Rabbi Yehuda's opinion.

items.text: Second answer: Rabbi Yochanan's testimony about Rabbi Yannai's practice
items.text_en: Second answer: Rabbi Yochanan's testimony about Rabbi Yannai's practice
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan testifies that he saw Rabbi Yannai pray and then pray again, suggesting that Rabbi Yannai himself may have prayed as an individual when necessary, contradicting his earlier rejection.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan testifies that he saw Rabbi Yannai pray and then pray again, providing evidence that Rabbi Yannai himself practiced praying twice.

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Zeira
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Zeira
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya objects that perhaps Rabbi Yannai's first prayer lacked proper intention (כוונה), so he prayed again with intention.
Rabbi Zeira rejects the objection, arguing that Rabbi Yannai was too great a sage to have prayed without intention.

items.text: Gemara's clarification: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi's practice
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi's practice
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi, despite having thirteen synagogues in Tiberias, only prayed between the pillars where they studied, indicating that individual prayer in a study context is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi, despite having thirteen synagogues in Tiberias, only prayed between the pillars where they studied, demonstrating that individual prayer in a study context is valid.

items.text: Halachic ruling: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Abdimi's statement
items.text_en: Halachic ruling: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Abdimi's statement
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Abdimi states the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda's opinion cited from Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, confirming that individual prayer is valid when the community cannot gather.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Abdimi states that the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda's opinion cited from Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya.

items.text: Gemara's objection: Rabbi Zeira's question about Rabbi Chiyya's double prayer
items.text_en: Gemara's objection: Rabbi Zeira's question about Rabbi Chiyya's double prayer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira questions why Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba prayed twice, suspecting lack of concentration, but Rabbi Chiyya explains he did so because he forgot Rosh Chodesh, not due to distraction.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba why he prayed twice, suggesting it might be due to lack of concentration, citing Rabbi Eliezer's rule that one should only pray if able to concentrate.
Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba answers that he prayed again for the correct reason: he forgot that it was Rosh Chodesh, not due to distraction.

items.text: Tannaic source: Forgetting Rosh Chodesh in evening prayer
items.text_en: Tannaic source: Forgetting Rosh Chodesh in evening prayer
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if one forgets to mention Rosh Chodesh in evening prayer, they do not repeat it because they can say it in the morning; similarly for morning and musaf, they can say it in mincha.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that if one forgets to mention Rosh Chodesh in evening prayer, they do not repeat it because they can say it in the morning; similarly for morning and musaf, they can say it in mincha.

items.text: Gemara's analysis: Distinction between full and deficient months
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis: Distinction between full and deficient months
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the baraita, noting that the rule applies only to a full month (30 days) where Rosh Chodesh is known; for a deficient month (29 days) where the new moon is not yet declared, one must repeat the prayer.

sub.desc_en: Ameimar states that Rav's ruling applies only to a full month (30 days).
Ameimar adds that in a deficient month (29 days), one must repeat the prayer.
Rav Ashi objects that since Rav gave a reason (the court sanctifies only by day), there should be no distinction between full and deficient months.
Rav Ashi concludes that there is no difference between a full and deficient month.

items.text: Objection: Rav Ashi challenges Ameimar's distinction
items.text_en: Objection: Rav Ashi challenges Ameimar's distinction
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi argues that since Rav stated the halacha without specifying month type, the distinction between full and deficient is irrelevant; the rule should apply uniformly.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects to Ameimar's distinction between full and deficient months, arguing that since Rav gave a reason (that the court sanctifies only by day), the rule should apply uniformly regardless of month type.

items.text: Conclusion: Halacha follows Rav's uniform ruling
items.text_en: Conclusion: Halacha follows Rav's uniform ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the halacha follows Rav's original statement, which applies to both full and deficient months without distinction, as per Rav Ashi's reasoning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the halacha follows Rav's uniform ruling, applying equally to full and deficient months, as per Rav Ashi's reasoning.

items.text: Mishna: Proper posture and concentration for prayer
items.text_en: Mishna: Proper posture and concentration for prayer
items.desc_en: The Mishna teaches that one should not stand to pray except with a heavy head (reverence), and the early pious ones would wait an hour before praying to focus their hearts on their Father in heaven.

sub.desc_en: The Mishna rules that one must stand for prayer only with a heavy head (reverence), and the early pious ones would wait an hour before praying to focus their hearts on their Father in heaven, and even if a king greets him or a snake is coiled around his heel, he should not interrupt.

items.text: Gemara's source: Scriptural basis for reverence
items.text_en: Gemara's source: Scriptural basis for reverence
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Elazar's derivation from the verse 'And she was bitter of soul' (Hannah) to establish that prayer requires a heavy head (reverence), not just any emotional state.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the Mishnah's requirement that one must pray with reverence (כובד ראש).
Rabbi Elazar cites the verse about Hannah — 'וְהִיא מָרַת נָפֶשׁ' (and she was bitter of soul) — to prove that prayer requires a state of heaviness and reverence.

items.text: Objection: Hannah's case is unique
items.text_en: Objection: Hannah's case is unique
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Hannah's bitterness might be exceptional, not a general rule; perhaps only someone in extreme distress should pray with heavy head.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the proof from Hannah is inconclusive, since her extreme bitterness may be exceptional and not a general rule for prayer preparation.

items.text: Alternative source: Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina's derivation
items.text_en: Alternative source: Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina's derivation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina cites a different verse: 'And I, through Your abundant kindness, will enter Your house, I will bow toward Your holy sanctuary in fear of You' to establish that reverence is required for prayer.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina cites the verse 'And I, through Your abundant kindness, will enter Your house, I will bow toward Your holy sanctuary in fear of You' to establish that reverence (יראה) is required for prayer.

items.text: Objection: David's case might be special
items.text_en: Objection: David's case might be special
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that David, who wrote this verse, might have been particularly fearful due to his circumstances, not establishing a general rule.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that David's case might be exceptional, as he was particularly distressed and given to much prayer, so his practice does not establish a general rule.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's alternative: 'Worship with trembling'
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's alternative: 'Worship with trembling'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi cites the verse 'Worship the Lord with reverence and rejoice with trembling' to argue that joy must be accompanied by fear, establishing the need for a heavy head even in joy.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi derives the requirement for a heavy head from the verse 'Worship the Lord in the beauty of holiness' by reinterpreting 'beauty' as 'trembling'.

items.text: Objection: 'Hadrat' might mean literal adornment
items.text_en: Objection: 'Hadrat' might mean literal adornment
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that 'hadrat' could mean literal adornment (splendor), not trembling; citing Rav Yehuda who would adorn himself before prayer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that 'hadrat' might mean literal adornment (splendor), not trembling, citing Rav Yehuda who would adorn himself before prayer.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's resolution: Both meanings apply
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's resolution: Both meanings apply
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the verse 'Serve the Lord with joy, come before Him with singing' (Psalms 100:2) implies joy, but the earlier verse 'Worship the Lord with reverence' (Psalms 2:11) mandates trembling, so both are needed.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the contradiction by citing the verse 'עִבְדוּ אֶת ה׳ בְּיִרְאָה וְגִילוּ בִּרְעָדָה' (Serve the Lord with fear and rejoice with trembling), showing that both joy and trembling are required.

items.text: Gemara's explanation: Joy must be accompanied by fear
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation: Joy must be accompanied by fear
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that 'rejoice with trembling' means that in a place of joy, there should also be fear, as per Rav Ada bar Matna citing Rabbah.

sub.text: Rav Ada bar Matna citing Rabbah
sub.text_en: Rav Ada bar Matna citing Rabbah
sub.desc_en: Rav Ada bar Matna in the name of Rabbah explains that the verse 'וְגִילוּ בִּרְעָדָה' teaches that in a place of joy, there must also be fear.

items.text: Abaye's observation: Rabbah's joy without fear
items.text_en: Abaye's observation: Rabbah's joy without fear
items.desc_en: Abaye notices Rabbah laughing excessively and quotes the verse 'Rejoice with trembling', prompting Rabbah to explain he is wearing tefillin, which brings fear of God.

sub.desc_en: Abaye, sitting before Rabbah, sees him laughing excessively and quotes the verse 'Rejoice with trembling'.
Rabbah responds that he is wearing תפילין (phylacteries), which brings fear of God and justifies his joy.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's observation: Rabbi Zeira's excessive joy
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's observation: Rabbi Zeira's excessive joy
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya sees Rabbi Zeira laughing excessively and quotes 'In all sorrow there is profit' (Proverbs 14:23), implying joy should be moderated; Rabbi Zeira explains he is wearing tefillin.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya, seeing Rabbi Zeira laughing excessively, quotes Proverbs 14:23 to question whether such joy is appropriate.
Rabbi Zeira explains that his joy is justified because he is wearing תפילין (phylacteries), which brings a sense of holiness and joy.

items.text: Mar bar Ravina's wedding celebration: Joy with fear
items.text_en: Mar bar Ravina's wedding celebration: Joy with fear
items.desc_en: Mar bar Ravina hosts a wedding celebration for his son, and the rabbans are excessively joyful; he reminds them of the need for fear, citing 'Rejoice with trembling'.

sub.desc_en: Mar bar Ravina holds a wedding feast for his son and sees the rabbis excessively joyful.
Mar bar Ravina rebukes the rabbis for excessive joy, citing the verse 'Rejoice with trembling'.

items.text: Stories of breaking vessels to sober wedding guests
items.text_en: Stories of breaking vessels to sober wedding guests
items.desc_en: Mar bar Ravina and Rav Ashi break expensive vessels before their wedding guests to curb excessive joy, teaching that one should not be overly happy in this world. The rabbis then ask Rav Hamnuna Zuti to lead a song, and he responds with a lament about mortality.

sub.desc_en: Mar bar Ravina brings an expensive cup worth 400 zuz and breaks it before his wedding guests to sober them from excessive joy.
Rav Ashi similarly breaks a white glass cup at his son's wedding to curb the rabbis' excessive joy.

The rabbis ask Rav Hamnuna Zuti to lead a song at Mar bar Ravina's wedding, but he responds with a lament about mortality, and when asked what they should respond, he says: 'Where is the Torah and where is the commandment that will shield us?'

items.text: Prohibition against filling one's mouth with laughter
items.text_en: Prohibition against filling one's mouth with laughter
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai states that it is forbidden for a person to fill his mouth with laughter in this world, citing the verse that laughter will only be full in the future when the nations acknowledge God's greatness. Reish Lakish never laughed after hearing this from his teacher.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai that it is forbidden to fill one's mouth with laughter in this world, citing the verse that laughter will only be full in the future when the nations acknowledge God's greatness.
The gemara reports that Reish Lakish never filled his mouth with laughter after hearing this teaching from Rabbi Yochanan.

items.text: Entering prayer from a settled halakha
items.text_en: Entering prayer from a settled halakha
items.desc_en: The Gemara teaches that one should not stand to pray from a state of judgment or a matter of halakha, but from a settled halakha. Abaye, Rava, and an alternative explanation provide examples of settled halakhot, such as the stringency of women regarding menstrual blood, the exemption of untithed produce fed to animals, and the prohibition against benefiting from blood of sacrificial animals.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that one should not stand to pray from a state of judgment or a matter of halakha, but only from a settled halakha (הלכה פסוקה).
The Gemara asks: What is an example of a settled halakha (הלכה פסוקה)?
Abaye answers: Like the case of Rabbi Zeira, who taught that Jewish women have adopted a stringency that even seeing a drop of blood the size of a mustard seed requires seven clean days.

Rava answers: Like the case of Rav Hoshaya, who taught that one may circumvent the tithe obligation by bringing untithed produce in its chaff so that his animal eats it, and it is exempt from מעשר (tithe).

An alternative explanation is offered: Like the case of Rav Huna citing Rabbi Ze'ira, that one who bleeds a consecrated animal is forbidden from benefiting from the blood and is liable for מעילה (misuse of sacred property).
The Gemara concludes: The Rabbis act according to the Mishnah (praying from a settled halakha), while Rav Ashi acts according to the baraita (praying from a settled halakha as well).

items.text: Proper mindset for prayer and parting
items.text_en: Proper mindset for prayer and parting
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one should not pray from sadness, laziness, laughter, conversation, frivolity, or idle talk, but from the joy of a mitzvah. Similarly, one should not part from a friend with idle talk but with a matter of halakha, as found with the early prophets who ended with words of praise and comfort.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that one should not stand to pray from sadness, laziness, laughter, conversation, frivolity, or idle talk, but from the joy of a mitzvah.
The baraita extends the principle to parting from a friend, which should be with a matter of halakha, as exemplified by the early prophets who ended with words of praise and comfort.
Mari bar brei d'Rav Huna teaches that one should only part from a friend with a matter of halakha, so that the friend will remember him through it.

items.text: Stories of accompanying and parting with halakha
items.text_en: Stories of accompanying and parting with halakha
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana accompanied Rav Shimi bar Ashi and discussed the origin of the Babylonian pits from Adam's decree on settlement. Rav Mordechai accompanied Rav Shimi bar Ashi from Hagronya to Bei Keifei, illustrating the practice of parting with a halakhic discussion.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana accompanies Rav Shimi bar Ashi and asks about the origin of the Babylonian pits from Adam's decree on settlement.

sub.text: Rav Shimi bar Ashi citing Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina
sub.text_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi citing Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina
sub.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi responds by citing Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's teaching that any land Adam decreed for settlement was settled, and any he did not decree was not.
A second story illustrates the practice of parting with a halakhic discussion: Rav Mordechai accompanied Rav Shimi bar Ashi from Hagronya to Bei Keifei (or Bei Dura).

items.text: Laws of prayer: intention, brevity, and windows
items.text_en: Laws of prayer: intention, brevity, and windows
items.desc_en: The Gemara teaches that one must direct their heart to heaven in prayer, as per Abba Shaul. Rabbi Akiva would shorten his prayer with the congregation but pray extensively alone due to prostrations. Rabbi Chiya bar Abba says one should always pray in a house with windows, as per Daniel.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that one must direct their heart to heaven in prayer, and Abba Shaul provides a biblical sign for this.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Akiva's practice
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Akiva's practice
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda describes Rabbi Akiva's practice: he shortened his prayer with the congregation to avoid burdening them, but when praying alone he was found prostrating in different corners.
Rabbi Chiya bar Abba rules that one should always pray in a house with windows, as derived from Daniel's practice.

items.text: Deriving prayer laws from biblical figures
items.text_en: Deriving prayer laws from biblical figures
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives various laws of prayer from Daniel, David, Hannah, and Solomon: fixed prayer times, facing Jerusalem, not raising one's voice, and the order of requests. It concludes that one may ask personal needs after the prayer, even as lengthy as the Yom Kippur confession.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the possibility that one may pray all day, and immediately rejects it by citing Daniel's fixed prayer times.
The Gemara asks whether the obligation to pray three times began only in exile, and answers from Daniel that he prayed this way before the exile.
The Gemara asks whether one may pray facing any direction, and answers from the verse that one must face Jerusalem.
The Gemara asks whether one may combine all three prayers into one, and answers from David's verse that they are distinct times.
The Gemara asks whether one may raise one's voice in prayer, and answers from Hannah that her voice was not heard.
The Gemara asks whether one may ask personal needs before prayer, and answers from Solomon that prayer (תפילה) comes before supplication (רנה).
The Gemara concludes that one may not insert personal requests after 'Emet veYatziv' in the morning, but after the prayer (the Amidah) one may say even a lengthy confession like Yom Kippur's.

sub.text: Rav Chiya bar Ashi in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chiya bar Ashi in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Ashi cites Rav to support the ruling: although one may ask personal needs in 'Shomea Tefillah', after the prayer one may say even a Yom Kippur-style confession.

items.text: Laws from Hannah's prayer
items.text_en: Laws from Hannah's prayer
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna derives several halakhot from the verses about Hannah's prayer: intention of the heart, moving the lips, not raising one's voice, and that a drunk person is forbidden to pray. Rabbi Elazar adds a lesson from Eli's rebuke.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna derives four halakhot from the verses about Hannah's prayer: intention of the heart, moving the lips, not raising one's voice, and that a drunk person is forbidden to pray.
Rabbi Elazar adds a lesson from Eli's rebuke of Hannah, that one who sees something improper in a colleague must judge him favorably.

items.text: Hannah's response to Eli's suspicion
items.text_en: Hannah's response to Eli's suspicion
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Hannah's response to Eli's accusation that she was drunk. Two versions are given: one where she says he is not a master in this matter and the Divine Spirit does not rest upon him, and another where she questions why he judged her unfavorably.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that one must rebuke improper behavior, then presents Ulla's (or Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's) version of Hannah's response to Eli: she tells him he is not a master in this matter and the Divine Spirit does not rest upon him for suspecting her.
An alternative version is given: Hannah asked Eli if he is not a master, questioning why he judged her unfavorably rather than favorably, and reminding him that she is a woman of sorrowful spirit.

items.text: One suspected must inform
items.text_en: One suspected must inform
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar derives from Hannah's statement that she did not drink wine that one who is suspected of something they did not do must inform the accuser.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar derives from Hannah's statement that she did not drink wine that one who is suspected of something they did not do must inform the accuser.

items.text: Praying while drunk is like idolatry
items.text_en: Praying while drunk is like idolatry
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar derives from the phrase 'daughter of Belial' that a drunk person who prays is like an idol worshipper, using a verbal analogy with the verse about idolatry.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar derives from the phrase 'בת בליעל' (daughter of Belial) that a drunk person who prays is like an idol worshipper, using a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) with the verse about idolatry.

items.text: One who suspects must appease and bless
items.text_en: One who suspects must appease and bless
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar derives from Eli's response that one who suspects another of something they did not do must appease them and even bless them.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar derives from Eli's response that one who suspects another of something they did not do must appease them and even bless them.

items.text: Hannah's prayer and the name 'Tzevaot'
items.text_en: Hannah's prayer and the name 'Tzevaot'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar notes that Hannah was the first to call God 'Tzevaot'. The Gemara then recounts Hannah's argument before God using a parable of a king's feast, and her threat to seclude herself with her husband to force God to fulfill the sotah verse.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar notes that Hannah was the first person to call God by the name 'Tzevaot'.
Hannah asks God rhetorically whether among all the hosts He created, it is too difficult to give her one son.
The Gemara presents a parable of a poor man at a king's feast to illustrate Hannah's argument.
Rabbi Elazar reports that Hannah said to God: 'If You see (my plight) — good; if not — You will see (my drastic action).'
Hannah threatens to seclude herself with her husband Elkanah, forcing God to fulfill the sotah verse that promises children to the innocent woman.

items.text: The dispute about the sotah verse
items.text_en: The dispute about the sotah verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva regarding the verse 'and she shall be cleared and shall conceive seed'. One says it means a barren woman is remembered, the other that it changes the nature of childbirth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: the verse 'וְנִקְּתָה וְנִזְרְעָה זָרַע' works well for the opinion that a barren woman is remembered, but what about the opinion that it changes the nature of childbirth?

The baraita cites the dispute: Rabbi Yishmael says the verse teaches that a barren woman is remembered, while Rabbi Akiva says it teaches that a woman who gave birth in pain will give birth easily, short children become tall, etc.

items.text: The Torah speaks in human language
items.text_en: The Torah speaks in human language
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the double expression 'if seeing, you will see' as the Torah speaking in human language.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the double expression 'if seeing, you will see' as the Torah speaking in human language (דִּבְּרָה תּוֹרָה כִּלְשׁוֹן בְּנֵי אָדָם).

items.text: The three 'amotecha' and the three mitzvot of women
items.text_en: The three 'amotecha' and the three mitzvot of women
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina explains that Hannah's three mentions of 'amotecha' correspond to the three mitzvot for which women die: niddah, challah, and lighting the Shabbat candles.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the three verses from Hannah's prayer that each contain the word 'amotecha' (Your maidservant).

Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina explains that Hannah's three mentions of 'amotecha' correspond to the three mitzvot for which women die: niddah, challah, and lighting the Shabbat candles, and she protests that she has not violated any of them.

items.text: Interpretations of 'zera anashim'
items.text_en: Interpretations of 'zera anashim'
items.desc_en: Various Amoraim interpret the phrase 'zera anashim': Rav says a man among men, Shmuel says seed that anoints two men (Saul and David), Rabbi Yochanan says seed equal to two men (Moses and Aaron), and the Rabbis say seed that is absorbed among men.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the meaning of the phrase 'zera anashim' (seed of men) in Hannah's prayer.
Rav interprets 'zera anashim' as a man among men, i.e., a son who is a man among other men.
Shmuel interprets 'zera anashim' as seed that anoints two men, namely Saul and David.
Rabbi Yochanan interprets 'zera anashim' as seed equal to two men, namely Moses and Aaron.
The Rabbis interpret 'zera anashim' as seed that is absorbed among men, i.e., a son who is not outstanding.
Rav Dimi adds that the son was neither tall nor short, neither wise nor foolish, elaborating on the Rabbis' interpretation.

items.text: Sitting within four cubits of prayer
items.text_en: Sitting within four cubits of prayer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi derives from Hannah's statement that it is forbidden to sit within four cubits of one who is praying.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi derives from Hannah's statement 'אֲנִי הָאִשָּׁה הַנִּצֶּבֶת עִמְּכָה בָּזֶה' that it is forbidden to sit within four cubits of one who is praying.

items.text: Samuel taught halakha before his teacher Eli
items.text_en: Samuel taught halakha before his teacher Eli
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains that Samuel taught halakha before his teacher Eli, ruling that slaughter by a non-priest is valid. Eli rebuked him, saying one who teaches halakha before their teacher is liable to death, but Hannah intervened and Eli blessed her.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asserts that Samuel taught halakha before his teacher Eli, citing the verse about bringing the boy to Eli.

The gemara explains the context: Eli sought a priest to slaughter, but Samuel ruled that slaughter by a non-priest (זר) is valid, citing the verse 'וְהִקְרִיבוּ הַכֹּהֲנִים' to prove that slaughter is not limited to priests.

Eli acknowledges Samuel's correct ruling but rebukes him for teaching halakha before his teacher, declaring him liable to death; Hannah then intervenes, reminding Eli that she prayed for this specific child.

items.text: Hannah's argument about the purpose of body parts
items.text_en: Hannah's argument about the purpose of body parts
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra explains that Hannah argued before God that every body part has a purpose, and her breasts were for nursing, so she should be given a son.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains that Hannah argued before God that every body part has a purpose, including her breasts for nursing, so she should be given a son.

items.text: Fasting on Shabbat and its remedy
items.text_en: Fasting on Shabbat and its remedy
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra says that one who fasts on Shabbat has their decree of seventy years torn up, but they are still punished for the enjoyment of Shabbat. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says the remedy is to fast another fast.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar citing Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar citing Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra states that one who fasts on Shabbat has their decree of seventy years torn up, but they are still punished for the enjoyment of Shabbat.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak provides the remedy: one should fast another fast to atone for the lost enjoyment of Shabbat.

items.text: Hannah and Elijah spoke harshly to God
items.text_en: Hannah and Elijah spoke harshly to God
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar says that Hannah spoke harshly to God, as indicated by the phrase 'prayed upon God'. Similarly, Elijah spoke harshly to God, and Rabbi Shmuel bar Rabbi Yitzchak says that God eventually agreed with Elijah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that Hannah spoke harshly to God, as derived from the phrase 'prayed upon God'.
Rabbi Elazar adds that Elijah also spoke harshly to God, citing the verse 'And You turned their heart backward'.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Rabbi Yitzchak asserts that God ultimately agreed with Elijah, though the proof text is not fully cited here.

items.text: Three verses that prevent Israel's downfall
items.text_en: Three verses that prevent Israel's downfall
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina and Rav Papa cite three or four verses that show God's control over Israel's fate, implying that without these verses, Israel would have been destroyed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing the verse 'וַאֲשֶׁר הֲרֵעֹתִי' (and that which I have done evil).

Rabbi Chama bar Chanina states that without three specific verses, Israel's enemies would have stumbled, listing them: the opening verse, 'הִנֵּה כַחֹמֶר' (like clay in the potter's hand), and 'וַהֲסִרֹתִי אֶת לֵב הָאֶבֶן' (I will remove the heart of stone).
Rav Papa adds a fourth verse from Ezekiel: 'וְאֶת רוּחִי אֶתֵּן בְּקִרְבְּכֶם' (I will put My spirit within you).

items.text: Moses' boldness against Heaven
items.text_en: Moses' boldness against Heaven
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar interprets the verse 'Vayitpallel Moshe el Hashem' as 'against Hashem', indicating Moses spoke insolently. The school of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov supports this by reading alef as ayin.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that Moses spoke insolently toward Heaven, interpreting the verse 'וַיִּתְפַּלֵּל מֹשֶׁה אֶל ה׳' as if it read 'עַל ה׳' (against Hashem).

sub.text: School of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.text_en: School of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov supports this reading by noting that they interchange the letters alef and ayin, allowing 'אֶל' to be read as 'עַל'.

items.text: The wealth that led to the Golden Calf
items.text_en: The wealth that led to the Golden Calf
items.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yannai and others argue that Israel's abundance of silver and gold caused them to sin. Various parables and verses illustrate that wealth and satiety lead to rebellion.

sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yannai interprets the verse 'וְדִי זָהָב' (enough of gold) to mean that the abundance of silver and gold caused Israel to make the Golden Calf.
The school of Rabbi Yannai offers a parable: a lion only roars from a basket of meat, not straw, implying that wealth causes rebellion.
Rabbi Oshaya gives a parable of a lean but strong cow that kicks after being fed vetch, showing that satiety leads to rebellion.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan gives a parable of a father who bathes, anoints, feeds, and gives money to his son, then places him at a brothel entrance, implying that wealth without restraint leads to sin.

sub.text: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Huna quoting Rav Sheshet
sub.text_en: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Huna quoting Rav Sheshet
sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet cites the folk saying 'a full belly leads to bad behavior' and supports it with the verse 'כְּמַרְעִיתָם וַיִּשְׂבָּעוּ שָׂבְעוּ וַיָּרׇם לִבָּם עַל כֵּן שְׁכֵחוּנִי' (as they were fed they became full, their heart was exalted, therefore they forgot Me).
Rav Nachman cites the verse 'וְרָם לְבָבֶךָ וְשָׁכַחְתָּ אֶת ה׳' (your heart becomes haughty and you forget the Lord) as proof that wealth leads to forgetting God.
The Rabbis cite the verse 'וְאָכַל וְשָׂבַע וְדָשֵׁן וּפָנָה' (he ate, became full, grew fat, and turned away) as another proof that satiety leads to rebellion.

items.text: God concedes to Moses
items.text_en: God concedes to Moses
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quotes Rabbi Yonatan that God admitted Moses was right, as per the verse 'And silver I multiplied for them, and gold they made for Baal'.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quoting Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quoting Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan proves that God conceded to Moses from the verse 'וישמן ישורון ויבעט' (Jeshurun grew fat and kicked), citing the continuation 'וכסף הרביתי להם וזהב עשו לבעל' (and I multiplied silver for them, and gold they made for Baal).

items.text: Moses' descent from greatness and his prayer
items.text_en: Moses' descent from greatness and his prayer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains that God told Moses to descend from his greatness because it was only for Israel. Moses then realized the matter depended on him and strengthened himself in prayer. A parable illustrates this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara quotes the verse 'Go, descend' and asks what it means.
Rabbi Elazar explains that God told Moses to descend from his greatness because it was only for Israel, and Moses became weak and unable to speak.
When God said 'Let Me be and I will destroy them,' Moses realized the matter depended on him and strengthened himself in prayer.
A parable of a king who was angry at his son and a friend who realized he could intervene and saved the son.

items.text: Moses seizes God and argues from the patriarchs
items.text_en: Moses seizes God and argues from the patriarchs
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu says Moses metaphorically seized God by His garment, demanding forgiveness. Rabbi Elazar adds that Moses argued that if a three-legged stool (patriarchs) cannot stand before God's anger, a one-legged stool (himself) certainly cannot, and he would be embarrassed before the patriarchs.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu states that Moses metaphorically seized God by His garment, demanding forgiveness for Israel.
Rabbi Elazar adds that Moses argued from the patriarchs (a three-legged stool) that he, a one-legged stool, cannot stand before God's anger, and would be embarrassed before them.

items.text: Interpretations of 'Vayechal Moshe'
items.text_en: Interpretations of 'Vayechal Moshe'
items.desc_en: Various Amoraim interpret the word 'vayechal' in different ways: Rabbi Elazar says Moses made God sick, Rava says he annulled God's vow, Shmuel says he endangered himself, Rava bar Yitzchak says he brought mercy, and the Rabbis say he said it is profane for God to do this. Rabbi Eliezer HaGadol says he was seized by trembling.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar interprets 'vayechal' to mean that Moses stood in prayer until he made God sick (i.e., weakened His resolve).

Rava interprets 'vayechal' to mean that Moses annulled God's vow, citing a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from the verse 'לֹא יַחֵל דְּבָרוֹ' (he shall not break his word), where others may annul it for him.
Shmuel interprets 'vayechal' to mean that Moses endangered himself to death for Israel, as it says 'מְחֵנִי נָא מִסִּפְרְךָ' (erase me from Your book).
Rava bar Yitzchak interprets 'vayechal' to mean that Moses brought the attribute of mercy (מידת רחמים) upon Israel.
The Rabbis interpret 'vayechal' to mean that Moses said to God: 'It is profane (חולין) for You to do this thing.'
A baraita cites Rabbi Eliezer HaGadol who interprets 'vayechal' to mean that Moses stood in prayer until trembling (אחילו) seized him.
Abaye explains that 'אחילו' (trembling) refers to 'אשתא דגרמי' (a fever of the bones).

items.text: Moses' argument from God's oath
items.text_en: Moses' argument from God's oath
items.desc_en: Moses argues that since God swore by His great name, which is eternal, the oath is eternal. Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani debate whether the subsequent verse is the student's or the teacher's words, concluding Moses asked what to tell Israel.

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites the verse where Moses invokes God's oath and asks what the word 'בך' (by You) implies.
Rabbi Elazar explains that Moses argued: had God sworn by heaven and earth, the oath could be voided, but since He swore by His great name which is eternal, the oath is eternal.
The gemara notes a textual anomaly: the verse says 'אשר אמרתי' (which I said) instead of the expected 'אשר אמרת' (which You said).
Rabbi Elazar resolves the anomaly: the first part of the verse is the student's (Moses') words, and the latter part is God's words.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani objects that both parts are the student's words, and explains that Moses asked what to tell Israel now that God's promise seems unfulfilled.

items.text: The nations' claim and God's concession
items.text_en: The nations' claim and God's concession
items.desc_en: Moses argues that the nations will say God's power is weak like a female. God responds that they saw miracles at the sea, but Moses counters that they might say He could stand against one king but not thirty-one. Rabbi Yochanan says God conceded, as per the verse 'Salachti kidevarecha'.

sub.desc_en: The gemara questions the biblical wording 'מבלתי יכלת ה (from lack of God's ability)', noting it should have said 'יכול ה (God is able)'.
Rabbi Elazar explains that Moses argued before God that the nations would say God's power is weak like a female (נקבה) and unable to save.
God objects that the nations already saw the miracles and mighty acts He performed for Israel at the sea.
Moses rejects God's objection, arguing the nations could still say God could stand against one king but not against thirty-one kings.

Rabbi Yochanan concludes that God conceded to Moses, as the verse says 'סלחתי כדבריך (I have forgiven according to your words)', and the school of Rabbi Yishmael adds that the nations will indeed say this.

items.text: Fortunate student whose teacher concedes
items.text_en: Fortunate student whose teacher concedes
items.desc_en: Rava bar Yitzchak says that God told Moses 'You have revived Me with your words', indicating that God conceded to Moses' argument.

sub.desc_en: Rava bar Yitzchak declares that a fortunate student is one whose teacher concedes to him, citing the verse where God tells Moses 'You have revived Me with your words'.

items.text: Order of prayer: praise before petition
items.text_en: Order of prayer: praise before petition
items.desc_en: Rabbi Simlai derives from Moses that one should first praise God and then pray, as Moses did in his prayer to enter the land. The segment ends with a mnemonic list of topics.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Simlai teaches that one should always arrange praise of God before praying, citing Moses who first praised God before petitioning to enter the land.
The gemara cites the verses from Moses' prayer to demonstrate the pattern of praise before petition.
The gemara provides a mnemonic list of topics (deeds, charity, sacrifice, priest, fast, shoe, iron) for the preceding discussion.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's comparisons: prayer vs. good deeds, fasting vs. charity, prayer vs. sacrifices
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's comparisons: prayer vs. good deeds, fasting vs. charity, prayer vs. sacrifices
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asserts three comparisons: prayer is greater than good deeds, as even Moses was only answered through prayer; fasting is greater than charity because it involves one's body; and prayer is greater than sacrifices, as shown by a verse from Isaiah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asserts that prayer is greater than good deeds, citing Moses who was only answered through prayer.
Rabbi Elazar asserts that fasting is greater than charity because it involves one's body, not just money.
Rabbi Elazar asserts that prayer is greater than sacrifices, citing a verse from Isaiah.

items.text: A priest who killed may not raise his hands
items.text_en: A priest who killed may not raise his hands
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that a priest who has killed a person may not perform the priestly blessing, citing the verse 'your hands are full of blood'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that a priest who has killed a person may not perform the priestly blessing (נשיאת כפים), citing the verse 'your hands are full of blood'.

items.text: Gates of prayer locked, but gates of tears not locked; iron wall separates Israel from God
items.text_en: Gates of prayer locked, but gates of tears not locked; iron wall separates Israel from God
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that since the Temple's destruction, the gates of prayer are locked, but the gates of tears are not. Rava would not decree a fast on a cloudy day. Rabbi Elazar adds that an iron wall separates Israel from their Father in heaven.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that since the Temple's destruction, the gates of prayer are locked, but the gates of tears are not locked.
Rava would not decree a fast on a cloudy day, citing the verse that clouds prevent prayer from passing.
Rabbi Elazar adds that an iron wall separates Israel from their Father in heaven.

items.text: Lengthy prayer: beneficial or harmful?
items.text_en: Lengthy prayer: beneficial or harmful?
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanin says one who lengthens prayer will not return empty-handed, citing Moses. Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba objects, citing Rabbi Yochanan that lengthy prayer with intent leads to heartache, and the remedy is Torah study. The Gemara resolves the contradiction: one who lengthens and focuses leads to heartache, but one who lengthens without focusing does not.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanin in the name of Rabbi Chanina states that one who lengthens prayer will not return empty-handed, citing Moses as proof.

sub.text: Gemara's objection via Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection via Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, who says that one who lengthens prayer and focuses on it will ultimately suffer heartache, and the remedy is Torah study.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: one who lengthens and focuses leads to heartache, but one who lengthens without focusing does not.

items.text: Four things requiring strengthening: Torah, good deeds, prayer, and derech eretz
items.text_en: Four things requiring strengthening: Torah, good deeds, prayer, and derech eretz
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina says if one prays and is not answered, he should pray again. The Sages teach that four things require strengthening: Torah, good deeds, prayer, and derech eretz, each supported by a biblical verse.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina rules that if one prayed and was not answered, he should pray again, citing the verse 'קַוֵּה אֶל ה׳ חֲזַק וְיַאֲמֵץ לִבֶּךָ וְקַוֵּה אֶל ה׳'.
The Sages teach in a baraita that four things require strengthening: Torah, good deeds, prayer, and derech eretz (proper conduct).

sub.text: Baraita (Sages) — proof for Torah and good deeds
sub.text_en: Baraita (Sages) — proof for Torah and good deeds
sub.desc_en: The baraita derives Torah and good deeds from the verse 'רַק חֲזַק וֶאֱמַץ מְאֹד', interpreting 'חֲזַק' as Torah and 'וֶאֱמַץ' as good deeds.
The baraita derives prayer from the same verse used by Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina, 'קַוֵּה אֶל ה׳ חֲזַק וְיַאֲמֵץ לִבֶּךָ וְקַוֵּה אֶל ה׳'.
The baraita derives derech eretz (proper conduct) from the verse 'חֲזַק וְנִתְחַזַּק בְּעַד עַמֵּנוּ', referring to military or communal strengthening.

items.text: Allegory of Zion's complaint and God's response
items.text_en: Allegory of Zion's complaint and God's response
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse 'Zion said, God has forsaken me'. Resh Lakish explains that Israel complains God forgot them like a man who remarries. God responds by describing the vast cosmos created for Israel. The dialogue continues with God recalling the sacrifices in the desert, Israel's concern about the Golden Calf, and God's promise not to forget Sinai. Rabbi Elazar bar Oshaya identifies the 'these' as the Golden Calf and 'I will not forget you' as Sinai.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse repeats 'forsaken' and 'forgotten' if they are synonymous.
Resh Lakish explains that Israel complains God forgot them like a man who remarries and forgets his first wife.
God responds by describing the vast cosmos created for Israel, questioning how they could think He forgot them.
God asks if He could forget the sacrifices Israel offered in the desert.
Israel asks whether God will forget the sin of the Golden Calf.
God responds that the sin of the Golden Calf will be forgotten.
Israel asks whether God will forget the revelation at Sinai.
God promises not to forget the events of Sinai.
Rabbi Elazar bar Oshaya identifies 'these' as the Golden Calf and 'I will not forget you' as Sinai.

items.text: The practice of the early pious ones: tarrying before and after prayer
items.text_en: The practice of the early pious ones: tarrying before and after prayer
items.desc_en: The early pious ones would tarry one hour before prayer. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi derives this from Psalms. He also says one must tarry one hour after prayer. A baraisa confirms this, and the Gemara asks how they had time for Torah and work, answering that because they were pious, their Torah was preserved and their work blessed.

sub.desc_en: The mishna states that the early pious ones would tarry one hour before prayer.
The Gemara asks: From where are these matters derived?
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi answers that the source is the verse 'אַשְׁרֵי יוֹשְׁבֵי בֵיתֶךָ' (Happy are those who dwell in Your house).

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi adds that one must also tarry one hour after prayer, citing the verse 'אַךְ צַדִּיקִים יוֹדוּ לִשְׁמֶךָ יֵשְׁבוּ יְשָׁרִים אֶת פָּנֶיךָ' (Surely the righteous will give thanks unto Your name, the upright will sit before You).
A baraita is cited that supports the requirement to tarry one hour before and one hour after prayer, with the same prooftexts.
The Gemara cites a baraita detailing the full practice (tarry, pray, tarry) and asks: If they spend nine hours daily in prayer, how is their Torah preserved and their work accomplished?
The Gemara answers: Because they were pious, their Torah was preserved and their work was blessed.

items.text: Interrupting prayer for a greeting: kings and danger
items.text_en: Interrupting prayer for a greeting: kings and danger
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that even if a king greets one during prayer, one should not respond. Rav Yosef limits this to Jewish kings, but for non-Jewish kings one may stop. An objection is raised about seeing danger; the Gemara resolves that if one can shorten, he should, otherwise he stops. A story is told of a pious man who did not return a greeting from a hegemon, and the man explains that if he were standing before a mortal king, he would not interrupt.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that even if a king greets one during prayer, one should not respond.
Rav Yosef limits the Mishnah's ruling to Jewish kings, but for non-Jewish kings one may interrupt prayer.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that says if one sees danger approaching, he should not interrupt but shorten his prayer.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: if one can shorten the prayer, he should; otherwise, he interrupts.
A baraita tells a story of a pious man who did not return a greeting from a hegemon during prayer, and the hegemon threatened him.
The pious man explains that if he were standing before a mortal king, he would not interrupt, so how much more so before the King of kings.

items.text: Story of the pious man and the hegemon
items.text_en: Story of the pious man and the hegemon
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the story of a pious man who did not interrupt his prayer to greet a hegemon. The hegemon initially threatened him, but after the pious man explained his reasoning with a kal vachomer, the hegemon was appeased and let him go in peace.

sub.desc_en: The hegemon asks the pious man whether he would return a greeting, and the man answers no; the hegemon then asks what would be done to him, and the man explains he would be executed.
The pious man argues by קל וחומר (a fortiori) that since he would not interrupt for a mortal king, he certainly should not interrupt for the King of Kings.
The hegemon is immediately appeased, and the pious man departs to his home in peace.

items.text: Interruption for a snake vs. scorpion
items.text_en: Interruption for a snake vs. scorpion
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that even if a snake is wrapped around one's heel, one should not interrupt prayer. Rav Sheshet qualifies this: only for a snake, but for a scorpion one may interrupt. A challenge is raised from a baraita about testifying that someone who fell into a pit of snakes and scorpions is dead, implying scorpions are as dangerous as snakes. The Gemara answers that there, due to the crowding, they harm each other.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one should not interrupt prayer even if a snake is wrapped around one's heel.
Rav Sheshet qualifies the Mishnah: the rule applies only to a snake, but for a scorpion one may interrupt prayer.
The Gemara challenges Rav Sheshet from a baraita that one may testify to the death of someone who fell into a pit of snakes and scorpions, implying scorpions are as deadly as snakes.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: in the pit, due to crowding, the scorpions harm each other and become more dangerous, but in the open they are less aggressive.

items.text: Interruption for a bull and the story of the arvad
items.text_en: Interruption for a bull and the story of the arvad
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak says that if one sees bulls (charging), one may interrupt prayer, citing a baraita about distancing from a tam bull. A tradition from Rabbi Meir advises climbing to a roof and removing the ladder. Shmuel limits this to a black bull in Nisan when the Satan dances between its horns.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak rules that one who sees bulls may interrupt prayer, citing a baraita of Rav Hoshaya about distancing from a tam bull and a muad bull.
A tradition in the name of Rabbi Meir advises that if a bull's head is in a basket, one should climb to the roof and remove the ladder.
Shmuel limits the danger to a black bull in Nisan, because the Satan dances between its horns.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa and the arvad
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa and the arvad
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates a story about a place where an arvad (a dangerous creature) was harming people. Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa placed his heel on its hole, the arvad bit him and died. He carried it to the study hall and taught that it is sin that kills, not the creature. The people declared woe to one who meets the arvad, and woe to the arvad that meets Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa.

sub.desc_en: The baraita relates that in a certain place an arvad (a dangerous creature) was harming people; Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa placed his heel on its hole, the arvad bit him and died.
Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa carries the dead arvad to the study hall and teaches that it is sin that kills, not the creature.
The people declare woe to one who meets the arvad, and woe to the arvad that meets Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on the placement of rain, request, and Havdalah
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on the placement of rain, request, and Havdalah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that rain is mentioned in the resurrection blessing, request in the blessing of the years, and Havdalah in Chonen HaDa'at. Rabbi Akiva says to say it as a separate fourth blessing, Rabbi Eliezer says in the thanksgiving blessing. The Gemara asks the reasons: Rav Yosef says rain is equal to resurrection, request is sustenance, Havdalah is wisdom. The Rabbis say Havdalah is placed in the blessing of weekday because it is a weekday matter.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the placement of rain, request, and Havdalah in the Amidah, with dissenting opinions from Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Eliezer.
The Gemara asks the reason for mentioning rain in the resurrection blessing.
Rav Yosef explains that rain is mentioned in the resurrection blessing because it is equivalent to resurrection.
The Gemara asks the reason for placing the request for rain in the blessing of the years.
Rav Yosef explains that the request for rain is placed in the blessing of the years because it is a matter of sustenance (פרנסה).
The Gemara asks the reason for placing Havdalah in the blessing of Chonen HaDa'at.
Rav Yosef explains that Havdalah is placed in the blessing of wisdom because it is a matter of wisdom (חכמה).
The Rabbis explain that Havdalah is placed in the blessing of weekday because it is a weekday matter (חול).

items.text: Greatness of da'at and the digression on nekama
items.text_en: Greatness of da'at and the digression on nekama
items.desc_en: Rav Ami says da'at is great because it was placed at the beginning of the weekday blessing and between two letters. Rabbi Elazar says the Temple is great because it was placed between two letters. Rav Acha bar Chinana objects that nekama is also between two letters. The Gemara answers that nekama is indeed great in its context, citing Ulla about two types of nekama: one for good and one for evil.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ami declares that da'at (knowledge/wisdom) is great because it was placed at the beginning of the weekday blessing (ברכת חונן הדעת).
Rav Ami adds that da'at is great because it is placed between two letters of God's name (אֵל דֵּעוֹת), and one without da'at is forbidden to receive mercy.
Rabbi Elazar states that the Temple (מקדש) is great because it is placed between two letters of God's name (פָּעַלְתָּ ה׳ מִקְּדָשׁ ה׳).
Rabbi Elazar adds that a person with da'at is as if the Temple was built in his days, linking the two concepts.
Rav Acha bar Chinana objects that by the same logic, nekama (vengeance) is also great because it appears between two letters (אֵל נְקָמוֹת ה׳).
The Gemara answers that nekama is indeed great in its own context, citing Ulla that there are two types of vengeance: one for good and one for evil.

items.text: History of Havdalah and the requirement to recite it over wine
items.text_en: History of Havdalah and the requirement to recite it over wine
items.desc_en: The Gemara returns to the Mishnah's dispute. Rav Shemen bar Abba asks Rabbi Yochanan where Havdalah was instituted. Rabbi Yochanan explains that initially it was in the prayer, when they became wealthy they instituted it over wine, when they became poor they returned it to the prayer, but they said one who recites it in prayer must also recite it over wine. This is supported by Rabbi Chiya bar Abba and by Rabba and Rav Yosef. Rava cites a baraita that one who forgets rain or request is returned, but for Havdalah he is not returned because he can say it over wine. The Gemara corrects the wording to 'because he says it over wine'. Rabbi Yosei asks Rabbi Yochanan and he confirms the requirement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's dispute regarding where to recite Havdalah, beginning with Rabbi Akiva's opinion.
Rav Shemen bar Abba asks Rabbi Yochanan where the members of the Great Assembly originally instituted Havdalah.

Rabbi Yochanan explains the historical stages: initially Havdalah was in the prayer, then over wine, then back to prayer, with the rule that one who recites it in prayer must also recite it over wine.

sub.text: Supporting baraita via Rabbi Chiya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita via Rabbi Chiya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: A supporting tradition is cited: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba reports the same historical account from Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.text: Supporting statement from Rabba and Rav Yosef
sub.text_en: Supporting statement from Rabba and Rav Yosef
sub.desc_en: Another supporting tradition: Rabba and Rav Yosef both rule that one who recites Havdalah in prayer must also recite it over wine.
Rava raises an objection from a baraita that distinguishes between forgetting rain/request (requires return) and forgetting Havdalah (no return because one can recite it over wine).
The Gemara resolves the objection by correcting the baraita's wording from 'because he can recite' to 'because he recites' over wine, implying obligation.

sub.text: Supporting inquiry from Rabbi Yosei to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Supporting inquiry from Rabbi Yosei to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: A further supporting tradition: Rabbi Yosei asked Rabbi Yochanan and received the same ruling that one must recite Havdalah over wine.

items.text: Further discussions on Havdalah: kal vachomer, beracha she'eina tzricha, and forgetting both
items.text_en: Further discussions on Havdalah: kal vachomer, beracha she'eina tzricha, and forgetting both
items.desc_en: A dilemma is raised: if one recites Havdalah over wine, must he also recite it in prayer? Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers with a kal vachomer from prayer. Rav Acha bar Chanina teaches that reciting Havdalah in prayer is more praiseworthy than over wine, but if one does both, blessings rest on his head. The Gemara objects that this would be a beracha she'eina tzricha, which violates 'lo tisa'. The text is corrected to 'if he recited in one and not the other'. Rav Chisda asks Rav Sheshet about one who forgot both, and he answers that he returns to the beginning.

sub.desc_en: A dilemma is raised: if one recites Havdalah over the cup, what is the ruling regarding whether he must also recite it in the prayer?
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers with a kal vachomer: if one who recited Havdalah in prayer must also recite over the cup, then one who recited over the cup certainly must recite in prayer.
Rav Acha Arikha teaches a baraita: one who recites Havdalah in prayer is more praiseworthy than one who recites over the cup, and if he does both, blessings rest on his head.
The Gemara objects that the baraita is self-contradictory: if prayer alone suffices, then reciting both would be an unnecessary blessing, violating 'lo tisa'.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by emending the baraita to read: if he recited in one and not the other, blessings rest on his head.
Rav Chisda asks Rav Sheshet about one who forgot Havdalah in both prayer and over the cup, and Rav Sheshet answers that he returns to the beginning.

items.text: Ravina asks Rava about the law of Havdalah
items.text_en: Ravina asks Rava about the law of Havdalah
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rava what the halakha is regarding Havdalah. Rava compares it to Kiddush: just as one who recites Kiddush in prayer must also recite it over a cup of wine, so too one who recites Havdalah in prayer must recite it over a cup of wine.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rava what the halakha is regarding Havdalah.
Rava answers that just as one who recites Kiddush in prayer must also recite it over a cup of wine, so too one who recites Havdalah in prayer must recite it over a cup of wine.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's opinion on Havdalah placement
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's opinion on Havdalah placement
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer states that Havdalah is recited in the 'Thanksgiving' blessing (Modim) of the Amidah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer states that Havdalah is recited in the Thanksgiving blessing (Modim) of the Amidah.

items.text: Debate about the halakha on a festival after Shabbat
items.text_en: Debate about the halakha on a festival after Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks Rabbi Chiyya bar Abin whether the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer on a festival that falls after Shabbat. Rabbi Chiyya confirms. The Gemara questions whether this implies a dispute, and examines whether the Sages and Rabbi Akiva disagree specifically in that case. The Gemara concludes that the Sages' dispute applies only during the rest of the year, not after Shabbat, and that Rabbi Akiva's opinion is not followed even then due to the number of blessings instituted.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks Rabbi Chiyya bar Abin whether the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer on a festival after Shabbat, and Rabbi Chiyya confirms.
The Gemara questions whether the statement 'halakha' implies that the Sages dispute Rabbi Eliezer's position.
The Gemara objects that the Sages indeed dispute Rabbi Eliezer's view.
The Gemara answers that the Sages' dispute applies only during the rest of the year, not on a festival after Shabbat.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Akiva disputes even in that case.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Akiva's opinion is not followed even then, because the number of blessings was instituted as seven, not eight.

items.text: Correction: 'Matin' rather than 'Halakha'
items.text_en: Correction: 'Matin' rather than 'Halakha'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira is told that the tradition was not 'halakha' but 'matin' (inclining). The Gemara cites a dispute: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi said 'halakha' in the name of Rabbeinu, while others said 'matin'.

sub.desc_en: The informant corrects Rabbi Zeira: the tradition was not 'halakha' but 'matin' (inclining).
The Gemara cites a dispute: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi said 'halakha' in the name of Rabbeinu, while others said 'matin'.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's versions, and Rabbi Zeira's endorsement
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's versions, and Rabbi Zeira's endorsement
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan said 'modim' (they agree), while Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said 'nir'in' (they appear). Rabbi Zeira advises holding Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's version because he was precise, like Rachava of Pumbedita. Rav Yosef says he knows neither version but knows the 'pearl' instituted by Rav and Shmuel in Babylonia.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports two versions of the ruling: Rabbi Yochanan said 'modim' (they agree), while Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said 'nir'in' (they appear).
Rabbi Zeira advises holding Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's version because he was precise in transmitting his master's teaching, like Rachava of Pumbedita.
The Gemara cites Rachava's precise description of the Temple Mount's double portico as an example of the precision Rabbi Zeira praised.
Rav Yosef says he knows neither version but knows the 'pearl' (the blessing formula) instituted by Rav and Shmuel in Babylonia.

items.text: The 'pearl' text for Havdalah in prayer
items.text_en: The 'pearl' text for Havdalah in prayer
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents the full text of the Havdalah blessing instituted by Rav and Shmuel, which distinguishes between the sanctity of Shabbat and that of the festival.

sub.desc_en: The full text of the Havdalah blessing instituted by Rav and Shmuel is presented, distinguishing between the sanctity of Shabbat and the festival.

items.text: Mishnah: Which prayer additions warrant silencing
items.text_en: Mishnah: Which prayer additions warrant silencing
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who says 'Upon a bird's nest may Your mercies reach', 'May Your name be mentioned for good', or 'Modim, modim' is silenced. The Gemara explains the reasons: 'Modim, modim' appears like two authorities; 'for good' implies only for good, contradicting the obligation to bless for evil; and regarding the bird's nest, two Amoraim in the West dispute: one says it casts jealousy on creation, the other says it makes God's attributes mercy when they are decrees.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists three prayer additions that warrant silencing the one who says them: mentioning mercy on a bird's nest, saying 'for good may Your name be mentioned', and repeating 'Modim'.

The Gemara explains the reasons for silencing 'Modim, modim' (appears like two authorities) and 'for good' (implies only for good, contradicting the obligation to bless for evil), then asks why the bird's nest phrase is silenced.
