Two Amoraim in the West dispute the reason: one says it casts jealousy on creation, the other says it makes God's attributes mercy when they are decrees.

items.text: Story of the one who prayed 'You had mercy on the bird's nest'
items.text_en: Story of the one who prayed 'You had mercy on the bird's nest'
items.desc_en: A person prayed before Rabbah saying 'You had mercy on the bird's nest, have mercy on us.' Rabbah praised him, but Abaye objected that the Mishnah says such a person is silenced. The Gemara explains that Rabbah only said this to sharpen Abaye.

sub.desc_en: A person descended before Rabbah and prayed 'You had mercy on the bird's nest, have mercy on us.'
Rabbah praised the person, saying how well he knows to appease his Master.
Abaye objected that the Mishnah explicitly says such a person is silenced.
The Gemara explains that Rabbah only said this to sharpen Abaye's understanding.

items.text: Story of the one who added many praises to God
items.text_en: Story of the one who added many praises to God
items.desc_en: A person prayed before Rabbi Chanina and added many adjectives praising God. Rabbi Chanina waited until he finished and then rebuked him, explaining that even the three standard praises (great, mighty, awesome) would not be said if not instituted by Moses and the Men of the Great Assembly. Adding more is like praising a king with silver when he has gold.

sub.desc_en: A person comes before Rabbi Chanina in prayer and recites many adjectives praising God beyond the standard three.
Rabbi Chanina rebukes the person, comparing excessive praise of God to praising a king who has gold with silver.

items.text: Discussion on fear of Heaven
items.text_en: Discussion on fear of Heaven
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina says everything is in Heaven's hands except fear of Heaven. The Gemara questions whether fear of Heaven is a small matter, citing Rabbi Chanina's own statement that God's treasury contains only the treasure of fear of Heaven. The Gemara resolves that relative to Moses it is a small matter, using a parable about a large vessel seeming small to one who has it.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina states that everything is in Heaven's hands except fear of Heaven, citing the verse 'וְעַתָּה יִשְׂרָאֵל מָה ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ שֹׁאֵל מֵעִמָּךְ כִּי אִם לְיִרְאָה'.

The Gemara objects: is fear of Heaven a small matter? It cites Rabbi Chanina in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai that God's treasury contains only the treasure of fear of Heaven, as per the verse 'יִרְאַת ה׳ הִיא אוֹצָרוֹ'.
The Gemara resolves that relative to Moses it is a small matter, using Rabbi Chanina's parable: a large vessel seems small to one who has it, but a small vessel seems large to one who lacks it.

items.text: The case of repeating 'Shema'
items.text_en: The case of repeating 'Shema'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira says one who says 'Shema, Shema' is like one who says 'Modim, modim'. The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that one who repeats Shema is merely 'disgraced' but not silenced. The Gemara resolves this by distinguishing between repeating a phrase and repeating a verse. Rav Pappa asks Abaye about a case where one did not intend initially but intended later, and Abaye responds.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that one who repeats 'We give thanks, we give thanks' is silenced.
Rabbi Zeira says that one who says 'Shema, Shema' is like one who says 'Modim, modim' and is silenced.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that one who repeats Shema is merely 'disgraced' but not silenced.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between repeating a single word (merely disgraced) and repeating an entire verse (silenced).
Rav Pappa asks Abaye: perhaps one who repeated Shema did not intend initially but intended later, so the repetition is justified?
Abaye begins his response to Rav Pappa (the text is cut off in the daf).

items.text: Gemara's opening question on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's opening question on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether there can be 'friendship' with Heaven, and states that if one does not intend from the beginning, he is struck until he does.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether there can be 'friendship' with Heaven, and states that if one does not intend from the beginning, he is struck until he does.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of the prayer leader
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of the prayer leader
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who says 'May the good bless you' is following heretical ways. If the prayer leader errs, another replaces him without refusal, starting from where he erred. The leader should not answer 'Amen' after the priests due to confusion, and if he is the only priest, he may not raise his hands unless he is confident.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that one who says 'May the good bless you' is following heretical ways.

The Mishnah continues with additional laws: the prayer leader should not answer 'Amen' after the priests due to confusion, and if he is the only priest, he may not raise his hands unless he is confident.

items.text: Gemara: On refusal and the three things
items.text_en: Gemara: On refusal and the three things
items.desc_en: The Gemara teaches that the prayer leader should refuse modestly, like a dish with salt; too much refusal spoils it. A baraita lists three things whose majority is bad and minority good: leaven, salt, and refusal.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that the prayer leader should refuse modestly: first refusal, second hesitation, third proceeding; too little or too much refusal is compared to a dish lacking or oversalted.
A second baraita lists three things whose majority is harmful and minority beneficial: leaven, salt, and refusal, supporting the earlier teaching on measured refusal.

items.text: Where to resume after an error in prayer
items.text_en: Where to resume after an error in prayer
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that if one errs in the first three blessings, he returns to the beginning; in the middle ones, to 'You graciously grant'; in the last, to 'Service'. Rav Asi says the middle blessings have no order. Rav Sheishet objects from the Mishnah that one resumes from the beginning of the blessing where he erred. Rav Huna responds that all middle blessings are considered one long blessing.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that if one errs in the first three blessings of the Amidah, he returns to the beginning; in the middle ones, to 'You graciously grant'; in the last three, to 'Service'.
Rav Asi objects that the middle blessings have no fixed order, implying a different rule for resumption after error.

sub.text: Rav Sheishet's objection from the Mishnah
sub.text_en: Rav Sheishet's objection from the Mishnah
sub.desc_en: Rav Sheishet objects from the Mishnah that one resumes from the beginning of the blessing where he erred, which contradicts Rav Huna's rule.
Rav Huna responds that all middle blessings are considered one long blessing, so resuming from 'You graciously grant' is equivalent to resuming from the beginning of the blessing where he erred.

items.text: When to ask personal needs in prayer
items.text_en: When to ask personal needs in prayer
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says one should never ask personal needs in the first or last three blessings, only in the middle ones, citing Rabbi Chanina's analogy of a servant who praises, requests, and departs.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that one should never ask personal needs in the first three or last three blessings of the Amidah, only in the middle ones.

Rabbi Chanina supports the ruling with an analogy: the first blessings are like a servant praising his master, the middle ones like requesting a gift, and the last ones like departing after receiving it.

items.text: Stories of Rabbi Eliezer on length of prayer
items.text_en: Stories of Rabbi Eliezer on length of prayer
items.desc_en: Two stories: a student who prayed too long, and another who prayed too short, before Rabbi Eliezer. His students criticized both, but Rabbi Eliezer defended them by citing Moses, who prayed long (40 days) and short ('Please, God, heal her').

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with a story about a student who prayed too long before Rabbi Eliezer.
The students criticize the lengthy prayer, calling it excessive.
Rabbi Eliezer defends the student by citing Moses, who prayed for forty days and nights.
The baraita shifts to a second story about a student who prayed too short before Rabbi Eliezer.
The students criticize the short prayer, calling it excessively brief.
Rabbi Eliezer defends the short prayer by citing Moses, who prayed briefly 'אֵל נָא רְפָא נָא לָהּ' (Please, God, heal her).

items.text: Praying for another without mentioning name
items.text_en: Praying for another without mentioning name
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov said in the name of Rav Chisda that one who prays for a friend need not mention the friend's name, as Moses prayed for Miriam without naming her.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov in the name of Rav Chisda states that one who prays for a friend need not mention the friend's name, citing Moses' prayer for Miriam as proof.

items.text: Bowing during prayer
items.text_en: Bowing during prayer
items.desc_en: A baraita lists blessings where one bows: at the beginning and end of 'Avot' and 'Hoda'ah'. If one wishes to bow elsewhere, he is taught not to. Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi quotes Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi in the name of Bar Kappara that a commoner does as stated.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists the blessings where one bows (Avot and Hoda'ah at beginning and end) and teaches that if one wishes to bow elsewhere, he is instructed not to.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi quoting Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi in the name of Bar Kappara
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi quoting Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi in the name of Bar Kappara
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi transmits in the name of Bar Kappara that a commoner (הדיוט) acts according to the baraita's stated rule.

items.text: Postures for prayer: commoner, High Priest, and king
items.text_en: Postures for prayer: commoner, High Priest, and king
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the commoner bows at the beginning and end of each blessing, the High Priest at the end of each blessing, and the king at the beginning and end of each blessing. Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nachmani clarifies in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that the commoner does as stated, the High Priest bows at the beginning of each blessing, and the king, once he bows, does not straighten up, as derived from Solomon's prayer.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the bowing postures for the commoner, High Priest, and king during prayer.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nachmani clarifies the Mishnah's postures and adds that the king, once bowing, does not straighten up, citing Solomon's prayer.

items.text: Definitions of Kiddah, Kri'ah, and Hishtachava'ah
items.text_en: Definitions of Kiddah, Kri'ah, and Hishtachava'ah
items.desc_en: A baraisa defines three types of prostration: Kiddah is falling on one's face, Kri'ah is bowing on one's knees, and Hishtachava'ah is spreading out one's hands and feet, each with a biblical prooftext.

sub.desc_en: A baraisa defines three types of prostration: Kiddah (קידּה) is falling on one's face, Kri'ah (כריעה) is bowing on one's knees, and Hishtachava'ah (השתחוואה) is spreading out one's hands and feet, each with a biblical prooftext.

items.text: Abaye and Rava's practice of extended prostration
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava's practice of extended prostration
items.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Rav Huna reports that he saw Abaye and Rava prostrating themselves fully (extending their limbs) during prayer.

sub.text: Rav Chiya bar Rav Huna's testimony
sub.text_en: Rav Chiya bar Rav Huna's testimony
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Rav Huna testifies that he saw Abaye and Rava prostrating themselves fully (extending their limbs) during prayer.

items.text: Contradiction about bowing in Hoda'ah and its resolution
items.text_en: Contradiction about bowing in Hoda'ah and its resolution
items.desc_en: Two baraisos contradict each other: one says bowing in Hoda'ah is praiseworthy, the other says it is disgraceful. The Gemara resolves this by distinguishing between bowing at the beginning (praiseworthy) and at the end (disgraceful). Rava's practice of bowing at both beginning and end is challenged, and he cites the precedent of Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet. The Gemara further distinguishes between the Hoda'ah of the Amidah and that of Hallel and Birkat HaMazon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents two contradictory baraisos: one says bowing in Hoda'ah is praiseworthy, the other says it is disgraceful.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: bowing at the beginning of Hoda'ah is praiseworthy, at the end is disgraceful.
The Sages challenge Rava for bowing both at the beginning and end of Hoda'ah, and Rava defends his practice by citing the precedent of Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet.
The Gemara objects by citing the baraita that says bowing in Hoda'ah is disgraceful, seemingly contradicting Rava's practice.
The Gemara answers that the baraita about disgraceful bowing refers to the Hoda'ah in Hallel, not the Amidah.
The Gemara objects further by citing a baraita that explicitly mentions both Hoda'ah in general and Hoda'ah of Hallel as disgraceful.
The Gemara resolves the objection by distinguishing that the baraita about disgraceful bowing refers to the Hoda'ah in Birkat HaMazon, not the Amidah.

items.text: Mishnah: One who errs in prayer, and the Gemara's clarification
items.text_en: Mishnah: One who errs in prayer, and the Gemara's clarification
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one errs in prayer it is a bad sign, and for a prayer leader it is a bad sign for his senders. It recounts Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa's ability to know if his prayer for the sick was accepted. The Gemara asks which blessing he refers to, and Rav Chiya bar Rav Safra answers in the name of a student of Rabbi's house: the Avot blessing. A second version of the teaching applies this to the requirement of kavanah (intent).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who errs in prayer receives a bad sign, and for a prayer leader it is a bad sign for his senders; it then recounts Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa's ability to know if his prayer for the sick was accepted based on whether his prayer was fluent.
The Gemara asks which blessing Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa refers to when he says his prayer is fluent.

sub.text: Rav Chiya bar Rav Safra in the name of a student of Rabbi's house
sub.text_en: Rav Chiya bar Rav Safra in the name of a student of Rabbi's house
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Rav Safra answers in the name of a student of Rabbi's house that the reference is to the Avot blessing.
A second version applies the teaching to the requirement of intent (kavanah) in prayer: one must intend in all blessings, but if unable, at least in one.

sub.text: Rav Chiya bar Rav Safra in the name of a student of Rabbi's house
sub.text_en: Rav Chiya bar Rav Safra in the name of a student of Rabbi's house
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Rav Safra again answers in the name of a student of Rabbi's house that the one blessing where intent is required is the Avot blessing.

items.text: Source for Rabbi Chanina's knowledge and the reward of Torah scholars
items.text_en: Source for Rabbi Chanina's knowledge and the reward of Torah scholars
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi derives from a verse that fluent prayer is accepted. Rabbi Yochanan states that all prophets only prophesied about the reward for those who support Torah scholars, but for the scholars themselves, 'no eye has seen.' A dispute with Shmuel limits messianic prophecy to political redemption, and with Rabbi Avahu about the superior status of penitents. The Gemara then explains the verse 'no eye has seen' as referring to the wine preserved since creation or to Eden, and clarifies that the Garden of Eden is distinct from Eden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa's ability to know if his prayer is accepted.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi cites the verse 'בּוֹרֵא נִיב שְׂפָתָיִם' (creating the fruit of the lips) to prove that fluent prayer is accepted.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that all prophets only prophesied about the reward for those who support Torah scholars, but for the scholars themselves, 'no eye has seen' (עַיִן לֹא רָאָתָה).

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan (second statement)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan (second statement)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan adds that all prophets only prophesied about the days of the Messiah, but for the World to Come, 'no eye has seen'.
Shmuel disputes Rabbi Yochanan, asserting that the only difference between this world and the days of the Messiah is political subjugation, citing the verse that the poor will never cease.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan (third statement)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan (third statement)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that all prophets only prophesied about penitents (בַּעֲלֵי תְשׁוּבָה), but for completely righteous individuals, 'no eye has seen'.

Rabbi Avahu disputes Rabbi Yochanan, arguing that penitents stand in a place where even completely righteous individuals cannot stand, citing the verse 'שָׁלוֹם שָׁלוֹם לָרָחוֹק וְלַקָּרוֹב' (peace to the far and then to the near).

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan interprets 'far' as one who was originally far from sin, and 'near' as one who was near sin but has now distanced himself, thus reconciling the verse with his view.
The Gemara asks for the interpretation of the phrase 'עַיִן לֹא רָאָתָה' (no eye has seen).
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explains that 'no eye has seen' refers to the wine preserved in its grapes since the six days of creation.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani explains that 'no eye has seen' refers to Eden, which no creature's eye has ever seen.
The Gemara anticipates a question: where was Adam? He was in the Garden (גַּן), not in Eden itself.
The Gemara clarifies that the Garden (גַּן) and Eden (עֵדֶן) are distinct, citing the verse 'וְנָהָר יוֹצֵא מֵעֵדֶן לְהַשְׁקוֹת אֶת הַגָּן' (a river flows from Eden to water the garden).

items.text: Stories of Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa's prayer for the sick
items.text_en: Stories of Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa's prayer for the sick
items.desc_en: Two stories illustrate Rabbi Chanina's power of prayer: one where he heals Rabban Gamliel's son by knowing the fever broke, and another where he heals Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai's son. Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai explains that Rabbi Chanina is like a servant before the king, while he is like a minister.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with a story: Rabban Gamliel's son falls ill, he sends two sages to Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa to pray; Rabbi Chanina ascends to the upper chamber, prays, and upon descending declares the fever has broken.
The sages ask Rabbi Chanina in astonishment: Are you a prophet that you know the fever broke?
Rabbi Chanina explains he is not a prophet but has a tradition: if his prayer is fluent in his mouth, he knows it is accepted; if not, he knows it is rejected.
The sages record the exact hour; upon returning to Rabban Gamliel, he confirms that at that very hour the fever broke and his son asked for water.
A second story: Rabbi Chanina goes to study with Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai; when Rabbi Yochanan's son falls ill, Rabbi Chanina prays and the son recovers.
Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai remarks that even if he (Ben Zakkai) had prayed all day, they would not have paid attention to him.

sub.text: Wife of Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai's question
sub.text_en: Wife of Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai's question
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan's wife asks: Is Chanina greater than you?
Rabbi Yochanan explains: Chanina is like a servant before the king, while I am like a minister before the king.

items.text: Laws of prayer location and confession
items.text_en: Laws of prayer location and confession
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that one should only pray in a house with windows, citing Daniel's practice. Rav Kahana declares that one who prays in a valley is arrogant, and one who publicly confesses his sins is also arrogant, citing a verse about covering sin.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan via Rabbi Chiya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan via Rabbi Chiya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that one should only pray in a house with windows, citing Daniel's practice of opening windows toward Jerusalem.
Rav Kahana declares that one who prays in a valley is arrogant.
Rav Kahana declares that one who publicly confesses his sins is arrogant, citing a verse about covering sin.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah specifies the blessings recited over various foods: for tree fruit (except wine) one says "בּוֹרֵא פְּרִי הָעֵץ", for wine "בּוֹרֵא פְּרִי הַגֶּפֶן", for earth produce (except bread) "בּוֹרֵא פְּרִי הָאֲדָמָה", for bread "הַמּוֹצִיא לֶחֶם מִן הָאָרֶץ", and for vegetables "בּוֹרֵא פְּרִי הָאֲדָמָה". Rabbi Yehuda adds a separate blessing for vegetables: "בּוֹרֵא מִינֵי דְשָׁאִים".

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing the blessings for tree fruit, wine, earth produce, and bread.
Rabbi Yehuda adds a separate blessing for vegetables: 'בּוֹרֵא מִינֵי דְשָׁאִים'.

items.text: Gemara's question and initial derivation
items.text_en: Gemara's question and initial derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where are these matters derived? It cites a baraita that interprets "קֹדֶשׁ הִלּוּלִים" to teach that foods require a blessing before and after eating. From this, Rabbi Akiva deduces that one may not taste anything before reciting a blessing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where are these matters (the blessings on foods) derived?
A baraita is cited: the verse 'קֹדֶשׁ הִלּוּלִים לַה׳' teaches that foods require a blessing before and after eating.
Rabbi Akiva deduces from the baraita that one may not taste anything before reciting a blessing.

items.text: Challenge to the derivation from "קֹדֶשׁ הִלּוּלִים"
items.text_en: Challenge to the derivation from "קֹדֶשׁ הִלּוּלִים"
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: is the phrase "קֹדֶשׁ הִלּוּלִים" really needed for blessings? It is required for another teaching: that God exchanged the fruit and then permitted it (referring to neta revai). Alternatively, it teaches that only something requiring song (wine) requires "חִלּוּל" (redemption). Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani cites Rabbi Yonatan that song is only said over wine, based on the verse about the vine.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the phrase 'קֹדֶשׁ הִלּוּלִים' is exclusively needed for the derivation of blessings.
The first answer explains that the phrase is needed for the teaching that God exchanged the fruit of neta revai and then permitted it.
The second answer teaches that only something requiring song (wine) requires חִלּוּל (redemption).

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani cites Rabbi Yonatan that song is only said over wine, based on the verse about the vine.

items.text: Debate between "נטע רבעי" and "כרם רבעי"
items.text_en: Debate between "נטע רבעי" and "כרם רבעי"
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the previous derivation works for the Tanna who teaches "נֶטַע רְבָעִי" (fourth-year planting), but for the one who teaches "כֶּרֶם רְבָעִי" (fourth-year vineyard), a different approach is needed. It cites a dispute between Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Shimon beRabbi. For the "כֶּרֶם רְבָעִי" view, if one learns a gezerah shavah, the extra "הִלּוּל" is available for blessings. If not, the source for blessings is unclear. The Gemara then derives the blessing before eating via a kal vachomer: if one blesses when full, certainly when hungry.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the previous derivation works for the Tanna who teaches 'נֶטַע רְבָעִי' (fourth-year planting), but asks what can be said for the one who teaches 'כֶּרֶם רְבָעִי' (fourth-year vineyard).
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi learns a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) between 'תבואתו' and 'תבואת הכרם', which leaves an extra 'הילול' for blessings.

The Gemara asks: if one does not learn the גזירה שווה (verbal analogy), where is the source for blessings; and even if one does, we find only the blessing after eating, but where is the blessing before eating?
The Gemara resolves that the blessing before eating is derived by קל וחומר (a fortiori): if one blesses when full (after eating), certainly one should bless when hungry (before eating).

items.text: Deriving blessings for all foods from the vineyard
items.text_en: Deriving blessings for all foods from the vineyard
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we found a source for the vineyard, but from where do we derive blessings for other items? It attempts to learn from the vineyard via a binyan av, but faces challenges (e.g., the vineyard is subject to gleanings). It then tries to learn from grain, but that is subject to challah. The common denominator is that both are enjoyable and require a blessing, but this is challenged because both have an aspect of the altar. The Gemara then tries to learn from the seven species, but they are subject to first fruits. The blessing before eating is again derived via kal vachomer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we found a source for the vineyard, but from where do we derive blessings for other items?

The Gemara attempts to learn from the vineyard via a בִּנְיָן אָב (building a paradigm): just as the vineyard is an enjoyable thing requiring a blessing, so too everything enjoyable requires a blessing.
An objection is raised: the vineyard is unique because it is subject to the law of gleanings (עוֹלֵלוֹת), so it cannot serve as a paradigm.
The Gemara responds by bringing grain (קָמָה) as a counterexample, but that too is challenged because grain is subject to חַלָּה (the priestly portion of dough).
The Gemara resolves by finding the common denominator (הַצַּד הַשָּׁוֶה) between vineyard and grain: both are enjoyable and require a blessing, so all enjoyable things require a blessing.
An objection is raised: the common denominator is flawed because both vineyard and grain have an aspect of the altar (צַד מִזְבֵּחַ), and the olive also has an aspect of the altar.
Rav Pappa rejects the objection: the olive is called 'כֶּרֶם זַיִת' (vineyard of olives) but not 'כֶּרֶם' (vineyard) in the absolute sense, so it does not share the altar aspect.
The Gemara persists: the common denominator still has the altar aspect, so the derivation is invalid.
The Gemara offers an alternative derivation from the seven species (שִׁבְעַת הַמִּינִין): just as they are enjoyable and require a blessing, so too all enjoyable things require a blessing.
An objection is raised: the seven species are unique because they are subject to first fruits (בִּכּוּרִים), and additionally, we only have a source for the blessing after eating, not before.
The Gemara resolves: the blessing before eating is derived via a קַל וָחוֹמֶר (a fortiori) argument — if one blesses when full (after eating), certainly one should bless when hungry (before eating).

items.text: Source for non-plant foods: sevara
items.text_en: Source for non-plant foods: sevara
items.desc_en: For the Tanna who says "נֶטַע רְבָעִי", the derivation works for things that are planted, but for non-planted items like meat, eggs, and fish, the source is a sevara (logical reasoning): it is forbidden for a person to benefit from this world without a blessing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for the Tanna who teaches the term 'נטע רבעי' (fourth-year planting), the source covers planted items, but for non-planted items like meat, eggs, and fish, where is the source derived?
The Gemara answers: it is a sevara (logical reasoning) — it is forbidden for a person to benefit from this world without a blessing.

items.text: The severity of benefiting without a blessing
items.text_en: The severity of benefiting without a blessing
items.desc_en: A baraita states: it is forbidden to benefit from this world without a blessing, and one who does so commits an act of sacrilege (מעל). The remedy is to go to a sage. Rava clarifies: go to a sage from the outset to learn blessings, so as not to come to sacrilege. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel says: one who benefits without a blessing is as if they benefited from the sacred things of Heaven, citing the verse "לַה׳ הָאָרֶץ וּמְלוֹאָהּ". Rabbi Levi resolves a contradiction between this verse and another, distinguishing between before and after the blessing.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that benefiting from this world without a blessing is forbidden and constitutes sacrilege (מעל), and the remedy is to go to a sage.
The gemara objects: going to a sage after the fact cannot undo the prohibition already committed.
Rava resolves: go to a sage from the outset to learn blessings, so as not to come to sacrilege.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel says that one who benefits without a blessing is as if they benefited from sacred things of Heaven, citing the verse 'לַה׳ הָאָרֶץ וּמְלוֹאָהּ'.
Rabbi Levi resolves a contradiction between two verses by distinguishing: before the blessing the earth belongs to God, after the blessing it is given to humanity.

items.text: Opening: blessing without benefit is theft
items.text_en: Opening: blessing without benefit is theft
items.desc_en: Rabbi Hanina bar Papa argues that enjoying the world without a blessing is like robbing God and the Jewish people, citing verses about father and mother.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces the principle that the discussion applies after a blessing.
Rabbi Hanina bar Papa states that one who enjoys the world without a blessing is like a robber of God and the Jewish people, citing a verse.

items.text: Gemara's question: blessing on oil vs. fruit
items.text_en: Gemara's question: blessing on oil vs. fruit
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether oil is blessed as a fruit of the tree or as a condiment, citing Rabbi Yehuda's opinion that oil is blessed as a fruit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the meaning of the phrase 'חָבֵר הוּא לְאִישׁ מַשְׁחִית' (he is a companion to a destructive man).
Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa explains that the phrase refers to one who is a companion to Jeroboam ben Nevat, who corrupted Israel before their Father in Heaven.
Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa raises a contradiction between two verses: one says 'I will take My grain in its time' and the other says 'you shall gather your grain'.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: one verse refers to when Israel does God's will, the other to when they do not.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yishmael explains that the verse 'you shall gather your grain' teaches that one should engage in worldly occupation alongside Torah study.
Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai objects: if one engages in all agricultural tasks, what will become of Torah? He argues that when Israel does God's will, their work is done by others.
Abaye notes that many followed Rabbi Yishmael's approach and succeeded, while those who followed Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai did not succeed.
Rava instructs the rabbis not to appear before him during Nisan and Tishrei, so they will not be distracted by their food concerns all year.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai: earlier generations made Torah primary and work secondary, and both succeeded; later generations reversed this and failed.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan (second statement)
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan (second statement)
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana reports another statement: earlier generations brought produce through the main entrance to obligate it in tithes, while later generations brought it through roofs and courtyards to exempt it, citing Rabbi Yannai's principle that produce is not obligated in tithes until it sees the face of the house.
Rabbi Yochanan adds that even a courtyard determines liability for tithes, citing the verse 'and they shall eat in your gates and be satisfied'.

items.text: Objection: oil as condiment vs. fruit
items.text_en: Objection: oil as condiment vs. fruit
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if oil is a condiment, it should be blessed as 'shehakol', but if it is a fruit, it should be blessed as 'borei pri ha'etz'. Mar Zutra argues oil is not a fruit because olives are the fruit, and oil is extracted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why oil is not blessed with a special fruit blessing, and answers that the olive itself is called 'zayit' (olive), so the blessing would be redundant.
Mar Zutra argues that wine is nourishing (זָיֵין) but oil is not nourishing, so oil does not receive the blessing of 'borei pri ha'etz'.

The Gemara objects that oil is indeed nourishing, citing a baraita that one who vows against 'food' (מזון) is permitted only water and salt, implying all other items including oil are considered food.

items.text: Gemara's resolution: oil is a condiment
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution: oil is a condiment
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that oil is a condiment, not a fruit, because it does not sustain like food, and wine is both sustaining and joyful, while bread only sustains.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection against Rav and Shmuel from the Mishnah that oil is considered מזון (sustenance), implying it should require a different blessing.
The Gemara distinguishes: oil sustains (זיין) but does not satisfy (סעיד), while wine both satisfies and gladdens.
The Gemara objects that wine does not satisfy, citing Rava's practice of drinking wine before Passover to stimulate appetite, concluding that a large amount stimulates and a small amount satisfies.
The Gemara objects further from a verse that only bread satisfies, and resolves that wine has both properties: it satisfies and gladdens, while bread only satisfies.
The Gemara asks: if wine satisfies, why not recite the full Grace After Meals (שלש ברכות) over it?
The Gemara answers: people do not establish their meals on wine alone.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak asks Rava: if one does establish a meal on wine, what then?
Rava answers that such a practice is not normative; it awaits Elijah's confirmation, and currently one's intention is disregarded by all.

items.text: Further discussion: wine's dual nature
items.text_en: Further discussion: wine's dual nature
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that wine both sustains and gladdens, while bread only sustains, so wine requires three blessings. However, if wine is the main course, it may be blessed as the primary food.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why wine is singled out for a different blessing, noting that oil also changes for the better but its blessing does not change.
Mar Zutra answers that wine sustains (זָיֵין) while oil does not sustain.
The Gemara objects that oil does sustain, citing a mishnah about a vow from food (מָזוֹן) which includes oil.
The Gemara rejects the distinction, concluding that wine satisfies (סָעֵיד) while oil does not satisfy.
The Gemara objects that wine does not satisfy, citing Rava's practice of drinking wine to stimulate appetite, and distinguishes between a little (satisfies) and a lot (stimulates).
The Gemara objects further from a verse that only bread satisfies, and resolves that wine has both properties: it satisfies and gladdens, while bread only satisfies.
The Gemara asks why wine does not require three blessings, and answers that people do not set their meals on it.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's question to Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's question to Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak asks Rava what the law is if one does set a meal on wine, and Rava defers the answer to Elijah.
The Gemara concludes that in practice, since people do not set meals on wine, one's intention to do so is disregarded.

items.text: Final ruling: oil blessing as 'borei pri ha'etz'
items.text_en: Final ruling: oil blessing as 'borei pri ha'etz'
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that oil is blessed as 'borei pri ha'etz' when drunk directly, but as a condiment when eaten with bread, following the rule that the primary food determines the blessing.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel, and Rabbi Yitzchak citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel, and Rabbi Yitzchak citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that oil is blessed as 'borei pri ha'etz' when drunk directly, but as a condiment when eaten with bread, following the rule that the primary food determines the blessing.

items.text: דין ברכת אניגרון לחושש בגרונו
items.text_en: Blessing on anigron for a sore throat
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier ruling that one blesses 'borei pri ha'adamah' on anigron, arguing that if oil is secondary to the leeks, the blessing should be on the leeks alone. It resolves that the case involves a person with a sore throat who swallows oil mixed with anigron for healing, and despite the medicinal intent, since there is benefit, a blessing is required.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה בברכת אניגרון (מי זיתים כבושים) כאשר השמן טפל לעיקר. נאמר שאם השמן הוא העיקר, מברכים עליו ופוטר את הטפל. אך כאן מדובר בחושש בגרונו, שנותן שמן רב לתוך האניגרון ובולע, ולמרות שהכוונה לרפואה, כיון שיש הנאה, צריך לברך.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier ruling on anigron, arguing that if oil is secondary to the leeks, the blessing should be on the leeks alone, citing the rule that one blesses on the primary item and exempts the secondary.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בהנחה שכל התערובות הן של ירקות שלוקים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the case involves a person with a sore throat who swallows oil mixed with anigron for healing, citing a baraita that permits this on Shabbat.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שמדובר בחושש בגרונו, שנותן שמן הרבה לתוך האנגרון והשמן עיקרי לרפואה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that despite the medicinal intent, since there is benefit from the oil, a blessing is required, dispelling the notion that no blessing is needed.
sub.desc: הגמרא מבהירה שאף שמכוון לרפואה, כיון שיש לו הנאה מהשמן, צריך לברך.

items.text: מחלוקת בברכת קמח חיטים
items.text_en: Blessing on wheat flour
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda and Rav Nachman dispute the blessing on wheat flour: Rav Yehuda says 'borei pri ha'adamah', Rav Nachman says 'shehakol'. Rava supports Rav Yehuda by citing a parallel from oil, but the Gemara objects that flour can be made into bread, a higher purpose. It then discusses barley flour and concludes that even barley flour requires 'shehakol', despite its harshness, because one derives benefit.
items.desc: רב יהודה ורב נחמן נחלקו בברכת קמח חיטים: רב יהודה אומר 'בורא פרי האדמה', ורב נחמן אומר 'שהכל נהיה בדברו'. רבא סובר כרב יהודה, ומביא ראיה משמן זית שאף על פי שנשתנה, ברכתו 'בורא פרי העץ'. הגמרא דוחה את הראיה, ומביאה ראיה אחרת מקרא חייא וקמח שעורים. לבסוף, הגמרא מביאה ראיה ממלח וזמית שצריך לברך עליהם 'שהכל', ומסיקה שגם על קמח שעורים מברכים 'שהכל'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda and Rav Nachman dispute the blessing on wheat flour: Rav Yehuda says 'borei pri ha'adamah', Rav Nachman says 'shehakol'.
sub.desc: רב יהודה ורב נחמן נחלקו בברכת קמח חיטים: רב יהודה מברך 'בורא פרי האדמה', ורב נחמן מברך 'שהכל נהיה בדברו'.

sub.desc_en: Rava supports Rav Yehuda by citing a parallel from oil, which retains its original blessing despite change.
sub.desc: רבא מביא ראיה לרב יהודה מדברי רבי יוחנן ושמואל על שמן זית, שאף על פי שנשתנה ברכתו 'בורא פרי העץ', וכך גם קמח חיטים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the parallel fails because flour can be elevated to bread, a higher purpose, unlike oil.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה את הראיה: בשמן זית אין עלוי אחר, אבל בקמח חיטים יש עלוי אחר בפת.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether having a higher purpose precludes the original blessing, citing a baraita about barley flour that implies wheat flour gets 'borei pri ha'adamah'.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מברייתא על אקרא חייא וקמח שעורים, ומשמע שקמח חיטים מברכים 'בורא פרי האדמה'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that even wheat flour requires 'shehakol', not 'borei pri ha'adamah'.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה: גם על קמח חיטים מברכים 'שהכל נהיה בדברו'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if wheat flour requires 'shehakol', the baraita should have mentioned wheat flour first, and barley flour would follow a fortiori.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מדוע לא השמיעו דין קמח חיטים וכל שכן שעורים?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that if only wheat flour were mentioned, one might think barley flour requires no blessing at all, so the baraita teaches both.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת: אילו השמיעו דין חיטים, הייתי אומר שדווקא חיטים מברכים, אבל שעורים אין מברכים כלל, לכן השמיעו דין שעורים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that even barley flour requires 'shehakol', because one derives benefit, just as salt and brine require a blessing despite their harshness.
sub.desc: הגמרא מסיקה שגם קמח שעורים מברכים 'שהכל', ואינו גרוע ממלח וזמית, כיון שיש הנאה ממנו.

items.text: מחלוקת בברכת קורא
items.text_en: Blessing on gourd (kora)
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda and Shmuel dispute the blessing on gourd: Rav Yehuda says 'borei pri ha'adamah' because it is a fruit, Shmuel says 'shehakol' because it hardens. Shmuel concedes to Rav Yehuda based on the precedent of radish, but the Gemara distinguishes: people plant radish for the root, but not gourd for its hardened state. The halakha follows Shmuel despite his praise of Rav Yehuda.
items.desc: רב יהודה ושמואל נחלקו בברכת הקורא (כרוב): רב יהודה אומר 'בורא פרי האדמה' כי הוא פרי, ושמואל אומר 'שהכל' הואיל וסופו להקשות. שמואל מודה לרב יהודה מצנון, אך הגמרא דוחה כי צנון נטוע על דעת פוגלא, אבל קורא לא נטוע על דעתו. הגמרא מקשה מצלף, ומתרצת שצלף נטוע על דעת שותא. למרות ששמואל קלסיה לרב יהודה, ההלכה כמותו.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that the blessing on gourd (קוֹרָא) is 'בּוֹרֵא פְּרִי הָאֲדָמָה' (Creator of the fruit of the ground).
sub.desc: רב יהודה ושמואל נחלקו בברכת הקורא: רב יהודה מברך 'בורא פרי האדמה' ושמואל מברך 'שהכל'.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states that the blessing on gourd is 'שֶׁהַכֹּל נִהְיֶה בִּדְבָרוֹ' (by Whose word all things exist).
sub.desc: הגמרא מבהירה את טעמי המחלוקת: רב יהודה רואה בקורא פרי, ושמואל סובר שכיוון שסופו להקשות אינו נחשב פרי.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rav Yehuda's reasoning: gourd is a fruit (פֵּירָא).
sub.desc: שמואל מודה לרב יהודה שהלכה כמותו, ומביא ראיה מצנון שסופו להקשות ומברכים עליו 'בורא פרי האדמה', אך הגמרא דוחה את הראיה כי צנון נטועים על דעת הפוגל, אבל קורא לא נטועים על דעת הקורא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains Shmuel's reasoning: since the gourd eventually hardens (סוֹפוֹ לְהַקְשׁוֹת), it is not considered a fruit for blessing purposes.
sub.desc: הגמרא מבהירה את טעמי המחלוקת: רב יהודה רואה בקורא פרי, ושמואל סובר שכיוון שסופו להקשות אינו נחשב פרי.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel tells Rav Yehuda that his view seems correct, citing the precedent of radish (צְנוֹן) which also hardens yet receives the blessing 'בּוֹרֵא פְּרִי הָאֲדָמָה'.
sub.desc: שמואל מודה לרב יהודה שהלכה כמותו, ומביא ראיה מצנון שסופו להקשות ומברכים עליו 'בורא פרי האדמה', אך הגמרא דוחה את הראיה כי צנון נטועים על דעת הפוגל, אבל קורא לא נטועים על דעת הקורא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the analogy: people plant radish for the root (פוּגְלָא), but they do not plant gourd for its hardened state (קוֹרָא).
sub.desc: שמואל מודה לרב יהודה שהלכה כמותו, ומביא ראיה מצנון שסופו להקשות ומברכים עליו 'בורא פרי האדמה', אך הגמרא דוחה את הראיה כי צנון נטועים על דעת הפוגל, אבל קורא לא נטועים על דעת הקורא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if people do not plant for the final state, do we not bless? But consider the caper bush (צָלָף), planted for its buds, yet the Mishnah rules that on its leaves and shoots one says 'בּוֹרֵא פְּרִי הָאֲדָמָה' and on its berries and capers 'בּוֹרֵא פְּרִי הָעֵץ'.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: הרי צלף שנטועים על דעת הפרח, ומברכים על העלים והתמרות 'בורא פרי האדמה' ועל האביונות והקפריסין 'בורא פרי העץ', ומכאן שדין הצמח תלוי בשימוש העיקרי.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves: people plant the caper bush for its shoots (שׁוּתָא), but they do not plant gourd for its hardened state.
sub.desc: רב נחמן בר יצחק מתרץ: צלף נטועים על דעת השותא (הפרי), אבל קורא לא נטועים על דעת הקורא, ולמרות ששמואל קלס את רב יהודה, ההלכה כשמואל.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes: although Shmuel praised Rav Yehuda, the halakha (הלכה) follows Shmuel.
sub.desc: רב נחמן בר יצחק מתרץ: צלף נטועים על דעת השותא (הפרי), אבל קורא לא נטועים על דעת הקורא, ולמרות ששמואל קלס את רב יהודה, ההלכה כשמואל.

items.text: דין צלף של ערלה בחוץ לארץ
items.text_en: Caper bush: orlah and blessings
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav rules that for caper bush (tzalaf) outside the land, one discards the berries (aviyonot) and eats the caper-fruit (kafrisin), implying berries are fruit and caper-fruit is not. This contradicts a mishna that both require 'borei pri ha'etz'. The Gemara explains Rav follows Rabbi Akiva, who says only berries are fruit for tithes. The Gemara clarifies that this leniency applies only outside the land, not in Israel.
items.desc: רב יהודה אמר רב: צלף של ערלה בחוץ לארץ זורק את האביונות ואוכל את הקפריסין. הגמרא מקשה מברייתא שמברכים על שניהם 'בורא פרי העץ'. מתרץ שזה כרבי עקיבא, הסובר שרק אביונות הם פרי. הגמרא דנה מדוע לא אמר 'הלכה כרבי עקיבא' ומסבירה שצריך לפרט כדי למנוע טעות.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav rules that for a caper bush (צָלָף) in its orlah years outside the land, one discards the berries (אֲבִיּוֹנוֹת) and eats the caper-fruit (קַפְרֵיסִין).
sub.desc: רב יהודה בשם רב פוסק שבצלף של ערלה בחוץ לארץ זורק את האביונות ואוכל את הקפריסין.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers that Rav considers berries fruit and caper-fruit not fruit, and questions this.
sub.desc: רב יהודה בשם רב פוסק שבצלף של ערלה בחוץ לארץ זורק את האביונות ואוכל את הקפריסין.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a mishna that requires the blessing 'בורא פרי העץ' (Who creates fruit of the tree) over both berries and caper-fruit, implying both are fruit.
sub.desc: רב יהודה בשם רב פוסק שבצלף של ערלה בחוץ לארץ זורק את האביונות ואוכל את הקפריסין.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that Rav follows Rabbi Akiva, who holds that only the berries are considered fruit for tithing, not the caper-fruit.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שרב סובר כרבי עקיבא, הסובר שרק האביונות הם פרי, ולכן רק הם אסורים בערלה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rav did not simply state that the halakha follows Rabbi Akiva.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מדוע רב לא אמר בפשטות 'הלכה כרבי עקיבא', ומתרצת שהיה נטעה לחשוב שזה אפילו בארץ, ולכן פירט שרק בחוץ לארץ מיקל.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that had Rav said the halakha follows Rabbi Akiva, one might think it applies even in Israel; therefore Rav specifies that the leniency is only outside the land.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מדוע לא אמר 'הלכה כרבי עקיבא בחוץ לארץ', ומתרצת שהיה נטעה לחשוב שזה דווקא במעשר אילן שהוא דרבנן, אבל בערלה שהיא דאורייתא בארץ, היינו גוזרים גם בחוץ לארץ.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara further asks why Rav did not simply say the halakha follows Rabbi Akiva outside the land.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מדוע לא אמר 'הלכה כרבי עקיבא בחוץ לארץ', ומתרצת שהיה נטעה לחשוב שזה דווקא במעשר אילן שהוא דרבנן, אבל בערלה שהיא דאורייתא בארץ, היינו גוזרים גם בחוץ לארץ.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that had Rav said that, one might think the leniency applies only to tithing (rabbinic), but for orlah (Torah law) one might decree even outside the land; therefore Rav teaches that the leniency applies to orlah as well.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מדוע לא אמר 'הלכה כרבי עקיבא בחוץ לארץ', ומתרצת שהיה נטעה לחשוב שזה דווקא במעשר אילן שהוא דרבנן, אבל בערלה שהיא דאורייתא בארץ, היינו גוזרים גם בחוץ לארץ.

items.text: מעשה רבינא עם מר בר רב אשי וספק ערלה בצלף
items.text_en: Ravina's observation and the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.desc_en: Ravina finds Mar bar Rav Ashi discarding berries and eating caper-fruit, following Rabbi Akiva's leniency. Ravina suggests following Beit Shammai who are even more lenient regarding kilayim, but the Gemara notes a contradiction: Beit Shammai consider caper a vegetable for kilayim but a tree for orlah. The Gemara resolves that Beit Shammai are uncertain and rule stringently in both cases, leading to a doubt about orlah, which is prohibited in Israel but permitted outside.
items.desc: רבינא מצא את מר בר רב אשי זורק אביונות ואוכל קפריסין, ותמה עליו מדוע לא עשה כבית שמאי המקילים יותר. הגמרא מקשה מברייתא שבית שמאי מחמירים גם בכלאים וגם בערלה, ומתרצת שהם מסתפקים ועושים לחומרא. מכל מקום, ספק ערלה בחוץ לארץ מותר.

sub.desc_en: Ravina finds Mar bar Rav Ashi discarding the berries and eating the buds of a caper-bush, following Rabbi Akiva's lenient position.
sub.desc: רבינא מצא את מר בר רב אשי זורק אביונות ואוכל קפריסין, ושאלו מדוע אינו נוהג כבית שמאי המקילים יותר.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Mar bar Rav Ashi why he follows Rabbi Akiva's leniency when Beit Shammai are even more lenient regarding kilayim.
sub.desc: רבינא מצא את מר בר רב אשי זורק אביונות ואוכל קפריסין, ושאלו מדוע אינו נוהג כבית שמאי המקילים יותר.

sub.desc_en: Ravina cites a mishnah: Beit Shammai consider the caper-bush a diverse kind in a vineyard, while Beit Hillel do not, yet both agree it is obligated in orlah.
sub.desc: רבינא מצא את מר בר רב אשי זורק אביונות ואוכל קפריסין, ושאלו מדוע אינו נוהג כבית שמאי המקילים יותר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the mishnah is self-contradictory: Beit Shammai treat the caper as a vegetable for kilayim but as a tree for orlah.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מברייתא זו סתירה פנימית: מדברי בית שמאי משמע שצלף ירק, ומחיוב ערלה משמע שהוא אילן.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Beit Shammai are uncertain about the caper's classification and rule stringently in both cases.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שבית שמאי מסתפקים אם צלף ירק או אילן, ולכן מחמירים בשני הדינים. מכל מקום, ספק ערלה בחוץ לארץ מותר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that for Beit Shammai the caper has uncertain orlah status, which is forbidden in Eretz Yisrael but permitted in Syria and outside the land.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שבית שמאי מסתפקים אם צלף ירק או אילן, ולכן מחמירים בשני הדינים. מכל מקום, ספק ערלה בחוץ לארץ מותר.

items.text: פתיחת הסוגיה: דין לוקט פירות ערלה
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Taking fruit without seeing the owner
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses a case where one takes fruit without seeing the owner, and the Gemara clarifies that this is permitted only if the owner is not watching.
items.desc: הקטע פותח בדין לוקט פירות ערלה, תוך אזכור תנאי שלא יראנו לוקט, ומציג את הרקע לדיון על דיני ערלה.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may take fruit without seeing the owner, provided the owner does not see him picking.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בדין לוקט פירות ערלה, ומציגה תנאי שהלוקח לא יראה את הלוקט.

items.text: כלל פסיקה: רבי עקיבא במקום רבי אליעזר
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Rabbi Akiva vs Rabbi Eliezer and Beit Shammai vs Beit Hillel
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether we follow Rabbi Akiva's position (in place of Rabbi Eliezer) and Beit Shammai (in place of Beit Hillel) in a specific Mishnah, noting that this is not a standard Mishnah.
items.desc: הקטע קובע כלל הלכתי: במקום מחלוקת בין רבי עקיבא לרבי אליעזר פוסקים כרבי עקיבא, ואילו מחלוקת בית שמאי ובית הלל אינה נחשבת למשנה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes a general principle: we follow Rabbi Akiva against Rabbi Eliezer, but Beit Shammai against Beit Hillel is not a Mishnah.
sub.desc: קובע כלל פסיקה: הלכה כרבי עקיבא נגד רבי אליעזר, ומחלוקת בית שמאי ובית הלל אינה נחשבת למשנה.

items.text: Gemara's objection: The protector becomes a fruit?
items.text_en: Gemara's objection: The protector becomes a fruit?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if a part (like a pit or peel) becomes a protector for the fruit, then the Torah's phrase 'and you shall orlah its fruit' includes the protector as part of the fruit, contradicting the Mishnah's exclusion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: why not derive that the caper's protective part becomes a שומר לפרי (guard for the fruit), and the verse 'וערלתם ערלתו את פריו' includes what is secondary to the fruit?

items.text: Rava's clarification: Protector status depends on attachment
items.text_en: Rava's clarification: Protector status depends on attachment
items.desc_en: Rava explains that a part becomes a protector for the fruit only when it is attached (in the ground), not when detached (plucked), and the Mishnah's case involves detached fruit.

sub.desc_en: Rava answers: we say something is a שומר לפרי only when it exists both when attached and when detached; here the caper's protective part exists when attached but not when detached.

items.text: קושיית אביי: פיטמא של רימון והנץ
items.text_en: Abaye's counterexample: Pomegranate pit and blossom
items.desc_en: Abaye cites a Mishnah about orlah where pomegranate peels and blossoms are liable, implying they are fruit, contradicting Rava's claim that detached parts are not protectors.
items.desc: אביי מקשה על רבא מברייתא: פיטמא של רימון מצטרפת לשיעור ערלה, והנץ אינו מצטרף, ומכאן שהנץ אינו אוכל. אך בברייתא אחרת שנינו שקליפי רימון והנץ חייבים בערלה, סתירה לכאורה.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects with a baraita: the pitma (crown) of a pomegranate joins, but its netz (calyx) does not join, and the netz is not food; yet the Mishnah in Orlah says pomegranate peels and its netz are obligated in orlah, implying the netz is a שומר לפרי.
sub.desc: אביי מקשה על רבא מברייתא: פיטמא של רימון מצטרפת לשיעור ערלה, והנץ אינו מצטרף, ומכאן שהנץ אינו אוכל.

items.text: תשובת רבא: שומר בשעת גמר פרי
items.text_en: Rava's resolution: Protector status at time of fruit completion
items.desc_en: Rava distinguishes: a part becomes a protector only when the fruit is fully formed (gemar peira), but the pomegranate blossom (nitz) is not present at that stage, so it is not a fruit.
items.desc: רבא עונה: שומר לפרי נחשב רק כשהוא קיים בשעת גמר הפרי, וקפריסין אינם קיימים בשעת גמר הפרי.

sub.desc_en: Rava revises: we say something is a שומר לפרי only when it exists at the time the fruit ripens; the caper's protective part does not exist at that time.
sub.desc: רבא עונה: שומר לפרי נחשב רק כשהוא קיים בשעת גמר הפרי, וקפריסין אינם קיימים בשעת גמר הפרי.

items.text: Rav Nachman's statement: Capers are forbidden as protectors
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's statement: Capers are forbidden as protectors
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites a tradition that capers (metachlei) are forbidden due to orlah because they become protectors for the fruit, contradicting Rava's earlier point.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Rav Nachman said in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha that the unripe caper buds (מתוחלי) of orlah are forbidden because they become a שומר לפרי, and that protection exists in the early stage (כופרא), yet he calls it a שומר לפרי.

items.text: Rav Nachman's view aligns with Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's view aligns with Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman holds like Rabbi Yosei, who considers smadar (unripe fruit) as fruit, and the Rabbis disagree, but the Gemara notes that for other trees the Rabbis do not dispute.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains: Rav Nachman follows Rabbi Yosei, who holds that the semadar (early bud) is considered fruit, but the Rabbis disagree with him.

items.text: Rav Shimi's challenge: Dispute only for capers?
items.text_en: Rav Shimi's challenge: Dispute only for capers?
items.desc_en: Rav Shimi from Nehardea challenges: do the Rabbis only dispute regarding capers? He cites a Mishnah about cutting trees in the seventh year that shows disagreement for all trees.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shimi challenges: do the rabbis dispute this for all trees? A Mishnah on Sheviit cutting shows Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagree on when cutting is permitted, implying dispute exists for all trees.

items.text: Rav Asi's identification: Boser, Gerua, Pol haLavan
items.text_en: Rav Asi's identification: Boser, Gerua, Pol haLavan
items.desc_en: Rav Asi identifies three stages of unripe fruit: boser (sour), gerua (bitter?), pol haLavan (white bean?), and clarifies that the measure for orlah is like pol haLavan.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi clarifies: 'בוסר' (unripe grape) equals 'גרוע' (inferior) and 'פול הלבן' (white bean). The rabbis who say 'בוסר is fruit, סמדר is not' also rule that all other trees are cut only when they produce (יוציאו).
The Gemara asks who holds that boser is fruit but semadar is not, answering that it is the Rabbis.
The Gemara cites the Mishnah that for other trees the orlah prohibition begins when they produce (yotzi'u), supporting the Rabbis' view.

items.text: Rava's further clarification: Protector kills the fruit
items.text_en: Rava's further clarification: Protector kills the fruit
items.desc_en: Rava explains that a part is a protector only if removing it kills the fruit; for capers, removing the caper does not kill the fruit, so it is not a protector.

sub.desc_en: Rava gives a third criterion: we say something is a שומר לפרי only when removing it causes the fruit to die; here, removing the caper's protective part does not kill the fruit.

items.text: Practical test: Removing caper does not kill pomegranate
items.text_en: Practical test: Removing caper does not kill pomegranate
items.desc_en: A case occurred: they took a caper from a pomegranate, the pomegranate survived; they took a blossom from a citron, the citron survived — proving they are not protectors.

sub.desc_en: A practical incident is cited: they removed the netz (calyx) of a pomegranate and the pomegranate dried up, but they removed the percha (flower) of a melon and the melon survived, supporting Rava's criterion.

items.text: Halakhic ruling: Capers are not fruit, blessing is 'Borei Peri haAdamah'
items.text_en: Halakhic ruling: Capers are not fruit, blessing is 'Borei Peri haAdamah'
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that capers are not fruit (for orlah), so the blessing over them is 'Borei Peri haAdamah' (creator of fruit of the ground), not 'Borei Peri haEtz'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rules like Mar bar Rav Ashi that capers are not fruit for orlah, so the blessing over them is 'Borei Peri haAdamah' (creator of fruit of the ground), not 'Borei Peri haEtz'.
The Gemara shifts to a dispute about the blessing over peppers: Rav Sheshet says 'Shehakol', Rava says no blessing at all, consistent with Rava's view that chewing pepper on Yom Kippur is exempt.

items.text: Pepper: Rabbi Meir's view that it is a tree fruit
items.text_en: Pepper: Rabbi Meir's view that it is a tree fruit
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir learns from the verse 'etz ma'achal' that pepper is a tree fruit, liable for orlah, and teaches that Eretz Yisrael lacks nothing.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi Meir learns from the verse 'עץ מאכל' (tree for food) that pepper is a tree fruit, liable for ערלה (orlah), and that Eretz Yisrael lacks nothing.

items.text: Distinction: Fresh vs dry pepper for blessing
items.text_en: Distinction: Fresh vs dry pepper for blessing
items.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes: fresh pepper gets 'Borei Peri haAdamah', dry pepper gets 'Shehakol' (or 'Borei Peri haEtz'? — unresolved).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: no difficulty — the baraita refers to fresh pepper, while the dispute refers to dry pepper.

items.text: דין זנגביל: ברכתו ופטור מיוה"כ
items.text_en: Ginger: Fresh vs dry for blessing and Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that fresh ginger gets 'Borei Peri haAdamah', dry ginger is exempt from blessing and from Yom Kippur prohibition (since not a fruit).
items.desc: רבנן מקשים על מרימר מדברי רבא שהתיר הימלתא (זנגביל) הבאה מהודו ומברכים עליה 'בורא פרי האדמה', ומתרצים: הא ברטיבתא הא ביבשתא.

sub.desc_en: The Rabbis ask Marimar: is eating ginger on Yom Kippur exempt? But Rava said that ginger from India is permitted and one recites 'בורא פרי האדמה' over it.
sub.desc: רבנן מקשים על מרימר: כיצד זנגביל פטור מיוה"כ, הרי הוא מאכל?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: no difficulty — fresh ginger is considered fruit, dry ginger is not.
sub.desc: רבנן מקשים על מרימר: כיצד זנגביל פטור מיוה"כ, הרי הוא מאכל?

items.text: Debate: Blessing over cooked dish with five grains
items.text_en: Debate: Blessing over cooked dish with five grains
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says 'Shehakol' for a cooked dish (dayisa) because honey is primary; Rav Kahana says 'Borei Minei Mezonot' because flour (semida) is primary; Rav Yosef agrees with Rav Kahana.

sub.desc_en: Regarding a cooked dish (חביץ קדרה) and porridge (דייסא): Rav Yehuda says the blessing is 'שהכל', Rav Kahana says 'בורא מיני מזונות', and Rav Yosef rules like Rav Kahana, citing Rav and Shmuel that anything containing the five grains requires 'בורא מיני מזונות'.

sub.text: Gemara's clarification and Rav Yosef's support
sub.text_en: Gemara's clarification and Rav Yosef's support
sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that all agree on plain דייסא (דייסא גרידא) that the blessing is 'בורא מיני מזונות'; the dispute is only about דייסא mixed with honey (כעין חביץ קדרה), and Rav Yosef supports Rav Kahana's view, citing Rav and Shmuel's principle that anything containing the five grains receives the blessing 'בורא מיני מזונות'.
Rav Yosef rules in accordance with Rav Kahana, citing Rav and Shmuel who both say that anything containing the five grains requires the blessing 'Borei Minei Mezonot'.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel's rule: Any mix of five grains gets 'Borei Minei Mezonot'
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel's rule: Any mix of five grains gets 'Borei Minei Mezonot'
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel both rule that any food containing any of the five grains (wheat, barley, etc.) gets the blessing 'Borei Minei Mezonot'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the actual statement: Rav and Shmuel both say that anything containing the five grains requires the blessing 'בורא מיני מזונות'.
The Gemara explains that both formulations of the rule are necessary: one for the grain in its own form, and one for mixtures, to avoid misunderstanding.

items.text: Clarification: 'All that is' vs 'by mixture' for blessing
items.text_en: Clarification: 'All that is' vs 'by mixture' for blessing
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that if we only heard 'all that is' we might think blessing applies only to visible grains, but 'by mixture' teaches it applies even when grains are mixed in.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains why both formulations of Rav and Shmuel's statement are necessary: if only 'anything that is' were stated, one might think it applies only when the grain is intact, but not in a mixture.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's phrase 'all that has' teaches that only the five grains warrant 'Borei Minei Mezonot', excluding rice and millet even when whole, to counter a possible inference that any grain in a mixture would qualify.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: The Mishnah's phrase 'all that has' implies that only the five grains warrant 'Borei Minei Mezonot', excluding rice and millet even when whole, to counter a possible inference that any grain in a mixture would qualify.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita on rice bread
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita on rice bread
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the exclusion of rice and millet by citing a baraita that says rice bread is blessed with a beginning and end blessing like a cooked dish, which for cooked dishes includes 'Borei Minei Mezonot' initially and 'Me'ein Shalosh' finally.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers: But if it is whole in its natural state, we would say that even rice and millet also warrant 'Borei Minei Mezonot'.

The Gemara cites a baraita that states rice bread and millet bread receive a beginning and end blessing like a cooked dish, which for cooked dishes includes 'Borei Minei Mezonot' initially and 'Me'ein Shalosh' finally.

items.text: Distinction between rice bread and cooked dishes
items.text_en: Distinction between rice bread and cooked dishes
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that rice bread is 'like a cooked dish but not exactly a cooked dish': it has a beginning and end blessing like a cooked dish, but the blessings differ—rice bread gets 'Shehakol' initially and 'Borei Nefashot' finally, unlike cooked dishes which get 'Mezonot' and 'Me'ein Shalosh'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: But we do not recite 'Borei Minei Mezonot' over rice and millet? Yet a baraita teaches: If they brought before him bread of rice and bread of millet, he recites the blessing at the beginning and end like a pot-cooked dish.

items.text: Challenge that rice is a cooked dish and attribution to Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri
items.text_en: Challenge that rice is a cooked dish and attribution to Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that rice is listed among cooked dishes in a baraita. It answers that the baraita follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, who considers rice a grain, but the Rabbis disagree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that rice is listed among cooked dishes (מעשה קדרה) in a baraita, implying it should receive the blessing of 'Borei Minei Mezonot'.
The Gemara answers that the baraita follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, who considers rice a grain, but the Rabbis disagree.

items.text: Baraita on wheat and rice blessings
items.text_en: Baraita on wheat and rice blessings
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita detailing blessings for wheat and rice: for wheat, when kernels are whole it gets 'Borei Pri Ha'adamah', and when ground and baked into bread with intact pieces it gets 'HaMotzi' and three blessings, otherwise 'Mezonot' and 'Me'ein Shalosh'. For rice, even with intact pieces, it gets 'Mezonot' initially and 'Me'ein Shalosh' finally.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Rabbis' position by citing a baraita that details the blessings for wheat and rice.
The baraita rules that for rice, even when the pieces are intact, the initial blessing is 'Borei Minei Mezonot' and the final blessing is one blessing summarizing the three.

items.text: Refutation of Rav and Shmuel's position
items.text_en: Refutation of Rav and Shmuel's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if the baraita followed Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, it would require 'HaMotzi' and three blessings for rice, not just 'Mezonot'. Therefore it must follow the Rabbis, providing a refutation of Rav and Shmuel who held that rice does not get 'Mezonot'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the baraita about rice follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, who considers rice a grain, it would require the full 'HaMotzi' blessing and three blessings after, not just 'Mezonot'.
The Gemara concludes: rather, the baraita must follow the Rabbis, providing a refutation of Rav and Shmuel who held that rice does not receive the 'Mezonot' blessing.
The Gemara affirms the refutation with a single word: 'תְּיוּבְתָּא' (a conclusive refutation).

items.text: Reconciliation of blessing for chewing wheat
items.text_en: Reconciliation of blessing for chewing wheat
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: one baraita says chewing wheat gets 'Borei Pri Ha'adamah', another says 'Borei Minei Zera'im'. It resolves that the first follows the Rabbis and the second follows Rabbi Yehuda, who says 'Borei Minei Desha'im' for vegetables.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara digresses: Mar said: One who chews wheat recites 'Borei Pri Ha'adama' over it. Yet a baraita teaches 'Borei Minei Zeraim'! It is not difficult: This is Rabbi Yehuda, and that is the Rabbis. For we learned: Over vegetables one says 'Borei Pri Ha'adama'; Rabbi Yehuda says 'Borei Minei Desha'im'.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by attributing the first baraita to the Rabbis and the second to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that the blessing for vegetables is 'Borei Minei Desha'im'.

items.text: Reconciliation of final blessing for rice and dispute of Rabban Gamliel
items.text_en: Reconciliation of final blessing for rice and dispute of Rabban Gamliel
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: one baraita says rice gets 'Me'ein Shalosh' finally, another says nothing. Rav Sheshet resolves that the first follows Rabban Gamliel (who requires three blessings for the seven species) and the second follows the Rabbis. A story illustrates Rabban Gamliel's position and Rabbi Akiva's ruling that the law follows the majority.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Blessings for non-grain foods
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Blessings for non-grain foods
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for foods not from the seven species or grain, Rabban Gamliel says one blessing (me'ein shalosh) and the Sages say no blessing at all.

items.text: Gemara's first question: Which opinion is cited?
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: Which opinion is cited?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's ruling aligns with Rabban Gamliel or the Sages, noting that the continuation about broken pieces suggests Rabban Gamliel's view.

items.text: Objection: Rabban Gamliel's three blessings vs. one blessing
items.text_en: Objection: Rabban Gamliel's three blessings vs. one blessing
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the ruling follows Rabban Gamliel, then the later statement about a single blessing contradicts his requirement of three blessings.

items.text: Resolution: The Sages' view prevails
items.text_en: Resolution: The Sages' view prevails
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah actually follows the Sages, and the later statement about a single blessing aligns with them, not Rabban Gamliel.

items.text: Rava's ruling on flour-based foods
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on flour-based foods
items.desc_en: Rava distinguishes between foods where flour is primary (blessing 'Borei Minei Mezonot') and where honey is primary (blessing 'Shehakol Nihya Bidvaro').

items.text: Rav and Shmuel's general rule for five grains
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel's general rule for five grains
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel state that any food containing any of the five grains receives the blessing 'Borei Minei Mezonot'.

items.text: Rav Yosef's ruling on habitzah (porridge)
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's ruling on habitzah (porridge)
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef rules that if habitzah contains olive-sized pieces of bread, it requires 'Hamotzi' and three blessings afterward; otherwise, it requires 'Borei Minei Mezonot' and one blessing.

items.text: Abaye's challenge: Does the blessing depend on bread pieces?
items.text_en: Abaye's challenge: Does the blessing depend on bread pieces?
items.desc_en: Abaye questions Rav Yosef's distinction, citing a baraita where eating olive-sized pieces of matzah fulfills the Passover obligation, implying that the blessing should be 'Hamotzi' regardless of piece size.

items.text: Clarification: The case of 'she'ersan' (soaked grains)
items.text_en: Clarification: The case of 'she'ersan' (soaked grains)
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the discussion is about 'she'ersan' (soaked grains), and the baraita's phrase 'she'achalan' should be 'she'achalo' (he ate it).

items.text: Rav Sheshet's ruling on habitza (porridge)
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's ruling on habitza (porridge)
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet rules that even if habitza lacks olive-sized bread pieces, one still recites 'Hamotzi' if there is a crust of bread on it.

items.text: Troknin: Exemption from challah
items.text_en: Troknin: Exemption from challah
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses 'troknin' (a type of bread) and whether it is exempt from challah, with Abaye defining it as 'kuba d'ara' (a round loaf).

items.text: Tritah: Exemption from challah
items.text_en: Tritah: Exemption from challah
items.desc_en: Abaye says 'tritah' is exempt from challah, with various opinions on what it is (boiled grits, Indian bread, or bread for kutach).

items.text: Baraita: Bread for kutach is exempt from challah
items.text_en: Baraita: Bread for kutach is exempt from challah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya teaches that bread made for kutach is exempt from challah, but a contradictory baraita says it is liable; Rabbi Yehuda explains that the appearance proves it is bread.

items.text: Blessing over a kuba (earth oven bread)
items.text_en: Blessing over a kuba (earth oven bread)
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef what blessing to recite over a kuba (a bread baked in an earthen pit). Rav Yosef responds that it is not considered bread but a gubla (a type of cake), and the blessing is 'Borei minei mezonot'.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef what blessing to recite over a kuba (earth oven bread).
Rav Yosef responds that a kuba is not bread but a gubla (cake), and the blessing is 'Borei minei mezonot'.

items.text: Mar Zutra's practice and Mar bar Rav Ashi's ruling on kuba for Passover
items.text_en: Mar Zutra's practice and Mar bar Rav Ashi's ruling on kuba for Passover
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra would establish his meal on the kuba and recite 'Hamotzi' and the three blessings. Mar bar Rav Ashi adds that one can fulfill their obligation with this bread on Passover because it is called 'lechem oni' (poor bread).

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra would establish his meal on the kuba (a type of bread) and recite 'המוציא' and the three blessings.
Mar bar Rav Ashi adds that one can fulfill their obligation with this bread on Passover because it is called 'לחם עוני' (poor bread).

items.text: Blessing over date honey and its support from a Tanna
items.text_en: Blessing over date honey and its support from a Tanna
items.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi rules that the blessing over date honey is 'Shehakol' because it is merely sweat (exudate) from the dates. This is supported by a Tanna who debates whether date honey is considered a fruit product for the laws of terumah.

sub.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi rules that the blessing over date honey is 'Shehakol' because it is merely sweat (exudate) from the dates.

The Gemara supports Mar bar Rav Ashi's ruling by citing a Tanna who debates whether date honey is considered a fruit product for the laws of תרומה (priestly portion), with Rabbi Eliezer deeming it liable and Rabbi Yehoshua exempting it.

items.text: Blessing over trimah (date paste) and the discussion with Rava
items.text_en: Blessing over trimah (date paste) and the discussion with Rava
items.desc_en: A certain rabbi asks Rava about the blessing for trimah (a date preparation). After some confusion, Rava recalls Rav Asi's teaching that trimah from terumah dates is permitted, and rules that the blessing is 'Borei pri ha'etz' because the dates retain their original form.

sub.text: A certain rabbi's question to Rava
sub.text_en: A certain rabbi's question to Rava
sub.desc_en: A certain rabbi asks Rava what blessing is recited over trimah (date paste).

sub.text: Gemara's narrative: Rava's confusion and Ravina's clarification
sub.text_en: Gemara's narrative: Rava's confusion and Ravina's clarification
sub.desc_en: Rava does not understand the question, and Ravina, sitting before him, asks whether he means trimah of sesame, safflower, or other seeds.

sub.text: Rava's answer and citation of Rav Asi
sub.text_en: Rava's answer and citation of Rav Asi
sub.desc_en: Rava recalls the question refers to date trimah and cites Rav Asi's ruling that terumah dates may be made into trimah but not into date beer.
Rava rules that the blessing over date trimah is 'Borei pri ha'etz' because the dates retain their original form.

items.text: Blessing over shatita (a barley drink) and the dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.text_en: Blessing over shatita (a barley drink) and the dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel disagree on the blessing for shatita: Rav says 'Shehakol', Shmuel says 'Borei minei mezonot'. Rav Chisda resolves that they do not dispute: thick shatita is for eating (mezonot), thin is for drinking (Shehakol). Rav Yosef objects based on a mishnah about drinking a medicinal drink on Shabbat, but Abaye resolves that the intention is for eating, and the medicinal effect is incidental. The Gemara concludes that even if intended for medicine, since one derives benefit, a blessing is required.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the dispute: Rav says the blessing over shatita (a barley drink) is 'Shehakol', Shmuel says it is 'Borei minei mezonot'.
Rav Chisda resolves that Rav and Shmuel do not dispute: thick shatita is for eating (mezonot), thin is for drinking (Shehakol).
Rav Yosef objects from a mishnah that permits stirring shatita on Shabbat and drinking it, implying it is for eating, not medicine, since medicine is forbidden on Shabbat.
Abaye answers that the person intends for eating, not medicine, as supported by a baraita that all foods may be eaten for healing on Shabbat.
In an alternative version, Abaye explains that the person intends for eating, and the healing effect is incidental (ממילא).
The Gemara concludes that even if one intends for healing, since one derives benefit (הנאה), a blessing is required, thus supporting Rav and Shmuel's dispute.

items.text: The wording of the blessing over bread: 'Hamotzi' vs. 'Motzi'
items.text_en: The wording of the blessing over bread: 'Hamotzi' vs. 'Motzi'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states the blessing over bread is 'Hamotzi'. The Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Nechemiah dispute whether to say 'Hamotzi' or 'Motzi'. Rava explains that all agree 'Motzi' implies past tense (God brought out), but they dispute about 'Hamotzi': the Rabbis hold it means past tense (as in 'who brought out water from the rock'), while Rabbi Nechemiah holds it means present tense (as in 'who brings you out from under the burdens'). The Gemara explains the Rabbis' interpretation of the verse used by Rabbi Nechemiah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that over bread one says 'Hamotzi'.
A baraita records the dispute: Tanna Kamma says the blessing is 'Hamotzi', while Rabbi Nechemiah says 'Motzi'.

Rava explains that all agree 'Motzi' means past tense (as in the verse 'אל מוציאם ממצרים'), but they dispute about 'Hamotzi': the Rabbis hold it means past tense (as in 'המוציא לך מים מצור החלמיש'), while Rabbi Nechemiah holds it means present tense (as in 'המוציא אתכם מתחת סבלות מצרים').

The Gemara explains the Rabbis' interpretation of the verse used by Rabbi Nechemiah: God told Israel that when He brings them out, He will do something so they know He is the one who brought them out of Egypt, as written 'וידעתם כי אני ה' אלהיכם המוציא'.

items.text: A story about Rabbi Zeira testing a sage's knowledge of blessings
items.text_en: A story about Rabbi Zeira testing a sage's knowledge of blessings
items.desc_en: The Sages praise Bar Rav Zevid as a great man knowledgeable in blessings. Rabbi Zeira tests him by having bread brought, and Bar Rav Zevid begins with 'Motzi'. Rabbi Zeira criticizes him, implying he should have said 'Hamotzi'.

sub.desc_en: The Sages praise Bar Rav Zevid to Rabbi Zeira as a great man knowledgeable in blessings.
Rabbi Zeira instructs the Sages to bring Bar Rav Zevid to him when he comes their way.
On one occasion Bar Rav Zevid came to Rabbi Zeira, bread was brought, and he began the blessing with 'מוציא' (without the definite article).
Rabbi Zeira criticizes Bar Rav Zevid, implying that a truly knowledgeable person would have said 'המוציא' (with the definite article) instead of 'מוציא'.
