items.text: Conclusion of the earlier dispute about 'מוציא' and ruling like Rabbanan
items.text_en: Conclusion of the earlier dispute about 'מוציא' and ruling like Rabbanan
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the halakha follows the Rabbanan that 'המוציא לחם מן הארץ' is the correct blessing, and explains that the one who says 'מוציא' was merely avoiding the dispute.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the halakha follows the Rabbanan that 'המוציא לחם מן הארץ' is the correct blessing, and explains that the one who says 'מוציא' was merely avoiding the dispute.

items.text: Derivation that cooked vegetables require 'בורא פרי האדמה'
items.text_en: Derivation that cooked vegetables require 'בורא פרי האדמה'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's comparison of vegetables to bread implies that just as bread is changed by fire, so too vegetables changed by fire (cooked) require 'בורא פרי האדמה'. Ravnai cites Abaye to support this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's comparison of vegetables to bread implies that just as bread is changed by fire, so too cooked vegetables require the blessing 'בורא פרי האדמה'.
Ravnai cites Abaye that this proves cooked vegetables require 'בורא פרי האדמה', based on the comparison to bread.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan on cooked vegetables, with resolution
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan on cooked vegetables, with resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda cites Rav that cooked vegetables require 'בורא פרי האדמה', while Ulla cites Rabbi Yochanan that they require 'שהכל נהיה בדברו'. The Gemara then presents a rule: anything whose raw blessing is 'בורא פרי האדמה' becomes 'שהכל' when cooked, and vice versa. Examples are given for each case.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda teaches in the name of Rav that cooked vegetables require the blessing 'בורא פרי האדמה'.
Ulla cites Rabbi Yochanan that cooked vegetables require the blessing 'שהכל נהיה בדברו', contradicting Rav.
The Gemara states a rule: anything whose raw blessing is 'בורא פרי האדמה' becomes 'שהכל' when cooked, and vice versa.
The Gemara questions how to find an example for the second case of the rule (raw 'שהכל' becoming 'בורא פרי האדמה' when cooked).
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers that the example is beets and leeks (תומי וכרתי).

items.text: Second version of the dispute: Shmuel vs. Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Second version of the dispute: Shmuel vs. Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites Shmuel that cooked vegetables require 'בורא פרי האדמה', while Ulla again cites Rabbi Yochanan that they require 'שהכל נהיה בדברו'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman teaches in the name of Shmuel that cooked vegetables require the blessing 'בורא פרי האדמה'.
Ulla cites Rabbi Yochanan that cooked vegetables require the blessing 'שהכל נהיה בדברו'.

items.text: Attempt to connect the dispute to a Tannaitic source and resolution
items.text_en: Attempt to connect the dispute to a Tannaitic source and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute is rooted in a Tannaitic argument about matzah: Rabbi Meir permits cooked matzah, while Rabbi Yosei prohibits it. However, the Gemara rejects this, explaining that Rabbi Yosei's concern is the taste of matzah, not the blessing; regarding cooked vegetables, even Rabbi Yosei agrees they require 'בורא פרי האדמה'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute about blessings on cooked vegetables is rooted in a Tannaitic argument about matzah: Rabbi Meir permits cooked matzah, while Rabbi Yosei prohibits it.
The Gemara rejects the connection, explaining that Rabbi Yosei's concern is the taste of matzah, not the blessing; regarding cooked vegetables, even Rabbi Yosei agrees they require 'בורא פרי האדמה'.

items.text: Conflicting reports from Rabbi Yochanan and resolution by Rabbi Zeira
items.text_en: Conflicting reports from Rabbi Yochanan and resolution by Rabbi Zeira
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet both cite Rabbi Yochanan but with opposite rulings. Rabbi Zeira questions this, arguing that Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba was more precise and reviewed his learning with Rabbi Yochanan, while Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet did not. A practical case of a turnip cooked seven times confirms that Rabbi Yochanan ruled 'בורא פרי האדמה'.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba reports that Rabbi Yochanan ruled that cooked vegetables (שלוקות) require the blessing 'בורא פרי האדמה'.

sub.text: Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet contradicts, citing Rabbi Yochanan that cooked vegetables require 'שהכל נהיה בדברו'.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that Ulla fixed his error (שבשתא) in line with Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet's version.
Rabbi Zeira questions how Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet's report can be compared to Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's.
Rabbi Zeira argues that Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba was precise in learning from Rabbi Yochanan, while Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet was not.
Rabbi Zeira adds that Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba reviewed his learning with Rabbi Yochanan every thirty days, unlike Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet.
Rabbi Zeira cites a case where a turnip cooked seven times was brought to Rabbi Yochanan, who ruled 'בורא פרי האדמה', confirming Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's version.

items.text: Proof from Rabbi Yochanan's blessing on a salted olive
items.text_en: Proof from Rabbi Yochanan's blessing on a salted olive
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba testifies that he saw Rabbi Yochanan eat a salted olive and recite both a beginning and ending blessing. This proves that cooked items retain their original blessing status, as the olive required 'בורא פרי העץ' initially and 'מעין שלש' at the end. The Gemara considers the possibility that if cooked items lost their status, the ending blessing would be 'בורא נפשות'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba testifies that he saw Rabbi Yochanan eat a salted olive and recite both a beginning blessing (בורא פרי העץ) and an ending blessing (מעין שלש), proving that cooked items retain their original blessing status.
The Gemara asks: if cooked items lose their original status, what ending blessing would Rabbi Yochanan have recited on the olive?
The Gemara suggests that the ending blessing would be 'בורא נפשות' (the general after-blessing for non-bread foods).

items.text: Objection from the law of bitter herbs and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from the law of bitter herbs and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel objects: if cooked vegetables retain their status, why can't one fulfill the obligation of maror with cooked bitter herbs? The Gemara answers that the requirement for the taste of maror is different, so the objection is rejected.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel objects from a baraita: if cooked vegetables retain their original identity (בְּמִילְּתַיְיהוּ קָיְימִי), why can one not fulfill the obligation of maror with cooked bitter herbs on Passover?

The Gemara resolves the objection by distinguishing the case of maror, where the taste of bitterness (טַעַם מָרוֹר) is required and is absent after cooking, so the baraita does not contradict the principle that cooked vegetables retain their identity.

items.text: Question about the blessing on a salted olive after removing the pit
items.text_en: Question about the blessing on a salted olive after removing the pit
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira: how does Rabbi Yochanan bless on a salted olive after its pit is removed? This question sets up the next discussion.

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Zeira
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Zeira
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira how Rabbi Yochanan would recite the blessing on a salted olive after its pit has been removed.

items.text: The size of an olive for blessing
items.text_en: The size of an olive for blessing
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the required olive size for blessing is a medium olive, not a large one. It cites a mishnah defining the medium olive as 'Agori', and discusses its alternate names.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the reduced olive size that was brought before Rabbi Yochanan.
The answer explains that the required size is a medium olive, not a large one, and the olive brought was large even after removing its pit.
The Gemara cites a mishnah defining the medium olive as 'Agori', and Rabbi Avahu discusses its alternate names and etymology.

items.text: The dispute between two students of Bar Kappara
items.text_en: The dispute between two students of Bar Kappara
items.desc_en: A story is told of two students who brought vegetables and meat dishes before Bar Kappara. One blessed on the meat, the other mocked him. Bar Kappara initially was angry at the mocker, then at the blesser. The Gemara analyzes whether they disagreed about the blessing for cooked vegetables (shehakol vs borei pri ha'adamah) or about which item is more beloved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a story of two students before Bar Kappara, where one blessed on the meat and the other mocked him.
Bar Kappara initially expresses anger at the mocker, rebuking him for mocking someone who clearly values meat.
Bar Kappara reverses his position and now expresses anger at the blesser, questioning his wisdom and age.
A baraita reports that both students did not complete their year (i.e., died within the year).

The Gemara proposes that the dispute is about the blessing for cooked vegetables: one holds it is 'shehakol' and thus the beloved item takes priority, the other holds it is 'borei pri ha'adamah' and thus the fruit (vegetable) takes priority.

The Gemara rejects the previous analysis and explains that both agree the blessing is 'shehakol', but they disagree about which item is more beloved: the blesser holds the beloved (meat) is preferred, the mocker holds the cabbage (which is nourishing) is preferred.

items.text: The blessing on turnip stalks
items.text_en: The blessing on turnip stalks
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira reports that in Rav Huna's house, large-cut turnip stalks require 'borei pri ha'adamah', while small-cut ones require 'shehakol'. In Rav Yehuda's house, both require 'borei pri ha'adamah', and the cutting is only to sweeten the taste.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira reports that in Rav Huna's house, large-cut turnip stalks require 'borei pri ha'adamah', while small-cut ones require 'shehakol'.
Rabbi Zeira adds that in Rav Yehuda's house, both large and small cuts require 'borei pri ha'adamah', and the cutting is only to sweeten the taste.

items.text: The blessing on cooked beets and turnips with flour
items.text_en: The blessing on cooked beets and turnips with flour
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi reports that in Rav Kahana's house, a beet dish with little flour requires 'borei pri ha'adamah', while a turnip dish with much flour requires 'borei minei mezonot'. He then retracts, saying both require 'borei pri ha'adamah', and the flour is only to bind the dish.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi reports that in Rav Kahana's house, a beet dish with little flour requires 'borei pri ha'adamah', while a turnip dish with much flour requires 'borei minei mezonot'.
Rav Ashi retracts, stating that both require 'borei pri ha'adamah', and the flour is only to bind the dish.

items.text: The health benefits of beet stew
items.text_en: The health benefits of beet stew
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda praises beet stew as good for the heart, eyes, and intestines. Abaye adds that it is effective when placed on the coals and cooked thoroughly.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that beet stew is beneficial for the heart, eyes, and especially the intestines.
Abaye adds that the benefit applies only when the beets are placed on coals and cooked until they make a 'tuch tuch' sound.

items.text: The status of cooking water and the herb shevet
items.text_en: The status of cooking water and the herb shevet
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa states that the water of cooked beets and turnips has the same status as the vegetables themselves. He questions whether the water of the herb shevet is used to sweeten or to remove bitterness. A baraita resolves that it is used to sweeten, as it loses its terumah status after imparting flavor.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa states that the water of cooked beets, turnips, and all cooked vegetables has the same status as the vegetables themselves.
Rav Pappa questions whether the water of the herb shevet is used to sweeten the dish or to remove bitterness.
A baraita is cited: once shevet has imparted its flavor into the pot, it loses its terumah status and is no longer susceptible to food impurity.
The Gemara concludes from the baraita that shevet is used to sweeten, not to remove bitterness.

items.text: The blessing on a bread crumb in a bowl
items.text_en: The blessing on a bread crumb in a bowl
items.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Ashi rules that a bread crumb in a bowl requires 'hamotzi'. This contradicts Rabbi Chiya, who requires that the blessing conclude with the bread. Rava objects: why should a crumb be different? Even on a whole loaf, the blessing ends on a piece.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers by citing a baraita: shibta once it imparts flavor to the pot is not subject to terumah laws and does not convey food impurity — implying it is used for sweetening, not bitterness removal.

items.text: Rava's ruling on blessing before breaking bread
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on blessing before breaking bread
items.desc_en: Rava states that one should bless first and then break the bread. The Nehardeans follow Rabbi Chiyya's practice of finishing the blessing with the bread, while the Rabbis follow Rava. Ravina reports that his father followed Rabbi Chiyya, but the halakha is like Rava.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rabbi Yochanan on whole vs. broken loaves
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rabbi Yochanan on whole vs. broken loaves
items.desc_en: When both broken pieces and whole loaves are present, Rav Huna says one blesses on the broken pieces and exempts the whole loaves. Rabbi Yochanan says a whole loaf is preferable (mitzvah min hamuvchar). However, if a broken wheat loaf and a whole barley loaf are present, all agree one blesses on the wheat broken piece.

items.text: Analogy from terumah: importance vs. completeness
items.text_en: Analogy from terumah: importance vs. completeness
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba compares the dispute to a Tannaitic debate about terumah: whether to give a small whole onion or a half of a large onion. One opinion values importance (chashuv), the other values completeness (shalem). The Gemara clarifies that when a priest is present, all agree importance is preferred; the dispute is only when no priest is present, citing a Mishnah about terumah.

items.text: Mar bar Ravina's practice and the praise of Shalman
items.text_en: Mar bar Ravina's practice and the praise of Shalman
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says a God-fearing person fulfills both opinions by placing a broken piece within a whole loaf and breaking it. He identifies Mar bar Ravina as such a person. A Tanna teaches before Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak that one places the broken piece inside the whole loaf, breaks, and blesses; Rav Nachman praises him, saying his name Shalman indicates peace between the students.

items.text: Passover: placing broken piece within whole loaf
items.text_en: Passover: placing broken piece within whole loaf
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa states that all agree on Passover one places a broken piece within a whole loaf and breaks it, because the Torah calls matzah 'poor bread' (lechem oni), implying brokenness.

items.text: Shabbat: requirement of two whole loaves
items.text_en: Shabbat: requirement of two whole loaves
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba says on Shabbat one must break bread on two whole loaves, because the Torah writes 'lechem mishneh' (double bread).

items.text: Practices of Rav Kahana and Rabbi Zeira regarding two loaves
items.text_en: Practices of Rav Kahana and Rabbi Zeira regarding two loaves
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi saw Rav Kahana holding two loaves but breaking only one. Rabbi Zeira would break on the entire loaf (i.e., the whole loaf). Ravina questions whether this appears gluttonous, but Rav Ashi responds that since he does not do so daily, it is not seen as gluttony.

items.text: Blessing on eiruv bread as a second mitzvah
items.text_en: Blessing on eiruv bread as a second mitzvah
items.desc_en: Rav Ami and Rav Asi, when they had bread from the eiruv, would recite the blessing 'hamotzi lechem min ha'aretz' over it, reasoning that since it fulfilled one mitzvah (the eiruv), they should perform another mitzvah with it (eating it for a meal).

items.text: Dispute about when a blessing is required before eating
items.text_en: Dispute about when a blessing is required before eating
items.desc_en: Rav, Rabbi Yochanan, and Rav Sheshet debate whether certain phrases like 'Take, blessed' or 'Bring salt' require a blessing before eating. Rav Sheshet cites a verse to support that one must feed one's animal before eating oneself.

items.text: Rava bar Shmuel's ruling on breaking bread
items.text_en: Rava bar Shmuel's ruling on breaking bread
items.desc_en: Rava bar Shmuel rules in the name of Rabbi Chiyya that the one who breaks bread must wait until salt or a relish is brought before each person. When he himself broke bread immediately at the Exilarch's house, he explained that there was no need for delay there.

items.text: Rava bar Shmuel's advice on urination
items.text_en: Rava bar Shmuel's advice on urination
items.desc_en: Rava bar Shmuel states in the name of Rabbi Chiyya that urine is only absorbed while sitting. Rav Kahana adds that with loose soil it can be absorbed even while standing. If there is no loose soil, one should stand on a high place and urinate onto a slope.

items.text: Health advice about salt and water after eating
items.text_en: Health advice about salt and water after eating
items.desc_en: Rava bar Shmuel advises eating salt after every meal and drinking water after every drink to avoid harm. A baraita supports this, and another baraita warns that failing to do so can cause bad breath by day and askara (croup) by night.

items.text: Drinking water with meals prevents stomach illness
items.text_en: Drinking water with meals prevents stomach illness
items.desc_en: The Sages taught that one who dilutes his food with water will not suffer from stomach illness. Rav Chisda specifies the amount: a kiton (small cup) for bread.

items.text: Health benefits of lentils, mustard, small fish, and ketzach
items.text_en: Health benefits of lentils, mustard, small fish, and ketzach
items.desc_en: Rav Mari reports that eating lentils once every thirty days prevents askara, but daily use harms breath. Similarly, mustard once every thirty days prevents illness but daily harms the heart. Small fish prevent stomach illness and promote growth. Rabbi Chama bar Chanina says ketzach prevents heart pain, but a baraita calls it deadly; the Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between its smell and taste.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's blessing and a lesson about God's measure
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's blessing and a lesson about God's measure
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira (or Rabbi Chinana bar Pappa) states that the halakha does not follow Rabbi Yehuda, who said the blessing for vegetables is 'Borei minei desha'im'. He explains Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning: just as one blesses God each day with appropriate blessings, so too each species should receive its appropriate blessing. Then he contrasts God's measure with that of humans: a full vessel holds, but an empty one does not, citing a verse about listening.

items.text: Mishnah: Blessings for fruit of the tree and ground
items.text_en: Mishnah: Blessings for fruit of the tree and ground
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one recited 'Borei pri ha'adamah' over tree fruit, he has fulfilled his obligation; but if he recited 'Borei pri ha'etz' over ground fruit, he has not. For any food, if he said 'Shehakol nihyeh bidvaro', he has fulfilled his obligation.

items.text: Gemara: Identifying the Tanna and Rabbi Yehuda's view on wheat
items.text_en: Gemara: Identifying the Tanna and Rabbi Yehuda's view on wheat
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who holds that the tree's essence is the ground, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak identifies it as Rabbi Yehuda. It then questions the ruling about ground fruit, explaining that it was necessary for Rabbi Yehuda, who considers wheat a tree. The Gemara cites a dispute about the Tree of Knowledge: Rabbi Meir says it was a vine, Rabbi Nechemya a fig, and Rabbi Yehuda wheat. Finally, the Gemara clarifies that the blessing for wheat is not 'Borei pri ha'etz' because a tree must have a permanent trunk that remains when fruit is taken.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Blessing for fruit without a pit
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Blessing for fruit without a pit
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a fruit's pit is removed and the fruit does not regenerate, one recites 'Borei Pri Ha'adamah' instead of 'Borei Pri Ha'etz'. It also notes that if one says 'Shehakol' for any food, they fulfill their obligation.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rabbi Yochanan on 'Shehakol' for bread and wine
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rabbi Yochanan on 'Shehakol' for bread and wine
items.desc_en: Rav Huna says 'Shehakol' is valid for all foods except bread and wine, while Rabbi Yochanan says it is valid even for bread and wine. The Gemara attempts to align their views with a Tannaitic dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei, but each Amora explains that their position is consistent even with the opposing Tanna's view under specific conditions.

items.text: Story of Binyamin the Shepherd: Blessing in Aramaic
items.text_en: Story of Binyamin the Shepherd: Blessing in Aramaic
items.desc_en: Binyamin the shepherd recited a blessing over bread in Aramaic without mentioning God's name explicitly. Rav ruled that he fulfilled his obligation, but the Gemara clarifies that he actually said 'Berich Rachamana' (Blessed is the Merciful). The Gemara then questions whether this suffices for the first blessing of Birkat Hamazon, and concludes that it teaches that blessings may be recited in any language, even if not in the formula established by the Sages.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan: Blessing must include God's name and kingship
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan: Blessing must include God's name and kingship
items.desc_en: Rav states that any blessing without God's name is invalid, while Rabbi Yochanan adds that it must also include mention of God's kingship. Abaye supports Rav with a baraita, but Rabbi Yochanan interprets the same baraita as requiring both name and kingship.

items.text: Mishnah: Blessings for non-produce items and multiple foods
items.text_en: Mishnah: Blessings for non-produce items and multiple foods
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that for items not grown from the earth, one says 'Shehakol'. It lists vinegar, unripe dates (novlot), and locusts as examples. Rabbi Yehuda says one does not bless over items that are a curse. If one has multiple types of food, Rabbi Yehuda says to bless over a species of the Seven Species, while the Sages say one may bless over whichever they prefer.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying 'not grown from the earth' – mushrooms and truffles
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying 'not grown from the earth' – mushrooms and truffles
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists items that require 'Shehakol', including meat, milk, eggs, and spoiled foods. It questions why mushrooms and truffles are included, since they grow from the earth. Abaye explains that they grow from the earth but do not draw nourishment from it, so the text should read 'not nourished from the earth'.

items.text: Dispute over 'novlot': unripe dates or pressed dates
items.text_en: Dispute over 'novlot': unripe dates or pressed dates
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Ila'a disagree on what 'novlot' are: one says unripe dates (buslei kamra), the other says pressed dates (tamrei dezikah). The Gemara analyzes the implications for Rabbi Yehuda's ruling and for tithing, concluding that the dispute is specifically about 'novlot temarah' (date novlot), and that the context of demai (doubtfully tithed produce) supports the interpretation of unripe dates.

items.text: Alternative version of the dispute
items.text_en: Alternative version of the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative formulation of the dispute regarding novlot, suggesting a different interpretation of the disagreement.

items.text: Resolution of the date terminology contradiction
items.text_en: Resolution of the date terminology contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction between two opinions about the meaning of 'novlot' by showing that the difficulty remains for one opinion, concluding with 'kashya'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by showing that for the opinion that 'novlot' means dates from a palm branch, the terminology is consistent, but for the opinion that it means unripe dates, the inconsistency remains as a difficulty (קשיא).

items.text: Ulla's explanation of the Mishnah dispute
items.text_en: Ulla's explanation of the Mishnah dispute
items.desc_en: Ulla explains that the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis applies only when the blessings are identical; when they differ, all agree one blesses each separately.

sub.desc_en: Ulla explains that the Mishnah dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis applies only when the blessings are identical; when they differ, all agree one blesses each separately.

items.text: Challenge from the radish and olive baraita
items.text_en: Challenge from the radish and olive baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Ulla with a baraita where radish and olive have different blessings yet one blessing exempts the other. It answers that the radish is primary, but then questions whether Rabbi Yehuda accepts the principle of primary and secondary. A further baraita shows he does.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: if a radish and an olive are before him, he recites a blessing over the radish and exempts the olive, even though their blessings differ.
The Gemara answers that the baraita deals with a case where the radish is the primary component, so its blessing exempts the secondary olive.
The Gemara objects: if the radish is primary, why does Rabbi Yehuda in the latter clause say to bless the olive? Does Rabbi Yehuda reject the principle that the primary exempts the secondary?

The Gemara rejects the objection by citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda explicitly says that if the olive comes because of the radish, one blesses the radish and exempts the olive, showing he does accept the primary-secondary principle.

items.text: Reformulation of the baraita to resolve the contradiction
items.text_en: Reformulation of the baraita to resolve the contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara reinterprets the baraita as missing a clause: when radish is primary, one blessing suffices; when not, all agree each requires its own blessing; the dispute is only when blessings are identical.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by reinterpreting the baraita as missing a clause: when radish is primary, one blessing suffices; when not, all agree each requires its own blessing; the dispute is only when blessings are identical.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappaha
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappaha
items.desc_en: Two Amoraim disagree about the scope of the Mishnah dispute: one says it is only when blessings are identical, the other says it applies even when blessings differ.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute between Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappaha regarding the scope of the Mishnah's disagreement.

sub.text: Rabbi Ammi (or Rabbi Yitzchak Nappaha) — first position
sub.text_en: Rabbi Ammi (or Rabbi Yitzchak Nappaha) — first position
sub.desc_en: One Amora states that the Mishnah's dispute applies only when the blessings are identical, but when they differ, all agree one recites a blessing on each food separately.

sub.text: Rabbi Ammi (or Rabbi Yitzchak Nappaha) — second position
sub.text_en: Rabbi Ammi (or Rabbi Yitzchak Nappaha) — second position
sub.desc_en: The other Amora holds that the dispute applies even when the blessings are not identical.

items.text: Clarification of the second opinion
items.text_en: Clarification of the second opinion
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the second Amora's dispute is about, and Rabbi Yirmeya answers: it is about which food to bless first.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the opinion that the dispute applies even when the blessings are different, what exactly is the dispute about?
Rabbi Yirmeya answers: the dispute is about which food to bless first (להקדים).

items.text: The principle of precedence from the verse
items.text_en: The principle of precedence from the verse
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef (or Rabbi Yitzchak) states that the order of the seven species in the verse determines the order of blessings.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef (or Rabbi Yitzchak) states that the order of the seven species in the verse determines the order of blessings, citing the verse 'אֶרֶץ חִטָּה וּשְׂעֹרָה וְגֶפֶן וּתְאֵנָה וְרִמּוֹן אֶרֶץ זֵית שֶׁמֶן וּדְבָשׁ'.

items.text: Rabbi Chanan's alternative interpretation of the verse
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanan's alternative interpretation of the verse
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanan argues that the entire verse is for halakhic measurements, not precedence, and the Gemara lists examples for each species.

sub.text: Stam's introduction of Rabbi Chanan's position
sub.text_en: Stam's introduction of Rabbi Chanan's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Rabbi Chanan's alternative view that the entire verse is for halakhic measurements, not precedence.
The Gemara cites a baraita about a leprous house to show that wheat is used for the measurement of 'כדי אכילת פרס' (the time to eat a half-loaf).
The Gemara cites a baraita about a bone the size of a barley grain to show that barley is used for the measurement of טומאת מת (impurity from a corpse).

sub.text: Supporting baraita for grape, fig, and pomegranate
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita for grape, fig, and pomegranate
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites measurements for grape (a quarter-log of wine for a nazirite), fig (a dried fig for Shabbat carrying), and pomegranate (the size of a pomegranate for vessel impurity).

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Shiurim as olives
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Shiurim as olives
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the measure for olive-sized items is like olives, and Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina interprets 'land of olive oil' as a land where all measures are olive-sized, but clarifies that most measures are olive-sized, not all.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the measure for olive-sized items is like olives, and Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina interprets 'land of olive oil' as a land where all measures are olive-sized, but clarifies that most measures are olive-sized, not all.

items.text: Gemara's question on honey measure
items.text_en: Gemara's question on honey measure
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the measure for honey, citing a verse about a 'thick honeycomb' on Yom Kippur, and notes that these measures are rabbinic, with scriptural support as mere hints.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Ḥanina
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Ḥanina
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, interprets the verse 'a land of olive oil' as a land whose measures are like olives.
The Gemara explains that 'honey' alludes to the measure of a large date on Yom Kippur.
The Gemara asks whether these measures are explicitly written in the Torah.
The Gemara concludes that these measures are rabbinic, and the verse is merely a support.

items.text: Rav Chisda and Rav Hamnuna debate blessing precedence
items.text_en: Rav Chisda and Rav Hamnuna debate blessing precedence
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda and Rav Hamnuna sit at a meal; Rav Hamnuna blesses dates first. Rav Chisda questions this based on Rav Yosef's rule that what is earlier in a verse gets precedence. Rav Hamnuna responds that dates are second to 'land' and pomegranates fifth, so dates come first.

sub.desc_en: Sets the scene: Rav Chisda and Rav Hamnuna sit at a meal, dates and pomegranates are brought, and Rav Hamnuna recites the blessing over the dates first.
Rav Chisda challenges Rav Hamnuna, citing Rav Yosef's (or Rabbi Yitzchak's) rule that the food mentioned earlier in the verse takes precedence in blessing.
Rav Hamnuna justifies his action: the date is second to the word 'land' in the verse, while the pomegranate is fifth, so the date indeed comes first.
Rav Chisda expresses admiration, wishing for iron legs to serve Rav Hamnuna and hear his novel teachings.

items.text: Rav Papa's ruling on blessings during a meal
items.text_en: Rav Papa's ruling on blessings during a meal
items.desc_en: Rav Papa states the halakha: items that come from the meal itself require no blessing before or after; items not from the meal require a blessing before but not after; after the meal, both require blessings before and after.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute about the blessings required for figs and grapes brought during a meal.
Rav Huna rules that figs and grapes require a blessing before eating but not after, as Grace after Meals exempts them.
Rav Naḥman concurs with Rav Huna's ruling.
Rav Sheshet argues that they require blessings both before and after, since only bread-like pastry is exempt from a blessing after.
The Gemara notes that both Rav Huna and Rav Sheshet disagree with Rabbi Ḥiyya, who holds that bread exempts all foods and wine exempts all drinks.
Rav Pappa rules the halakha: items from the meal require no blessing before or after; items not from the meal require a blessing before but not after; after the meal, both blessings are required.

items.text: Ben Zoma's question on why items during a meal need no blessing
items.text_en: Ben Zoma's question on why items during a meal need no blessing
items.desc_en: Ben Zoma asks why items that come from the meal itself require no blessing before or after. He answers that bread exempts them. The Gemara then questions whether wine also is exempted by bread, but distinguishes wine as different.

sub.desc_en: The students ask Ben Zoma why foods that come as part of the meal during the meal require no blessing before or after.
Ben Zoma answers that bread exempts them from blessings.
The students object that if bread exempts, then wine should also be exempted by bread.
The Gemara responds that wine is different, implying a distinction is to be explained.

items.text: Rav Huna, Rav Nachman, and Rav Sheshet on blessing figs and grapes
items.text_en: Rav Huna, Rav Nachman, and Rav Sheshet on blessing figs and grapes
items.desc_en: Rav Huna and Rav Nachman say figs and grapes brought during a meal require a blessing before but not after. Rav Sheshet says they require blessings both before and after, except for bread in baskets. Rabbi Chiya says bread exempts all foods and wine exempts all drinks.

sub.desc_en: Introduces the case of figs and grapes brought during a meal.
Rav Huna rules that figs and grapes require a blessing before but not after.
Rav Nachman agrees with Rav Huna.
Rav Sheshet argues that they require blessings both before and after, except for bread in baskets.
Rabbi Chiya's statement that bread exempts all foods and wine exempts all drinks, which disagrees with both Rav Huna and Rav Sheshet.

items.text: Rav Papa's halakha on blessings during a meal (repeated)
items.text_en: Rav Papa's halakha on blessings during a meal (repeated)
items.desc_en: Rav Papa restates the halakha: items from the meal need no blessing; items not from the meal need a blessing before but not after; after the meal, both need blessings before and after.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa rules that foods brought due to the meal during the meal require no blessing before or after; foods not due to the meal require a blessing before but not after; after the meal, both require blessings before and after.

items.text: Ben Zoma's question on why items during a meal need no blessing (repeated)
items.text_en: Ben Zoma's question on why items during a meal need no blessing (repeated)
items.desc_en: Ben Zoma asks why items from the meal need no blessing; he answers that bread exempts them. The Gemara questions whether wine also is exempted, but distinguishes wine.

sub.desc_en: The students ask Ben Zoma why foods that come as part of the meal during the meal require no blessing before or after.
Ben Zoma answers that bread exempts these foods from blessings.
The students object that if bread exempts, then wine should also be exempted by bread.
The Gemara responds that wine is different, implying a distinction that will be explained.

items.text: Gemara's discussion on when one must recite a blessing
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion on when one must recite a blessing
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rav Huna's practice of eating thirteen loaves without blessing, and Rav Nachman explains that one must bless only when others would establish a meal on that food.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the concept of one who causes a blessing for himself, setting up the discussion.
Rav Nachman explains that Rav Huna's practice of eating thirteen loaves without blessing is valid, but one must bless only when others would establish a meal on that food.

items.text: The blessing on bread baked in a pan (פת הבאה בכסנין)
items.text_en: The blessing on bread baked in a pan (פת הבאה בכסנין)
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda hears his son's household reciting 'HaMotzi' on bread baked in a pan, and initially questions them. They cite a baraita of Rabbi Muna in the name of Rabbi Yehuda, and Shmuel's ruling that the law follows Rabbi Muna. Rav Yehuda then distinguishes between when one establishes a meal on it and when one does not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda is occupied with his son's household, and they bring before them bread baked in a pan (פת הבאה בכסנין); he hears them reciting the blessing 'HaMotzi'.
Rav Yehuda asks them: 'What is this 'tzitzi' I hear? Are you perhaps reciting 'HaMotzi lechem min ha'aretz'?'
They answer yes, citing a baraita of Rabbi Muna in the name of Rabbi Yehuda that one recites 'HaMotzi' on this bread, and Shmuel's ruling that the law follows Rabbi Muna.
Rav Yehuda objects: 'Was it indeed stated that the law follows Rabbi Muna?'
They challenge him: 'But the Master himself said in Shmuel's name that one may use לחמניות (small bread rolls) for an עירוב (eruv) and recite 'HaMotzi' over them?'
Rav Yehuda resolves: 'There it is different because one establishes one's meal on them, but here where one does not establish one's meal on them — no.'

items.text: The prohibition of eating after the meal is over (סילק)
items.text_en: The prohibition of eating after the meal is over (סילק)
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa and later Rava and Rabbi Zeira encounter situations where food is brought after the meal has ended. Rav Pappa explains that the prohibition applies only when the table is formally removed (סילק), while Rabbi Zeira relies on the table of the Exilarch not being formally removed.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa visits the house of Rav Huna son of Rav Natan, and after the meal ends, food is brought; Rav Pappa begins to eat.
The hosts ask Rav Pappa: does the master not hold that once the meal is finished (גמר), it is forbidden to eat?
Rav Pappa responds that the prohibition was stated only regarding סילק (formal removal of the table), not merely finishing the meal.
Rava and Rabbi Zeira visit the Exilarch's house; after the table is removed, they are sent a dish from the Exilarch's kitchen.
Rava asks Rabbi Zeira: does the master not hold that after the table is removed (סילק), it is forbidden to eat?
Rabbi Zeira explains that he relies on the table of the Exilarch not being formally removed, so eating is permitted.

items.text: The principle of תכיפה (immediacy) and the blessing after hand-washing
items.text_en: The principle of תכיפה (immediacy) and the blessing after hand-washing
items.desc_en: Rav states that one accustomed to oil is delayed by it. Rav Ashi reports that in Rav Kahana's house, oil delays them. The Gemara concludes that the law follows Rabbi Chiya bar Ashi's statement about three instances of תכיפה, including that hand-washing must be immediately followed by the blessing. Abaye adds that the blessing of Torah scholars follows immediately after their presence, citing verses.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that one who is accustomed to oil is delayed by it.
Rav Ashi reports that in Rav Kahana's house, oil delays them.
The Gemara concludes that the law follows Rabbi Chiya bar Ashi's statement about three instances of תכיפה (immediacy), including that hand-washing must be immediately followed by the blessing.
Abaye adds that the blessing of Torah scholars follows immediately after their presence, citing verses.

items.text: Mishnah: Which blessings exempt others
items.text_en: Mishnah: Which blessings exempt others
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a blessing on wine before the meal exempts wine after the meal, and similarly for appetizers. Blessing on bread exempts appetizers, but not vice versa. Beit Shammai add that it does not exempt cooked dishes. The Mishnah also discusses when individuals bless for themselves versus one blessing for all.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that a blessing on wine before the meal exempts wine after the meal, and a blessing on bread exempts appetizers but not vice versa.
Beit Shammai add that the blessing on bread does not exempt cooked dishes.
The Mishnah concludes that when seated individually each person blesses for himself, but when they recline together one blesses for all.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if wine is brought during the meal, each person recites a blessing for himself; after the meal, one recites for all. It also mentions the blessing over incense, which is only brought after the meal.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for blessing on wine brought during or after a meal, and mentions the fragrant smoke (מוגמר) brought after the meal.

items.text: Gemara's distinction: Shabbat and festivals vs. weekdays
items.text_en: Gemara's distinction: Shabbat and festivals vs. weekdays
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan limits the Mishnah's leniency to Shabbat and festivals when one fixes his meal on wine; on weekdays, each cup requires its own blessing. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi adds occasions like leaving a bathhouse or bloodletting.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan limits the Mishnah's leniency to Shabbat and festivals when one fixes his meal on wine; on weekdays, each cup requires its own blessing.

sub.text: Rabba bar Mari citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Rabba bar Mari citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Mari adds in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that the same leniency applies when leaving a bathhouse or after bloodletting, but on weekdays each cup requires its own blessing.

items.text: Anecdotes: Rabba bar Mari and Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef
items.text_en: Anecdotes: Rabba bar Mari and Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef
items.desc_en: Rabba bar Mari visited Rava on a weekday and saw him bless before and after the meal, approving. Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef visited Abaye on a festival and saw him bless each cup; when questioned about Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling, he said he was undecided.

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Mari visited Rava on a weekday, saw him bless before and after the meal, and approved, citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's support.
Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef visited Abaye on a festival, saw him bless each cup, and when questioned about Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling, Abaye said he was undecided.

items.text: Inquiry: Does wine during the meal exempt wine after the meal?
items.text_en: Inquiry: Does wine during the meal exempt wine after the meal?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether wine brought during the meal exempts wine after the meal from a blessing, given that the former is for drinking and the latter for digestion. Rav, Rav Nachman, and others hold it exempts; Rav Kahana, Rav Sheshet, and Rav Huna's school hold it does not. Rava challenges Rav Nachman from the Mishnah, and Rav Nachman reinterprets the Mishnah.

items.text: Mishnah: Blessing over bread exempts accompaniments; Beit Shammai's dispute
items.text_en: Mishnah: Blessing over bread exempts accompaniments; Beit Shammai's dispute
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that blessing over bread exempts accompaniments, but not vice versa. Beit Shammai adds that even cooked dishes are not exempted by bread. The Gemara inquires whether Beit Shammai disputes the first clause or the latter, and concludes with 'teiku' (undecided).

items.text: Mishnah: Reclining vs. sitting for group blessing; resolution and anecdote
items.text_en: Mishnah: Reclining vs. sitting for group blessing; resolution and anecdote
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says that if they were sitting, each blesses individually; if they reclined, one blesses for all. A contradiction is raised from a baraita where sitting together suffices. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that the baraita refers to when they said 'let us go eat at a certain place.' An anecdote about Rav's students illustrates the uncertainty.

items.text: Opening story: Rav's death and the question of reclining
items.text_en: Opening story: Rav's death and the question of reclining
items.desc_en: A story is told about Rav's death, where his garment was torn and a second tear was made. An elder resolves a contradiction between a Mishnah and a baraita by explaining that the moment people say 'let us go eat at a certain place' is considered like reclining.

sub.desc_en: A story about Rav's death: his garment was torn, and a second tear was made. An elder resolves a contradiction between a Mishnah and a baraita by explaining that the moment people say 'let us go eat at a certain place' is considered like reclining.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan on reclining for wine
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan on reclining for wine
items.desc_en: Two versions of a dispute are presented: Rav says the rule that one person blesses for all applies only to bread, which requires reclining, but not to wine; Rabbi Yochanan says even wine requires reclining. The second version frames the dispute in terms of whether reclining benefits the item.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the dispute: Rav says only bread requires reclining, not wine; Rabbi Yochanan says even wine requires reclining.

items.text: Baraita on the order of reclining
items.text_en: Baraita on the order of reclining
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited describing the order of reclining: guests sit until all arrive, then wash one hand, then each blesses for himself over wine; after reclining, they wash both hands, and one blesses for all over wine.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited describing the order of reclining: each person washes one hand, then each blesses for himself, but when wine comes after they have reclined, one person blesses for all — implying wine requires reclining.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction for both versions of Rav's statement
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction for both versions of Rav's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita contradicts both versions of Rav's statement. For the first version, the beginning of the baraita (where each blesses for himself before reclining) is problematic, but is resolved by saying guests intend to leave. For the second version, the end of the baraita (where one blesses for all after reclining) is problematic, but is resolved by saying that since reclining benefits bread, it also benefits wine.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: according to the first version of Rav's statement (that wine does not require reclining), the beginning of the baraita (where each guest blesses for himself before reclining) is problematic.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that guests are different because they intend to leave, so they do not yet have the status of reclining.

The Gemara raises a contradiction: according to the second version of Rav's statement (that reclining does not benefit wine), the end of the baraita (where one blesses for all after reclining) is problematic.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that since reclining benefits bread, it also benefits wine in this context.

items.text: Ben Zoma's explanation for wine during the meal
items.text_en: Ben Zoma's explanation for wine during the meal
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when wine is brought during the meal, each person blesses for himself, but after the meal, one blesses for all. Ben Zoma explains this is because the throat is not yet clear during the meal.

sub.desc_en: Ben Zoma asks: Why is the rule that when wine comes during the meal each blesses for himself, but after the meal one blesses for all?
Ben Zoma answers that during the meal the throat is not yet clear, so each person must bless individually.

items.text: Who leads the blessing over incense and the rule of washing first
items.text_en: Who leads the blessing over incense and the rule of washing first
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah says 'he says over the incense' implying there is someone better, and answers that it is because he washed his hands first after the meal. This supports Rav's statement that the one who washes first after the meal leads the blessing. A story illustrates this with Rabbi, Rav, and Rabbi Chiyya.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah says 'he says over the incense' implying there is someone better, and questions why that is.
The Gemara answers that it is because he washed his hands first after the meal.

sub.text: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi citing Rav
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav's statement that the one who washes his hands first after the meal leads the blessing, supporting the answer.

sub.text: Story about Rabbi, Rav, and Rabbi Chiyya
sub.text_en: Story about Rabbi, Rav, and Rabbi Chiyya
sub.desc_en: A story illustrates that Rabbi instructed Rav to wash first, and Rabbi Chiyya explained that this was to lead the blessing over the meal.

items.text: When to bless on fragrance: from when the smoke rises
items.text_en: When to bless on fragrance: from when the smoke rises
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira quotes Rava bar Yirmeya that one blesses on fragrance from when its column of smoke rises. Rabbi Zeira objects that one hasn't yet smelled it, but Rava bar Yirmeya compares it to the blessing over bread, where one blesses before eating because he intends to eat; here too, one intends to smell.

sub.desc_en: Rav says: One who washes his hands first at the end is privileged to the blessing.
Rabbi Zeira objects that one hasn't yet smelled the fragrance at that point.
Rava bar Yirmeya answers by comparing to the blessing over bread, where one blesses before eating because he intends to eat; here too, one intends to smell.

items.text: Blessing on musk and the challenge from a baraita
items.text_en: Blessing on musk and the challenge from a baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda quotes Rav that all incenses receive the blessing 'Borei Atzei Besamim' except musk, which is from an animal, so one says 'Borei Minei Besamim'. A baraita challenges this by listing only specific items for 'Borei Atzei Besamim', and the Gemara declares it a refutation.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda quotes Rav (or Ze'iri) that all incenses receive the blessing 'Borei Atzei Besamim' except musk, which is from an animal, so one says 'Borei Minei Besamim'.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that lists only specific items for 'Borei Atzei Besamim', challenging Rav's ruling.
The Gemara declares the baraita a refutation (תיוּבְתָּא) of Rav's statement.

items.text: Blessing on persimmon oil
items.text_en: Blessing on persimmon oil
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks Rav Yitzchak what blessing is said on persimmon oil. Rav Yitzchak quotes Rav Yehuda saying 'Borei Shemen Artzeinu', but Rav Chisda objects that this is only for Rav Yehuda who loves the Land of Israel. Rav Yitzchak then quotes Rabbi Yochanan saying 'Borei Shemen Arev'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks Rav Chisda to Rav Yitzchak: what blessing on persimmon oil? He says: 'Borei shemen artzenu' (Creator of the oil of our land). Rav Chisda asks: but Rabbi Yehuda loves the Land of Israel, for the whole world what?

items.text: Blessing on different types of oil: fresh, pickled, ground
items.text_en: Blessing on different types of oil: fresh, pickled, ground
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava says that on fresh oil (כשרתא) one says 'Borei Atzei Besamim', but not on pickled oil. Rav Kahana adds even pickled oil, but not ground oil. The Nehardeans say even ground oil.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects with a baraita: We only bless 'Borei atzei besamim' on persimmon of Rabbi's house, persimmon of Caesar's house, and myrtle everywhere — implying musk is excluded.
Rav Kahana adds that even pickled oil receives the blessing, but not ground oil.
The Nehardeans rule that even ground oil receives the blessing 'Borei Atzei Besamim'.

items.text: Blessings for specific fragrant plants
items.text_en: Blessings for specific fragrant plants
items.desc_en: Rav Giddel, Rav Chananel, Mar Zutra, Rav Mesharshiya, and Rav Sheishes each state the appropriate blessing for a particular aromatic plant: simlak, chalfei d'yama, narkom, and siglei. Mar Zutra adds a blessing for smelling an etrog or quince.

items.text: Blessing for blossoming trees and source for blessing on scent
items.text_en: Blessing for blossoming trees and source for blessing on scent
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda teaches the blessing for seeing trees blossom in Nisan. Rav Zutra bar Tuvia quotes Rav to derive the obligation to bless over scent from the verse 'All souls praise God', identifying scent as that which benefits the soul but not the body.

items.text: Three homilies by Rav Zutra bar Tuvia quoting Rav
items.text_en: Three homilies by Rav Zutra bar Tuvia quoting Rav
items.desc_en: Rav Zutra bar Tuvia quotes Rav on three matters: that the youth of Israel will emit a good fragrance like Lebanon, that God made each person's craft beautiful in its time, and Rav Papa notes this explains the folk saying about hanging a gourd on something else.

items.text: The status of a torch regarding the evil spirit
items.text_en: The status of a torch regarding the evil spirit
items.desc_en: Rav Zutra bar Tuvia quotes Rav that a torch is like two people and the moon is like three regarding protection from harmful spirits. The Gemara questions whether a torch counts as two including itself or excluding itself, and proves from the moon that it includes itself.

items.text: Preferring to be thrown into a furnace rather than shame another
items.text_en: Preferring to be thrown into a furnace rather than shame another
items.desc_en: Rav Zutra bar Tuvia (or others) quotes that it is better for a person to throw himself into a fiery furnace than to publicly shame another, deriving this from Tamar's example.

items.text: Dispute over the order of blessings for oil and myrtle
items.text_en: Dispute over the order of blessings for oil and myrtle
items.desc_en: A baraita records a dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on whether to bless oil or myrtle first. Rabban Gamliel 'decides' for oil because it provides both scent and anointment. Rabbi Yochanan rules like the decider. Rav Papa later blesses myrtle first, citing Rava that the law follows Beit Hillel, but he does so to avoid an honorific.

items.text: Dispute over the order of blessings for oil and wine
items.text_en: Dispute over the order of blessings for oil and wine
items.desc_en: A baraita records a dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on how to hold and bless oil and wine. Beit Hillel says to hold wine in the right hand and bless it first, then anoint the attendant. If the attendant is a scholar, he anoints the wall to avoid appearing perfumed in public.

items.text: Six (or eight) things unbecoming a Torah scholar
items.text_en: Six (or eight) things unbecoming a Torah scholar
items.desc_en: A baraita lists six things that are disgraceful for a Torah scholar: going out perfumed, alone at night, in patched shoes, talking with a woman in the market, sitting with ignoramuses, and entering the study hall last. Some add not taking large strides and not walking erect. The Gemara explains each item with reasons and qualifications.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Blessing for salted fish with bread
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Blessing for salted fish with bread
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if salted fish is brought first with bread, one recites the blessing over the fish and exempts the bread, because the bread is secondary. The general rule: whatever is primary with something secondary, one blesses over the primary and exempts the secondary.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: when salted fish is brought first with bread, one blesses over the fish and exempts the bread, because the bread is secondary; the general principle is that one blesses over the primary and exempts the secondary.

items.text: Gemara's question and answer about salted fish as primary
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answer about salted fish as primary
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether salted fish can ever be primary and bread secondary. Rav Acha bar Avira in the name of Rav Ashi answers that the Mishnah refers to those eating Ginossar fruits, where the fish is eaten as a relish with the fruit, and bread is secondary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether there is any case where salted fish is considered primary and bread secondary.
Rav Ashi answers that the Mishnah was taught regarding those who eat Ginosar fruits, where the fish is the main dish.

items.text: Stories of eating Ginossar fruits and related tales
items.text_en: Stories of eating Ginossar fruits and related tales
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana recounts how they would follow Rabbi Yochanan to eat Ginossar fruits, with large quantities consumed. Further stories are told by Rav Dimi, Ravin, and Rabbi Yitzchak about the abundance of fruits in the land of Israel, including a city that produced sixty myriad se'ah of dried figs and a tree that yielded forty se'ah of pigeons.

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana recounts how they would follow Rabbi Yochanan to eat Ginossar fruits, with large quantities consumed, and a textual correction from 'ziyuna' to 'mezonah'.
Stories of Rabbi Avahu, Rabbi Ami, Rabbi Asi, and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish eating large quantities, and Rabbi Yochanan sending for Rabbi Yehuda Nesia.
Rav Dimi recounts a city of King Yannai that produced sixty myriad se'ah of dried figs for fig cutters each week.
Ravin tells of a tree yielding forty se'ah of pigeons monthly, and Rabbi Yitzchak tells of a city with many priestly couples, concluding that Rav Chisda's daughters married non-priests.

items.text: Rav and Rabbi Yochanan on essential components of a meal
items.text_en: Rav and Rabbi Yochanan on essential components of a meal
items.desc_en: Rav states that any meal without salt is not a meal. Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan says that any meal without a roasted dish is not a meal.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that any meal without salt is not considered a meal.
Rabbi Yochanan states that any meal without a roasted dish (שריף) is not considered a meal.

items.text: Mishnah: Blessings after eating fruits and drinking water
items.text_en: Mishnah: Blessings after eating fruits and drinking water
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: Rabban Gamliel says that after eating grapes, figs, and pomegranates, one recites the full three blessings of Birkat HaMazon. The Sages say one recites a single blessing summarizing the three. Rabbi Akiva says even if one ate a vegetable and it was his meal, he recites three blessings. One who drinks water to quench thirst recites 'Shehakol'. Rabbi Tarfon says 'Borei Nefashot'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: Rabban Gamliel says one who ate grapes, figs, or pomegranates recites the full Grace After Meals (שלוש ברכות); the Sages say a shortened blessing (ברכה אחת מעין שלוש); Rabbi Akiva says even if one ate a vegetable that is his sustenance, he recites the full Grace; one who drinks water for thirst recites 'שהכל נהיה בדברו'; Rabbi Tarfon says 'בורא נפשות רבות וחסרונן'.
Answer: Because verses: 'Eretz chita u-seora…', 'Eretz asher lo be-miskenut tochal bah lechem…', 'Ve-achalta ve-savata u-verachta…'.
Rabbi Akiva adds that even if one ate a vegetable and it was his meal, he recites three blessings.
The Mishnah states that one who drinks water to quench thirst recites the blessing 'Shehakol'.
Rabbi Tarfon says the blessing is 'Borei Nefashot'.

items.text: Gemara: Scriptural basis for Rabban Gamliel's position
items.text_en: Gemara: Scriptural basis for Rabban Gamliel's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabban Gamliel's reasoning: the verse mentions the Seven Species and then commands blessing after eating, implying a full blessing. The Sages argue that the word 'land' interrupts the context. Rabban Gamliel counters that the word 'land' is needed to exclude one who chews wheat (not eating it properly).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural basis of Rabban Gamliel's position that one who eats the Seven Species must recite a full three-blessing grace after meals, citing the verses that list the land of Israel and command blessing after eating.
The Sages object that the word 'אֶרֶץ' (land) interrupts the context, so the verses do not directly connect the Seven Species to the blessing command.
Rabban Gamliel responds that the word 'אֶרֶץ' is indeed an interruption, but it is necessary to exclude one who chews wheat (rather than eating it properly) from the obligation of blessing.

items.text: Blessings for the Five Species and Seven Species
items.text_en: Blessings for the Five Species and Seven Species
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi in the name of Rabbi Chanina states that for anything from the Five Species, one initially recites 'Borei Minei Mezonot' and concludes with the one blessing summarizing three. Rabba bar Mari in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says for anything from the Seven Species, one initially recites 'Borei Pri HaEtz' and concludes with the one blessing summarizing three. Abaye asks Rav Dimi what this blessing is, and Rav Dimi explains the text for fruits and for the Five Species.

sub.text: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi in the name of Rabbi Chanina
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi in the name of Rabbi Chanina
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi in the name of Rabbi Chanina rules that for anything from the Five Species, one initially recites 'Borei Minei Mezonot' and concludes with the one blessing summarizing three.

sub.text: Rabba bar Mari in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Rabba bar Mari in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Mari in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi adds that for anything from the Seven Species, one initially recites 'Borei Pri HaEtz' and concludes with the one blessing summarizing three.
Abaye asks Rav Dimi what exactly is the text of the one blessing summarizing three.
Rav Dimi explains the full text of the blessing for fruits of the tree, beginning with 'על העץ ועל פרי העץ' and ending with 'כי אתה טוב ומטיב לכל'.
Rav Dimi then provides the text of the blessing for the Five Species, beginning with 'על המחיה ועל הכלכלה' and concluding with the signature 'על הארץ ועל המחיה'.

items.text: Dispute on the concluding formula of the blessing
items.text_en: Dispute on the concluding formula of the blessing
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how to conclude the blessing. Rav Dimi reports that Rav concluded for Rosh Chodesh with 'Blessed is He who sanctifies Israel and the New Months'. Here, Rav Chisda says conclude 'Al HaAretz VeAl Peiroteha', and Rabbi Yochanan says 'Al HaAretz VeAl HaPeirot'. Rav Amram says they do not disagree: one is for us (in Babylonia) and one is for them (in Israel). Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects: they eat and we bless? Rather, reverse: Rav Chisda said 'Al HaAretz VeAl HaPeirot', Rabbi Yochanan said 'Al HaAretz VeAl Peiroteha'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how to conclude the blessing for fruits, citing Rav Dimi's report that Rav concluded for Rosh Chodesh with a specific formula, and now asks what the conclusion should be here.
Rav Chisda states that the conclusion is 'על הארץ ועל פירותיה' (on the land and on its fruits).
Rabbi Yochanan states that the conclusion is 'על הארץ ועל הפירות' (on the land and on the fruits).
Rav Amram says they do not disagree: one formula is for us (Babylonia) and the other is for them (Israel).
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects: they (in Israel) eat the fruits, and we (in Babylonia) bless? That is illogical.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak reverses the attributions: Rav Chisda said 'על הארץ ועל הפירות' and Rabbi Yochanan said 'על הארץ ועל פירותיה'.

items.text: Blessings on eggs and vegetables
items.text_en: Blessings on eggs and vegetables
items.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Abdimi states that for eggs and fried foods, one first blesses 'Shehakol' and then 'Borei Nefashot'; for vegetables, no after-blessing. Rav Yitzchak says even vegetables need an after-blessing, but not water. Rav Papa says even water needs an after-blessing.

items.text: Mar Zutra and Rav Shimi's practices
items.text_en: Mar Zutra and Rav Shimi's practices
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra follows Rav Yitzchak bar Abdimi, Rav Shimi follows Rav Yitzchak. Rav Ashi sometimes follows one, sometimes the other.

items.text: Mishna: Blessings before and after
items.text_en: Mishna: Blessings before and after
items.desc_en: The Mishna states: everything that requires an after-blessing also requires a before-blessing; some require a before-blessing but no after-blessing. The Gemara discusses exceptions like vegetables and water.

items.text: Gemara's question on exceptions
items.text_en: Gemara's question on exceptions
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the Mishna excluding? For Rav Yitzchak bar Abdimi, it excludes vegetables; for Rav Yitzchak, it excludes water; for Rav Papa, what does it exclude?

items.text: Answer: excluding mitzvot
items.text_en: Answer: excluding mitzvot
items.desc_en: Rav Papa says the Mishna excludes mitzvot (commandments) that require a blessing before but not after, like putting on tefillin.

items.text: Westerners' blessing after tefillin
items.text_en: Westerners' blessing after tefillin
items.desc_en: The Westerners (people of the West) bless after removing tefillin: 'Who sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to keep His statutes.' The Gemara asks: what does this exclude?

items.text: Answer: excluding spices
items.text_en: Answer: excluding spices
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers: it excludes spices (reihanai) that require a blessing before but not after, since they are not substantial foods.

items.text: Rav Yannai: egg better than bread
items.text_en: Rav Yannai: egg better than bread
items.desc_en: Rav Yannai citing Rav: anything the size of an egg — an egg is better than it. Ravin says: a boiled egg is better than fine wheat flour bread. Rav Dimi says: a boiled egg is better than bread from four things, and a cooked egg is better than anything the size of an egg, except meat.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva: even cooked vegetables
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva: even cooked vegetables
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva says even if one ate cooked vegetables (shelek), he still needs an after-blessing. The Gemara asks: is shelek a meal? Rav Ashi says: it refers to a stalk of cabbage.

items.text: Tanna's teaching on health effects
items.text_en: Tanna's teaching on health effects
items.desc_en: The Tanna teaches: spleen is good for teeth and bad for intestines; leeks are bad for teeth and good for intestines; all raw vegetables make one pale; small ones make one smaller; every soul restores the soul; what is close to the soul restores the soul; cabbage for food, radishes for healing; woe to a house where leek passes through.

items.text: Mar's advice on spleen and leeks
items.text_en: Mar's advice on spleen and leeks
items.desc_en: Mar says: spleen is good for teeth and bad for intestines. Remedy: chew it and spit. Leeks are bad for teeth and good for intestines. Remedy: boil and swallow.

items.text: Rav Yitzchak: raw vegetables before 4 hours
items.text_en: Rav Yitzchak: raw vegetables before 4 hours
items.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak says: all raw vegetables make one pale; in the first meal after fasting, it is forbidden to eat raw vegetables before 4 hours due to smell. Also forbidden to eat raw vegetables before 4 hours generally.

items.text: Amemar, Mar Zutra, Rav Ashi: eating raw vegetables
items.text_en: Amemar, Mar Zutra, Rav Ashi: eating raw vegetables
items.desc_en: Amemar, Mar Zutra, and Rav Ashi were sitting; raw vegetables were brought before them before 4 hours. Amemar and Rav Ashi ate, Mar Zutra did not. They asked him why; he cited Rav Yitzchak's prohibition. They argued: we eat and talk! He replied: I follow Rav Yitzchak's view.

items.text: Rav Chisda: small fish kill in 7, 17, 27 days
items.text_en: Rav Chisda: small fish kill in 7, 17, 27 days
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda says: a small salted fish can kill in 7, 17, or 27 days. Some say in 23. Only if not roasted well; if roasted well, no harm. If not roasted well and one drinks beer after, no harm.

items.text: Rav Papa: every soul restores the soul
items.text_en: Rav Papa: every soul restores the soul
items.desc_en: Rav Papa says: even gildanei (fish intestines) restore the soul. Rav Acha bar Yaakov says: unka (a fish) restores the soul. Rava tells his attendant: when you bring me meat sauce, bring it from near the 'Baruch' place.

items.text: Cabbage for food, radishes for healing
items.text_en: Cabbage for food, radishes for healing
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses: cabbage for food, radishes for healing — but the Tanna taught six things that heal: cabbage, radishes, honey, dates, spleen, and liver. So 'cabbage for food' is wrong? It means cabbage is also for food, but primarily for healing.

items.text: Woe to house where leek passes
items.text_en: Woe to house where leek passes
items.desc_en: The Gemara says: woe to the house where leek passes through. Is that so? Rava told his attendant: when you see leek in the market, don't tell me 'how to wrap bread'!

items.text: Abaye and Rava: without meat or wine
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava: without meat or wine
items.desc_en: Abaye says: without meat. Rava says: without wine. It was stated: Rav says: without meat. Shmuel says: without wood. Rabbi Yochanan says: without wine.

items.text: Rava to Rav Papa: break it with meat and wine
items.text_en: Rava to Rav Papa: break it with meat and wine
items.desc_en: Rava tells Rav Papa (Sudani): we break it (the leek) with meat and wine; you, who have little wine, break it with wood, like Rav Papa's wife who breaks it with 80 Persian ovens.

items.text: Small salted fish: death timing
items.text_en: Small salted fish: death timing
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda says: a small salted fish can kill in 7, 17, or 27 days. Some say in 23. Only if not roasted well; if roasted well, no harm. If not roasted well and one drinks beer after, no harm.

items.text: Drinking water for thirst
items.text_en: Drinking water for thirst
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what does 'drinking water for thirst' exclude? Rav Idi bar Avin says: it excludes to remove something (like a bone).

items.text: Conclusion of previous Mishnah and Rabbi Tarfon's blessing
items.text_en: Conclusion of previous Mishnah and Rabbi Tarfon's blessing
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the previous discussion about blessings after eating, mentioning Rabbi Tarfon's formula 'Borei nefashot rabot vechesronan'. Rava bar Rav Chanan asks Abaye about the halakha, and is told to follow the practice of the people.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the previous discussion with a case of someone choked by a piece of meat and drank water without a blessing.
The Mishnah cites Rabbi Tarfon's blessing formula for water: 'Borei nefashot rabot vechesronan'.
Rava bar Rav Chanan asks Abaye (or Rav Yosef) what the halakha is regarding the dispute.
Abaye tells him to go out and observe what the people are doing and act accordingly.

items.text: Conclusion of chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of chapter
items.desc_en: The phrase 'Hadran alach keitzad mevarchin' marks the end of the previous chapter.

sub.desc_en: The phrase 'הדרן עלך כיצד מברכין' (we return to you, chapter 'How does one recite blessings') marks the conclusion of the previous chapter.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Who is obligated in zimmun
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Who is obligated in zimmun
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that three who ate together are obligated to form a zimmun. It lists those who may be counted for zimmun (e.g., one who ate a kezayit of demai, a Samaritan) and those who may not (e.g., one who ate tevel, a gentile). Women, slaves, and minors are not counted. The minimum amount for zimmun is a kezayit; Rabbi Yehuda says a k'beitzah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that three who ate together are obligated to form a zimmun, and lists those who may be counted for zimmun, including one who ate a kezayit of demai, first tithe from which teruma was taken, redeemed second tithe and consecrated food, a waiter who ate a kezayit, and a Samaritan.

The Mishnah lists those who may not be counted for zimmun, including one who ate tevel, first tithe from which teruma was not separated, unredeemed second tithe and consecrated food, a waiter who ate less than a kezayit, and a gentile; women, slaves, and minors are not counted; the minimum amount for zimmun is a kezayit, but Rabbi Yehuda says a k'beitzah.

items.text: Source for zimmun from the Torah
items.text_en: Source for zimmun from the Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the biblical source for zimmun. Rav Asi cites 'Gadlu laHashem iti' (Psalms 34:4), and Rabbi Avahu cites 'Ki shem Hashem ekra havu godel leloheinu' (Deuteronomy 32:3).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the biblical source for the obligation of זימון (zimmun).
Rav Asi cites the verse 'גַּדְּלוּ לַה׳ אִתִּי וּנְרוֹמְמָה שְׁמוֹ יַחְדָּו' (Psalms 34:4) as the source for זימון (zimmun).
Rabbi Avahu cites a different verse, 'כִּי שֵׁם ה׳ אֶקְרָא הָבוּ גֹדֶל לֵאלֹהֵינוּ' (Deuteronomy 32:3), as the source for זימון (zimmun).

items.text: The responder's voice should not be louder than the blesser
items.text_en: The responder's voice should not be louder than the blesser
items.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Abba derives from 'Gadlu laHashem iti' that the one answering 'Amen' should not raise his voice louder than the one blessing.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Abba derives from the verse 'גדלו לה' אתי ונרוממה שמו יחדו' (Praise God with me, and we will exalt His name together) that one who answers 'אמן' (amen) should not raise his voice louder than the one reciting the blessing.

items.text: The translator's voice should not be louder than the reader
items.text_en: The translator's voice should not be louder than the reader
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi derives from 'Moshe yedaber vehaElohim ya'anenu bekol' that the translator may not raise his voice louder than the Torah reader. A baraisa supports this, adding that if necessary, the reader should lower his voice.

sub.desc_en: רבי שמעון בן פזי (Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi) derives from the verse 'משה ידבר והאלהים יעננו בקול' (Moses spoke, and God responded in a voice) that the translator may not raise his voice louder than the Torah reader, interpreting 'בקול' (in a voice) to mean in Moses' voice.

A ברייתתא (baraita) supports this ruling, stating that the translator may not raise his voice louder than the reader, and if the translator cannot match the reader's volume, the reader should lower his voice.

items.text: Dispute about two who ate together: may they form a zimmun?
items.text_en: Dispute about two who ate together: may they form a zimmun?
items.desc_en: Rav and Rabbi Yochanan dispute whether two who ate together may form a zimmun if they wish. The Gemara attempts to prove from the Mishnah and other sources that only three are obligated, but distinguishes between obligation and permission. A baraisa about a waiter eating with two or three is also addressed, but the Gemara deflects it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rav and Rabbi Yochanan dispute whether two who ate together may form a zimmun if they wish.
The Gemara objects from the Mishnah that only three are obligated, implying two cannot form a zimmun.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah discusses obligation, while the dispute is about permission.
The Gemara brings a baraisa that three who ate together may not disperse, implying two cannot form a zimmun.
The Gemara rejects the proof, distinguishing that the three established themselves as obligated from the outset.
The Gemara cites a baraisa about a waiter eating with two or three, implying two cannot form a zimmun.
The Gemara begins to reject this proof as well, but the argument is cut off.

items.text: Gemara's initial assumption about Rav's view
items.text_en: Gemara's initial assumption about Rav's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara assumes that Rav holds that if three people ate together and one left, they can still call him back and include him in zimmun, because they were already obligated from the start.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah about women and slaves
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah about women and slaves
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav's view by citing a Mishnah that says women may form their own zimmun and slaves may form their own zimmun, implying that even a large group of women (like 100) cannot join with men, contradicting the idea that obligation from the start allows inclusion.

items.text: First answer: distinction due to diverse opinions
items.text_en: First answer: distinction due to diverse opinions
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the case of women is different because they have diverse opinions (da'ot) and cannot be considered a unified group like men.

items.text: Counter-challenge from the same Mishnah's continuation
items.text_en: Counter-challenge from the same Mishnah's continuation
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the reason is diverse opinions, then why does the Mishnah say that women and slaves who wish to join with men may not do so? There too there are diverse opinions, so they should be allowed.

items.text: Second answer: distinction due to licentiousness
items.text_en: Second answer: distinction due to licentiousness
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the case of women and men together is different because of licentiousness (peritzuta), which prevents them from forming a proper zimmun.
