items.text: Attempt to conclude that Rav holds 'if they wish, they may not join'
items.text_en: Attempt to conclude that Rav holds 'if they wish, they may not join'
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to prove that Rav holds the view that women and slaves who wish to join with men may not do so, citing Rav Dimi bar Yosef's statement that if one of three who ate together left to the market, they call him and include him in zimmun, implying that if they don't call him, they don't include him.

items.text: Rejection: distinction due to initial obligation
items.text_en: Rejection: distinction due to initial obligation
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof, saying that the case of three who ate together is different because they were already obligated in zimmun from the start, unlike women and slaves who never had that obligation.

items.text: Attempt to conclude that Rabbi Yochanan holds 'if they wish, they may not join'
items.text_en: Attempt to conclude that Rabbi Yochanan holds 'if they wish, they may not join'
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to prove that Rabbi Yochanan holds the view that women and slaves who wish to join may not do so, citing his statement that two who ate together, one may fulfill the other's blessing, which Rabbi Zeira explains means there is no zimmun between them.

items.text: Rava bar Rav Huna's question and resolution
items.text_en: Rava bar Rav Huna's question and resolution
items.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Huna asks Rav Huna about the Western sages who say 'if they wish, they may join' — did they hear this from Rabbi Yochanan? Rav Huna answers that they heard it from Rav before he descended to Babylonia.

items.text: Rav's ruling on calling back one who left
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on calling back one who left
items.desc_en: The Gemara returns to Rav's statement: three who ate together and one left to the market — they call him and include him in zimmun. Abaye adds that this is only if they call him and he responds.

items.text: Mar Zutra's limitation and Rav Ashi's objection, with halakhic conclusion
items.text_en: Mar Zutra's limitation and Rav Ashi's objection, with halakhic conclusion
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra limits Rav's ruling to a group of three, but for ten they must wait until he comes. Rav Ashi objects, arguing the opposite: nine appear as ten, but two do not appear as three. The halakha follows Mar Zutra because mentioning God's name requires ten.

items.text: Abaye's ruling on two who ate together
items.text_en: Abaye's ruling on two who ate together
items.desc_en: Abaye states that two who ate together should separate (each bless individually). A baraita supports this, with the exception that if one is a scholar and the other ignorant, the scholar blesses and the ignorant fulfills his obligation.

items.text: Rava's ruling on one interrupting for two
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on one interrupting for two
items.desc_en: Rava rules that in a group of three, one may interrupt his meal to join the other two for zimmun, but two may not interrupt for one. The Gemara notes that Rav Pappa did interrupt for his son and another, but that was beyond the letter of the law.

items.text: Case of three equals and Marimar's ruling
items.text_en: Case of three equals and Marimar's ruling
items.desc_en: Three sages of equal stature ate together and each blessed individually. They asked Marimar, who ruled that they fulfilled the blessing but not zimmun, and they cannot retroactively perform zimmun.

items.text: What to say when joining a group already blessing
items.text_en: What to say when joining a group already blessing
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid and Rav Pappa dispute what one says when he finds others already blessing: Rav Zevid says 'Baruch u-mevorach', Rav Pappa says 'Amen'. The Gemara resolves that it depends on whether they are saying 'Nevarech' or 'Baruch'.

items.text: Contradiction about answering Amen after one's own blessings
items.text_en: Contradiction about answering Amen after one's own blessings
items.desc_en: Two baraitot contradict each other: one says answering Amen after one's own blessings is praiseworthy, another says it is disgraceful. The Gemara resolves: the first refers to the blessing 'Boneh Yerushalayim' (in Birkat Hamazon), the second to other blessings.

items.text: Abaye and Rav Ashi's practices regarding 'HaTov veHaMeitiv'
items.text_en: Abaye and Rav Ashi's practices regarding 'HaTov veHaMeitiv'
items.desc_en: Abaye would answer the blessing 'HaTov veHaMeitiv' loudly so workers would hear and get up to work, since it is not biblical. Rav Ashi would answer quietly so as not to demean the blessing.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's illness and the meal
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's illness and the meal
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira falls ill; Rabbi Avahu visits and vows to make a feast if he recovers. When he does, Rabbi Avahu asks Rabbi Zeira to recite the blessing over bread, but Rabbi Zeira defers, citing Rabbi Yochanan's rule that the host breaks bread. Later, when it's time for the blessing after the meal, Rabbi Avahu asks Rabbi Zeira to lead, but Rabbi Zeira defers again, citing Rav Huna's rule that the one who breaks bread also recites the blessing.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira falls ill; Rabbi Avahu visits and vows to make a feast for the rabbis if he recovers.
When it's time to break bread, Rabbi Avahu asks Rabbi Zeira to recite the blessing over bread.
Rabbi Zeira defers, citing Rabbi Yochanan's rule that the host breaks bread, and Rabbi Avahu then breaks bread for them.
When it's time for the blessing after the meal, Rabbi Avahu asks Rabbi Zeira to lead the blessing.
Rabbi Zeira defers again, citing Rav Huna's rule that the one who breaks bread also recites the blessing after the meal.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is Rabbi Zeira's own opinion? It answers that he holds like Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: the host breaks bread (to do so generously) and the guest recites the blessing (to bless the host).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is Rabbi Zeira's own opinion regarding who breaks bread and who recites the blessing?
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Zeira holds like Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: the host breaks bread (to do so generously) and the guest recites the blessing (to bless the host).

items.text: Content of the guest's blessing
items.text_en: Content of the guest's blessing
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains what the guest blesses: a prayer that the host not be ashamed in this world nor disgraced in the next. Rabbi adds further requests for success, protection from Satan, and freedom from sinful thoughts.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the guest blesses and provides the basic text of the guest's blessing.
Rabbi adds further requests for success, protection from Satan, and freedom from sinful thoughts.

items.text: Extent of the zimmun blessing
items.text_en: Extent of the zimmun blessing
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: until which point in Grace after Meals does the invitation to bless (zimmun) extend? Rav Nachman says until 'Nevarekh' (the invitation itself), and Rav Sheshet says until 'Hazan' (the first blessing).

items.text: Attempt to align with Tannaitic disputes
items.text_en: Attempt to align with Tannaitic disputes
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet's dispute corresponds to a Tannaitic dispute: one baraita says Grace after Meals has two and three blessings (counting Hazan as the first), another says three and four (counting Nevarekh as the first). The Gemara assumes all agree that Hatov veHametiv is not biblical, so the dispute is about the extent of zimmun.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is Rav Nachman's reasoning?

items.text: Rejection and alternative explanations
items.text_en: Rejection and alternative explanations
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the alignment and instead explains each Amora's view independently: Rav Nachman holds that all agree zimmun extends until 'Nevarekh', and the Tannaitic dispute is about workers' blessings (who skip Hatov veHametiv). Rav Sheshet holds that all agree zimmun extends until 'Hazan', and the dispute is about whether Hatov veHametiv is biblical.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the attempted alignment of Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet with the Tannaitic dispute, stating that each Amora explains the baraitot according to his own reasoning.

Rav Nachman explains that all agree zimmun extends until 'Nevarekh'; the Tannaitic dispute is about workers' blessings, where workers skip Hatov veHametiv and include 'Boneh Yerushalayim' in the land blessing.
Rav Sheshet explains that all agree zimmun extends until 'Hazan'; the Tannaitic dispute is about whether Hatov veHametiv is biblical (d'Oraita) or rabbinic.

items.text: Proof that Hatov veHametiv is not biblical
items.text_en: Proof that Hatov veHametiv is not biblical
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef proves that Hatov veHametiv is not biblical because workers omit it. Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta in the name of Rav proves it because it begins with 'Barukh' but does not end with 'Barukh', unlike most blessings, as per a baraita listing exceptions.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef argues that Hatov veHametiv is not biblical because workers omit it.

sub.text: Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta in the name of Rav provides a second proof: Hatov veHametiv begins with 'Barukh' but does not end with 'Barukh', unlike most blessings, as per a baraita listing exceptions.

items.text: Opening statement about 'HaTov veHaMetiv'
items.text_en: Opening statement about 'HaTov veHaMetiv'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that some blessings conclude with 'Baruch' but do not open with it, while 'HaTov veHaMetiv' opens with 'Baruch' but does not conclude with it, implying it is an independent blessing.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that some blessings conclude with 'Baruch' but do not open with it, while 'HaTov veHaMetiv' opens with 'Baruch' but does not conclude with it, implying it is an independent blessing.

items.text: Proof that 'HaTov veHaMetiv' is not biblical
items.text_en: Proof that 'HaTov veHaMetiv' is not biblical
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak proves that 'HaTov veHaMetiv' is not biblical because it is omitted in a house of mourning. A baraita is cited: in a house of mourning they say 'Baruch HaTov veHaMetiv'; Rabbi Akiva says 'Baruch Dayyan HaEmet'. The Gemara corrects the baraita to include both blessings.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak asserts that 'HaTov veHaMetiv' is not biblical because it is omitted in a house of mourning.
A baraita is cited: in a house of mourning they say 'Baruch HaTov veHaMetiv'; Rabbi Akiva says 'Baruch Dayyan HaEmet'.
The Gemara objects: the baraita implies only 'HaTov veHaMetiv' is said, not 'Dayyan HaEmet'?
The Gemara corrects the baraita to include both blessings: 'Baruch HaTov veHaMetiv' and 'Baruch Dayyan HaEmet'.

items.text: Mar Zutra's blessing in a time of trouble
items.text_en: Mar Zutra's blessing in a time of trouble
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra, when a bad thing happened to him at Rav Ashi's house, opened with a blessing combining 'HaTov veHaMetiv' and 'Dayyan HaEmet', along with other praises.

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra, visiting Rav Ashi's house when a misfortune occurred, recited a long blessing combining 'HaTov veHaMetiv' with 'Dayyan Emet' and a prayer for repair.

items.text: Where does one return if interrupted?
items.text_en: Where does one return if interrupted?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if one is interrupted during a blessing, where does he resume? Rav Zevid in the name of Abaye says he returns to the beginning; the Rabbis say he returns to where he stopped. The halakha follows the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks where one who interrupts the blessing returns to, and records the dispute between Rav Zevid in the name of Abaye (returns to the beginning) and the Rabbis (returns to where he stopped), concluding the halacha is to return to where he stopped.

sub.text: Rav Zevid in the name of Abaye
sub.text_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Abaye says he returns to the beginning of the blessing.
The Rabbis say he returns to the place where he stopped.
The halakha is ruled in accordance with the Rabbis: he returns to where he stopped.

items.text: Order of reclining at a meal
items.text_en: Order of reclining at a meal
items.desc_en: The Exilarch asks Rav Sheshet about the order of reclining for two or three couches. Rav Sheshet questions how one can speak with the person above if they are far apart; the Exilarch explains that Persians signal with a whip.

sub.desc_en: The Exilarch asks Rav Sheshet about the order of reclining for two or three couches, explaining the Persian custom.
Rav Sheshet objects that if the second person is above the first, one cannot easily speak with the person above.
The Exilarch explains that Persians signal with a whip, so distance does not hinder communication.

items.text: Order of hand-washing: first and last waters
items.text_en: Order of hand-washing: first and last waters
items.desc_en: The Exilarch asks about the order of first waters (before the meal) and last waters (after the meal). Rav Sheshet answers: first waters begin with the greatest; last waters begin with the smallest. He also addresses concerns about the greatest waiting with dirty hands.

sub.desc_en: The Exilarch asks Rav Sheshet where the first waters (hand-washing before the meal) begin.
Rav Sheshet answers that the first waters begin with the greatest (most important person).
The Exilarch objects that the greatest would have to sit and guard his hands until everyone else washes.
Rav Sheshet answers that they immediately bring a basin before the greatest so he does not have to wait.
The Exilarch asks where the last waters (hand-washing after the meal) begin.
Rav Sheshet answers that the last waters begin with the smallest (least important person).
The Exilarch objects that the greatest would have to sit with dirty hands until everyone else washes.
Rav Sheshet answers that they do not remove the basin from before the greatest until the water reaches him, so he does not wait long.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's baraita on the order of reclining and hand-washing
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's baraita on the order of reclining and hand-washing
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet cites a baraita that details the order of reclining for two or three couches, and the order of first and last waters. For last waters, if there are five people, they start with the greatest; if one hundred, they start with the smallest until the fifth, then return to the greatest. This supports Rav's statement that one who washes last waters first is destined for blessing.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet declares that he knows a baraita, and then cites the baraita detailing the order of reclining for two or three couches, and the order of first and last waters, including the rule that for last waters with one hundred people, they start from the smallest until the fifth, then return to the greatest.
The gemara notes that the baraita supports Rav's statement, cited by Rabbi Chiya bar Ashi in Rav's name, that one who washes last waters first is destined for blessing.

items.text: Rav and Rabbi Chiya before Rabbi
items.text_en: Rav and Rabbi Chiya before Rabbi
items.desc_en: Rav and Rabbi Chiya were sitting at a meal before Rabbi. Rabbi told Rav to wash his hands; Rav trembled, thinking he was being asked to leave. Rabbi reassured him that he was only referring to the blessing after the meal.

sub.text: Story of Rav and Rabbi Chiya
sub.text_en: Story of Rav and Rabbi Chiya
sub.desc_en: Rabbi told Rav to wash his hands, and when Rav trembled, Rabbi explained he meant to focus on the blessing after the meal (בִּרְכַּת מְזוֹנָא), not to wash first.
Rabbi tells Rav: 'Get up, wash your hands' — which Rav misunderstands as a dismissal.
Rav trembles, thinking Rabbi is telling him to leave the meal.
Rabbi reassures Rav: 'Son of a nobleman, I was only referring to the blessing after the meal (i.e., wash for the final hand-washing before Grace).'

items.text: Beginning of a baraita on honoring
items.text_en: Beginning of a baraita on honoring
items.desc_en: The baraita begins: 'One does not honor (others) on roads or on bridges...'

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that one does not honor people on roads or bridges.

items.text: Opening Mishnah fragment
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah fragment
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that one should not break bread with soiled hands.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that one should not break bread with soiled hands.

items.text: Gemara's story about honoring at the door
items.text_en: Gemara's story about honoring at the door
items.desc_en: Ravin and Abaye were traveling; Ravin's donkey went ahead, and Abaye initially thought Ravin was arrogant. When they reached the synagogue, Ravin invited Abaye to enter, and Abaye questioned why he wasn't honored earlier. Ravin cited Rabbi Yochanan that honor is only given at a door that has a mezuzah. The Gemara clarifies that this means a door fit for a mezuzah, not necessarily one that has one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Ravin and Abaye were traveling; Ravin's donkey went ahead, and Abaye suspected Ravin of arrogance for not inviting him to lead.
When they reached the synagogue door, Ravin invited Abaye to enter, and Abaye questioned why he was not honored earlier.
Ravin replied citing Rabbi Yochanan that honor is only given at a door that has a mezuzah.
The Gemara objects that if the rule is limited to doors with a mezuzah, then synagogues and study halls without one would never receive honor, which is absurd.
The Gemara resolves that the rule applies to a door fit for a mezuzah, not necessarily one that actually has one.

items.text: The one who breaks bread must taste first
items.text_en: The one who breaks bread must taste first
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Rav says that the diners may not eat anything until the one who breaks bread tastes. Rav Safra clarifies that the word used is 'to taste' (לִטְעוֹם), not 'to eat'. The Gemara explains the practical difference: one must use the language of one's teacher.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Rav says that a person must say the blessing in the language of his teacher, and the Gemara clarifies that the word used is 'to taste' (לִטְעוֹם), not 'to eat'.

items.text: Baraita on waiting and the one who breaks bread
items.text_en: Baraita on waiting and the one who breaks bread
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that two people wait for each other at the bowl, but three do not. The one who breaks bread extends his hand first, but may honor his teacher or a greater person.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that two wait for each other at the bowl, three do not; the one who breaks bread extends his hand first but may honor his teacher or a greater person.

items.text: Waiting for 'Amen' before breaking bread
items.text_en: Waiting for 'Amen' before breaking bread
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chanah taught his son that the one who breaks bread may not break until the 'Amen' from the responders is finished. Rav Chisda says from the majority of responders. Rami bar Chama questions why the majority is different from the minority, and Rabba bar bar Chanah answers that one who says 'Amen' excessively is mistaken.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chanah teaching his son
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chanah teaching his son
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chanah teaches his son that the one who breaks bread may not break until the 'Amen' from the responders is finished.
Rav Chisda qualifies that the waiting is only until the majority of responders finish saying 'Amen'.
Rami bar Chama questions why the majority is different from the minority, since the blessing is not yet finished for either.
Rabba bar bar Chanah answers that one who says 'Amen' excessively is mistaken, so the minority may be prolonging unnecessarily.

items.text: Baraita on proper 'Amen' response
items.text_en: Baraita on proper 'Amen' response
items.desc_en: A baraita lists improper ways to say 'Amen': snatched, cut off, orphaned, and not to throw the blessing from one's mouth. Ben Azzai adds that one who says an orphaned 'Amen' will have orphaned children, etc., and one who lengthens 'Amen' has his days lengthened.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists four improper ways to respond 'Amen': snatched, cut off, orphaned, and not to throw the blessing from one's mouth.
Ben Azzai adds that responding with an orphaned 'Amen' leads to orphaned children, and lengthening 'Amen' lengthens one's days.

items.text: Stories about joining a meal and who blesses
items.text_en: Stories about joining a meal and who blesses
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel were eating; Rav Shimi bar Chiya came and ate quickly to join them. Rav questioned him, and Shmuel defended him. In another story, Rav's students thought Rav Acha would bless because he was a great man, but Rav Acha taught that the main person of the meal blesses. The Gemara concludes that the great one blesses even if he came last.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Rav and Shmuel were sitting at a meal when Rav Shimi bar Chiya came and ate quickly.
Rav asks Rav Shimi bar Chiya if he intends to join their meal, noting that they have already eaten.
Shmuel defends Rav Shimi bar Chiya, arguing that if choice foods were brought to him, he would also eat quickly.

items.text: Discussion on demai and terumah
items.text_en: Discussion on demai and terumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the status of demai produce: since one can renounce ownership and become poor, it is fit for a poor person. Rav Huna cites a dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel. Then it discusses first tithe from which terumat ma'aser was taken but not terumah gedolah, citing Rabbi Abahu in the name of Reish Lakish. Rav Pappa questions Abaye about a similar case, and Abaye responds with a verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how demai produce can be considered fit for a meal invitation, since it is not fit for the host himself.

The Gemara answers that since the host can renounce ownership of his property and become poor, demai is fit for him as a potential poor person, citing a Mishnah that one may feed demai to the poor and guests.
Rav Huna cites a Tanna that Beit Shammai disagree and say one may not feed demai to the poor and guests.

items.text: Clarification of the source for the Mishnah's first clause
items.text_en: Clarification of the source for the Mishnah's first clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah derives the law of tithes from a specific verse, and answers that it distinguishes between produce that has been processed and produce that has not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara quotes the verse 'מכל מעשרותיכם תרימו' (from all your tithes you shall set apart) and asks: what is the basis for the distinction?
The Gemara answers: this produce has been processed (אידגן) and that has not, establishing the distinction between processed and unprocessed produce.

items.text: Clarification of second tithe and consecrated produce that were redeemed
items.text_en: Clarification of second tithe and consecrated produce that were redeemed
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why this case is necessary, and explains that it deals with one who paid the principal but not the additional fifth, teaching that the fifth does not impede the redemption.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the case of second tithe and consecrated produce that were redeemed is necessary, since it seems obvious.
The Gemara explains that the case deals with one who paid the principal but not the additional fifth, teaching that the fifth does not impede the redemption.

items.text: Clarification of the attendant who ate an olive's bulk
items.text_en: Clarification of the attendant who ate an olive's bulk
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why this case is necessary, and explains that it teaches that an attendant does establish a fixed meal for zimun.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the case of an attendant who ate an olive's bulk is necessary, since it seems obvious.
The Gemara explains that the case teaches that an attendant does establish a fixed meal for zimun, countering a potential assumption otherwise.

items.text: Discussion of including a Samaritan in zimun
items.text_en: Discussion of including a Samaritan in zimun
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a Samaritan may be included, since he is at least an am ha'aretz, and a baraita prohibits including an am ha'aretz. Abaye and Rava offer different answers: Abaye says the Samaritan is a haver, while Rava says the Mishnah follows the opinion that an am ha'aretz is defined by tithing, and Samaritans are meticulous about tithing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a Samaritan (כותי) may be included in zimun, given that he is at least an am ha'aretz (ignoramus), and a baraita prohibits including an am ha'aretz.
The Gemara cites a baraita that one does not include an am ha'aretz in zimun.
Abaye answers that the Samaritan (כותי) is a haver (companion), i.e., a learned and observant person, not an am ha'aretz.

Rava answers that even if the Samaritan is an am ha'aretz, the Mishnah follows the opinion that an am ha'aretz is defined by failure to tithe, and Samaritans are meticulous about tithing, as they are strict about all commandments they observe.

items.text: Baraita defining an am ha'aretz
items.text_en: Baraita defining an am ha'aretz
items.desc_en: A baraita lists various definitions of an am ha'aretz according to different Tannaim, and concludes with the ruling of Rav Huna that the halakha follows the opinion of Aherim, who define an am ha'aretz as one who has studied but not served Torah scholars.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by asking 'Who is an am ha'aretz?' and presents the first definition: one who does not recite the Shema, according to Rabbi Eliezer.
Rabbi Yehoshua defines an am ha'aretz as one who does not wear tefillin.
Ben Azzai defines an am ha'aretz as one who lacks tzitzit on his garment.
Rabbi Natan defines an am ha'aretz as one who lacks a mezuzah on his door.
Rabbi Natan bar Yosef defines an am ha'aretz as one who has children but does not raise them to study Torah.
Aherim define an am ha'aretz as one who has studied and repeated but has not served Torah scholars.
Rav Huna rules that the halakha follows the opinion of Aherim.

items.text: Story of Rami bar Hama and Rav Menashya bar Tahalifa
items.text_en: Story of Rami bar Hama and Rav Menashya bar Tahalifa
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Rami bar Hama did not include Rav Menashya bar Tahalifa in a zimun, and Rava said this caused his death. The Gemara questions this in light of the baraita, and answers that Rav Menashya was different because he heard teachings from rabbis and studied them, making him like a Torah scholar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Rami bar Hama did not include Rav Menashya bar Tahalifa in a zimun, even though the latter had studied Sifra, Sifrei, and halakhot.
Rava declares that Rami bar Hama's death was caused by his failure to include Rav Menashya in the zimun.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that says even one who read and studied but did not serve Torah scholars is considered an ignoramus.
The Gemara answers that Rav Menashya was different because he heard teachings from rabbis and studied them, making him like a Torah scholar, and Rami bar Hama simply did not check on him.
An alternative version states that Rav Menashya heard teachings from the mouths of rabbis and studied them, thus he is considered like a Torah scholar.

items.text: Clarifications of the remaining Mishnah clauses
items.text_en: Clarifications of the remaining Mishnah clauses
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains each of the remaining cases in the Mishnah: tevel refers to rabbinically prohibited untithed produce, first tithe refers to one who preceded the Levite, second tithe and consecrated produce refer to improper redemption, and the attendant who ate less than an olive's bulk is simply the counterpart of the earlier clause.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah lists tevel (untithed produce) at all, since it is obviously prohibited.
The Gemara explains that the case refers to tevel that is only rabbinically prohibited, such as produce grown in an unperforated pot.
The Gemara asks why first tithe is mentioned, since it too is obviously prohibited.
The Gemara explains that the case is where the Levite preceded the priest in taking the tithe, and the Mishnah teaches that this is still prohibited.
The Gemara asks why second tithe and consecrated produce are listed, since they too are obviously prohibited.

The Gemara explains that the case is where the produce was redeemed improperly: second tithe was redeemed on a coin without a minted image, and consecrated produce was redeemed on land rather than with silver.

items.text: Clarification of the attendant who ate less than an olive's bulk
items.text_en: Clarification of the attendant who ate less than an olive's bulk
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this clause is obvious, and explains that it was taught as the counterpart to the earlier clause about an olive's bulk.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the clause about the attendant who ate less than an olive's bulk was necessary, since it seems obvious.
The Gemara explains that the clause was taught as the counterpart to the earlier clause about an olive's bulk, to maintain the parallel structure.

items.text: Clarification of the gentile who may not be included
items.text_en: Clarification of the gentile who may not be included
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why this is necessary, and explains that it deals with a convert who was circumcised but did not immerse, citing Rabbi Zeira quoting Rabbi Yochanan that such a person is still a gentile.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah's statement that a gentile is not included in zimmun is obvious.
The Gemara answers that the case involves a convert who was circumcised but did not yet immerse.
Rabbi Zeira quotes Rabbi Yochanan that such a person is still a gentile until both circumcision and immersion are completed.

items.text: Discussion of including a minor in zimun
items.text_en: Discussion of including a minor in zimun
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that women, slaves, and minors are not included. Rabbi Yosei says a minor in a cradle may be included. The Gemara questions this contradiction, and explains that Rabbi Yosei follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who says a minor may be used as an additional person to complete a minyan of ten.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that women, slaves, and minors are not included in the zimun (invitation to bless).
Rabbi Yosei says that a minor in a cradle may be included in the zimun.
The Gemara objects: but we already learned that women, slaves, and minors are not included — how can Rabbi Yosei say otherwise?

The Gemara resolves: Rabbi Yosei follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who says that although a minor in a cradle is not included in the zimun, he may be used as an additional person (סניף) to complete a minyan of ten.

items.text: Discussion of including a slave in a minyan
items.text_en: Discussion of including a slave in a minyan
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says nine and a slave may join together. The Gemara brings a story of Rabbi Eliezer freeing his slave to complete a minyan, and questions how he could violate the prohibition against freeing a slave. The Gemara answers that a public need is different.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi (רבי יהושע בן לוי) rules that nine free men and a slave (עבד) may join together to form a minyan (מנין).
The Gemara (גמרא) raises an objection from a story about Rabbi Eliezer (רבי אליעזר) who entered a synagogue and did not find ten men, and freed his slave to complete the minyan.
The Gemara (גמרא) infers from the story that only by freeing the slave did he complete the minyan, implying that a slave cannot join without being freed.
The Gemara (גמרא) clarifies that two men were needed, so he freed one slave and went out with the other.

The Gemara (גמרא) asks: How could Rabbi Eliezer (רבי אליעזר) do this? Rabbi Yehuda (רב יהודה) said that one who frees his slave violates a positive commandment (עשה) from the verse 'לעולם בהם תעבודו' (they shall serve you forever).
The Gemara (גמרא) answers: For a matter of a mitzvah (מצוה) it is different — the need to complete a minyan overrides the prohibition.
The Gemara (גמרא) objects: But this is a mitzvah (מצוה) that comes through a transgression (עבירה) — freeing a slave is forbidden.
The Gemara (גמרא) resolves: For a public mitzvah (מצוה דרבים) it is different — the need of the community overrides the prohibition.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's advice to come early to synagogue
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's advice to come early to synagogue
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says one should always come early to synagogue to be counted among the first ten, as even if a hundred come after him, he receives reward equal to all of them. The Gemara corrects this to say he receives reward corresponding to all of them.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi (רבי יהושע בן לוי) states that one should always come early to synagogue to be counted among the first ten, and even if a hundred come after him, he receives reward equal to all of them.
The Gemara (גמרא) rejects the literal reading of 'reward equal to all of them' and corrects it to 'they give him reward corresponding to all of them'.

items.text: Discussion of nine and an ark joining together
items.text_en: Discussion of nine and an ark joining together
items.desc_en: Rav Huna says nine and an ark may join together. Rav Nachman objects, and Rav Huna clarifies that he meant nine who appear as ten may join. There is a dispute about whether this applies when they are gathered or when they are dispersed.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states that nine people and an ark (containing a Torah scroll) may join together to form a minyan.
Rav Nachman objects, asking whether an ark is considered a person (i.e., can it count as a man?).
Rav Huna clarifies that he meant nine people who appear as ten (due to the presence of the ark) may join together.
Some say the ruling applies when the nine are gathered together (as a group).
And others say it applies when they are dispersed (i.e., the ark makes them appear as a minyan even when scattered).

items.text: Discussion of two Torah scholars and Shabbat joining together
items.text_en: Discussion of two Torah scholars and Shabbat joining together
items.desc_en: Rav Ammi says two and Shabbat may join together. Rav Nachman objects, and Rav Ammi clarifies that he meant two Torah scholars who sharpen each other in halakha may join. Rav Chisda and Rav Sheshet give examples.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ammi states that two Torah scholars and Shabbat may join together to form a quorum for zimmun.
Rav Nachman objects, questioning how Shabbat can be considered a person to join the quorum.
Rav Ammi clarifies that he meant two Torah scholars who sharpen each other in halakha may join together, not Shabbat itself.
Rav Chisda gives an example of such a pair: himself and Rav Sheshet.
Rav Sheshet reciprocates, giving the same example of himself and Rav Chisda.

items.text: Discussion of a minor who has reached puberty
items.text_en: Discussion of a minor who has reached puberty
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says a minor who has developed pubic hair may be included in zimun. A baraita supports this, but the Gemara notes a contradiction within the baraita itself, and asks what the baraita comes to include.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan (רבי יוחנן) states that a minor who has developed pubic hair (קטן פורח) may be included in the zimun (זימון) for Grace after Meals.
A supporting baraita (תניא נמי הכי) is cited: a minor who has grown two pubic hairs is included in zimun; one who has not is not included.

The Gemara (הא גופא קשיא) notes an internal contradiction in the baraita: it first says that a minor with two hairs is included and one without is not, but then adds that one should not be strict about a minor.
The Gemara (והדר תני) points out that the baraita then repeats: 'one does not scrutinize a minor' — asking what this second clause comes to include.
The Gemara (לאתויי מאי) asks: what does this second statement come to include? It suggests that it must be referring to a case where the minor has not yet reached full puberty.

items.text: Conclusion regarding a minor leading a mezuman
items.text_en: Conclusion regarding a minor leading a mezuman
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects all earlier traditions and adopts Rav Nachman's ruling: a minor who knows to Whom blessings are directed may be counted for a mezuman.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the earlier discussion was meant to include a minor who is 'blossoming' (close to majority) in the mezuman.
The Gemara rejects all earlier traditions and adopts Rav Nachman's ruling: a minor who knows to Whom blessings are directed may be counted for a mezuman.

items.text: Story of Abaye and Rava before Rabbah
items.text_en: Story of Abaye and Rava before Rabbah
items.desc_en: Rabbah tests Abaye and Rava by asking to Whom they bless; their responses show their understanding, and Rabbah declares them both scholars.

sub.desc_en: The gemara sets the scene: Abaye and Rava were sitting before Rabbah.
Rabbah asks them: 'To Whom do we bless?'
They answer: 'To the Merciful One.'
Rabbah asks: 'And where does the Merciful One dwell?'
Rava points to the sky (the ceiling).
Abaye goes outside and points to the heavens.
Rabbah declares them both scholars, citing the proverb: 'Pumpkins — from their stalks they are known.'

items.text: Joining for a mezuman with different foods
items.text_en: Joining for a mezuman with different foods
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that nine who ate grain and one who ate vegetables join for a mezuman. Rabbi Zeira asks about eight or seven, and Rabbi Yirmeya explains the reasoning is based on a majority, but Rabbi Zeira thought a recognizable majority was needed.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules in Rav's name that nine who ate grain and one who ate vegetables join for a mezuman.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira's question to Rav Yehuda
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's question to Rav Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks Rav Yehuda about the case of eight or seven who ate grain and the rest vegetables.
Rav Yehuda answers that it is no different, and that six certainly does not need to be asked.
Rabbi Yirmeya explains that the reasoning is based on a majority (רוב), and here too there is a majority.

sub.text: Stam's clarification of Rabbi Zeira's misunderstanding
sub.text_en: Stam's clarification of Rabbi Zeira's misunderstanding
sub.desc_en: The gemara clarifies that Rabbi Zeira thought a recognizable majority (רובא דמינכר) was required.

items.text: Story of Yannai the king and Shimon ben Shetach
items.text_en: Story of Yannai the king and Shimon ben Shetach
items.desc_en: Yannai the king and his queen had no one to bless after their meal because they had killed the Sages. The queen brought her brother Shimon ben Shetach, who refused to be subservient, and when given a cup to bless, he blessed in a way that honored Yannai.

sub.desc_en: The story opens: King Yannai and his queen ate together, but since he had killed the Sages, no one was available to bless; the queen swore Yannai not to harm her brother Shimon ben Shetach and brought him.

sub.text: Shimon ben Shetach's response to Yannai
sub.text_en: Shimon ben Shetach's response to Yannai
sub.desc_en: Shimon ben Shetach is seated between the king and queen; when Yannai boasts of the honor, Shimon retorts that the honor is due to the Torah, not to Yannai, and the queen observes that Shimon refuses subservience.
Given a cup to bless, Shimon ben Shetach asks how to bless — 'Blessed is He from whose property Yannai and his companions have eaten' — then drinks that cup, receives another, and blesses properly.

items.text: Requirement of eating a kezayit of grain to discharge others
items.text_en: Requirement of eating a kezayit of grain to discharge others
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that Shimon ben Shetach acted for himself, as one can only discharge the obligation of others if he ate a kezayit of grain.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that Shimon ben Shetach's action was for himself, because one can only discharge the obligation of others if he ate a kezayit of grain.

items.text: Distinction between joining and discharging others
items.text_en: Distinction between joining and discharging others
items.desc_en: A baraita of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is cited: one who joins the group even with a dried fig joins for a mezuman, but to discharge others he must eat a kezayit of grain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel stating that one who joins the group even with a single dried fig joins for a mezuman.
The Gemara resolves the baraita: joining (הצטרפות) is permitted with minimal food, but to discharge others (להוציא את הרבים) one must eat a kezayit of grain.

items.text: Supporting statement from Rava
items.text_en: Supporting statement from Rava
items.desc_en: Rav Hana bar Yehuda cites Rava that even if one did not eat a kezayit of grain, he can still join for a mezuman, but the text is cut off.

sub.text: Rav Hana bar Yehuda citing Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Hana bar Yehuda citing Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Hana bar Yehuda cites Rava that even if one did not eat a kezayit of grain, he can still join for a mezuman, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Requirements for leading Birkat HaMazon
items.text_en: Requirements for leading Birkat HaMazon
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a baraita stating that one who ate a minimal amount (e.g., a dried fig) joins the zimun, but cannot lead the blessing unless he ate a kezayit of grain. Rav Hana bar Yehuda cites Rava's ruling that eating a leaf or drinking wine suffices for joining but not for leading.

items.text: Historical institution of the blessings
items.text_en: Historical institution of the blessings
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman explains that each blessing of Birkat HaMazon was instituted at a specific historical moment: 'HaZan' by Moses when the manna fell, 'Birkat HaAretz' by Joshua upon entering the land, 'Boneh Yerushalayim' by David and Solomon, and 'HaTov VeHaMetiv' by the Sages in Yavneh after the burial of the martyrs of Beitar.

items.text: Order of blessings and dispute about Shabbat
items.text_en: Order of blessings and dispute about Shabbat
items.desc_en: A baraita presents the standard order of the four blessings, with a special insertion for Shabbat. Rabbi Eliezer allows reciting the Shabbat insertion in any of the blessings, while the Sages restrict it to the third blessing (Nechemah). The Gemara notes that the dispute is only about whether one who did so fulfills his obligation post facto.

items.text: Biblical source for Birkat HaMazon after eating
items.text_en: Biblical source for Birkat HaMazon after eating
items.desc_en: A baraita derives the four blessings from the verse 'And you shall eat and be satisfied and bless' (Deut. 8:10), interpreting each phrase as a different blessing. It also derives the obligation to bless before eating via a kal vachomer argument: if one blesses when full, certainly when hungry.

items.text: Rabbi's alternative derivation
items.text_en: Rabbi's alternative derivation
items.desc_en: Rabbi argues that the verse only teaches Birkat HaMazon after eating, but the blessing before eating (zimun) is derived from 'Gadlu LaHashem Iti'. He also notes that 'HaTov VeHaMetiv' was instituted in Yavneh, and derives the obligation to bless before eating from the phrase 'asher natan lach'—from the moment He gave you.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak's proof for blessing before eating
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak's proof for blessing before eating
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak derives the obligation to bless before eating from the verse 'And I will bless your bread and your water' (Ex. 23:25), reading 'uverach' as 'uvareich' (bless), implying blessing is required before eating bread.

items.text: Rabbi Natan's proof and reasons for Samuel's practice
items.text_en: Rabbi Natan's proof and reasons for Samuel's practice
items.desc_en: Rabbi Natan derives the obligation to bless before eating from the story of Samuel blessing the sacrifice before the people ate. The Gemara then explains why Samuel did this: because women are talkative (to gather them), to allow gazing at Saul's beauty, or because one kingdom does not overlap with another even a hair's breadth.

items.text: Source for blessing before Torah study
items.text_en: Source for blessing before Torah study
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of blessing before Torah study. Rabbi Yishmael uses a kal vachomer: if one blesses over temporal life, certainly over eternal life. Rabbi Chiya bar Nachmani cites Rabbi Yishmael that it is derived from the verse 'upon the good land which He gave you', linking to the giving of the Torah.

items.text: Blessing on bad as on good
items.text_en: Blessing on bad as on good
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir derives from the verse 'asher natan lecha Hashem Elohecha' that one must bless on bad just as on good, interpreting 'dayyanecha' as accepting God's judgment in all measures, whether good or punitive.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's interpretation of 'tovah' and 'hatovah'
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's interpretation of 'tovah' and 'hatovah'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira argues that the verse's 'tovah' refers to the Torah and 'hatovah' to the building of Jerusalem, citing prooftexts for each.

items.text: Required phrases in the blessings
items.text_en: Required phrases in the blessings
items.desc_en: A baraita records Rabbi Eliezer's requirement to mention 'eretz chemdah tovah urechavah' in Birkat HaAretz and 'malchut beit David' in Boneh Yerushalayim. Nachum HaZaken requires mentioning the covenant, Rabbi Yosei requires mentioning the Torah, and Pelimo requires mentioning the covenant before the Torah because it was given with three covenants.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the blessing of the land was given with thirteen covenants.

items.text: Rabbi Abba's ruling on Birkat HaMazon
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba's ruling on Birkat HaMazon
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba rules that one must include thanksgiving at the beginning and end of the blessing, and that one who omits the mention of brit and Torah in the blessing of the land, or malchut in the blessing of Jerusalem, has not fulfilled their obligation.

items.text: Support for Rabbi Ila'a
items.text_en: Support for Rabbi Ila'a
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a statement from Rabbi Ila'a in the name of Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha quoting Rabbeinu, which supports the requirement to mention brit, Torah, and malchut.

items.text: Dispute about malchut in HaTov VeHaMeitiv
items.text_en: Dispute about malchut in HaTov VeHaMeitiv
items.desc_en: Abba Yosef ben Dostai and the Rabbis disagree whether the blessing 'HaTov VeHaMeitiv' requires mention of malchut; one holds it is rabbinic and requires malchut, the other holds it is biblical and does not.

items.text: Conclusion of the blessing of Jerusalem
items.text_en: Conclusion of the blessing of Jerusalem
items.desc_en: A baraitha discusses the proper conclusion for the blessing of Jerusalem; Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda says 'Moshia Yisrael', and the Gemara clarifies that one should say 'Boneh Yerushalayim' as well.

items.text: The rule against sealing with two themes
items.text_en: The rule against sealing with two themes
items.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna sealed with two themes, and Rav Chisda objects, citing Rabbi's ruling that one does not seal with two. The Gemara examines exceptions and explains the reason: one does not make bundles of mitzvot.

items.text: Rav Sheshet and Rav Nachman on the conclusion
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet and Rav Nachman on the conclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the halacha is. Rav Sheshet rules that if one began with 'Rachem al amcha Yisrael' one concludes with 'Moshia Yisrael', and if with 'Rachem al Yerushalayim' one concludes with 'Boneh Yerushalayim'. Rav Nachman says even if one began with 'Rachem al Yisrael' one concludes with 'Boneh Yerushalayim' based on a verse.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's inquiry and Rav Chisda's story
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's inquiry and Rav Chisda's story
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks Rav Chisda to teach him, but Rav Chisda declines, recounting how he was once punished by Rav Sheshet for omitting brit, Torah, and malchut in Birkat HaMazon, despite relying on Rav's lenient opinion.

items.text: Requirement of two malchuyot in HaTov VeHaMeitiv
items.text_en: Requirement of two malchuyot in HaTov VeHaMeitiv
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that HaTov VeHaMeitiv requires malchut. Rabbi Zeira explains it needs two malchuyot: its own and that of Boneh Yerushalayim. The Gemara questions why not three, and answers that Birkat HaAretz is adjacent, but Boneh Yerushalayim is also adjacent; Rav Pappa clarifies it needs two malchuyot besides its own.

items.text: Formulations for forgetting Shabbat, Yom Tov, and Rosh Chodesh
items.text_en: Formulations for forgetting Shabbat, Yom Tov, and Rosh Chodesh
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira, sitting behind Rav Giddel, reports Rav's rulings: if one forgot Shabbat, one says a specific blessing; similarly for Yom Tov; for Rosh Chodesh, the formulation is uncertain regarding 'simcha' and the conclusion.

items.text: Rav Nachman's error
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's error
items.desc_en: Giddel bar Minyome stood before Rav Nachman, who made an error.

items.text: Opening: Rabbi Sheila's ruling on error in Birkat HaMazon
items.text_en: Opening: Rabbi Sheila's ruling on error in Birkat HaMazon
items.desc_en: Rabbi Sheila (via Rav) rules that if one errs in Birkat HaMazon, they return to the beginning, but Rav Huna (via Rav) says they say 'Baruch she'natam' instead. The Gemara resolves: the dispute is only when one did not open with 'HaTov veHaMetiv'; if they did, they return to the start.

items.text: Gemara's question: Why differ between prayer and Birkat HaMazon?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why differ between prayer and Birkat HaMazon?
items.desc_en: Rav Avin asks Rav Amram why prayer (where error requires return) differs from Birkat HaMazon (where error does not require return). Rav Nachman answers via Samuel: prayer is a 'debt' (obligation), so one must return; Birkat HaMazon is optional (if one doesn't eat, no blessing), so no return.

items.text: Gemara's extension: Shabbatot and Yom Tovim
items.text_en: Gemara's extension: Shabbatot and Yom Tovim
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: on Shabbat/Yom Tov where eating is mandatory, if one errs in Birkat HaMazon, do they return? Rabbi Sheila (via Rav) says yes, but Rav Huna (via Rav) says they say 'Baruch she'natam'. The dispute is only when not opening with 'HaTov veHaMetiv'; if they did, they return.

items.text: Mishna: How many are called to lead Birkat HaMazon?
items.text_en: Mishna: How many are called to lead Birkat HaMazon?
items.desc_en: The Mishna specifies: for 3, the leader says 'Nevarekh'; for 3+1 (a fourth), 'Bar'khu'. For 10, 'Nevarekh Eloheinu'; for 10+1, 'Bar'khu'. For 100, 'Nevarekh HaShem Eloheinu'; for 100+1, 'Bar'khu'. For 1000, 'Nevarekh laHaShem Eloheinu Elohei Yisrael'; for 1000+1, 'Bar'khu'. For 10000, 'Nevarekh laHaShem Eloheinu Elohei Yisrael Elohei Tzevaot yoshev haKeruvim al haMazon she'achalnu'; for 10000+1, 'Bar'khu'.

items.text: Gemara on Mishna: How the leader responds to the call
items.text_en: Gemara on Mishna: How the leader responds to the call
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains: as the leader blesses, the others respond 'Baruch HaShem Eloheinu Elohei Yisrael Elohei Tzevaot yoshev haKeruvim al haMazon she'achalnu'. Rabbi Yosei HaGlili says: according to the majority, they bless, citing 'Bemakhelot bar'khu Elohim HaShem miMekor Yisrael'. Rabbi Akiva says: as in synagogue, one among many or few says 'Bar'khu et HaShem'. Rabbi Yishmael says: 'Bar'khu et HaShem haMevorakh'.

items.text: Gemara: Samuel's rule on never excluding oneself from the group
items.text_en: Gemara: Samuel's rule on never excluding oneself from the group
items.desc_en: Samuel says: one should never exclude oneself from the group. The Gemara cites the Mishna: in a group of 3+1, the fourth says 'Bar'khu' (not 'Nevarekh'), confirming Samuel's point.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda on return size
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda on return size
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute: Rabbi Meir says returning to the start requires an olive-sized piece; Rabbi Yehuda says an egg-sized piece. They differ on interpretation of 've'achalta ve'sava'ta': Rabbi Meir sees 'achalta' as eating (olive), 'sava'ta' as drinking; Rabbi Yehuda sees both as eating with satiety (egg).

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Yochanan's statement on the dispute
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Yochanan's statement on the dispute
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says the dispute is 'muchlefet haShita' (the positions are reversed). Abaye says: never reverse. Here in the verses they differ: Rabbi Meir reads 've'achalta' as eating (olive), 've'sava'ta' as drinking; Rabbi Yehuda reads both as eating with satiety (egg).

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the dispute on return size
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the dispute on return size
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies: the dispute is about the size for returning to the start. Rabbi Meir holds return size equals impurity size (egg), Rabbi Yehuda holds return size equals prohibition size (olive). They differ on the verse: Rabbi Meir sees 'achalta' as eating (olive), 'sava'ta' as drinking; Rabbi Yehuda sees both as eating with satiety (egg).

items.text: Mishna: How to invite for zimmun
items.text_en: Mishna: How to invite for zimmun

items.text: Preference for 'Nevarech' over 'Barchu'
items.text_en: Preference for 'Nevarech' over 'Barchu'
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that 'Nevarech' is the superior formulation for the zimmun invitation, citing a baraita about six people dividing into two groups of three. It proves this by noting that if 'Barchu' were better, there would be no reason to divide.

items.text: Baraita on the discerning grammarian
items.text_en: Baraita on the discerning grammarian
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that while neither 'Barchu' nor 'Nevarech' is grounds for reprimand, the grammarians (nakdanim) do reprimand. It then teaches that a person's character is discernible from their blessing language: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi states that saying 'u'vetuvo' marks a scholar, while 'umituvo' marks a boor.

items.text: Abaye's objection and resolution regarding 'umituvo'
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and resolution regarding 'umituvo'
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges the baraita by citing a verse where David uses 'umituvo' (from Your blessing). The Gemara resolves that the verse refers to a request (she'elah), not a blessing. A further objection about 'harchev picha' is answered by saying that verse deals with Torah study.

items.text: Another baraita on 'betuvo' vs. 'chayyim'
items.text_en: Another baraita on 'betuvo' vs. 'chayyim'
items.desc_en: A second baraita from Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi distinguishes between a scholar who says 'betuvo chayyinu' and a boor who says 'chayyim'. The Nehardeans reverse the ruling, but the halakha does not follow them.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's distinction and Rav Acha's objection
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's distinction and Rav Acha's objection
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that saying 'Nevarech she'achalnu mishelo' marks a scholar, while 'lemi she'achalnu mishelo' marks a boor. Rav Acha bar Rava objects, citing the Haggadah where we say 'lemi she'asah...'. Rav Ashi answers that there the context makes clear that God is the subject.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's second distinction
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's second distinction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan further distinguishes: saying 'Baruch she'achalnu mishelo' marks a scholar, while 'al hamazon she'achalnu' marks a boor.

items.text: Rav Huna's qualification for a group of ten
items.text_en: Rav Huna's qualification for a group of ten
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua qualifies the previous rulings: they apply only to a group of three where God's name is not mentioned, but in a group of ten where God's name is invoked, the context makes the meaning clear, as per the Mishnah.

items.text: Contradiction in the Mishnah and resolution via Tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Contradiction in the Mishnah and resolution via Tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction in the Mishnah: it says ten and ten thousand are the same, yet later distinguishes between one hundred, one thousand, and ten thousand. Rav Yosef resolves this by attributing the first view to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and the second to Rabbi Akiva. The Gemara then explains how Rabbi Akiva interprets the verse used by Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.

items.text: Halakha follows Rabbi Akiva; practical story
items.text_en: Halakha follows Rabbi Akiva; practical story
items.desc_en: Rava rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Akiva. A story is told of Ravina and Rav Chama bar Buzi who went to the Exilarch's house; Rav Chama sought a group of one hundred, but Ravina told him that Rava had already ruled like Rabbi Akiva, so it was unnecessary.

items.text: Rava's practice at the Exilarch's house
items.text_en: Rava's practice at the Exilarch's house
items.desc_en: Rava explains that when they ate at the Exilarch's house, they would bless in groups of three rather than ten, because the Exilarch would be offended by a large group, and the crowd was too noisy to hear the Exilarch's blessing.

items.text: Rule of zimmun retroactively
items.text_en: Rule of zimmun retroactively
items.desc_en: Rabba Tosfa'ah rules that if three people ate together and one of them blessed prematurely on his own, the other two may fulfill their obligation through his zimmun, but he does not fulfill his obligation through theirs, because zimmun cannot be done retroactively.

items.text: Practice of 'Barchu et Hashem hamevorach'
items.text_en: Practice of 'Barchu et Hashem hamevorach'
items.desc_en: A story is told of Rafram bar Papa who began with 'Barchu et Hashem' without 'hamevorach', and the congregation completed it. Rava criticizes this, saying one should not involve himself in a dispute, and the world follows Rabbi Yishmael's practice of saying the full phrase.

items.text: Mishnah: Rules for splitting a group for zimmun
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rules for splitting a group for zimmun
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that three, four, or five who ate together may not split; six may split into two groups of three, up to ten; ten may not split until twenty.

items.text: Mishnah: Two groups in one house
items.text_en: Mishnah: Two groups in one house
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if two groups eat in the same house and can see each other, they may combine for zimmun; otherwise, each group blesses separately.

items.text: Mishnah: Blessing on undiluted wine
items.text_en: Mishnah: Blessing on undiluted wine
items.desc_en: The Mishnah records a dispute: Rabbi Eliezer says one may not bless on wine until water is added; the Sages say one may bless even without water.

items.text: Gemara: What does the Mishnah teach?
items.text_en: Gemara: What does the Mishnah teach?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah adds, since we already know three who ate together are obligated to invite. It answers that the Mishnah teaches a new point from Shmuel: three who sat down to eat together but have not yet eaten may not split.

items.text: Alternative versions of Shmuel's statement and Rav Huna's addition
items.text_en: Alternative versions of Shmuel's statement and Rav Huna's addition
items.desc_en: An alternative version of Shmuel's statement is given: even if each eats from his own loaf, they may not split. Rav Huna adds that three who came from three different groups may not split. Rav Chisda specifies that this applies when the three groups each had three people.

items.text: Rava's statement (unfinished)
items.text_en: Rava's statement (unfinished)
items.desc_en: The daf ends with Rava beginning a statement, which is cut off.

items.text: Zimmun for separate groups
items.text_en: Zimmun for separate groups
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that if two groups have already recited zimmun separately, the obligation is lifted. Rava proves this from a mishna about a bed that, once divided, loses its impurity; similarly, once zimmun is recited, the obligation departs.

items.text: Server connects two groups
items.text_en: Server connects two groups
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if a waiter serves between two groups, he can join them for zimmun.

items.text: Blessing on undiluted wine
items.text_en: Blessing on undiluted wine
items.desc_en: A baraita records a dispute: Rabbi Eliezer says undiluted wine gets 'Borei Pri HaEtz' and may be used for handwashing, while diluted wine gets 'Borei Pri HaGefen' and may not. The Sages say both get 'Borei Pri HaGefen' and neither may be used for handwashing. The Gemara identifies Shmuel's ruling with Rabbi Eliezer, and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina notes that the Sages agree with Rabbi Eliezer regarding the cup of blessing, requiring dilution for the mitzvah.

items.text: Use of undiluted wine
items.text_en: Use of undiluted wine
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira explains that undiluted wine is fit for medicinal purposes (kuryatei), answering what it is good for.

items.text: Four rules about bread and food throwing
items.text_en: Four rules about bread and food throwing
items.desc_en: A baraita lists four rules about bread: no raw meat on it, no full cup over it, no throwing bread, no supporting a bowl with it. An incident with Amemar, Mar Zutra, and Rav Ashi leads to a contradiction about throwing food, resolved by distinguishing between foods that become repulsive and those that do not.

items.text: Customs at weddings
items.text_en: Customs at weddings
items.desc_en: A baraita describes practices at weddings: pouring wine through channels, throwing parched grain and nuts in summer but not winter, and never throwing hard cakes.

items.text: Food in mouth without a blessing
items.text_en: Food in mouth without a blessing
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that if one put food in mouth without a blessing, he should move it aside and bless. Three contradictory baraitot are reconciled: for liquids, swallow; for non-repulsive solids, spit out; for repulsive solids, move aside.

items.text: Gemara's question on blessing over repulsive items
items.text_en: Gemara's question on blessing over repulsive items
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why one cannot simply move repulsive items aside and bless. Rav Yitzchak Kasksa'ah explains in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that it is because of the verse 'Let my mouth be filled with Your praise.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why one cannot simply move aside a non-repulsive item and recite the blessing.

sub.text: Rav Yitzchak Kasksa'ah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Yitzchak Kasksa'ah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak Kasksa'ah explains that one must spit it out because of the verse 'Let my mouth be filled with Your praise.'

items.text: Whether one who ate without blessing must return to bless
items.text_en: Whether one who ate without blessing must return to bless
items.desc_en: The students asked Rav Chisda if one who ate and drank without blessing must return to bless. He answered with a parable about garlic. Ravina then ruled that even if one finished the meal, he must return to bless, citing a baraita about immersion. The Gemara rejects this, distinguishing between the cases.

sub.desc_en: The students ask Rav Chisda whether one who ate and drank without reciting a blessing must return and bless.
Rav Chisda answers with a parable: should one who ate garlic and has bad breath eat another garlic to restore the odor?
Ravina rules that even if one finished his meal, he must return and recite the blessing.
Ravina cites a baraita about immersion: one who immersed and emerged recites the blessing after the act.
The Gemara rejects the parallel: in the immersion case, the person was initially unfit to bless; here, he was fit and excluded himself, so he remains excluded.

items.text: Properties of isparagos (wine drink)
items.text_en: Properties of isparagos (wine drink)
items.desc_en: A baraita states that isparagos is good for the heart and eyes, especially for the intestines. The Gemara questions a contradiction with another baraita about old wine. It resolves that the first baraita refers to aged wine, citing a mishnah about a vow.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that isparagos (a wine drink) is good for the heart and eyes, especially for the intestines, and habitual use benefits the whole body, but drunkenness harms it.

The Gemara questions a contradiction: another baraita says isparagos is beneficial for L-E-T (heart, eyes, spleen) but harmful for R-M-T (head, intestines, hemorrhoids), contradicting the claim that it is especially good for the intestines.
The Gemara resolves that the first baraita refers to aged wine, citing a mishnah about a vow where old wine is acknowledged as beneficial for the intestines, while new wine is harmful.

items.text: Six rules of isparagos and a contradiction
items.text_en: Six rules of isparagos and a contradiction
items.desc_en: A baraita lists six rules for drinking isparagos, including that it must be supported only by its own type. Another baraita says it must be supported by bread. The Gemara resolves: one refers to wine, the other to beer.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists six rules for drinking isparagos, including that it must be supported only by its own kind.
The Gemara objects by citing another baraita that says isparagos must be supported only by bread.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: one baraita refers to wine-based isparagos, the other to beer-based isparagos.

items.text: Contradictions about isparagos' effects and spitting
items.text_en: Contradictions about isparagos' effects and spitting
items.desc_en: Two baraitot contradict each other about whether isparagos is good for the stomach or the head. Another contradiction about spitting after drinking. Both are resolved by distinguishing between wine and beer.

sub.desc_en: One baraita states that asparagus is beneficial for L-E-T (heart, eyes, spleen) and harmful for R-M-T (head, intestines, hemorrhoids).
Another baraita contradicts the first, stating that asparagus is beneficial for R-M-T and harmful for L-E-T.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the first baraita refers to wine-based asparagus, the second to beer-based asparagus.
One baraita states that spitting after drinking asparagus causes illness.
Another baraita contradicts, stating that not spitting after drinking asparagus causes illness.
The Gemara resolves this contradiction similarly: the first baraita refers to wine-based asparagus, the second to beer-based asparagus.

items.text: Rav Ashi's ruling on spitting after isparagos
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's ruling on spitting after isparagos
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi concludes that since not spitting after isparagos is punishable, one may spit even in front of the king.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi rules that since failing to spit after drinking isparagos (asparagus) is punishable, one may spit even in the presence of the king.

items.text: Angel Suriel's three warnings and the Angel of Death's advice
items.text_en: Angel Suriel's three warnings and the Angel of Death's advice
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha reports three things told by the angel Suriel: not to take one's garment from the attendant, not to wash hands from one who hasn't, and not to return the isparagos cup except to the giver. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi reports three things from the Angel of Death, including not to stand before women returning from a funeral. The Gemara provides remedies if one encounters them.

sub.desc_en: רבי ישמעאל בן אלישע (Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha) reports three warnings from the angel סוריאל (Suriel): not to take one's garment from the attendant, not to wash hands from one who hasn't, and not to return the אספרגוס (asparagus) cup except to the giver, because demons lie in wait.

רבי יהושע בן לוי (Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi) reports three things from the Angel of Death: not to take one's garment from the attendant, not to wash hands from one who hasn't, and not to stand before women returning from a funeral, because the Angel of Death dances before them with his sword.
The Gemara asks: if one encounters women returning from a funeral, what is his remedy?
The Gemara provides remedies: jump four cubits away, cross a river, take another path, stand behind a wall, or turn away and recite a verse from Zechariah until they pass.

items.text: Ten things said about the cup of blessing
items.text_en: Ten things said about the cup of blessing
items.desc_en: A baraita lists ten requirements for the cup of blessing: rinsing, washing, live, full, adornment, wrapping, taking with two hands, giving to the right, lifting a handbreadth, and looking at it. Rabbi Yochanan reduces to four. The Gemara elaborates on each, including verses and debates about the left hand assisting the right.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists ten requirements for the cup of blessing: rinsing, washing, live, full, adornment, wrapping, taking with two hands, giving to the right, lifting a handbreadth, and looking at it, with an additional opinion about sending it as a gift.
Rabbi Yochanan reduces the ten requirements to four: rinsing, washing, live, and full, and explains that rinsing is from the inside and washing from the outside.
Rabbi Yochanan promises a boundless inheritance for one who blesses over a full cup, citing a verse; Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina adds that such a person inherits both this world and the World-to-Come.
The Gemara discusses adornment of the cup: Rav Yehuda adorns it with students, Rav Chisda with other cups; Rabbi Chanan specifies undiluted wine, and Rav Sheshet adds the blessing of the land.
The Gemara discusses wrapping: Rav Pappa wraps himself in his prayer shawl, and Rav Asi spreads a cloth on his head.
Rabbi Chinana bar Pappa cites a verse to support taking the cup with two hands.
The early Sages ask whether the left hand may assist the right when taking the cup.
Rav Ashi notes that since the early Sages raised this dilemma and it was not resolved, the matter remains undecided.

items.text: Laws of lifting the cup and giving it as a gift
items.text_en: Laws of lifting the cup and giving it as a gift
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the requirement to lift the cup of blessing a handbreadth from the ground, citing a verse. It also explains that one should look at the cup to avoid distraction, and that sending the cup to one's household brings blessing.

items.text: The story of Ulla, Rav Nachman, and Yalta
items.text_en: The story of Ulla, Rav Nachman, and Yalta
items.desc_en: Ulla visits Rav Nachman, blesses the meal, and gives the cup of blessing to Rav Nachman. Rav Nachman asks him to send it to Yalta, but Ulla cites Rabbi Yochanan that a woman's blessing comes from her husband. Yalta hears this, becomes angry, and breaks 400 barrels of wine. Rav Nachman then asks Ulla to send another cup, but Ulla sends a message that the blessing is already given, leading to a sharp retort from Yalta.

items.text: Laws of the cup of blessing and the cup of punishment
items.text_en: Laws of the cup of blessing and the cup of punishment
items.desc_en: Rav Asi rules that one may not speak over the cup of blessing and that one should not bless over a cup of punishment, which is identified as a second cup. A baraita supports this, stating that one who drinks two cups should not bless, citing a verse.

items.text: The law of blessing while standing or sitting
items.text_en: The law of blessing while standing or sitting
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu or a baraita states that one who eats while walking blesses standing, one who eats standing blesses sitting, and one who eats reclining blesses while sitting. The halakha is that in all cases one sits and blesses.

items.text: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter 'Three who ate' with the standard formula.

items.text: Mishnah: Disputes between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding the meal
items.text_en: Mishnah: Disputes between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding the meal
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists several disputes between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel concerning the order of blessings, hand-washing, and other practices during a meal, including the order of Havdalah, blessings over fire and spices, and the law of one who forgot to bless.

items.text: Gemara: Analysis of the dispute regarding blessing on the day and wine
items.text_en: Gemara: Analysis of the dispute regarding blessing on the day and wine
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the reasoning of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding the order of blessing on the day and wine. Beit Hillel offers two reasons: wine causes the sanctification to be said, and the blessing over wine is more frequent. The Gemara questions the need for the second reason and discusses the halakha after the Bat Kol.

items.text: Attribution to Rabbi Yehoshua
items.text_en: Attribution to Rabbi Yehoshua
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the earlier mishnah as following Rabbi Yehoshua, who holds that one does not heed a bat kol.

items.text: Challenge: Beit Shammai's view on the order of blessings
items.text_en: Challenge: Beit Shammai's view on the order of blessings
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Beit Shammai prioritizes the blessing of the day, citing a baraita about entering one's home on Saturday night. It resolves that the baraita aligns with Beit Shammai according to Rabbi Yehuda.

items.text: Distinction between entering and leaving the day
items.text_en: Distinction between entering and leaving the day
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between bringing in the day (Shabbat) and taking it out: for bringing in, earlier is better; for taking out, later is better to avoid it being a burden.

items.text: Does Birkat HaMazon require a cup?
items.text_en: Does Birkat HaMazon require a cup?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Beit Shammai holds that Birkat HaMazon requires a cup, citing a mishnah. It addresses objections about tasting, diminishing the cup, and a baraita from Rabbi Chiya, concluding there are two tannaitic traditions.

items.text: Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the mishnah's statement of Beit Shammai's opinion.

items.text: Dispute about hand-washing and pouring the cup
items.text_en: Dispute about hand-washing and pouring the cup
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a baraita where Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel dispute the order of hand-washing and pouring the cup, with each side concerned about impurity from liquids. The discussion addresses purity rules.

items.text: Dispute over using a vessel whose exterior is impure
items.text_en: Dispute over using a vessel whose exterior is impure
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding the Mishnah's ruling on a vessel whose exterior is impure. Beit Shammai prohibits using it due to a decree lest sparks of liquid cause impurity, while Beit Hillel permits it, arguing that sparks are uncommon and the concern is about liquids on the hands becoming impure from the cup.

items.text: Beit Hillel's additional argument: immediate hand-washing before the meal
items.text_en: Beit Hillel's additional argument: immediate hand-washing before the meal
items.desc_en: Beit Hillel presents an additional argument to Beit Shammai: even according to their concern about sparks, the priority is that hand-washing should be immediately before the meal, as stated in the Mishnah. This supports their lenient position.

items.text: Dispute about drying hands: on the table or on a cushion
items.text_en: Dispute about drying hands: on the table or on a cushion
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the Mishnah's dispute about where to place the towel after drying hands. Beit Shammai says on the table, lest the towel become impure from the cushion and then re-impurify the hands. Beit Hillel says on the cushion, lest the towel become impure from the table and then re-impurify the food. The Gemara explains the underlying dispute: Beit Shammai prohibits using a secondary table due to a decree for terumah foods, while Beit Hillel permits it, trusting that terumah eaters are careful.

items.text: Beit Hillel's additional argument: hand-washing for non-sacred food is not Torah law
items.text_en: Beit Hillel's additional argument: hand-washing for non-sacred food is not Torah law
items.desc_en: Beit Hillel adds another argument: even if one is concerned about food impurity, hand-washing for non-sacred food is only rabbinic, so it is better that hands become impure than that foods (which have a Torah basis for impurity) become impure.

items.text: Dispute about sweeping the house before hand-washing
items.text_en: Dispute about sweeping the house before hand-washing
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Beit Shammai says to sweep the house first, then wash hands, while Beit Hillel says to wash hands first. The Gemara explains that Beit Shammai is concerned about crumbs, and Beit Hillel permits a learned servant to remove large crumbs. The underlying dispute is whether one may use an ignorant servant: Beit Hillel prohibits it, Beit Shammai permits it.

items.text: Ruling on the entire chapter: halakha follows Beit Hillel except one case
items.text_en: Ruling on the entire chapter: halakha follows Beit Hillel except one case
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina quotes Rav Huna that the halakha follows Beit Hillel throughout the chapter except for one case, but Rabbi Oshaya reverses it, and even in that case the halakha follows Beit Hillel.

items.text: Dispute about the order of Havdalah: candle, spices, or food first
items.text_en: Dispute about the order of Havdalah: candle, spices, or food first
items.desc_en: The Mishnah records a dispute about the order of Havdalah: Beit Shammai says candle, food, spices, and Havdalah; Beit Hillel says candle, spices, food, and Havdalah. Rava explains that according to Rabbi Meir they disagree, but Rabbi Yehuda says they agree that food comes first and Havdalah last, and they only disagree about candle and spices. Rabbi Yochanan says the people follow Beit Hillel according to Rabbi Yehuda.

items.text: Dispute about the blessing formula: 'bara' vs 'borei' and 'me'or' vs 'me'orei'
items.text_en: Dispute about the blessing formula: 'bara' vs 'borei' and 'me'or' vs 'me'orei'
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding the blessing over fire. Rava says all agree that 'bara' implies past creation, and they disagree about 'borei'.
