Rav Yosef objects with verses and says they disagree about 'me'or' (singular) vs 'me'orei' (plural), as Beit Shammai holds there is one light in fire, Beit Hillel holds there are many lights. A baraita supports Beit Hillel.

items.text: Why no blessing over a Gentile's candle or spices
items.text_en: Why no blessing over a Gentile's candle or spices
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one does not bless over a candle or spices of Gentiles. The Gemara asks why, and Rav Yehuda says it is because a Gentile's gathering is typically for idolatry. An objection is raised from the Mishnah's later clause about idolatry, and Rabbi Chanina from Sura explains that the first clause is also about idolatry, and the phrase 'what is the reason' explains it.

items.text: Definition of a fire that 'rested' for blessing
items.text_en: Definition of a fire that 'rested' for blessing
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that one blesses over a fire that 'rested' (shavat) and not over one that did not. It then asks what 'shavat' and 'lo shavat' mean.

items.text: Clarifying the meaning of 'rested'
items.text_en: Clarifying the meaning of 'rested'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a fire that did not rest from any work, even permitted work, can be blessed upon. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that 'rested' means it rested from forbidden work, and a supporting baraita is cited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether 'did not rest' means it did not rest from any labor, even permitted labor, citing a baraita that one may bless over fire kindled for a woman giving birth or a dangerously ill person on Shabbat.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that 'rested' means it rested from forbidden labor, and a supporting baraita is cited about a lantern burning all day on Shabbat.

items.text: Blessing over fire kindled by a non-Jew
items.text_en: Blessing over fire kindled by a non-Jew
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one may bless over fire kindled by a non-Jew from a Jew or a Jew from a non-Jew, but not a non-Jew from a non-Jew. The Gemara questions this distinction, suggesting that the fire from a non-Jew has not 'rested'. Various answers are proposed, including that the blessing is on the additional permitted flame, and a decree is made due to the first non-Jew and first flame.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that one may recite a blessing over fire kindled by a non-Jew from a Jew or a Jew from a non-Jew, but not a non-Jew from a non-Jew.
The Gemara questions why a non-Jew-from-non-Jew fire is invalid, suggesting the reason is that the fire did not rest on שבת (Sabbath), and then objects that a Jew-from-non-Jew fire also did not rest.

The Gemara rejects the answer that the prohibited flame is gone and a new flame is born, citing a Tosefta that one who carries out a flame on שבת (Sabbath) is liable, proving the flame is considered a single entity.
The Gemara answers that the prohibited flame still exists, and the blessing is on the permitted addition, but then objects that the same logic should apply to a non-Jew-from-non-Jew fire.
The Gemara resolves that fundamentally it is permitted, but a decree was issued due to the first non-Jew and the first pillar of flame.

items.text: Blessing over fire outside a city based on majority
items.text_en: Blessing over fire outside a city based on majority
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if one sees a fire outside a city, if the majority are non-Jews, one does not bless; if the majority are Jews, one blesses. The Gemara notes an internal contradiction regarding the case of half and half, and resolves it by explaining that the baraita's phrasing is imprecise.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if one sees a fire outside a city, the blessing depends on the majority: if most are non-Jews, one does not bless; if most are Jews, one blesses.
The Gemara points out an internal contradiction: the first clause implies that half-and-half permits a blessing, but the second clause implies that half-and-half does not permit a blessing.
The Gemara resolves that by right even half-and-half permits a blessing, but the baraita used the same expression 'majority' in both clauses for stylistic consistency.

items.text: Blessing over fire seen with a child near sunset
items.text_en: Blessing over fire seen with a child near sunset
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses seeing a child with a torch outside a city; if the child is Jewish, one blesses; if non-Jewish, one does not. The Gemara questions why a child is specified, and Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains that near sunset, an adult is certainly a non-Jew, but a child might be Jewish.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules: one who sees a child with a torch outside a city checks the child's identity; if Jewish, he recites a blessing; if non-Jewish, he does not.
The Gemara asks why the baraita specifies a child; even an adult would require investigation.

Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains that the case is near sunset; an adult is certainly a non-Jew (since a Jew would not take fire so soon after שבת (Sabbath)), but a child might be Jewish and happened to take the torch.

items.text: Blessing over fire from a furnace, oven, or synagogue
items.text_en: Blessing over fire from a furnace, oven, or synagogue
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one blesses over a fire as thick as a furnace opening. Contradictory baraitot are cited regarding fire from a furnace, oven, and synagogue. The Gemara resolves each contradiction: initially one blesses, later not; for a synagogue, it depends on whether an important person or a cantor is present, or whether there is moonlight.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that one blesses over a fire as thick as a furnace opening, otherwise not.
The Gemara cites contradictory baraitot: one permits blessing over furnace fire, the other forbids.
The Gemara resolves: the first baraita refers to the beginning when the fire is for heating, the second to the end when it is for light.
The Gemara cites another contradiction regarding oven or stove fire.
The Gemara resolves similarly: the distinction is between the beginning and the end of the fire's use.
The Gemara cites a contradiction regarding synagogue or study hall fire.
The Gemara resolves: the baraita that forbids refers to a case with an important person (fire for honor), the one that permits refers to a case without (fire for light).
An alternative resolution: both baraitot refer to a case with an important person; the distinction is whether a caretaker (חזנא) is present to use the light.
A further alternative: both baraitot refer to a case with a caretaker; the distinction is whether there is moonlight (no need for light) or not.

items.text: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on blessing over fire in the study hall
items.text_en: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on blessing over fire in the study hall
items.desc_en: A baraita presents a dispute: when fire is brought into the study hall, Beit Shammai say each person blesses individually, while Beit Hillel say one blesses for all, citing 'In a multitude of people is the king's glory'. The Gemara explains Beit Shammai's reasoning is due to interruption of study, and a supporting baraita is cited.

sub.desc_en: A baraita presents the dispute: when fire is brought into the study hall, Beit Shammai say each person recites a blessing for himself, while Beit Hillel say one recites for all, citing the verse 'In a multitude of people is the king's glory'.
The Gemara asks: Granted, Beit Hillel explain their reasoning, but what is the reason for Beit Shammai's position?
The Gemara answers: Beit Shammai hold that it is due to interruption of study in the study hall.
A supporting baraita is cited: the household of Rabban Gamliel would not say 'good health' in the study hall, due to interruption of study.

items.text: No blessing over fire or spices for the dead
items.text_en: No blessing over fire or spices for the dead
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one does not bless over fire or spices used for the dead, because the fire is for honor and the spices to remove odor. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav adds a criterion: if items are brought out both day and night, no blessing is said; if only at night, a blessing is said.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that one does not recite a blessing over the candle or spices of the dead, explaining that the candle is for honor and the spices to remove odor.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav adds a criterion: if items are brought out both day and night, no blessing is said; if only at night, a blessing is said.

items.text: Blessing over spices not intended for fragrance
items.text_en: Blessing over spices not intended for fragrance
items.desc_en: Rav Huna states that one does not bless over spices for the toilet or oil to remove filth. The Gemara challenges this with a baraita about a perfumer's shop, where one blesses repeatedly upon entering and exiting, even though the spices are not primarily for fragrance. The Gemara answers that they are indeed for fragrance, to attract customers.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that one does not recite a blessing over spices used for the toilet or oil made to remove filth, as they are not intended for fragrance.
The Gemara asks whether this implies that wherever something is not intended for fragrance, one does not recite a blessing over it.
The Gemara objects with a baraita about a perfumer's shop, where one recites a blessing each time upon entering and exiting, even though the spices are not primarily for fragrance.
The Gemara answers that in that case the spices are indeed intended for fragrance, to attract customers so they will come and buy.

items.text: Blessing over fragrance outside a city and in idolatrous contexts
items.text_en: Blessing over fragrance outside a city and in idolatrous contexts
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if one smells a fragrance outside a city, the blessing depends on the majority. Rabbi Yosei says even if the majority are Jews, one does not bless because Jewish women burn incense for sorcery. The Gemara questions this, concluding that a minority is for sorcery and another minority for finishing vessels, so the majority is not for fragrance. Rabbi Yochanan adds that in certain places at specific times, one does not bless because the fragrance is assumed to be for finishing vessels. A final baraita states that one who deliberately smells in an idolatrous market is a sinner.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that one who smells a fragrance outside a city recites a blessing if the majority are Jews, but not if the majority are gentiles.
רבי יוסי (Rabbi Yosei) argues that even with a Jewish majority one does not bless, because Jewish women burn incense for sorcery.
The Gemara questions whether all Jewish women burn incense for sorcery.
The Gemara answers that a minority is for sorcery and another minority for finishing vessels, so the majority is not for fragrance, and one does not bless.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: רבי חייא בר אבא (Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba) citing רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) adds that in Tiberias on Shabbat eve and Tzippori at Shabbat's conclusion, one does not bless because the fragrance is presumed to be for finishing vessels.
A final baraita states that one who deliberately smells incense in an idolatrous marketplace is a sinner.

items.text: Definition of 'ye'otu' for fire blessing
items.text_en: Definition of 'ye'otu' for fire blessing
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one does not recite a blessing over fire until 'ye'otu' (one benefits from its light). Rav Yehuda citing Rav clarifies that 'ye'otu' does not mean literal benefit, but rather that if one were standing close enough to use its light, even if actually far away. Rav Ashi confirms this interpretation.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one does not recite a blessing over fire until 'ye'otu' (one benefits from its light).
Rav Yehuda citing Rav clarifies that 'ye'otu' does not mean literal benefit, but rather that if one were standing close enough to use its light, even if actually far away.
Rav Ashi confirms this interpretation, stating that the Mishnah's ruling applies even at a distance.

items.text: Challenge and resolution regarding seeing and using the flame
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution regarding seeing and using the flame
items.desc_en: A baraita is brought as a challenge: one must both see the flame and use its light. The Gemara questions how one can see the flame without using its light, suggesting it must be far away. The answer is that the flame is flickering and moving, so one sees it but cannot use its light.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited as a challenge: one must both see the flame and use its light to recite the blessing.
The Gemara questions how one can see the flame without using its light, suggesting it must be far away.
The Gemara answers that the flame is flickering and moving, so one sees it but cannot use its light.

items.text: Blessing over coals and spelling of 'omemot'
items.text_en: Blessing over coals and spelling of 'omemot'
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one recites a blessing over glowing coals but not over dying embers. Rav Chisda defines glowing coals as those that ignite a splinter on their own. A question arises about the correct spelling of 'omemot' (dying embers), and Rav Chisda bar Avdimi cites a verse to support the spelling with an 'ayin.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one recites a blessing over glowing coals (גחלים לוחשות) but not over dying embers (אוממות).
The gemara asks what defines 'glowing coals' (לוחשות).
Rav Chisda defines glowing coals as those that ignite a splinter on their own.
A question arises about the correct spelling of the word for dying embers: 'אוממות' or 'עוממות'.
Rav Chisda bar Avdimi cites a verse (Ezekiel 31:8) using the spelling with an 'ayin (עממהו) to support that the correct spelling is 'עוממות'.

items.text: Literal interpretation of 'ye'otu' and its measure
items.text_en: Literal interpretation of 'ye'otu' and its measure
items.desc_en: Rava argues that 'ye'otu' means literal benefit. The Gemara then asks how much benefit is required. Ulla says enough to distinguish between an issar and a pundyon coin. Chizkiya says enough to distinguish between the coin of Tiberias and that of Tzippori.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that 'ye'otu' means literal benefit from the fire.
The Gemara asks how much benefit is required.
Ulla answers that the benefit must be enough to distinguish between an issar and a pundyon coin.
Chizkiya answers that the benefit must be enough to distinguish between the coin of Tiberias and that of Tzippori.

items.text: Practice of sages and not actively seeking fire
items.text_en: Practice of sages and not actively seeking fire
items.desc_en: The Gemara records that Rav Yehuda, Rava, and Abaye would recite the blessing over fire at specific places. Rav Yehuda citing Rav states that one should not actively seek out fire as one does for other mitzvot. Rabbi Zeira initially sought it but stopped after hearing this, only blessing if it comes his way.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara records that Rav Yehuda, Rava, and Abaye would recite the blessing over fire at specific places.
Rav Yehuda citing Rav states that one should not actively seek out fire as one does for other mitzvot.
Rabbi Zeira initially sought fire but stopped after hearing Rav's statement, only blessing if it comes his way.

items.text: Dispute about forgetting Grace after Meals: intentional vs. unintentional
items.text_en: Dispute about forgetting Grace after Meals: intentional vs. unintentional
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid (or Rav Dimi bar Abba) states that the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel about returning to one's place applies only when one forgot, but if intentional, all agree one must return. The Gemara questions this, noting the Mishnah says 'forgot', but the statement clarifies that the Mishnah's wording is to show Beit Shammai's stringency.

sub.text: Rav Zevid (or Rav Dimi bar Abba)
sub.text_en: Rav Zevid (or Rav Dimi bar Abba)
sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid (or Rav Dimi bar Abba) states that the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel applies only when one forgot, but if intentional, all agree one must return to one's place and bless.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah explicitly says 'forgot', so the ruling is obvious.

The Gemara explains that the statement was necessary to counter a possible assumption that the Mishnah's wording 'forgot' was only to highlight Beit Shammai's stringency, but the ruling applies even to intentional cases.

items.text: Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai's debate and a story
items.text_en: Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai's debate and a story
items.desc_en: A baraita records the debate: Beit Hillel argues that one who forgot Grace after Meals on a roof need not return, while Beit Shammai compares it to retrieving a lost purse. A story is told of two students: one acted like Beit Shammai unintentionally and found gold, the other acted like Beit Hillel intentionally and was eaten by a lion.

sub.desc_en: Beit Hillel challenges Beit Shammai: according to your logic, if one ate on a roof and forgot to bless, must he return to the roof to bless?
Beit Shammai responds: if one forgot a purse on a roof, he would return for it; for the honor of Heaven, all the more so should one return to bless.
A story is told: one student unintentionally acted like Beit Shammai and found gold, another intentionally acted like Beit Hillel and was eaten by a lion.

items.text: Rabba bar bar Chana's ruse to bless and the symbolism of the dove
items.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana's ruse to bless and the symbolism of the dove
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana, traveling with a caravan, forgot to recite Grace after Meals. To avoid embarrassment, he pretended to have lost a golden dove, went aside, blessed, and actually found a golden dove. The Gemara explains the dove symbolizes Israel, which is saved only through mitzvot.

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana, traveling with a caravan, forgot to recite Grace after Meals and pretended to have lost a golden dove to go aside and bless, then actually found one.
The Gemara explains the dove symbolizes Israel, which is saved only through mitzvot (מצות), citing the verse about the dove's wings.

items.text: Measure of digestion for Grace after Meals
items.text_en: Measure of digestion for Grace after Meals
items.desc_en: The Mishnah asks until when one can recite Grace after Meals. Rabbi Yochanan says as long as one is not hungry, Reish Lakish says as long as one is thirsty from the meal. A contradiction is raised from Reish Lakish's other statement that digestion takes the time to walk four mil. The resolution: one applies to a large meal, the other to a small meal.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah asks until when one may recite Grace after Meals.
Rabbi Yochanan says one may recite Grace as long as he is not hungry; Reish Lakish says as long as he is thirsty from the meal.

sub.text: Rav Yemar bar Shelemya to Mar Zutra
sub.text_en: Rav Yemar bar Shelemya to Mar Zutra
sub.desc_en: A contradiction is raised: Reish Lakish elsewhere said digestion takes the time to walk four mil, not the thirst-based measure.
The contradiction is resolved: one measure applies to a large meal, the other to a small meal.

items.text: One who did not eat with the group answering Amen
items.text_en: One who did not eat with the group answering Amen
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how one who did not hear the entire blessing can fulfill their obligation by answering Amen. Chiya bar Rav and Rav Nachman bar Abba explain this applies when one did not eat with them. Rav and Rav Huna instruct their sons to 'snatch and bless' (be the first to bless).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when wine is brought to the group during the meal, the one who recites the blessing over the wine is exempt from the blessing after the meal.
The Gemara questions how an Israelite who did not hear the entire blessing can fulfill his obligation by answering Amen.

sub.text: Chiya bar Rav and Rav Nachman bar Abba
sub.text_en: Chiya bar Rav and Rav Nachman bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Chiya bar Rav and Rav Nachman bar Abba explain that the Mishnah's ruling applies only when the Israelite did not eat with the group.
Rav and Rav Huna instruct their sons to 'snatch and bless' (be the first to recite the blessing), implying that the one who blesses is preferred over the one who answers Amen.

items.text: Who is greater: the one who blesses or the one who answers Amen?
items.text_en: Who is greater: the one who blesses or the one who answers Amen?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the one who blesses is greater than the one who answers Amen, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yosei says the one who answers Amen is greater. Rabbi Nehorai agrees, using a parable of soldiers and heroes. The Gemara concludes it is a dispute among Tannaim, with another baraita stating both are equal but the blesser is quicker.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the one who blesses is greater than the one who answers Amen, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yosei says the one who answers Amen is greater.
Rabbi Nehorai agrees with Rabbi Yosei, using a parable of soldiers and heroes to illustrate that the responder is greater.
The Gemara concludes it is a dispute among Tannaim, with another baraita stating both are equal but the blesser is quicker.

items.text: Answering Amen after schoolchildren
items.text_en: Answering Amen after schoolchildren
items.desc_en: Shmuel asks Rav whether one may answer Amen after the blessings of schoolchildren. Rav rules that one answers Amen after everyone except schoolchildren, since they recite for practice. However, if it is their time to be dismissed (and they recite seriously), one may answer.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel asks Rav whether one may answer Amen after the blessings of schoolchildren.
Rav rules that one answers Amen after everyone except schoolchildren, since they recite for practice.
The Gemara clarifies that if it is their time to be dismissed (and they recite seriously), one may answer Amen.

items.text: Oil as a requirement for the blessing after meals
items.text_en: Oil as a requirement for the blessing after meals
items.desc_en: A baraita records a dispute: Rabbi Zilai says oil is required for the blessing, Rabbi Zivai says it is not, Rabbi Acha says good oil is required, and Rabbi Zohamai compares soiled hands to disqualified priests. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says he does not know these names but knows a tradition that verses allude to the requirements: first water, last water, oil, and the blessing.

sub.desc_en: A baraita records four opinions: Rabbi Zilai says oil is required for the blessing, Rabbi Zivai says it is not, Rabbi Acha says good oil is required, and Rabbi Zohamai compares soiled hands to disqualified priests.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says he does not know these names but knows a tradition that verses allude to the requirements: first water, last water, oil, and the blessing.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Blessings for various sights and occasions
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Blessings for various sights and occasions
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists blessings recited upon seeing places where miracles occurred for Israel, places where idolatry was uprooted, natural phenomena (shooting stars, earthquakes, winds, lightning), mountains and seas, rains and good news, bad news, new possessions, and the rule to bless on bad as on good. It also discusses vain prayer and entering a city.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the blessings recited upon seeing a place where miracles were performed for Israel and a place from which idolatry was eradicated.

The Mishnah lists blessings for natural phenomena (zikin, earthquakes, thunder, winds, lightning) and for mountains, hills, seas, rivers, and deserts, with Rabbi Yehuda adding a special blessing for the great sea when seen intermittently.
The Mishnah states blessings for rain and good tidings, for bad tidings, for a new house or vessels, and the principle of blessing on bad as on good.

The Mishnah rules that crying out over the past is a vain prayer, giving examples of praying for a male child when the wife is already pregnant and praying that a scream heard in the city is not from one's own house.
The Mishnah concludes with the rule that one entering a city recites two prayers, while Ben Azzai says four, giving thanks for the past and crying out for the future.

items.text: Derivation of blessing on bad as on good
items.text_en: Derivation of blessing on bad as on good
items.desc_en: The Mishnah's rule to bless on bad as on good is derived from the verse 'And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart...' interpreted to mean with both inclinations, even if He takes your soul, and with all your money, and thanking Him for every measure.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the obligation to bless on bad as on good, citing the verse 'And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart...'
The Mishnah interprets 'with all your heart' as with both inclinations, the good and the evil.
The Mishnah interprets 'with all your soul' as even if God takes your soul.
The Mishnah interprets 'with all your might' as with all your money.
The Mishnah offers an alternative interpretation: 'with all your might' means with every measure He metes out to you, thank Him.

items.text: Laws of reverence for the Temple and greetings in God's name
items.text_en: Laws of reverence for the Temple and greetings in God's name
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches not to act frivolously opposite the Eastern Gate, not to enter the Temple Mount with staff, shoes, money belt, or dusty feet, and not to use it as a shortcut. It then discusses the change from 'until the world' to 'from the world until the world' due to heretics, and the enactment to greet others in God's name, citing Boaz and other verses.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah prohibits acting irreverently opposite the Eastern Gate and entering the Temple Mount with staff, shoes, money belt, or dusty feet, and forbids using it as a shortcut, with spitting derived via an a fortiori argument.

The Mishnah relates that all blessings in the Temple concluded with 'until the world,' but after heretics claimed there is only one world, the Sages instituted saying 'from the world until the world.'

The Mishnah records the enactment to greet others in God's name, citing verses about Boaz, the angel to Gideon, and the principle that it is time to work for God, with Rabbi Natan explaining the verse's meaning.

items.text: Gemara: Source for blessing on a miracle
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for blessing on a miracle
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the Mishnah's blessing on a place of miracles. Rabbi Yochanan answers from the verse where Jethro said 'Blessed is the Lord who delivered you...'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where are these matters (the obligation to bless on a miracle) derived?
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the verse states: 'And Jethro said: Blessed is the Lord who delivered you...' (Exodus 18:10), indicating that one blesses for a miracle.

items.text: Contradiction: Communal vs. individual miracles
items.text_en: Contradiction: Communal vs. individual miracles
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why only communal miracles require blessing, citing cases of individuals (a man saved from a lion, Mar bar Ravina saved from thirst and a camel) who were told to bless. The resolution: for a communal miracle everyone must bless; for an individual miracle, only the recipient is obligated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a blessing is recited only for a communal miracle and not for an individual miracle.
The Gemara cites the case of a man saved from a lion, to whom Rava instructed to recite a blessing upon returning to the site, proving that individual miracles also warrant a blessing.
The Gemara cites the case of Mar bar Ravina, who was saved from thirst by a miraculous spring, further demonstrating that individual miracles are blessed.
The Gemara cites another incident where Mar bar Ravina was saved from a wild camel, and he recited blessings at both locations, confirming that individual miracles are blessed.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: for a communal miracle everyone is obligated to bless, while for an individual miracle only the recipient is obligated.

items.text: Baraita: Additional sites requiring thanksgiving
items.text_en: Baraita: Additional sites requiring thanksgiving
items.desc_en: A baraita lists sites where one must give thanks: crossings of the Sea, Jordan, Arnon, hailstones at Beit Choron, Og's stone, Moses' stone, Lot's wife, and Jericho's wall. The Gemara provides scriptural sources for the Sea, Jordan, and Arnon, citing verses and a tradition about two lepers.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists sites of miracles (crossings of the Sea, Jordan, Arnon, etc.) and states that one must give thanks and praise upon seeing them.
The Gemara cites scriptural verses for the miracles at the Sea and the Jordan, showing they are explicitly recorded in the Torah.
The Gemara asks for the scriptural source for the miracle at the crossings of the Arnon, citing the verse from the Book of the Wars of the Lord.
The Tanna explains that the verse refers to two lepers who walked at the rear of Israel's camp, and when the Emorites came, a miracle occurred, as the narrative continues.

items.text: The miracle of the Aron at the Arnon River
items.text_en: The miracle of the Aron at the Arnon River
items.desc_en: The Gemara describes how the Aron miraculously caused mountains to merge, killing the Amorites who ambushed Israel, and how the blood flowing into the streams led to the song of 'Et Vahev'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara describes how the Amorites hid in caves, the Aron miraculously merged mountains to kill them, and the blood flowing into the Arnon streams led to the song of 'Et Vahev'.

items.text: The stones of 'Avnei Elgavish'
items.text_en: The stones of 'Avnei Elgavish'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the term 'Avnei Elgavish' as stones that stood for Moses and fell for Joshua, citing verses to support the interpretation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'avnei elgavish' (hailstones) refers to, and a baraita answers that they are stones that stood upon a man (Moses) and fell upon a man (Joshua), citing verses for each.
A Tanna explains that these are stones that stood for Moses and fell for Joshua, citing verses to support each identification.

items.text: The stone of Og, King of Bashan
items.text_en: The stone of Og, King of Bashan
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts how Og attempted to throw a mountain at Israel, but God caused it to collapse around his neck, and Moses killed him by jumping ten cubits and striking his ankle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts how Og, king of Bashan, planned to uproot a mountain and throw it at Israel, but God caused it to collapse around his neck.

sub.text: Gemara's narrative with Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish
sub.text_en: Gemara's narrative with Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish
sub.desc_en: The Gemara describes how Og could not remove the mountain and cites Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish's interpretation of the verse 'שיני רשעים שברת' (You broke the teeth of the wicked) as 'שרבבת' (You lengthened).
The Gemara concludes that Moses, who was ten cubits tall, took an axe of ten cubits, jumped ten cubits, and struck Og's ankle, killing him.

items.text: The stone Moses sat on and Lot's wife
items.text_en: The stone Moses sat on and Lot's wife
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists additional items for blessing: the stone Moses sat on, Lot's wife turned to salt, and the wall of Jericho that was swallowed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara lists three additional items for blessing: the stone Moses sat on, Lot's wife turned to salt, and the wall of Jericho that was swallowed, each supported by a biblical verse.

items.text: Blessing for Lot's wife and the resolution
items.text_en: Blessing for Lot's wife and the resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Lot's wife, a punishment, is included among miracles, and resolves that one says 'Dayyan HaEmet' for her and 'Zokher et HaTzaddikim' for Lot, citing Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Lot's wife, a punishment, is included among the miracles listed in the Mishnah.
The Gemara answers that one recites the blessing 'Dayyan HaEmet' (the True Judge) for her, which is a blessing of acceptance, not praise.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah lists the blessing as one of 'thanksgiving and praise', not a blessing of judgment.

A baraita is cited that resolves the objection: for Lot's wife one says 'Dayyan HaEmet', and for Lot one says 'Zokher et HaTzaddikim' (Who remembers the righteous), thus the Mishnah's 'thanksgiving and praise' refers to Lot's blessing.
Rabbi Yochanan adds a prooftext that even in God's anger, He remembers the righteous, citing the verse about Lot's rescue.

items.text: The wall of Jericho: swallowed, not fallen
items.text_en: The wall of Jericho: swallowed, not fallen
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the wall of Jericho was swallowed into the ground because its width and height were equal, reconciling the verse that says it fell.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the wall of Jericho fell, not was swallowed, as the verse says 'and the wall fell under it'.
The Gemara resolves that since the wall's width and height were equal, it was swallowed into the ground rather than falling outward.

items.text: Four who must give thanks
items.text_en: Four who must give thanks
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav lists four categories: those who crossed the sea, traveled the desert, recovered from illness, and were released from prison, each supported by verses from Psalms.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav lists four categories of people who must give thanks: seafarers, desert travelers, the recovered ill, and released prisoners.
The Gemara asks for the scriptural source for seafarers and cites multiple verses from Psalms 107.
The Gemara asks for the source for desert travelers and cites verses from Psalms 107.
The Gemara asks for the source for the recovered ill and cites verses from Psalms 107.
The Gemara asks for the source for released prisoners and cites verses from Psalms 107.

items.text: The blessing and requirement of ten
items.text_en: The blessing and requirement of ten
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states the blessing 'Baruch Gomel Chasadim Tovim', Abaye requires it before ten, Mar Zutra adds two Torah scholars, and Rav Ashi questions the proof, leaving the matter unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what blessing one recites when giving thanks for deliverance.
Rav Yehuda states the blessing: 'Baruch Gomel Chasadim Tovim' (Blessed is He who bestows acts of loving-kindness).
Abaye adds that one must offer thanks before ten people, citing the verse 'Let them exalt Him in the congregation of the people'.
Mar Zutra adds that two of the ten must be Torah scholars, citing the verse 'and praise Him in the assembly of elders'.
Rav Ashi objects: perhaps all ten must be Torah scholars, but the Gemara rejects this because the verse says 'congregation of the people', not 'congregation of elders'.
The Gemara raises a further objection: perhaps the requirement is ten ordinary people plus two Torah scholars, but this remains unresolved.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's recovery and the blessing
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's recovery and the blessing
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda recovers from illness, and visitors bless him; he says they exempted him from blessing, but the Gemara explains that since ten were present and he answered 'Amen', it sufficed.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda falls ill and recovers; Rav Chana Bagdata'ah and the rabbis visit and bless him, and he says they exempted him from blessing.
The Gemara objects: Abaye said one must bless before ten, but Rav Yehuda himself did not bless.
The Gemara resolves: ten were present, and Rav Yehuda answered 'Amen' after their blessing, so he was exempted.

items.text: Three who need protection
items.text_en: Three who need protection
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda lists three who need protection: a sick person, a groom, and a bride; a baraita adds a woman in childbirth, and some say a mourner or Torah scholars at night.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that three require protection: a sick person, a groom, and a bride.
A baraita adds a woman in childbirth to the list, and some add a mourner, and some add Torah scholars at night.
Some say a mourner (אבל) also needs protection.
Some say Torah scholars at night (תלמידי חכמים בלילה) also need protection.

items.text: Three things that prolong life
items.text_en: Three things that prolong life
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that lengthening prayer, mealtime, and bathroom time prolongs life, but the Gemara questions whether long prayer is praiseworthy, citing Rabbi Yochanan's objection.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that three things—lengthening one's prayer, mealtime, and bathroom time—prolong a person's life.
The Gemara questions whether lengthening one's prayer is indeed praiseworthy, given a potential objection.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's objection (via Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's objection (via Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Yochanan's teaching that contrasts with Rav Yehuda's praise of long prayer.

items.text: Prolonging prayer and its consequences
items.text_en: Prolonging prayer and its consequences
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a statement that one who prolongs prayer and focuses on it will eventually suffer heartache. It then cites Rabbi Yitzchak's list of three things that remind a person of their sins: a leaning wall, focusing on prayer, and handing over a friend's judgment to Heaven. The Gemara resolves a contradiction by distinguishing between focusing on prayer (which is bad) and merely prolonging it without focus (which is good, as it increases supplication).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a statement that one who prolongs prayer and focuses on it will eventually suffer heartache, citing a verse, and then adds Rabbi Yitzchak's list of three things that remind a person of their sins: a leaning wall, focusing on prayer, and handing over a friend's judgment to Heaven.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between focusing on prayer (which is bad) and merely prolonging it without focus (which is good, as it increases supplication).

items.text: Prolonging at the table
items.text_en: Prolonging at the table
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that prolonging at the table is praiseworthy because a poor person might come and receive food. It supports this by citing verses that equate the altar with the table, and Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar state that while the Temple stood, the altar atoned, but now a person's table atones for them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that prolonging at the table is praiseworthy because a poor person might come and receive food.
The Gemara cites verses that equate the altar with the table, showing a connection between the two.
Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar state that while the Temple stood, the altar atoned, but now a person's table atones for them.

items.text: Prolonging in the bathroom
items.text_en: Prolonging in the bathroom
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether prolonging in the bathroom is praiseworthy, citing a baraita listing ten things that bring a person to hemorrhoids, including lingering too long. It resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between one who lingers and strains (bad) and one who lingers without straining (good).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether prolonging in the bathroom is praiseworthy.
A baraita is cited listing ten things that bring a person to hemorrhoids, including lingering too long.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between one who lingers and strains (bad) and one who lingers without straining (good).

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's bathroom habit
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's bathroom habit
items.desc_en: A matron comments to Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai that his face looks like that of pig breeders or usurers. He responds that both are forbidden to him, but he visits twenty-four bathrooms between his lodging and the study hall, checking himself in all of them.

sub.desc_en: A matron tells Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai that his face resembles that of pig breeders or usurers.
Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai responds that both are forbidden to him, but he visits twenty-four bathrooms between his lodging and the study hall, checking himself in all of them.

items.text: Three things that shorten life
items.text_en: Three things that shorten life
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states three things that shorten a person's days and years: one who is given a Torah scroll to read and does not read, one who is given a cup of blessing to bless and does not bless, and one who conducts himself with authority. Each is supported by a verse, and Rabbi Chama bar Chanina explains that Joseph died before his brothers because he conducted himself with authority.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda lists three things that shorten a person's days and years: being given a Torah scroll to read and not reading, being given a cup of blessing to bless and not blessing, and conducting oneself with authority.
The Gemara supports the first two items with verses: the Torah is life and length of days, and God blesses those who bless Him.
Rabbi Chama bar Chanina explains that Joseph died before his brothers because he conducted himself with authority.

items.text: Three things needing mercy
items.text_en: Three things needing mercy
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that three things require mercy: a good king, a good year, and a good dream. Each is supported by a verse.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that three things require mercy: a good king, a good year, and a good dream, each supported by a verse.

items.text: Three things God Himself proclaims
items.text_en: Three things God Himself proclaims
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states three things that the Holy One, Blessed be He, Himself proclaims: famine, plenty, and a good leader. Rabbi Yitzchak adds that a leader is only appointed after consulting the community, as demonstrated by the appointment of Bezalel.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that God Himself proclaims three things: famine, plenty, and a good leader, citing verses for each.
Rabbi Yitzchak adds that a leader is only appointed after consulting the community, as demonstrated by the appointment of Bezalel.

items.text: Bezalel's wisdom and name
items.text_en: Bezalel's wisdom and name
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan explains that Bezalel was named for his wisdom. When Moses told him to make the Ark, vessels, and Tabernacle, Bezalel corrected the order, showing he knew that the Tabernacle should be built first. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav adds that Bezalel knew how to combine the letters with which heaven and earth were created.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan explains that Bezalel was named for his wisdom, recounting how Bezalel corrected Moses' order of construction, leading Moses to recognize his divine insight.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav adds that Bezalel knew how to combine the letters with which heaven and earth were created, citing verses linking חכמה (wisdom), תבונה (understanding), and דעת (knowledge) to creation.

items.text: Wisdom given to the wise
items.text_en: Wisdom given to the wise
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that God only gives wisdom to one who already has wisdom, citing a verse. Rav Tachlifa bar Ma'arva heard this and said it before Rabbi Avahu, who noted that they learn it from a different verse.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that God only gives wisdom to one who already has wisdom, citing the verse 'יָהֵב חׇכְמְתָא לְחַכִּימִין' (He gives wisdom to the wise).
Rav Tachlifa bar Ma'arva heard this teaching and repeated it before Rabbi Avahu.
Rabbi Avahu responds that they learn the same principle from a different verse: 'וּבְלֵב כׇּל חֲכַם לֵב נָתַתִּי חׇכְמָה' (And in the heart of every wise-hearted I have given wisdom).

items.text: Teachings about dreams
items.text_en: Teachings about dreams
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda makes several statements about dreams: every dream has some nonsense; an uninterpreted dream is like an unread letter; no dream is entirely fulfilled; a bad dream is better than a good one; the sadness of a bad dream suffices, and the joy of a good dream suffices. Rav Yosef adds that even for him, the joy of a good dream mitigates it. Rav Chisda says a bad dream is worse than flogging. Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai compares dreams to straw without grain. Rabbi Berechya notes that a dream is never entirely fulfilled, as seen with Joseph.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda opens with the principle that every dream contains some nonsense (לא טוות).
Rav Chisda compares an uninterpreted dream to an unread letter.
Rav Chisda states that no dream, good or bad, is entirely fulfilled.
Rav Chisda asserts that a bad dream is preferable to a good one.
Rav Chisda teaches that the sadness of a bad dream suffices as its fulfillment, and the joy of a good dream suffices as its fulfillment.
Rav Yosef adds that even for him, the joy of a good dream mitigates its potential harm.
Rav Chisda declares that a bad dream is worse than flogging, citing a verse and a tradition from Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan, citing Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, compares dreams to straw without grain, explaining that just as grain cannot exist without straw, a dream cannot exist without meaningless elements.
Rabbi Berechya concludes that a dream is never entirely fulfilled, as demonstrated by Joseph's dream where only part was realized.

items.text: The duration for which a good dream can be fulfilled
items.text_en: The duration for which a good dream can be fulfilled
items.desc_en: Rabbi Levi teaches that one should hope for the fulfillment of a good dream for up to twenty-two years, derived from Joseph's dreams. The calculation is based on the verses about Joseph's age at the time of his dreams and when he stood before Pharaoh.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that at that time, Joseph's mother was not alive, implying a question about the duration for dream fulfillment.
Rabbi Levi teaches that one should hope for a good dream's fulfillment up to twenty-two years, deriving this from Joseph's age at his dreams and when he stood before Pharaoh.

items.text: Good people see bad dreams and vice versa
items.text_en: Good people see bad dreams and vice versa
items.desc_en: Rav Huna states that a good person is not shown a good dream, and a bad person is not shown a bad dream. A baraita supports this with David and Achitophel. The Gemara reconciles this with a verse about protection from evil, explaining that the person himself does not see it, but others see it for him.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states that a good person is not shown a good dream, and a bad person is not shown a bad dream.
A baraita supports Rav Huna: David never saw a good dream, and Achitophel never saw a bad dream.
The Gemara objects with a verse promising protection from evil, and cites Rav Chisda's interpretation that it means bad dreams and bad thoughts will not frighten him.
The Gemara resolves: the person himself does not see the bad dream, but others see it for him.

items.text: The value of seeing a dream even if unknown
items.text_en: The value of seeing a dream even if unknown
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether not seeing a dream is praiseworthy, citing Rabbi Zeira that one who goes seven days without a dream is called 'bad'. The Gemara resolves that the earlier statement refers to one who sees a dream but does not know what he saw.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that not seeing a dream is not praiseworthy, citing Rabbi Zeira that one who goes seven days without a dream is called 'bad'.
The Gemara resolves that the good person does see a dream but does not know what he saw.
The Gemara resolves that the earlier statement refers to one who sees a dream but does not know what he saw.

items.text: Improving a bad dream before three people
items.text_en: Improving a bad dream before three people
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Ammi quotes Rabbi Yochanan that one whose soul is troubled by a dream should improve it before three people. The Gemara clarifies that it is not about interpretation but about having three people say specific verses of reversal, redemption, and peace. The verses for each category are listed.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Ammi quoting Rabbi Pedat quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Ammi quoting Rabbi Pedat quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Ammi quotes Rabbi Yochanan that one who sees a troubling dream should have it interpreted before three people.
The Gemara objects: 'Interpret it'? But Rav Chisda said an uninterpreted dream is like an unread letter, implying interpretation brings fulfillment.
The Gemara corrects: Rather say 'improve it' before three people, and the three should recite verses of transformation, redemption, and peace verses.
The Gemara lists the three transformation verses: 'You turned my mourning into dancing... and God turned the curse into a blessing.
The Gemara lists the three redemption verses: 'He redeemed my soul in peace... and the people rescued Jonathan.
The Gemara lists the three peace verses: 'Peace, peace to the far and near... and you shall say: peace to you and your house.'

items.text: Prayer for an unknown dream
items.text_en: Prayer for an unknown dream
items.desc_en: Amemar, Mar Zutra, and Rav Ashi each share a teaching. The first teaches that one who sees a dream and does not know what it is should stand before the priests during the Priestly Blessing and recite a specific prayer asking for the dream to be good or healed, concluding with the congregation's 'Amen'.

sub.desc_en: Amemar, Mar Zutra, and Rav Ashi sit together and agree that each will say something the others have not heard.

sub.text: First speaker (Amemar or Mar Zutra or Rav Ashi)
sub.text_en: First speaker (Amemar or Mar Zutra or Rav Ashi)
sub.desc_en: One of them begins and teaches the law for one who sees a dream and does not know what it is.

sub.text: First speaker (Amemar or Mar Zutra or Rav Ashi)
sub.text_en: First speaker (Amemar or Mar Zutra or Rav Ashi)
sub.desc_en: He prescribes standing before the priests during the Priestly Blessing and reciting a detailed prayer asking for good dreams to be strengthened and bad dreams to be healed, citing biblical precedents.

sub.text: First speaker (Amemar or Mar Zutra or Rav Ashi)
sub.text_en: First speaker (Amemar or Mar Zutra or Rav Ashi)
sub.desc_en: He instructs to conclude with the congregation's 'Amen' and provides a shorter alternative prayer for peace if one cannot recite the full formula.

items.text: Protection from the evil eye when entering a city
items.text_en: Protection from the evil eye when entering a city
items.desc_en: The second teaching is about one who enters a city and fears the evil eye. He should hold his right thumb in his left hand and his left thumb in his right hand and recite that he is from the seed of Joseph, over whom the evil eye has no power, citing verses. Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina adds a proof from the fish.

sub.text: Second sage (Amemar, Mar Zutra, or Rav Ashi)
sub.text_en: Second sage (Amemar, Mar Zutra, or Rav Ashi)
sub.desc_en: The second sage teaches a remedy for one who fears the evil eye when entering a city, involving grasping the thumb and reciting a verse about Joseph, and if fearing his own evil eye, looking at his left nostril.

Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina adds a proof from the verse 'וידגו לרוב בקרב הארץ' (and may they multiply like fish in the midst of the earth), comparing Joseph's descendants to fish that are covered by water and thus immune to the evil eye.

sub.text: Amemar, Mar Zutra, or Rav Ashi (the second speaker, continuation)
sub.text_en: Amemar, Mar Zutra, or Rav Ashi (the second speaker, continuation)
sub.desc_en: The sage adds that if one fears his own evil eye, he should look at the side of his left nostril.

items.text: When to reveal illness
items.text_en: When to reveal illness
items.desc_en: The third teaching is about one who is ill: on the first day he should not reveal it so as not to harm his fortune, but afterwards he may. Rava would announce his illness after the first day so that those who love him would pray and those who hate him would rejoice, citing a verse.

sub.text: Third sage (Amemar, Mar Zutra, or Rav Ashi)
sub.text_en: Third sage (Amemar, Mar Zutra, or Rav Ashi)
sub.desc_en: The third sage teaches that one who is ill should not reveal it on the first day to avoid harming his מזל (fortune), citing Rava's practice of announcing after the first day to gain prayers from friends and avoid joy from enemies.
The gemara cites Rava's practice: on the first day he would not reveal his illness, but afterward he would tell his attendant to announce it so that friends would pray and enemies would rejoice.
The gemara supports Rava's reasoning with a verse: when your enemy falls, do not rejoice, lest God see and turn His anger from him to you.

items.text: Dreams from angels vs. demons
items.text_en: Dreams from angels vs. demons
items.desc_en: Shmuel would say that vain dreams speak falsely for bad dreams, but for good dreams he would question that, citing a verse. Rava resolves the contradiction: dreams through an angel are true, but through a demon they are false.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel would cite a verse dismissing bad dreams as vain, but for good dreams he would question that by citing a contradictory verse.
Rava resolves the contradiction: dreams through an angel are true, but through a demon they are false.

items.text: Dreams follow the mouth
items.text_en: Dreams follow the mouth
items.desc_en: Rabbi Bizna bar Zavda quotes a chain of tradition that there were twenty-four dream interpreters in Jerusalem, and all their interpretations were fulfilled, confirming that all dreams follow the mouth. The Gemara questions if this is a verse, and Rabbi Elazar proves it from the verse about Joseph's interpretation. Rava adds that the interpretation must be appropriate to the dream.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Bizna bar Zavda transmits a tradition that all twenty-four dream interpreters in Jerusalem gave different interpretations, yet all were fulfilled, proving that dreams follow the mouth.
The Gemara questions whether the phrase 'all dreams follow the mouth' is actually a verse.
The Gemara answers that it is indeed a verse, as Rabbi Elazar derives it from the story of Joseph.
Rabbi Elazar proves from the verse 'as he interpreted for us, so it was' that dreams follow the interpretation.
Rava adds that the interpretation must be appropriate to the dream, as the verse says 'each man according to his dream he interpreted.'

items.text: How the baker knew Joseph's dream
items.text_en: How the baker knew Joseph's dream
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains that the verse 'And the chief baker saw' teaches that each was shown his own dream and the interpretation of his friend's dream.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the baker knew that Joseph's interpretation was correct.
Rabbi Elazar answers that each was shown his own dream and the interpretation of his fellow's dream.

items.text: Minor prophecy and dreams that are fulfilled
items.text_en: Minor prophecy and dreams that are fulfilled
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says that if a verse falls into one's mouth upon waking, it is a minor prophecy. He also lists three dreams that are fulfilled: a morning dream, a dream dreamt by another about him, and a dream interpreted within a dream. Some add a repeated dream.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that if one wakes up and a verse falls into his mouth, it is a minor prophecy (נבואה קטנה).
Rabbi Yochanan lists three dreams that are fulfilled: a morning dream, a dream dreamt by another about him, and a dream interpreted within a dream.
Some add that a repeated dream is also fulfilled, citing the verse 'וְעַל הִשָּׁנוֹת הַחֲלוֹם' (and concerning the repetition of the dream).

items.text: Dreams reflect one's thoughts
items.text_en: Dreams reflect one's thoughts
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quotes Rabbi Yonatan that a person is only shown dreams from the thoughts of his heart, citing verses. Rava adds that one is not shown a golden palm tree or an elephant going through the eye of a needle.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quoting Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quoting Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yonatan teaches that a person is only shown dreams from his own thoughts, and Rava adds that one is not shown a golden palm tree or an elephant going through the eye of a needle.
Rava adds a supporting proof that a person is not shown a golden palm tree or an elephant going through the eye of a needle, demonstrating that dreams reflect only plausible thoughts.

items.text: Opening stories: Caesar and Shapur ask for dream interpretations
items.text_en: Opening stories: Caesar and Shapur ask for dream interpretations
items.desc_en: Caesar asks Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya what he will see in his dream, and Rabbi Yehoshua interprets it as a negative omen. Similarly, King Shapur asks Shmuel for a dream interpretation, and Shmuel gives a negative interpretation. Both interpretations come true.

sub.desc_en: Caesar asks Rabbi Yehoshua to tell him what he will see in his dream; Rabbi Yehoshua predicts the Persians will enslave him, and the dream comes true.
King Shapur asks Shmuel to tell him what he will see in his dream; Shmuel predicts the Romans will capture him and force him to grind date pits, and the dream comes true.

items.text: Introduction of Bar Hedya and the dreams of Abaye and Rava
items.text_en: Introduction of Bar Hedya and the dreams of Abaye and Rava
items.desc_en: Bar Hedya is introduced as a dream interpreter who interprets favorably for those who pay him and unfavorably for those who do not. Abaye and Rava have dreams; Abaye pays him, Rava does not. They tell him they dreamed of a verse about one's ox being slaughtered, and he interprets it oppositely for each.

sub.desc_en: Introduces Bar Hedya as a dream interpreter who interprets favorably for those who pay him and unfavorably for those who do not.
Relates that Abaye and Rava both had a dream; Abaye paid Bar Hedya a zuz, but Rava did not.
They tell Bar Hedya that they dreamed the verse 'Your ox shall be slain before your eyes' (Deuteronomy 28:31) was read to them.
To Rava, he interprets the dream as his business will be lost and he will not eat due to sadness.
To Abaye, he interprets the dream as his business will profit and he will not eat due to joy.

items.text: Interpretations of dreams about children
items.text_en: Interpretations of dreams about children
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava tell Bar Hedya they dreamed of verses about bearing children and children being given to another nation. Bar Hedya interprets each verse favorably for Abaye and unfavorably for Rava, with Rava's interpretation including a teaching from Rav about a wife of the father.

sub.desc_en: Abaye and Rava report to Bar Hedya that they dreamed the verse 'בָּנִים וּבָנוֹת תּוֹלִיד' (You shall beget sons and daughters).
Abaye and Rava report that they dreamed the verse 'בָּנֶיךָ וּבְנֹתֶיךָ נְתֻנִים לְעַם אַחֵר' (Your sons and daughters shall be given unto another people).
Bar Hedya interprets the verse favorably for Abaye: his children will be numerous, and his wife will insist they marry her relatives, which is like another nation.
Bar Hedya interprets the verse unfavorably for Rava: his wife will die and his children will come under another woman's care.
Rava cites a tradition from Rav that the verse 'בָּנֶיךָ וּבְנֹתֶיךָ נְתֻנִים לְעַם אַחֵר' refers to the father's wife, the stepmother.

items.text: Interpretation of the dream about eating in joy
items.text_en: Interpretation of the dream about eating in joy
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava dream of the verse 'Go eat your bread in joy'. Bar Hedya interprets it favorably for Abaye (success and joy) and unfavorably for Rava (loss and fear).

sub.desc_en: Abaye and Rava report that they dreamed the verse 'Go eat your bread with joy'.
Bar Hedya interprets the dream favorably for Abaye: his business will profit and he will eat and drink with joy.
Bar Hedya interprets the same dream unfavorably for Rava: his business will be lost, and he will eat and drink only to allay his fears.

items.text: Interpretations of dreams about agricultural produce and honor
items.text_en: Interpretations of dreams about agricultural produce and honor
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava dream of verses about abundant seed, olives, and universal recognition. Bar Hedya interprets each verse's beginning favorably for Abaye and its end unfavorably for Rava. For the verse about recognition, he interprets it as Abaye becoming head of the academy and Rava being arrested, which later comes true.

sub.desc_en: They report dreaming of the verse about carrying much seed out to the field; Bar Hedya interprets the beginning for Abaye and the end for Rava.
They report dreaming of the verse about olive trees throughout the borders; again Bar Hedya interprets the beginning for Abaye and the end for Rava.

For the verse about all peoples seeing the name of the Lord, Bar Hedya tells Abaye he will become head of the academy, and tells Rava he will be arrested for theft; the next day Rava is indeed apprehended.

items.text: Series of dream interpretations about various objects
items.text_en: Series of dream interpretations about various objects
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava report dreams about lettuce, meat, a barrel, a pomegranate, a barrel falling into a well, and a donkey. Bar Hedya interprets each favorably for Abaye and unfavorably for Rava, with the last dream about a donkey leading to a discussion about Rava's tefillin.

sub.desc_en: Abaye and Rava report their dream of lettuce on the mouth of barrels.
Bar Hedya interprets the lettuce dream favorably for Abaye: his business will double like lettuce.
Bar Hedya interprets the same dream unfavorably for Rava: his work will be bitter like a lettuce stalk.
Abaye and Rava report their dream of meat on the mouth of barrels.
Bar Hedya interprets the meat dream favorably for Abaye: his wine will be sweet and everyone will buy from him.
Bar Hedya interprets the same dream unfavorably for Rava: his wine will spoil and people will buy meat to eat with it.
Abaye and Rava report their dream of a barrel hanging from a palm tree.
Bar Hedya interprets the barrel dream favorably for Abaye: his business will rise like a palm tree.
Bar Hedya interprets the same dream unfavorably for Rava: his work will be sweet like dates, indicating cheap prices.
Abaye and Rava report their dream of a pomegranate taking root on the mouth of barrels.
Bar Hedya interprets the pomegranate dream favorably for Abaye: his business will increase in value like a pomegranate.
Bar Hedya interprets the same dream unfavorably for Rava: his work will go sour like a pomegranate.
Abaye and Rava report their dream of a barrel falling into a pit.
Bar Hedya interprets the barrel-in-pit dream favorably for Abaye: his merchandise will be in demand, citing the adage about bread falling into a pit.
Bar Hedya interprets the same dream unfavorably for Rava: his merchandise will be ruined and thrown into a pit.
Abaye and Rava report their dream of a donkey foal standing near their heads and braying.
Bar Hedya interprets the donkey dream favorably for Abaye: he will become head of the yeshiva with an interpreter standing before him.
Bar Hedya interprets the same dream unfavorably for Rava: the words 'peter chamor' are erased from his tefillin.
Rava objects that he saw the words in his tefillin and they are present.
Bar Hedya insists that the letter vav of 'peter chamor' is certainly erased from Rava's tefillin.

items.text: Rava goes to Bar Hedya alone and receives negative interpretations
items.text_en: Rava goes to Bar Hedya alone and receives negative interpretations
items.desc_en: Rava goes to Bar Hedya alone and reports dreams of a door falling, teeth falling, two doves, and two turnip heads. Bar Hedya interprets each as a calamity: Rava's wife dies, his children die, he divorces two wives, and he receives two blows. These come true when Rava is hit by two blind men.

sub.desc_en: Rava goes alone to Bar Hedya and reports his first dream: the outer door fell.
Bar Hedya interprets the falling door as meaning Rava's wife will die.
Rava reports his second dream: his front and back teeth fell out.
Bar Hedya interprets the falling teeth as meaning Rava's sons and daughters will die.
Rava reports his third dream: two doves were flying.
Bar Hedya interprets the two doves as meaning Rava will divorce two wives.
Rava reports his fourth dream: two turnip heads.
Bar Hedya interprets the two turnip heads as meaning Rava will receive two blows with a club.

The narrative confirms the interpretation: Rava sits in the study hall all day, encounters two blind men fighting, and is struck twice; when they raise their staffs again, he says 'enough, I saw two'.

items.text: Rava pays Bar Hedya and receives favorable interpretations, then curses him
items.text_en: Rava pays Bar Hedya and receives favorable interpretations, then curses him
items.desc_en: Rava eventually pays Bar Hedya, who then interprets his dreams favorably: a wall falling means acquiring property, Abaye's palace falling means Abaye dies and Rava inherits his position, etc. Rava finds a book stating 'All dreams follow the mouth' and curses Bar Hedya for causing him suffering.

sub.desc_en: Rava finally pays Bar Hedya, who interprets his dream of a falling wall as acquiring property without boundaries.
Bar Hedya interprets Rava's dream of Abaye's palace falling as Abaye's death and Rava inheriting his yeshiva.
Bar Hedya interprets Rava's dream of his own palace falling as his teachings being disseminated worldwide.
Bar Hedya interprets Rava's dream of his head splitting as a feather falling from his pillow.
Bar Hedya interprets Rava's dream of reading the Egyptian Hallel as miracles being performed for him.
Bar Hedya travels with Rava on a ship, and a book falls from him.
Rava finds the book stating 'All dreams follow the mouth' and curses Bar Hedya for causing him suffering.
Rava forgives Bar Hedya for everything except the prediction about his wife, and prays that Bar Hedya be delivered to a merciless kingdom.

items.text: Bar Hedya's exile and downfall
items.text_en: Bar Hedya's exile and downfall
items.desc_en: Bar Hedya, fearing Rava's curse, exiles himself to Rome. He interprets dreams for the king's chief executioner but withholds the interpretation until paid, leading to the executioner's death. The king's men discover Bar Hedya's role and execute him.

sub.desc_en: Bar Hedya reflects on the curse of a Sage, concluding that exile atones for transgression, and decides to exile himself.
Bar Hedya goes into exile to Rome and sits at the entrance of the king's chief executioner, who then has a dream.
The chief executioner tells Bar Hedya his dream about a needle piercing his finger, but refuses to pay the fee.
Bar Hedya withholds the interpretation because he was not paid, and the executioner has a second dream about a worm between his fingers.
After the third dream about a worm on the whole hand, Bar Hedya finally interprets that the worm will destroy all the silk garments, leading to the executioner's death.
The king's men hear of the interpretation, execute the chief executioner, and then bring Bar Hedya to justice for his role in the ruin.

items.text: Opening anecdote: execution of the king's guards
items.text_en: Opening anecdote: execution of the king's guards
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates a story about the execution of the king's guards, describing how they were tied to two cedar trees and split apart. This serves as an introduction to the dream interpretations that follow.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates the execution of the king's guards, describing how they were tied to two cedar trees and split apart, serving as an introduction to the dream interpretations that follow.

items.text: Ben Dama's dream of two cheeks falling
items.text_en: Ben Dama's dream of two cheeks falling
items.desc_en: Ben Dama, Rabbi Yishmael's nephew, asks about a dream where his two cheeks fell. Rabbi Yishmael interprets this as two Roman legions plotting evil against him, and they died.

sub.desc_en: Ben Dama asks Rabbi Yishmael about his dream of his two cheeks falling off.
Rabbi Yishmael interprets the dream as two Roman legions plotting evil against Ben Dama, and they died.

items.text: Bar Kappara's dreams and Rabbi's interpretations
items.text_en: Bar Kappara's dreams and Rabbi's interpretations
items.desc_en: Bar Kappara asks Rabbi about several dreams: a nose falling off, hands cut off, feet cut off, and being told he will die in Adar and not see Nisan. Rabbi interprets each one positively.

sub.desc_en: Bar Kappara asks Rabbi about his dream of his nose falling off and his hands being cut off.
Rabbi interprets the nose dream as removal of anger and the hands dream as not needing manual labor.
Bar Kappara asks about his dream of legs cut off and the prophecy of dying in Adar.
Rabbi interprets the legs dream as riding a horse and the Adar prophecy as dying in glory without temptation.

items.text: A heretic's dreams and Rabbi Yishmael's interpretations
items.text_en: A heretic's dreams and Rabbi Yishmael's interpretations
items.desc_en: A heretic asks Rabbi Yishmael about a series of dreams: pouring oil on olives, plucking a star, swallowing a star, eyes kissing each other, kissing the moon, stepping on a bundle of myrtle, a bundle above and below, crows around his bed, doves around his bed, and holding two doves that fly away. Rabbi Yishmael interprets each as a sin. The heretic admits to all but one, and then a woman arrives confirming the last sin.

sub.desc_en: The heretic asks Rabbi Yishmael about his dream of watering olives with oil; Rabbi Yishmael interprets it as having relations with his mother.
Rabbi Yishmael interprets the dream of watering olives with oil as a sign that the heretic had relations with his mother.
The heretic asks about his dream of plucking a star; Rabbi Yishmael interprets it as kidnapping an Israelite.
Rabbi Yishmael interprets the dream of plucking a star as a sign that the heretic kidnapped an Israelite.
The heretic asks about his dream of swallowing a star; Rabbi Yishmael interprets it as selling the Israelite and spending the money.
Rabbi Yishmael interprets the dream of swallowing a star as a sign that the heretic sold the Israelite and used the proceeds.
The heretic asks about his dream of his eyes kissing each other; Rabbi Yishmael interprets it as having relations with his sister.
Rabbi Yishmael interprets the dream of eyes kissing as a sign of incest with his sister.
The heretic asks about his dream of kissing the moon; Rabbi Yishmael interprets it as sleeping with an Israelite woman.
Rabbi Yishmael interprets the dream of kissing the moon as a sign of sleeping with an Israelite woman.
The heretic asks about his dream of treading on a bundle of myrtle; Rabbi Yishmael interprets it as sleeping with a betrothed young woman.
Rabbi Yishmael interprets the dream of treading on myrtle as a sign of sleeping with a betrothed young woman.
The heretic asks about his dream of the bundle above and himself below; Rabbi Yishmael interprets it as his bed being upside-down.
Rabbi Yishmael interprets the dream of the bundle above as a sign that his bed is upside-down, indicating unnatural relations.
The heretic asks about his dream of crows circling his bed; Rabbi Yishmael interprets it as his wife committing adultery with many men.
Rabbi Yishmael interprets the dream of crows as a sign that his wife committed adultery with many men.
The heretic asks about his dream of doves circling his bed; Rabbi Yishmael interprets it as his having defiled many women.
Rabbi Yishmael interprets the dream of doves as a sign that the heretic defiled many women.
The heretic asks about his dream of holding two doves that flew away; Rabbi Yishmael interprets it as marrying two women and dismissing them without a get.
Rabbi Yishmael interprets the dream of two doves flying as a sign that the heretic married two women and divorced them without a get.
The heretic asks about his dream of peeling eggs; Rabbi Yishmael interprets it as stripping the dead.
Rabbi Yishmael interprets the dream of peeling eggs as a sign that the heretic stripped the dead.
The heretic admits that all interpretations are true except the last one about peeling eggs.
A woman arrives and confirms that the cloak the heretic is wearing belonged to a dead man he stripped, proving the last interpretation true.

items.text: Dream of inheritance in Kapodkya
items.text_en: Dream of inheritance in Kapodkya
items.desc_en: A man dreams he is told his father left him property in Kapodkya. Rabbi Yishmael deduces that it refers to a jar (קפא) at the head of ten (עשרה), which turns out to be a jar full of coins.

sub.desc_en: The man reports his dream that his father left him property in Kapodkya.
Rabbi Yishmael asks if the man has property in Kapodkya, and the man answers no.
Rabbi Yishmael asks if his father went to Kapodkya, and the man answers no.
Rabbi Yishmael interprets the dream as referring to a jar (קפא) at the head of ten (עשרה), and instructs him to look for it.
The man goes and finds the jar full of coins, confirming the interpretation.

items.text: Interpretations of seeing a well in a dream
items.text_en: Interpretations of seeing a well in a dream
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina, Rabbi Natan, and Rava offer different interpretations of seeing a well in a dream: peace, finding Torah, or actual life.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina interprets seeing a well in a dream as seeing peace, citing the verse about Isaac's servants finding a well of living water.
Rabbi Natan interprets seeing a well as finding Torah, linking the verse about finding life to the well of living water.
Rava interprets seeing a well as actual life.

items.text: Three symbols of peace: river, bird, pot
items.text_en: Three symbols of peace: river, bird, pot
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanan states that three things in a dream signify peace: a river, a bird, and a pot, each supported by a biblical verse. Rabbi Chanina adds that this applies only to a pot without meat.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanan states that three things in a dream signify peace: a river, a bird, and a pot, each supported by a biblical verse.
Rabbi Chanina adds that the pot as a sign of peace applies only to a pot without meat, citing a verse that associates meat in a pot with calamity.

items.text: Preemptive verses for dream symbols
items.text_en: Preemptive verses for dream symbols
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that one who sees a river, bird, pot, grapes, mountain, shofar, dog, lion, haircut, well, or reed in a dream should recite a positive verse before another negative verse comes to mind.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi opens with the general principle that one who sees a river in a dream should recite a positive verse before a negative one.
He applies the principle to a bird, instructing to recite a positive verse about birds before a negative one.
He applies the principle to a pot, instructing to recite a positive verse about a pot before a negative one.
He applies the principle to grapes, instructing to recite a positive verse about grapes before a negative one.
He applies the principle to a mountain, instructing to recite a positive verse about mountains before a negative one.
He applies the principle to a shofar, instructing to recite a positive verse about a shofar before a negative one.
He applies the principle to a dog, instructing to recite a positive verse about dogs before a negative one.
He applies the principle to a lion, instructing to recite a positive verse about lions before a negative one.
He applies the principle to a haircut, instructing to recite a positive verse about a haircut before a negative one.
He applies the principle to a well, instructing to recite a positive verse about a well before a negative one.
He applies the principle to a reed, instructing to recite a positive verse about a reed before a negative one.

items.text: Teachings on seeing a reed in a dream
items.text_en: Teachings on seeing a reed in a dream
items.desc_en: The Sages teach that seeing a reed in a dream portends wisdom, and seeing reeds portends understanding. Rabbi Zeira adds that certain Aramaic words for reed are all good. A baraita states that gourds are only shown to those who fear Heaven.

sub.desc_en: The Sages teach that seeing a reed in a dream portends wisdom, citing the verse 'קְנֵה חָכְמָה' (acquire wisdom).
The Sages add that seeing reeds (קָנִים) portends understanding, citing the verse 'וּבְכׇל קִנְיָנְךָ קְנֵה בִינָה' (with all your acquisition acquire understanding).
Rabbi Zeira lists several Aramaic words for reed-like items (קָרָא, קוּרָא, קִירָא, קַנְיָא) and states that all are good omens in a dream.
A baraita states that gourds (דִּלּוּעִין) are only shown in a dream to one who fears Heaven with all his might.

items.text: Seeing an ox in a dream
items.text_en: Seeing an ox in a dream
items.desc_en: One who sees an ox in a dream should recite a positive verse before a negative one.

sub.desc_en: One who sees an ox in a dream should recite a positive verse before a negative one.

items.text: Five things said about an ox in a dream
items.text_en: Five things said about an ox in a dream
items.desc_en: The Sages teach five interpretations for an ox in a dream: eating its flesh brings wealth, being gored yields Torah scholars, being bitten brings suffering, being kicked brings a distant journey, and riding it brings greatness. A contradiction is resolved: riding the ox oneself is good, but the ox riding him is bad.

sub.desc_en: The Sages teach five interpretations for an ox in a dream: eating its flesh brings wealth, being gored yields Torah scholars, being bitten brings suffering, being kicked brings a distant journey, and riding it brings greatness.
The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita taught that riding an ox in a dream is a sign of death.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: riding the ox oneself is good, but the ox riding him is bad.

items.text: Various dream symbols: donkey, cat, grapes, horse
items.text_en: Various dream symbols: donkey, cat, grapes, horse
items.desc_en: Seeing a donkey portends salvation, a cat brings either a nice song or a bad change depending on its name, white grapes are always good, black grapes in season are good, a white horse is always good, a red horse is good at rest but bad in pursuit.
