sub.desc_en: One who sees a donkey in a dream should anticipate salvation, as it is said: 'Behold, your king comes unto you... riding upon a donkey'.
One who sees a cat in a dream: if it is called shunra, a nice song will be composed for him; if it is called shinra, he will undergo a change for the worse.
One who sees white grapes in a dream, whether in season or not, it is good; black grapes in season are good, but out of season they are bad.
One who sees a white horse in a dream, whether walking or running, it is good; a red horse is good when walking but bad when running.

items.text: Seeing Yishmael or a camel in a dream
items.text_en: Seeing Yishmael or a camel in a dream
items.desc_en: Seeing Yishmael in a dream means one's prayer is heard, specifically Yishmael son of Abraham. Seeing a camel means a death sentence was decreed but rescinded, supported by verses from Rabbi Chama and Rav Nachman.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara teaches that seeing Ishmael in a dream indicates one's prayer is heard, specifically Ishmael son of Abraham, not a random Arab.
The Gemara teaches that seeing a camel in a dream indicates a death sentence was decreed from heaven but the dreamer was spared.
Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina cites a verse from Genesis where the acronym of 'gam alo' (also bring up) spells 'gamal' (camel), supporting the interpretation.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers an alternative proof from a verse in II Samuel where 'gam' (also) appears, linking to the word 'camel' and the promise of not dying.

items.text: Seeing Pinchas or an elephant in a dream
items.text_en: Seeing Pinchas or an elephant in a dream
items.desc_en: Seeing Pinchas in a dream brings a wonder, seeing an elephant brings wonders, and seeing elephants brings wonders of wonders. A contradiction is raised: all animals are good except the elephant and monkey. The Gemara resolves it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara teaches that seeing Pinchas in a dream portends a miracle, seeing an elephant portends miracles, and seeing elephants portends miracles upon miracles.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that all animals are good omens in a dream except the elephant and the monkey.
The Gemara begins to resolve the contradiction, indicating that the difficulty is not insurmountable.

items.text: Opening: distinctions in dream interpretations
items.text_en: Opening: distinctions in dream interpretations
items.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes between different types of dreams (e.g., with or without a specific detail) and interprets seeing certain names or a eulogy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes between dreams with and without a specific detail, and interprets seeing certain names or a eulogy in a dream.

items.text: Merits of answering and reciting
items.text_en: Merits of answering and reciting
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that one who answers 'Yehei Shmei Rabba' is assured of the World to Come, and one who recites Shema is worthy of the Divine Presence, but the generation is not worthy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that one who answers 'Yehei Shmei Rabba' is assured of the World to Come.
The Gemara adds that one who recites Shema is worthy of the Divine Presence, but the generation is not worthy.

items.text: Dreams of tefillin and prayer
items.text_en: Dreams of tefillin and prayer
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets seeing tefillin in a dream as a sign of greatness, citing Rabbi Eliezer Hagadol, and praying in a dream as a good sign, provided one did not finish.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that seeing oneself donning tefillin in a dream is a sign of greatness, citing a verse and a baraita of Rabbi Eliezer Hagadol.
The Gemara adds that praying in a dream is a good sign, provided one did not finish the prayer.

items.text: Dreams of forbidden relations
items.text_en: Dreams of forbidden relations
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets dreams of incestuous or adulterous relations as positive omens for wisdom, Torah, and the World to Come, with a condition regarding prior knowledge.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that one who dreams of relations with his mother should anticipate wisdom (בינה), citing a verse.
The Gemara states that one who dreams of relations with a betrothed young woman should anticipate Torah, via a wordplay on מוֹרָשָׁה (inheritance) and מְאוֹרָשָׂה (betrothed).
The Gemara states that one who dreams of relations with his sister should anticipate wisdom (חכמה), citing a verse.
The Gemara states that one who dreams of relations with a married woman is assured a share in the World to Come.
The Gemara qualifies that these positive interpretations apply only if the dreamer did not know the woman and had not thought about her the previous night.

items.text: Dreams of grains: wheat and barley
items.text_en: Dreams of grains: wheat and barley
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba interprets seeing wheat as peace and barley as atonement; Rabbi Zeira relates his personal experience of seeing barley before moving to Israel.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba interprets seeing wheat in a dream as peace and seeing barley as atonement for sins.
Rabbi Zeira relates that he did not ascend from Babylonia to the Land of Israel until he saw barley in a dream, confirming the positive omen.

items.text: Dreams of vine, fig, and pomegranate
items.text_en: Dreams of vine, fig, and pomegranate
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets seeing a laden vine as preventing miscarriage, a sorek as messianic hope, a fig as preserving Torah, and pomegranates as increasing business or, for a scholar, Torah, and for an ignoramus, mitzvot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets seeing a laden vine in a dream as a sign that one's wife will not miscarry, and seeing a sorek vine as hope for the Messiah.
The Gemara interprets seeing a fig as preserving Torah, and seeing pomegranates as increasing business or, for a scholar, Torah, and for an ignoramus, mitzvot.

items.text: Dreams of olives, oil, and dates
items.text_en: Dreams of olives, oil, and dates
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets seeing olives as business success or many children, olive oil as the light of Torah, and dates as the end of sins.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets seeing small olives in a dream as a sign that one's business will flourish like olives.
The Gemara clarifies that this applies to the fruit, but seeing olive trees signifies many children, citing a verse.
An alternative interpretation states that seeing an olive tree in a dream means a good name will go out for the dreamer, citing a verse.
The Gemara interprets seeing olive oil in a dream as a sign of the light of Torah, citing a verse.
The Gemara interprets seeing dates in a dream as a sign that one's sins have ended, citing a verse.

items.text: Dreams of goat, myrtle, etrog, and lulav
items.text_en: Dreams of goat, myrtle, etrog, and lulav
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef interprets seeing a goat as a blessed year; Ulla adds a condition about seeing them in their clusters. The Gemara also interprets myrtle as successful assets, etrog as being glorious before God, and lulav as having a single heart for God.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef interprets seeing a goat in a dream as a blessed year, citing a verse about goat's milk.
The Gemara interprets seeing myrtle in a dream as successful assets or an inheritance from elsewhere.
Ulla adds a condition that the myrtle must be seen in its clusters for the interpretation to apply.
The Gemara interprets seeing an etrog in a dream as being glorious before God, citing a verse.
The Gemara interprets seeing a lulav in a dream as having a single heart for God.

items.text: Dream of a goose
items.text_en: Dream of a goose
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets seeing a goose as wisdom, and having intercourse with it as becoming a head of a yeshiva; Rav Ashi testifies to this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that seeing a goose in a dream portends wisdom, citing the verse 'חכמות בחוץ תרנה' (wisdom cries out in the streets).
The Gemara adds that having intercourse with the goose in the dream means one will become a head of a yeshiva (ראש ישיבה).
Rav Ashi testifies that he saw a goose in a dream, had intercourse with it, and indeed rose to greatness.

items.text: Dreams of chicken, eggs, and breakable items
items.text_en: Dreams of chicken, eggs, and breakable items
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets seeing a rooster as a male child, a hen as a fine teaching and joy, and eggs or other breakable items as a pending request that is fulfilled if broken.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets seeing a rooster in a dream as a sign of a male child.
The Gemara extends the interpretation: multiple roosters signify multiple male children.
The Gemara interprets a hen in a dream as a sign of fine teaching and joy.
The Gemara interprets seeing eggs in a dream as a pending request.
The Gemara concludes that if the eggs or other breakable items are broken, the request is fulfilled.

items.text: Dreams of entering a city, shaving, sitting in a boat, and defecating
items.text_en: Dreams of entering a city, shaving, sitting in a boat, and defecating
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets entering a city as fulfilled desires, shaving as a good sign, sitting in a small boat as a good name, and defecating as a good sign if not wiping.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets entering a city in a dream as fulfilled desires, citing a verse.
The Gemara states that shaving one's head in a dream is a good sign, and shaving head and beard is good for the dreamer and his family.
The Gemara interprets sitting in a small boat as a good name, and in a large boat as good for the dreamer and his family, provided the boat is being rowed.
The Gemara interprets defecating in a dream as a good sign, citing a verse, but only if the dreamer does not wipe.

items.text: Dreams of ascending, tearing clothes, nakedness, and imprisonment
items.text_en: Dreams of ascending, tearing clothes, nakedness, and imprisonment
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets ascending a roof as greatness, tearing clothes as tearing one's decree, standing naked in Babylonia as sinless but in Israel as without mitzvot, and being imprisoned as receiving protection.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that ascending a roof in a dream signifies ascending to greatness.
The Gemara adds that descending from a roof in a dream signifies descending from greatness.
Abaye and Rava both rule that once one has ascended in a dream, he has ascended and will not descend.
The Gemara states that tearing one's clothes in a dream means his decree is torn up.
The Gemara interprets standing naked in a dream: in Babylonia it means sinless, in Israel it means without mitzvot.
The Gemara states that being imprisoned in a dream means protection is provided.
The Gemara adds that being put in a collar adds extra protection.
The Gemara qualifies that the extra protection applies only to a collar, not to mere ropes.

items.text: Dreams of entering a marsh or forest
items.text_en: Dreams of entering a marsh or forest
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets entering a marsh as becoming a head of a yeshiva, and a forest as head of a bridegroom's group. Rav Papa and Rav Huna's dreams are cited, with a variant about hanging a tablet.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that entering a marsh in a dream means becoming a head of a yeshiva, and entering a forest means becoming a head of a bridegroom's group.

sub.text: Rav Papa and Rav Huna's dreams
sub.text_en: Rav Papa and Rav Huna's dreams
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the dreams of Rav Papa and Rav Huna, which confirm the interpretation: Rav Papa entered a marsh and became head of a yeshiva, Rav Huna entered a forest and became head of a a bridegroom's group.
An alternative version states that both entered a marsh, but Rav Papa, who hung a tablet, became head of a yeshiva, while Rav Huna, who did not, became head of a bridegroom's group.
Rav Ashi testifies that he entered a marsh, hung a tablet, and barked in it, implying his own rise to leadership.

items.text: Dream of bloodletting: dispute resolved
items.text_en: Dream of bloodletting: dispute resolved
items.desc_en: A Tanna teaches before Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak that bloodletting in a dream means sins are forgiven. An objection is raised from another baraita that sins are arranged. The Gemara resolves: arranged for forgiveness.

sub.text: Tanna's teaching before Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
sub.text_en: Tanna's teaching before Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
sub.desc_en: A Tanna teaches before Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak that one who undergoes bloodletting in a dream has his sins forgiven.
The Gemara objects by citing a contradictory baraita that states his sins are arranged (not forgiven).
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that 'arranged' means arranged for forgiveness.

items.text: Dream of a snake: dispute with Rav Sheshet
items.text_en: Dream of a snake: dispute with Rav Sheshet
items.desc_en: A Tanna teaches before Rav Sheshet that seeing a snake means sustenance is ready, being bitten means doubled, and killing it means lost. Rav Sheshet argues that killing it doubles sustenance, citing his own dream.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna teaches before Rav Sheshet that seeing a snake in a dream means sustenance is ready, being bitten means it is doubled, and killing it means it is lost.
Rav Sheshet objects that killing the snake should double sustenance, not lose it.
The gemara resolves that the dispute is not general; Rav Sheshet's ruling was based on his own dream where he killed a snake and his sustenance was doubled.

items.text: Dream of wine: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling
items.text_en: Dream of wine: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling
items.desc_en: A Tanna teaches before Rabbi Yochanan that all drinks are good for a dream except wine, which can be good or bad. Rabbi Yochanan instructs the Tanna to teach that for a Torah scholar, wine is always good.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna teaches before Rabbi Yochanan that all drinks are good for a dream except wine, which can be good or bad, citing verses for each possibility.

Rabbi Yochanan instructs the Tanna to teach that for a Torah scholar, wine is always good, citing the verse 'לְכוּ לַחֲמוּ בְלַחֲמִי וּשְׁתוּ בְּיַיִן מָסָכְתִּי' (Come, eat of my bread and drink of the wine I have mixed).

items.text: Dream interpretations for kings, prophets, writings, sages, and students
items.text_en: Dream interpretations for kings, prophets, writings, sages, and students
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that a verse that comes to one's mouth upon waking is a minor prophecy. A baraita lists interpretations for seeing various figures in dreams: David, Solomon, Ahab; prophets; biblical books; sages like Rabbi, Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, Rabbi Yishmael; and students like Ben Azzai, Ben Zoma, and Acher.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that a verse that comes to one's mouth upon waking is a minor prophecy.
A baraita lists dream interpretations for seeing three kings: David, Solomon, and Ahab.
The baraita continues with interpretations for seeing three prophets: Kings, Ezekiel, Isaiah, and Jeremiah.
The baraita lists interpretations for seeing three major writings: Psalms, Proverbs, and Job.
The baraita lists interpretations for seeing three minor writings: Song of Songs, Ecclesiastes, Lamentations, and the Scroll of Esther.
The baraita lists interpretations for seeing three sages: Rabbi, Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, and Rabbi Yishmael.
The baraita lists interpretations for seeing three students: Ben Azzai, Ben Zoma, and Acher.

items.text: Animals in dreams and resolution of contradiction
items.text_en: Animals in dreams and resolution of contradiction
items.desc_en: A general rule states that all animals are good in dreams except the elephant, monkey, and porcupine. The Gemara notes a contradiction: earlier it was said that seeing an elephant is a wonder. The resolution: if the elephant is saddled it is good, if not it is bad.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states a general rule: all types of animals are good in dreams except the elephant, monkey, and porcupine.
The Gemara raises a contradiction: earlier it was said that seeing an elephant in a dream is a wonder, implying it is good.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: if the elephant is saddled (מסרג) it is good, if not it is bad.

items.text: Metals, fruits, vegetables, colors, and birds in dreams
items.text_en: Metals, fruits, vegetables, colors, and birds in dreams
items.desc_en: A baraita lists dream omens for metals (except a saw, chisel, and axe when seen with their handles), fruits (except unripe dates), vegetables (except heads of beets, with a resolution regarding Rav's experience), colors (except blue), and birds (except certain species).

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by listing metals that are good omens in dreams, except for a saw, chisel, and axe.
The baraita qualifies that the exception applies only when the tools are seen with their handles.
The baraita lists fruits as good omens, except for unripe dates.
The baraita lists vegetables as good omens, except for heads of beets.
The gemara objects that Rav said he only became wealthy after seeing heads of beets in a dream, contradicting the baraita's negative omen.
The gemara resolves that Rav saw the beets with their stalks, which is a good omen, unlike the heads alone.
The baraita lists colors as good omens, except for blue (תכלת).
The baraita lists birds as good omens, except for certain species: קַרְיָא, קִפּוֹפָא, and קוּרְפְּרַאי.

items.text: Three things that enter the body, three that benefit, and three that expand the mind
items.text_en: Three things that enter the body, three that benefit, and three that expand the mind
items.desc_en: A mnemonic introduces a series of threes: things that enter the body without benefit (dates, etc.), things that benefit without entering (bathing, anointing, and elimination), things that are a taste of the World to Come (Shabbat, sun, and elimination). The Gemara clarifies that 'elimination' refers to defecation, not marital relations. Then three things that restore one's mind (sound, sight, smell) and three that expand it (a beautiful home, wife, and vessels).

sub.desc_en: A mnemonic introduces the series of threes: things that enter the body, things that benefit without entering, things that are a taste of the World to Come, things that restore the mind, and things that expand it.

The baraita lists three things that enter the body without benefit (dates, etc.), three that benefit without entering (bathing, anointing, and elimination), and three that are a taste of the World to Come (Shabbat, sun, and elimination).
The Gemara asks: what does 'elimination' (תשמיש) refer to in the third list?
The Gemara objects: if it means marital relations, that weakens the body, so it cannot be a taste of the World to Come.
The Gemara resolves: it refers to defecation (תשמיש נקבים), which relieves the body.
The baraita concludes with three things that restore one's mind (sound, sight, smell) and three that expand it (a beautiful home, wife, and vessels).

items.text: Five, six, and ten as omens
items.text_en: Five, six, and ten as omens
items.desc_en: A baraita lists five things that are one-sixtieth of something else: fire (of Gehinnom), honey (of manna), Shabbat (of the World to Come), sleep (of death), and dreams (of prophecy).

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists five things that are one-sixtieth of something else: fire (of Gehinnom), honey (of manna), Shabbat (of the World to Come), sleep (of death), and dreams (of prophecy).

items.text: Six good signs for the sick and ten things that worsen illness
items.text_en: Six good signs for the sick and ten things that worsen illness
items.desc_en: A baraita lists six good signs for a sick person: sneezing, sweating, diarrhea, seminal emission, sleep, and dream, each with a biblical prooftext. Another baraita lists six things that heal the sick (cabbage, etc.) and ten things that return the sick to their illness (beef, etc.), with additional opinions.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by listing six good signs for a sick person (sneezing, sweat, diarrhea, seminal emission, sleep, dream) and provides a biblical prooftext for each.
A second baraita lists six things that heal the sick (cabbage, beets, dry sisin, stomach, womb, diaphragm) and adds that small fish also strengthen the body.

A third baraita lists ten things that return the sick to their illness (beef, fat meat, roast, bird meat, roasted egg, shaving, cress, milk, cheese, bath), with additional opinions adding nuts and cucumbers.

items.text: Cucumbers: hard or beneficial?
items.text_en: Cucumbers: hard or beneficial?
items.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael explains that cucumbers are called קשואים because they are as hard (קשים) as swords. The Gemara questions this from a verse about Rebecca, which is interpreted by Rav Yehuda citing Rav to refer to Antoninus and Rabbi, who always had cucumbers on their table. The resolution: large cucumbers are hard, small ones are beneficial.

sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that cucumbers are called קשואים because they are as hard (קשים) as swords.
The Gemara objects from a verse about Rebecca, interpreted by Rav Yehuda citing Rav to mean that Antoninus and Rabbi always had cucumbers on their table, implying cucumbers are beneficial.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: large cucumbers are hard, small ones are beneficial.

items.text: Omens from a dead person in the house and taking items
items.text_en: Omens from a dead person in the house and taking items
items.desc_en: A baraita states: if a dead person is in the house, it is peace; if one ate and drank, it is a good sign; if one took vessels, it is a bad sign. Rav Pappa explains this refers to shoes and sandals. Taking from a dead person is good except shoes and sandals; giving to a dead person is good except dust and mustard.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists three omens: a dead person in the house brings peace, eating and drinking is a good sign, and taking vessels is a bad sign.
Rav Pappa explains that the bad omen of taking vessels refers specifically to shoes and sandals.
A general rule states: taking from a dead person is good except for shoes and sandals; giving to a dead person is good except for dust and mustard.

items.text: Blessings upon seeing idolatry and places where it was uprooted
items.text_en: Blessings upon seeing idolatry and places where it was uprooted
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches: one who sees a Merkolis (idol) says a blessing for God's patience. Upon seeing a place where idolatry was uprooted, one says a blessing for its removal and prays for its removal from all Israel, and for the hearts of its worshippers to return. Outside the Land, one omits the prayer for return, but Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says to include it because they will convert.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches the blessing for seeing a Merkolis (idol) and the blessing for seeing a place where idolatry was uprooted, including a prayer for its removal from all Israel and for the hearts of its worshippers to return.
The baraita adds that outside the Land of Israel, one omits the prayer for return because most inhabitants are gentiles.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar objects and says that even outside the Land one must include the prayer, because the gentiles will eventually convert, as the verse states.

items.text: Blessings upon seeing Babylon and related practices
items.text_en: Blessings upon seeing Babylon and related practices
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna teaches that one who sees wicked Babylon must recite five blessings: upon seeing Babylon, Nebuchadnezzar's house, the lions' den or fiery furnace, a Merkolis, and a place where dust is taken. Rava would strike donkeys carrying dust and urge them to do their master's will. Mar bar Ravina would take dust from Babylon and throw it outside. Rav Ashi says he did not hear Rav Hamnuna's teaching but blessed all these from his own reasoning.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna teaches that one who sees wicked Babylon must recite five specific blessings for different sights.
Rava, upon seeing donkeys carrying dust from Babylon, would strike them and urge them to fulfill their master's will.
Mar bar Ravina would take dust from Babylon and throw it outside, fulfilling the verse about sweeping destruction.
Rav Ashi says he had not heard Rav Hamnuna's teaching but independently reasoned and blessed all these sights.

items.text: Opening statement on Babylon and Samaria
items.text_en: Opening statement on Babylon and Samaria
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya ben Elazar contrasts the curses on Babylon and Samaria: Babylon's curse extended to its neighbors, while Samaria's curse blessed its neighbors, citing biblical verses.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya ben Elazar contrasts the curses on Babylon and Samaria: Babylon's curse extended to its neighbors, while Samaria's curse blessed its neighbors, citing biblical verses.

items.text: Blessings upon seeing crowds of Israel and Gentiles
items.text_en: Blessings upon seeing crowds of Israel and Gentiles
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna teaches that seeing a crowd of Israel requires the blessing 'Chacham HaRazim', while seeing a crowd of Gentiles requires a verse of shame. The Tanna Kamma explains the reason: their minds and faces are not alike, and Ben Zoma adds a blessing upon seeing a crowd on the Temple Mount.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna teaches the blessings for seeing a crowd of Israel (חכם הרזים) and a crowd of Gentiles (a verse of shame).
The Tanna Kamma explains the reason for the blessing: their minds and faces are not alike.
Ben Zoma adds a blessing upon seeing a crowd on the Temple Mount, praising God who created all these to serve him.

items.text: Ben Zoma's reflections on human effort and the good and bad guest
items.text_en: Ben Zoma's reflections on human effort and the good and bad guest
items.desc_en: Ben Zoma reflects on the labor of Adam HaRishon to obtain bread and clothing, contrasting it with his own ease. He then contrasts the words of a good guest, who praises the host's efforts, with those of a bad guest, who belittles them, citing verses.

sub.desc_en: Ben Zoma reflects on the immense labor of Adam HaRishon to obtain bread and clothing, contrasting it with his own effortless access to these necessities.
Ben Zoma contrasts the words of a good guest, who praises the host's efforts, with those of a bad guest, who belittles them.
Ben Zoma cites verses: for the good guest, 'זְכֹר כִּי תַשְׂגִּיא פׇעֳלוֹ' (Job 36:24), and for the bad guest, 'לָכֵן יְרֵאוּהוּ אֲנָשִׁים' (Job 37:24).

items.text: Interpretation of a verse about an old man and definition of a crowd
items.text_en: Interpretation of a verse about an old man and definition of a crowd
items.desc_en: Rava, Rav Zevid, or Rav Oshaya identify the old man in the verse as Yishai, father of David, who went out, entered, and taught in a crowd. Ulla states there is no crowd in Babylonia, and a Tanna teaches a crowd is no less than 600,000.

sub.desc_en: Rava (or others) identifies the 'man in the days of Saul' as Jesse, who went out, entered, and taught among a multitude; Ulla states there is no multitude in Babylonia; a baraita defines a multitude as no fewer than 600,000.

sub.text: Rava / Rav Zevid / Rav Oshaya's identification
sub.text_en: Rava / Rav Zevid / Rav Oshaya's identification
sub.desc_en: Rava (or others) identifies the old man as Yishai, father of David, who went out, entered, and taught in a crowd (אוכלוסין).
Ulla states that there is no crowd (אוכלוסין) in Babylonia.
A Tanna teaches that a crowd (אוכלוסין) is no less than 600,000 people.

items.text: Blessings upon seeing sages and kings
items.text_en: Blessings upon seeing sages and kings
items.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma teaches blessings for seeing Jewish and gentile sages and kings. Rabbi Yochanan adds that one should always run to greet Jewish kings, and even gentile kings, to distinguish between them in the future.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma teaches the blessings recited upon seeing Jewish and gentile sages and kings.
Rabbi Yochanan adds that one should always run to greet Jewish kings, and even gentile kings, to distinguish between them in the future.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's encounter with a heretic and the king's arrival
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's encounter with a heretic and the king's arrival
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet, who was blind, goes with others to greet the king. A heretic mocks him, but Rav Sheshet correctly predicts the king's arrival based on the silence after the third legion, citing the verse about Elijah. When the king arrives, Rav Sheshet blesses him, and the heretic is punished.

sub.desc_en: The narrator introduces Rav Sheshet, who is blind, and describes how he goes with everyone to greet the king, encountering a heretic who mocks him.
Rav Sheshet explains to the heretic that he knew the king was coming because earthly kingship mirrors heavenly kingship, as described in the verse about Elijah.
When the king arrives, Rav Sheshet blesses him, and the heretic is punished—either his friends gouged out his eyes or Rav Sheshet caused him to become a pile of bones.

items.text: Rabbi Shila's trial and the killing of an informer
items.text_en: Rabbi Shila's trial and the killing of an informer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shila flogs a man who had relations with a gentile woman. The man informs the Persian authorities, who summon Rabbi Shila. Through a miracle involving Elijah, Rabbi Shila proves the man's guilt, then kills him as a pursuer, citing the principle 'If someone comes to kill you, rise early to kill him.'

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shila flogs a man who had relations with a gentile woman, and the man informs the Persian authorities that Rabbi Shila judges without royal authorization.
The Persian authorities summon Rabbi Shila and ask why he flogged the man.
Rabbi Shila answers that the man had relations with a donkey, and Elijah appears as a witness to confirm.
The authorities declare the man liable for death, but Rabbi Shila says Jews lack authority to execute; they give him a staff to judge the case.
The informer objects that Rabbi Shila called him a donkey, citing the verse 'their flesh is the flesh of donkeys'.
Rabbi Shila sees the informer going to report the insult, declares him a pursuer, and kills him with the staff, citing the principle 'If someone comes to kill you, rise early to kill him.'

items.text: Homiletical interpretations of 'Lecha Hashem Hagdulah'
items.text_en: Homiletical interpretations of 'Lecha Hashem Hagdulah'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shila, after the miracle, expounds the verse 'Lecha Hashem Hagdulah' as referring to various biblical events: creation, Exodus, sun standing for Joshua, fall of Rome, battle of Arnon, battle of Sisera, battle of Amalek, and war of Gog and Magog. Rav Chanan bar Rava adds that even a leader of a reed is appointed from heaven. A baraita in the name of Rabbi Akiva gives alternative interpretations.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shila, after the miracle, expounds each phrase of 'Lecha Hashem Hagdulah' as referring to a specific biblical event: creation, Exodus, sun standing for Joshua, fall of Rome, battle of Arnon, battle of Sisera, battle of Amalek, and war of Gog and Magog.

sub.text: Rav Chanan bar Rava citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Chanan bar Rava citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Rava in the name of Rabbi Yochanan adds that even a leader of a reed (a lowly position) is appointed from heaven.

sub.text: Baraita in the name of Rabbi Akiva
sub.text_en: Baraita in the name of Rabbi Akiva
sub.desc_en: A baraita in the name of Rabbi Akiva gives alternative interpretations: 'Hagdulah' is the splitting of the Red Sea, 'Gevurah' is the plague of the firstborn, 'Tiferet' is the giving of the Torah, 'Netzach' is Jerusalem, and 'Hod' is the Temple.

items.text: Opening Baraita on blessings for dwellings
items.text_en: Opening Baraita on blessings for dwellings
items.desc_en: The baraita teaches that upon seeing Jewish dwellings in habitation one says 'Blessed... who establishes the border of the widow', and in ruin 'Blessed... the true Judge'. For non-Jewish dwellings in habitation one says 'The house of the proud...', and in ruin 'God of vengeance...'.

items.text: Story of Ulla and Rav Chisda at the ruins of Rav Chana bar Chanilai
items.text_en: Story of Ulla and Rav Chisda at the ruins of Rav Chana bar Chanilai
items.desc_en: Ulla and Rav Chisda were walking. When they reached the door of Rav Chana bar Chanilai's house, Rav Chisda groaned. Ulla rebuked him citing Rav and Rabbi Yochanan that groaning breaks half or all of a person's body. Rav Chisda explained his grief over the ruined house that once hosted many guests. Rabbi Yochanan said that since the Temple's destruction, the houses of the righteous are decreed to be destroyed, but will be restored. Ulla comforted him: 'It is enough for a servant to be like his master.'

items.text: Baraita on blessings for graves
items.text_en: Baraita on blessings for graves
items.desc_en: The baraita teaches that upon seeing Jewish graves one says a blessing acknowledging God's judgment in creation, sustenance, gathering, and future resurrection. Mar bar Ravina adds a conclusion in the name of Rav Nachman. For non-Jewish graves one says 'Your mother is ashamed...'.

items.text: Blessing upon seeing a friend after 30 days or 12 months
items.text_en: Blessing upon seeing a friend after 30 days or 12 months
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that upon seeing a friend after 30 days one says 'Shehecheyanu', and after 12 months one says 'Blessed... who revives the dead'. Rav adds that a deceased is only forgotten from the heart after 12 months, citing a verse.

items.text: Story of Rav Pappa and Rav Huna meeting Rav Chanina
items.text_en: Story of Rav Pappa and Rav Huna meeting Rav Chanina
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua met Rav Chanina bar Rav Ika. They blessed him with two blessings: 'who gave of His wisdom to those who fear Him' and 'Shehecheyanu'. He responded that he considered them as 600,000 of Israel and blessed them with three, including 'Chacham Harazim'. They were amazed and cast their eyes on him, and he died.

items.text: Blessing for behakanim and the resolution of the contradiction
items.text_en: Blessing for behakanim and the resolution of the contradiction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says that upon seeing behakanim (people with skin discolorations) one says 'Blessed... who changes creatures'. A baraita objects: for a black person, albino, etc. one says 'Meshaneh habriyot', but for a cripple, blind, etc. and behakanim one says 'Dayyan ha'emet'. The Gemara resolves: the baraita refers to a congenital condition, while Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi refers to one acquired after birth, as indicated by the mention of a cripple.

items.text: Baraita on blessings for unusual animals and beautiful creations
items.text_en: Baraita on blessings for unusual animals and beautiful creations
items.desc_en: The baraita teaches that upon seeing an elephant, monkey, or kipof one says 'Blessed... who changes creatures'. Upon seeing beautiful creatures or trees one says 'Blessed... who has such in His world'.

items.text: Discussion of zikin, Kesil, Kimah, and astronomical phenomena
items.text_en: Discussion of zikin, Kesil, Kimah, and astronomical phenomena
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains 'zikin' as a comet. Shmuel says he knows the paths of heaven except for the comet. It is learned that the comet does not pass through the constellation of Kesil, but if it does the world would be destroyed. The Gemara resolves that only its light passes. Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua and Rav Ashi offer alternative explanations. Shmuel resolves a contradiction about the order of Kesil and Kimah, explaining their roles in sustaining the world. The Gemara discusses the sting of Scorpio and the meaning of 'Kimah' (about a hundred stars) and 'Ash' (the tail of Aries or the head of the calf).

items.text: The story of Kimah and Ayish
items.text_en: The story of Kimah and Ayish
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the constellation Ayish follows Kimah: because when God brought the flood, He took two stars from Kimah, and when He stopped it, He took two stars from Ayish. It then addresses why Ayish cannot be refilled from its own stars (the pit cannot fill from its own hole, and an accuser cannot become a defender) and why new stars cannot be created (there is nothing new under the sun). Rav Nachman concludes that God will eventually restore the stars to Ayish, as per the verse 'and Ayish will comfort her children.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Ayish follows Kimah because God took two stars from Kimah to bring the flood and two from Ayish to stop it.
The Gemara asks why Ayish cannot be refilled from its own stars.
Two answers are given: a pit cannot fill from its own hole, and an accuser cannot become a defender.
The Gemara asks why new stars cannot be created to replace the missing ones.

The Gemara answers that there is nothing new under the sun, and Rav Nachman concludes that God will eventually restore the stars to Ayish, as per the verse 'וְעַיִשׁ עַל בָּנֶיהָ תַנְחֵם' (and Ayish will comfort her children).

items.text: The nature of earthquakes (z'va'ot)
items.text_en: The nature of earthquakes (z'va'ot)
items.desc_en: Rav Katina identifies earthquakes (z'va'ot) as 'guha' (a rumbling sound). He recounts an incident where he encountered a cave of demons and heard a guha, and a demon named Oba Tamya explained that it is the sound of God's tears falling into the sea when He remembers His children in exile. Rav Katina then accuses the demon of lying, because the sound should be 'guha guha' (repeated), but the demon's claim is defended: the sound is indeed 'guha guha', but the demon denied it to prevent people from following him.

sub.desc_en: Rav Katina concludes that the demon lied, but the sound is indeed 'guha guha', and the demon denied it to prevent the whole world from following him.

items.text: God's actions during earthquakes
items.text_en: God's actions during earthquakes
items.desc_en: Various rabbis describe what God does during earthquakes: Rav Katina says He claps His hands (based on a verse), Rabbi Natan says He sighs, the Rabbis say He kicks the firmament, and Rav Acha bar Yaakov says He presses His feet under the Throne of Glory. Each view is supported by a biblical verse.

sub.desc_en: Rav Katina states that during an earthquake God claps His hands, citing the verse 'וְגַם אֲנִי אַכֶּה כַפִּי אֶל כַּפִּי וַהֲנִיחֹתִי חֲמָתִי'.
Rabbi Natan says God sighs during an earthquake, citing the verse 'וַהֲנִיחוֹתִי חֲמָתִי בָּם וְהִנֶּחָמְתִּי'.
The Rabbis say God kicks the firmament during an earthquake, citing the verse 'הֵידָד כְּדֹרְכִים יַעֲנֶה אֶל כׇּל יֹשְׁבֵי הָאָרֶץ'.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov says God presses His feet under the Throne of Glory during an earthquake, citing the verse 'כֹּה אָמַר ה׳ הַשָּׁמַיִם כִּסְאִי וְהָאָרֶץ הֲדֹם רַגְלָי'.

items.text: The nature of thunder (r'amin)
items.text_en: The nature of thunder (r'amin)
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains what thunder is: Shmuel says it is clouds rolling in a wheel (based on a verse), the Rabbis say it is clouds pouring water onto each other, Rav Acha bar Yaakov says it is a strong lightning bolt that breaks iron bars, and Rav Ashi says it is hollow clouds that wind blows into like a jar. The Gemara concludes that the view of Rav Acha bar Yaakov is most plausible, as lightning flashes, clouds rumble, and then rain comes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what thunder (רְעָמִים) is.
Shmuel says thunder is clouds rolling in a wheel, citing a verse.
The Rabbis say thunder is clouds pouring water onto each other, citing a verse.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov says thunder is a strong lightning bolt that breaks iron bars.
Rav Ashi says thunder is hollow clouds that wind blows into like a jar.
The Gemara concludes that Rav Acha bar Yaakov's view is most plausible, as lightning flashes, clouds rumble, and then rain comes.

items.text: The nature of winds (ruchot)
items.text_en: The nature of winds (ruchot)
items.desc_en: Abaye identifies winds as 'za'fa' (a storm). He states a tradition that a storm does not occur at night, but the Gemara objects that we see storms at night; Abaye responds that those storms began during the day. He also states that a storm does not last two hours, to fulfill the verse 'trouble does not arise twice,' but the Gemara objects that we see storms lasting longer; Abaye responds that they pause intermittently.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what type of wind is referred to in the Mishnah's blessing over winds.
Abaye identifies the winds as 'za'fa' (a storm).
Abaye states a tradition that a storm (za'fa) does not occur at night.
The Gemara objects that we see storms at night.
Abaye responds that those storms began during the day.
Abaye states another tradition that a storm does not last two hours, to fulfill the verse 'trouble does not arise twice'.
The Gemara objects that we see storms lasting longer than two hours.
Abaye responds that the storms pause intermittently, so they do not last continuously for two hours.

items.text: Lightning and the blessing for natural phenomena
items.text_en: Lightning and the blessing for natural phenomena
items.desc_en: Rava defines lightning as 'barka' and lists various types of lightning and clouds that are ominous. The Gemara asks what practical difference this makes, and answers: for praying for mercy. These signs are significant at night, but in the morning they are meaningless. Rabbi Shmuel bar Yitzchak supports this with a verse about morning clouds. Rav Pappa then cites a folk saying about morning clouds and rain, and Abaye distinguishes between clouds that are tied to the sky and those that are not.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that upon seeing lightning one recites the blessing 'Blessed… whose power and might fill the world'.
The Gemara asks: what exactly are 'ברקים' (lightning flashes)?
Rava defines 'ברקים' as 'ברקה' (lightning flash).
Rava lists various types of lightning and clouds that are ominous (bad signs).
The Gemara asks: what practical difference does this classification make?
The Gemara answers: the practical difference is for praying for mercy (when these signs appear).
The Gemara qualifies: these ominous signs apply only at night, but in the morning they have no substance.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Yitzchak supports the rule with a verse: 'your kindness is like a morning cloud' (Hosea 6:4).
Rav Pappa objects to Abaye citing a folk saying that morning clouds do bring rain, contradicting the claim that morning clouds are meaningless.
Abaye resolves the contradiction: the folk saying refers to clouds that are tied to the sky (עיבא), while the verse refers to clouds that are not tied (ענני).

items.text: The rainbow and its blessing
items.text_en: The rainbow and its blessing
items.desc_en: Rabbi Alexandri quoting Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says that thunder was created only to straighten the crookedness of the heart, and that one who sees a rainbow must fall on his face. In the West, they curse this practice because it looks like bowing to the rainbow, but one should certainly bless. The blessing is 'Zocher HaBrit' (Rememberer of the Covenant). Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka says 'Ne'eman Bivrito Vekayam Bema'amaro' (Faithful in His covenant and Fulfills His word). Rav Pappa concludes that we should say both.

sub.text: Rabbi Alexandri quoting Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Alexandri quoting Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Alexandri in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states that thunder was created only to straighten the crookedness of the heart, and that one who sees a rainbow must fall on his face, citing a verse.
In the West they curse this practice because it appears as if one is bowing to the rainbow.
The gemara concludes that one certainly does recite a blessing, and the blessing is 'Zocher HaBrit' (Rememberer of the Covenant).
A baraita teaches that Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka says the blessing is 'Ne'eman Bivrito Vekayam Bema'amaro' (Faithful in His covenant and Fulfills His word).
Rav Pappa rules that we should say both formulations together: 'Zocher HaBrit' and 'Ne'eman Bivrito Vekayam Bema'amaro'.

items.text: Blessing for mountains and hills, and the clear sky
items.text_en: Blessing for mountains and hills, and the clear sky
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why mountains and hills require a separate blessing of 'Oseh Ma'aseh Bereishit' when all these phenomena are acts of creation. Abaye says to include it in the general blessing, while Rava says one recites both 'Shekocho Malei Olam' and 'Oseh Ma'aseh Bereishit' for lightning, but for mountains only 'Oseh Ma'aseh Bereishit'. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says one who sees the sky in its clarity recites 'Oseh Ma'aseh Bereishit', and Abaye specifies this occurs after a night of rain when the morning wind clears the clouds. This disagrees with Rafram bar Pappa quoting Rav Chisda, who says that since the Temple was destroyed, the sky has never been seen in its clarity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why mountains and hills require a separate blessing of 'Oseh Ma'aseh Bereishit', since all the phenomena mentioned are acts of creation.
The Gemara cites the verse 'ברקים למטר עשה' (He makes lightning for the rain) to show that lightning is also an act of creation, yet it gets a special blessing.
Abaye answers that one should include the blessing for mountains and hills within the general blessing (i.e., recite it as part of the list).
Rava distinguishes: for lightning one recites both 'Shekocho Malei Olam' and 'Oseh Ma'aseh Bereishit', but for mountains only 'Oseh Ma'aseh Bereishit' is recited.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states that one who sees the sky in its clarity recites 'Oseh Ma'aseh Bereishit'.
The Gemara asks when this occurs (when is the sky seen in its clarity).
Abaye explains that this occurs after a night of rain when the morning wind clears the clouds.

sub.text: Rafram bar Pappa quoting Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Rafram bar Pappa quoting Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rafram bar Pappa quoting Rav Chisda disagrees, stating that since the Temple was destroyed, the sky has never been seen in its clarity, citing the verse 'אלביש שמים קדרות ושק אשים כסותם'.

items.text: Blessing for celestial phenomena and its timing
items.text_en: Blessing for celestial phenomena and its timing
items.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states that one who sees the sun at its solstice, the moon at its peak, stars in their paths, and constellations in their order recites 'Oseh Ma'aseh Bereshit'. Abaye explains that this occurs every 28 years when the Nisan solstice falls on the night of Tuesday-Wednesday.

items.text: Blessings for the sea and rivers
items.text_en: Blessings for the sea and rivers
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda says one who sees the sea recites the blessing periodically, defined by Rami bar Abba citing Rav Yitzchak as within 30 days. Rami bar Abba also states that one who sees the Euphrates at the bridge of Babylon recites 'Oseh Ma'aseh Bereshit', but now that Persians diverted it, the blessing is said from Bei Shapur upward (Rav Yosef says from Ihi Dekira upward). Similarly, one who sees the Tigris at the bridge of Shavistena recites the same blessing.

items.text: Etymology of Tigris and Euphrates, and traits of Mahoza residents
items.text_en: Etymology of Tigris and Euphrates, and traits of Mahoza residents
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that 'Chiddekel' (Tigris) means its waters are sharp and light, and 'Perat' (Euphrates) means its waters are fruitful and multiply. Rava attributes the sharpness of the residents of Mahoza to drinking Tigris water, their boldness to daytime marital relations, and their watery eyes to living in dark houses.

items.text: Blessing for rain: 'Hatov vehametiv' and its formulation
items.text_en: Blessing for rain: 'Hatov vehametiv' and its formulation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for rain one recites 'Hatov vehametiv'. The Gemara questions this, citing Rabbi Abahu (or a baraita) that the blessing for rain is recited when the groom goes out to meet the bride (i.e., when raindrops form bubbles). Rav Yehuda says the blessing is 'Modim anachnu lach al kol tipa v'tipa shehoradeta lanu', and Rabbi Yochanan concludes with a longer text ending with 'Baruch Atah Hashem, Rov Hahoda'ot'.

items.text: Dispute over the conclusion: 'Rov Hahoda'ot' vs. 'Ha'el Hahoda'ot'
items.text_en: Dispute over the conclusion: 'Rov Hahoda'ot' vs. 'Ha'el Hahoda'ot'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the phrase 'Rov Hahoda'ot' (the majority of thanksgivings) implying not all. Rava suggests saying 'Ha'el Hahoda'ot' (the God of thanksgivings). Rav Pappa concludes that one should say both phrases together.

items.text: Reconciling the blessing for rain with 'Hatov vehametiv'
items.text_en: Reconciling the blessing for rain with 'Hatov vehametiv'
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the Mishnah's 'Hatov vehametiv' for rain applies when one hears about rain (good news), but the baraita's blessing applies when one sees rain. Further, when seeing rain, if it is light rain one says the baraita's blessing, but if abundant, one says 'Hatov vehametiv'. Alternatively, both cases are abundant rain, but one with land says 'Hatov vehametiv' (benefiting himself and others), while one without land says the other blessing.

items.text: When does one say 'Hatov vehametiv'? Cases of partnership and benefit to others
items.text_en: When does one say 'Hatov vehametiv'? Cases of partnership and benefit to others
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether one with land says 'Hatov vehametiv', citing a Mishnah that for a new house or vessels one says 'Shehecheyanu' for his own, and 'Hatov vehametiv' for his and others'. It resolves that 'Hatov vehametiv' is said when one has a partner. Further challenges from a baraita about a wife giving birth to a son (where the wife benefits), inheriting a father (where brothers inherit), and changing wine (where drinking companions benefit) are all resolved by noting that others benefit alongside him.

items.text: Dispute on blessing for new items: Rav Huna vs. Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Dispute on blessing for new items: Rav Huna vs. Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Rav Huna says the Mishnah's rule that one recites a blessing for a new house or vessels applies only if one has no similar items, but if he has similar items, he need not bless. Rabbi Yochanan says even if he has similar items, he must bless.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rabbi Yochanan on blessing for repeated acquisitions
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rabbi Yochanan on blessing for repeated acquisitions
items.desc_en: Two versions of Rav Huna's statement are presented: in the first, if one acquired and then acquired again, all agree no blessing is needed; in the second, Rav Huna says only if he did not acquire previously, but if he did, no blessing is needed, while Rabbi Yochanan requires a blessing even then.

items.text: Supporting baraita from Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Supporting baraita from Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: for a new house or vessels without similar ones, one must bless; if he has similar ones, Rabbi Meir says no blessing, Rabbi Yehuda says always bless.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the versions against the baraita
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the versions against the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that according to the first version, Rav Huna aligns with Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yochanan with Rabbi Yehuda. But according to the second version, Rav Huna aligns with Rabbi Yehuda, while Rabbi Yochanan matches neither.

items.text: Resolution: Rabbi Yochanan's position and the reason for the baraita's formulation
items.text_en: Resolution: Rabbi Yochanan's position and the reason for the baraita's formulation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that according to Rabbi Yehuda, even if he acquired and then acquired again, he must bless; the baraita only disputes 'has and acquires' to show the strength of Rabbi Meir, who exempts even in that case. The Gemara questions why not show Rabbi Yehuda's strength instead, and answers that the lenient position is preferred.

items.text: Blessing on bad and good events
items.text_en: Blessing on bad and good events
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states one blesses on bad as on good. The Gemara explains: bad like finding a pit in his field that improves it, good like finding a treasure that might be taken by the king.

items.text: Prayer for a pregnant wife and the limits of prayer
items.text_en: Prayer for a pregnant wife and the limits of prayer
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says praying for a pregnant wife to give birth to a male is a vain prayer. Rav Yosef questions this with Leah's prayer that turned Dinah from a male to a female. Two answers: one says we do not mention miracles, another says Leah was within forty days when prayer is effective. Rav Yitzchak adds that if both parents emit simultaneously, prayer can affect the gender.

items.text: Fear and trust: Hillel and the disciples
items.text_en: Fear and trust: Hillel and the disciples
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses one who hears a cry and is confident it is not from his home. A baraita about Hillel illustrates this. Rava explains the verse can be read both ways. Two stories follow: Rabbi Yishmael rebukes a fearful student, and Rav Hamnuna rebukes Yehuda bar Natan for sighing, distinguishing fear of Torah from other fear.

items.text: Prayers upon entering and leaving a city
items.text_en: Prayers upon entering and leaving a city
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses entering a city. A baraita details the prayers: entering, after entering, before leaving, and after leaving. Rav Matna limits this to a city without capital punishment, but another version says even with it, one might need a defender.

items.text: Prayer upon entering a bathhouse and the danger of opening one's mouth to Satan
items.text_en: Prayer upon entering a bathhouse and the danger of opening one's mouth to Satan
items.desc_en: A baraita gives the prayer for entering a bathhouse. Abaye warns not to say it lest one open his mouth to Satan, citing Resh Lakish and Rav Yosef with a verse. Upon exiting, one says a blessing. A story about Rabbi Avahu illustrates the danger.

items.text: Prayer for bloodletting and the permission for doctors
items.text_en: Prayer for bloodletting and the permission for doctors
items.desc_en: Rav Acha gives the prayer for bloodletting. Abaye objects, citing the school of Rabbi Yishmael that doctors have permission to heal. Upon standing, one says 'Blessed is the Healer without charge.'

items.text: Prayer upon entering the bathroom and Abaye's correction
items.text_en: Prayer upon entering the bathroom and Abaye's correction
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents the formula for entering a bathroom, addressing the angels. Abaye objects that this might cause the angels to leave, and offers an alternative formula. It then gives the blessing upon exiting, praising God for creating the body's openings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the initial formula for entering a bathroom, addressing the ministering angels.
Abaye objects that the initial formula might cause the angels to leave him.
Abaye offers an alternative formula for entering the bathroom, asking the angels to guard and wait for him.
The Gemara presents the blessing recited upon exiting the bathroom, praising God for creating the body's openings.

items.text: Dispute over the concluding formula of the bathroom blessing
items.text_en: Dispute over the concluding formula of the bathroom blessing
items.desc_en: Rav suggests concluding with 'רוֹפֵא חוֹלִים', but Samuel objects that this implies everyone is sick. Rav Sheshet suggests 'מַפְלִיא לַעֲשׂוֹת'. Rav Pappa concludes that both should be said: 'רוֹפֵא כׇל בָּשָׂר וּמַפְלִיא לַעֲשׂוֹת'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what concluding formula should be used for the bathroom blessing.
Rav proposes concluding with 'רוֹפֵא חוֹלִים' (Healer of the sick).
Samuel objects that Rav's formula implies everyone is sick.
Samuel proposes concluding with 'רוֹפֵא כׇל בָּשָׂר' (Healer of all flesh).
Rav Sheshet proposes concluding with 'מַפְלִיא לַעֲשׂוֹת' (Who does wondrously).
Rav Pappa rules that both formulas should be combined: 'רוֹפֵא כׇל בָּשָׂר וּמַפְלִיא לַעֲשׂוֹת'.

items.text: Prayers for going to sleep and waking up
items.text_en: Prayers for going to sleep and waking up
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides the full text of the bedtime prayer, including reciting the first paragraph of Shema and a lengthy supplication. It then gives the morning prayer upon waking, thanking God for restoring the soul.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the bedtime prayer, which includes reciting the first paragraph of Shema and a blessing about sleep.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of the bedtime supplication
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of the bedtime supplication
sub.desc_en: The Gemara provides the full text of the lengthy supplication recited before sleep, asking for protection from evil and a peaceful rest.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of the morning prayer
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of the morning prayer
sub.desc_en: The Gemara provides the full text of the morning prayer upon waking, thanking God for restoring the soul.

items.text: Blessings for daily activities upon waking
items.text_en: Blessings for daily activities upon waking
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists a series of blessings to be recited upon hearing a rooster, opening eyes, sitting up, dressing, standing, stepping on the ground, walking, putting on shoes, girding a belt, covering the head, wrapping in tzitzit, donning tefillin, washing hands, and washing the face, each with its specific formula.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara instructs that upon hearing a rooster, one should recite the blessing 'who gave the rooster understanding to distinguish between day and night'.
Upon opening one's eyes, one recites the blessing 'who opens the eyes of the blind'.
Upon sitting up, one recites the blessing 'who releases the bound'.
Upon dressing, one recites the blessing 'who clothes the naked'.
Upon standing upright, one recites the blessing 'who straightens the bent'.
Upon stepping onto the ground, one recites the blessing 'who spreads the earth upon the waters'.
Upon walking, one recites the blessing 'who establishes the steps of a man'.
Upon putting on shoes, one recites the blessing 'who has provided me with all my needs'.
Upon girding a belt, one recites the blessing 'who girds Israel with strength'.
Upon covering the head, one recites the blessing 'who crowns Israel with glory'.
Upon wrapping in tzitzit, one recites the blessing 'who commanded us to wrap ourselves in tzitzit'.
Upon donning tefillin on the arm, one recites the blessing 'who commanded us to lay tefillin'.
Upon donning tefillin on the head, one recites the blessing 'who commanded us concerning the commandment of tefillin'.
Upon washing hands, one recites the blessing 'who commanded us concerning the washing of hands'.

Upon washing the face, one recites a longer blessing including 'who removes the bonds of sleep from my eyes' and a prayer for the day, concluding with 'who bestows good kindnesses upon His people Israel'.

items.text: Explanation of blessing on bad events as on good
items.text_en: Explanation of blessing on bad events as on good
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how one can bless on bad as on good, given the different blessings for good and bad news. Rava explains that the obligation is to receive both with joy, not to recite the same blessing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Mishnah's rule to bless on bad as on good can be literal, given that the blessings for good news (הטוב והמטיב) and bad news (דיין האמת) are different.
Rava resolves the difficulty by explaining that the Mishnah means one must receive both good and bad with joy, not recite the same blessing.

items.text: Biblical sources for blessing on both good and bad
items.text_en: Biblical sources for blessing on both good and bad
items.desc_en: Various amoraim cite verses to support the obligation to praise God for both good and bad: Rav Acha bar Levi from Psalms, Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani from Psalms, Rabbi Tanchum from Psalms, and the Rabbis from Job.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Levi in the name of Rabbi Levi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Levi in the name of Rabbi Levi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Levi cites Psalms 101:1 to show that one must praise God for both חסד (kindness) and משפט (judgment).
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani cites Psalms 56:11 to distinguish between praising God for the good measure and the punitive measure.
Rabbi Tanchum cites Psalms 116:13 and 116:3 to show that one calls upon God's name both in salvation and in distress.
The Rabbis cite Job 1:21 to teach that one must bless God's name both when He gives and when He takes away.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's maxim and story of trust in God
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's maxim and story of trust in God
items.desc_en: Rav Huna in the name of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Akiva teaches that one should always say 'כׇּל דְּעָבֵיד רַחֲמָנָא לְטָב עָבֵיד'. The Gemara illustrates this with a story of Rabbi Akiva who, despite losing his rooster, donkey, and lamp, maintained this faith, and was later saved from a marauding band that captured the town.

sub.text: Rav Huna citing Rav in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Rav Huna citing Rav in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna in the name of Rav citing Rabbi Meir teaches the maxim that one should always say 'כׇּל דְּעָבֵיד רַחֲמָנָא לְטָב עָבֵיד' (everything the Merciful One does is for good).

The Gemara illustrates the maxim with a story of Rabbi Akiva who, while traveling, was denied lodging, lost his rooster, donkey, and lamp, yet maintained faith, and was later saved from a marauding band that captured the town.

items.text: Opening statement on brevity before God
items.text_en: Opening statement on brevity before God
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by citing Rav Huna in the name of Rabbi Meir that one's words before God should be few, citing Ecclesiastes 5:1.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing Rav Huna in the name of Rav and Rabbi Meir, teaching that one's words before God should be few, quoting Ecclesiastes 5:1.

items.text: Two yetzers from the double yod in וייצר
items.text_en: Two yetzers from the double yod in וייצר
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda derives from the double yod in וייצר that God created two inclinations, good and evil. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects that animals also have an aggressive yetzer, and instead explains the double yod as referring to two faces (du partsufin) as per Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi and Rabbi Yirmeya ben Elazar.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's derasha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's derasha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda derives from the double yod in 'וייצר' that God created two inclinations, one good and one evil.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects that animals also have an aggressive yetzer, even though the double yod is not written regarding them.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative explanation
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative explanation
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak instead explains the double yod as referring to the two inclinations as per Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi's statement.

sub.text: Alternative support from Rabbi Yirmeya ben Elazar
sub.text_en: Alternative support from Rabbi Yirmeya ben Elazar
sub.desc_en: Alternatively, the double yod refers to the two faces (du partsufin) created in the first man, as per Rabbi Yirmeya ben Elazar.

items.text: Debate: Was the first woman created from a face or a tail?
items.text_en: Debate: Was the first woman created from a face or a tail?
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel debate whether the first woman was created from a face (partsuf) or a tail (zanav). The Gemara analyzes each view against verses like 'Achor vaKedem tzartani' and 'Vayiven... et hatzela', concluding that the tail view explains 'Achor' as referring to the Flood, not the serpent's curse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse about the building of the rib and introduces the debate between Rav and Shmuel over whether the first woman was created from a face (פרצוף) or a tail (זנב).
The Gemara notes that the face view fits the verse 'Achor vaKedem tzartani', but asks how the tail view explains that verse.
Rabbi Ammi explains that 'Achor' refers to the creation of the world and 'Kedem' to punishment.
The Gemara objects that the punishment of the serpent cannot be intended, because in curses the smaller is cursed first, contradicting the order of 'Achor vaKedem'.
The Gemara resolves that the punishment refers to the Flood, where the verse lists man before beast, fitting the order of 'Achor vaKedem'.

items.text: Further support for the tail view
items.text_en: Further support for the tail view
items.desc_en: The Gemara continues to reconcile the tail view with verses: the double yod in וייצר is explained by Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi's 'oy li miyotzri', 'Zachar u'nekevah' is explained by Rabbi Avahu's resolution, and 'Vayisgor basar tachtenah' refers to the place of the cut.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the tail view, how is the double yod in 'וייצר' (and He formed) explained?

Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi explains that the double yod alludes to the two inclinations: the yetzer tov and yetzer hara, as expressed in his exclamation 'oy li miyotzri oy li miyitzri' (woe to me from my Creator, woe to me from my inclination).
The Gemara asks: according to the tail view, how is the verse 'זכר ונקבה בראם' (male and female He created them) explained?
Rabbi Avahu resolves the apparent contradiction between 'זכר ונקבה בראם' and 'כי בצלם אלהים עשה את האדם' by explaining that initially God intended to create two, but ultimately only one was created.
The Gemara asks: according to the tail view, how is the verse 'ויסגר בשר תחתנה' (and He closed up the flesh in its place) explained?

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya / Rav Zevid / Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya / Rav Zevid / Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's answer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya (or alternatively Rav Zevid or Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak) explains that the verse refers to the place of the cut where the tail was removed.

items.text: Explaining 'Vayiven' for the face view
items.text_en: Explaining 'Vayiven' for the face view
items.desc_en: For the face view, 'Vayiven' is explained by Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya as braiding (kile'ah), and by Rav Chisda as building like a storehouse. The verse 'Vayevi'eha' teaches that God served as a groomsman, establishing the custom of a great person escorting a lesser one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the view that the first woman was created from a tail (זָנָב), the verse 'וַיִּבֶן' (He built) fits, but according to the view that she was created from a face (פַּרְצוּף), how is 'וַיִּבֶן' explained?
Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya explains that 'וַיִּבֶן' means God braided (קִלְּעָה) Eve's hair and brought her to Adam, since in coastal cities they call a braider 'בַּנָּיְיתָא' (builder).
Rav Chisda (or a baraita) explains that 'וַיִּבֶן' means God built Eve like a storehouse: narrow at the top and wide at the bottom to receive the fetus.
Rabbi Yirmeya ben Elazar teaches that the verse 'וַיְבִיאֶהָ' shows God served as a groomsman for Adam, establishing the custom that a great person escorts a lesser one without resentment.

items.text: Which part went first? And laws of walking behind a woman
items.text_en: Which part went first? And laws of walking behind a woman
items.desc_en: For the face view, Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak determines the man went first based on a baraita that a man should not walk behind a woman. The Gemara then discusses the prohibition of walking behind a woman, exceptions, and the severity of staring at a woman's hand. It also addresses the case of Manoach and Elkanah walking 'after' their wives, reinterpreted as following their advice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the view that Adam was created as a face (androgynous), which part (male or female) went first?
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers that the man went first, citing a baraita that a man should not walk behind a woman.
A baraita teaches that one who gives money to a woman to gaze at her will not be acquitted from the judgment of Gehinnom.
Rav Nachman objects that Manoach was an ignoramus because the verse says he walked after his wife.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak rejects the objection, explaining that 'after' in those verses means after her words and advice, not literally behind her.
Rav Ashi supports Rav Nachman's view that Manoach was an ignoramus, citing that even Rebecca walked after the man, not before him.
Rabbi Yochanan resolves the prohibition of walking behind a woman, listing exceptions such as carrying a load, having another entrance, riding a donkey, or wearing tefillin.

items.text: The nature of the evil inclination and the organs' functions
items.text_en: The nature of the evil inclination and the organs' functions
items.desc_en: Rav compares the evil inclination to a fly between the heart's openings; Shmuel compares it to a grain of wheat. A baraita describes the kidneys advising, the heart understanding, the tongue articulating, etc.

sub.desc_en: Rav compares the evil inclination (יצר הרע) to a fly sitting between the two openings of the heart, citing the verse 'זְבוּבֵי מָוֶת יַבְאִישׁ יַבִּיעַ שֶׁמֶן רוֹקֵחַ' (Dead flies make the perfumer's oil stink).
Shmuel offers an alternative comparison: the evil inclination is like a grain of wheat, citing the verse 'לַפֶּתַח חַטָּאת רוֹבֵץ' (Sin crouches at the door).

A baraita teaches that a person has two kidneys, one advising for good and one for evil, and it is reasonable that the good kidney is on the right and the evil on the left, as per the verse 'לֵב חָכָם לִימִינוֹ וְלֵב כְּסִיל לִשְׂמֹאלוֹ' (A wise heart is to his right, a foolish heart to his left).

A baraita lists the functions of the organs: the kidneys advise, the heart understands, the tongue articulates, the mouth completes, the esophagus (ושט) brings in and brings out all types of food, and the trachea (קנה) produces sound.

items.text: Functions of the bodily organs
items.text_en: Functions of the bodily organs
items.desc_en: A baraita describes the functions of various organs: the lung absorbs liquids, the liver causes anger, the gall bladder drops a drop and pacifies, the spleen laughs, the stomach grinds, the womb sleeps, and the nose wakes. If both sleep or both wake, one dies immediately.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists the functions of bodily organs and states that if both the nose and womb sleep or wake simultaneously, one dies immediately.

items.text: The yetzer governs the righteous, wicked, and intermediate
items.text_en: The yetzer governs the righteous, wicked, and intermediate
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili teaches that the righteous are judged by their good inclination, the wicked by their evil inclination, and the intermediate by both. Rabba considers himself intermediate, but Abaye objects. Rava and Rav then discuss the purpose of the world and how one can know if they are completely righteous.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili teaches that the righteous are judged by their good inclination, the wicked by their evil inclination, and the intermediate by both.
Rabba considers himself and his colleagues intermediate, but Abaye objects that this would leave no one alive.
Rava and Rav explain that the world was created only for the completely wicked or completely righteous, and Rav identifies Ahab and Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa as exemplars of this world and the next.

items.text: Interpretation of 'with all your soul' and 'with all your might'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'with all your soul' and 'with all your might'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer explains that the Torah uses both 'with all your soul' and 'with all your might' to cover two types of people: those who love their body more than their money, and those who love their money more than their body. Rabbi Akiva interprets 'with all your soul' to mean even if He takes your soul.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer explains the double language of 'בכל נפשך' and 'בכל מאדך' for those who value body or money more, and Rabbi Akiva interprets 'בכל נפשך' as even if He takes your soul.
Rabbi Eliezer answers that the two phrases cover different cases: one for those who love their body more than money, the other for those who love money more than their body.
Rabbi Akiva interprets 'בְּכָל נַפְשְׁךָ' to mean even if God takes your soul, i.e., martyrdom.

items.text: The martyrdom of Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: The martyrdom of Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts the story of Rabbi Akiva's arrest and execution by the Romans for teaching Torah publicly. He was combed with iron combs while reciting the Shema, and his soul departed as he said 'Echad'. A heavenly voice declared him worthy of the World to Come.

sub.desc_en: The baraita recounts that the evil kingdom decreed against Torah study, and Pappus ben Yehuda found Rabbi Akiva publicly teaching and warned him of the danger.
Rabbi Akiva responds with a parable of a fox and fish, arguing that if Torah is their life source, abandoning it for safety is even more dangerous.
The baraita relates that soon after, Rabbi Akiva was arrested and imprisoned alongside Pappus, and Rabbi Akiva declared Pappus fortunate for being arrested over Torah study.

The baraita describes Rabbi Akiva's martyrdom: as he was being combed with iron combs at the time of the Shema, he prolonged the word 'Echad' until his soul departed, and a heavenly voice declared him blessed.
The ministering angels questioned the justice of such suffering for Torah, and a heavenly voice responded that Rabbi Akiva is destined for the World to Come.

items.text: Restrictions on facing the Temple while relieving oneself
items.text_en: Restrictions on facing the Temple while relieving oneself
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav and Rabbi Yochanan limit the prohibition of facing the Temple to within the area of Tzofim, when one can see it, and when the Divine Presence rests there.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda citing Rav, and Rabbi Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav, and Rabbi Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav and Rabbi Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan limit the prohibition of treating the eastern gate lightly to within sight of the Temple, when the Divine Presence rests.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav limits the prohibition to within the area of Tzofim and when one can see the Temple.
Rabbi Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan adds that the prohibition also requires no partition and that the Divine Presence rests there.

items.text: Dispute about directions for relieving oneself in Judea and Galilee
items.text_en: Dispute about directions for relieving oneself in Judea and Galilee
items.desc_en: A baraita states that in Judea one should face north-south, in Galilee east-west, but Rabbi Yosei permits all directions with conditions. A second baraita adds Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Akiva's opinions. The Gemara notes the differences between the tannaim regarding the Temple's existence and outside the Land.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the Tanna Kamma's ruling: in Judea one must face north-south, in Galilee east-west.
Rabbi Yosei permits all directions, but only under specific conditions: when the Temple is visible, no fence, and the Divine Presence resides.
The Sages prohibit all directions unconditionally, disagreeing with Rabbi Yosei.
The Gemara asks: the Sages' position is identical to the Tanna Kamma's — what is the difference between them?
The Gemara resolves: the difference lies in the case of facing the sides (diagonals) — the Tanna Kamma forbids, the Sages permit.
A second baraita repeats the Tanna Kamma's ruling with slightly different wording.
Rabbi Yosei again permits, but here only mentions the condition of visibility (רוֹאֶה).
Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes: when the Temple stands it is forbidden, when it does not it is permitted.
Rabbi Akiva forbids facing east-west in all places, unconditionally.
The Gemara asks: Rabbi Akiva's position is identical to the Tanna Kamma — what is the difference between them?
The Gemara resolves: the difference is the case of outside the Land of Israel — the Tanna Kamma permits, Rabbi Akiva forbids.

items.text: Rabba's practice and Abaye's correction
items.text_en: Rabba's practice and Abaye's correction
items.desc_en: Rabba would relieve himself facing east-west, but Abaye turned him north-south. Rabba rebuked Abaye, stating he follows Rabbi Akiva who forbids facing any direction except north-south everywhere.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah's students faced east-west, Abaye turned them north-south, and Rabbah rebuked the one who disturbed him, stating he follows Rabbi Akiva who forbids in all places.
Rabba rebuked Abaye, asserting that he follows Rabbi Akiva who forbids facing east-west everywhere.

items.text: Stories of Rabbi Akiva and Ben Azzai learning bathroom conduct
items.text_en: Stories of Rabbi Akiva and Ben Azzai learning bathroom conduct
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva recounts entering the bathroom after Rabbi Yehoshua and learning three things: not to face east-west, to sit rather than stand, and to wipe with the left hand. Ben Azzai similarly learns from Rabbi Akiva, and both are challenged by their students but defend their actions as Torah study.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva recounts entering the bathroom after Rabbi Yehoshua and learning three rules of bathroom conduct.
Ben Azzai objects that Rabbi Akiva was impertinent to observe his teacher so closely.
Rabbi Akiva defends his actions, stating that it is Torah and he must learn.
Ben Azzai similarly recounts entering the bathroom after Rabbi Akiva and learning the same three rules.
Rabbi Yehuda objects that Ben Azzai was impertinent to his teacher.
Ben Azzai defends his actions with the same justification: it is Torah and he must learn.

items.text: Rav Kahana hides under Rav's bed
items.text_en: Rav Kahana hides under Rav's bed
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana hides under Rav's bed and observes his intimate conduct with his wife. When Rav discovers him, he rebukes him, but Rav Kahana defends himself by saying it is Torah and he needs to learn.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana hides under Rav's bed and observes Rav's intimate behavior with his wife.
Rav Kahana comments that Rav's mouth appears as if it has never tasted a cooked dish, implying lustful behavior.
Rav rebukes Rav Kahana for being there, stating that such behavior is improper.
Rav Kahana defends himself by stating that it is Torah and he must learn.

items.text: Reasons for wiping with the left hand
items.text_en: Reasons for wiping with the left hand
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why one should wipe with the left hand and not the right. Various amoraim give reasons: because the Torah was given with the right hand, because the right hand is close to the mouth, because one ties tefillin on the left arm, and because one points out the reasons of Torah with the right hand. A baraisa adds that Rabbi Eliezer says because one eats with the right hand, Rabbi Yehoshua says because one writes with it, and Rabbi Akiva says because one points out reasons of Torah with it.
