sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why one should wipe with the left hand and not the right.
Rava answers that the Torah was given with the right hand, citing the verse 'מימינו אש דת למו' (At His right hand was a fiery law unto them).
Rabba bar bar Chana answers that the right hand is close to the mouth, used for eating.
Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish answers that one ties תפילין (phylacteries) on the left arm with the right hand.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers that one points out the reasons of Torah with the right hand.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Eliezer says one should not wipe with the right hand because he eats with it.
Rabbi Yehoshua says one should not wipe with the right hand because he writes with it.
Rabbi Akiva says one should not wipe with the right hand because he points out the reasons of Torah with it.

items.text: Benefits of modesty in the bathroom
items.text_en: Benefits of modesty in the bathroom
items.desc_en: Rabbi Tanchum bar Chanilai says that one who is modest in the bathroom is saved from three things: snakes, scorpions, and harmful spirits. Some add that even his dreams are settled for him.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Tanchum bar Chanilai states that one who is modest in the bathroom is saved from snakes, scorpions, and harmful spirits.
Some add that such a person's dreams are also settled for him.

items.text: The dangerous bathroom in Tiberias
items.text_en: The dangerous bathroom in Tiberias
items.desc_en: There was a dangerous bathroom in Tiberias where two people entering together would be harmed even by day. Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi entered alone and were unharmed. When asked, they said they learned that the tradition for the bathroom is modesty and silence, and for suffering is silence and prayer.

sub.desc_en: Introduces the dangerous bathroom in Tiberias and how two people entering together would be harmed even by day.
Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi enter alone and are unharmed.
The rabbis ask Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi if they are not afraid.
They respond that they have a tradition: the tradition for the bathroom is modesty (צניעות) and silence, and for suffering is silence and prayer.

items.text: Practices of Abaye and Rava regarding bathroom accompaniment
items.text_en: Practices of Abaye and Rava regarding bathroom accompaniment
items.desc_en: Abaye's mother raised a lamb to accompany him to the bathroom, and the Gemara questions why not a goat, explaining that a goat might be confused with a demon. Rava, before becoming head of the academy, had his wife knock a nut on a jug for him; after becoming head, she made a hole and put her hand on his head.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Abaye's mother raised a lamb to accompany him to the bathroom.
The Gemara asks why a goat was not raised instead, and explains that a goat might be confused with a demon.
The Gemara recounts that before Rava became head, his wife Bat Rav Chisda would knock a nut on a jug for him, and after he became head, she made a hole and put her hand on his head.

items.text: Distance for modesty when relieving oneself
items.text_en: Distance for modesty when relieving oneself
items.desc_en: Ulla and Isi bar Nathan debate the required distance for modesty: behind a fence, one may relieve himself immediately, but in a field, one must wait until a sneeze is not heard or until no one sees him. The Gemara raises objections from a mishna about olive press workers, and resolves that purity laws are more lenient. Rav Ashi explains that Isi bar Nathan meant that no one sees his exposed flesh, but he himself can see it.

sub.desc_en: Ulla and Isi bar Nathan state the required distance for modesty when relieving oneself: behind a fence one may do so immediately, but in a field one must wait until a sneeze is not heard (Ulla) or until no one sees him (Isi bar Nathan).
The Gemara raises an objection from a mishna about olive press workers who go behind a fence and remain pure, implying immediate permission contradicts Ulla's requirement of waiting.
The Gemara answers that the mishna refers to purity laws, where the rabbis were lenient.
The Gemara objects further from a baraita that says one must be far enough that he can still see the other, contradicting Isi bar Nathan's condition that no one sees him.
The Gemara answers that the baraita deals with eaters of pure food, where the rabbis were lenient.
Rav Ashi resolves the contradiction by explaining that Isi bar Nathan meant that no one sees his exposed flesh, but he himself can see it.

items.text: The eulogizer and the definition of modesty
items.text_en: The eulogizer and the definition of modesty
items.desc_en: A eulogizer praised a deceased person as modest in his ways. Rav Nachman challenged him, saying only one who is modest in the bathroom can be called modest. The Gemara explains Rav Nachman's concern: because the eulogizer and those who respond will be punished if they lie.

sub.desc_en: A eulogizer descends before Rav Nachman and praises the deceased as modest in his ways.
Rav Nachman challenges the eulogizer, asking if he entered the bathroom with the deceased to verify his modesty.
The Gemara cites a baraita that one is only called modest if he is modest in the bathroom.
The Gemara asks why Rav Nachman cared about the accuracy of the eulogy.
The Gemara answers that Rav Nachman was concerned because a baraita teaches that punishment is exacted from eulogizers and those who respond for false praise.

items.text: Definition of a modest person and the practice of regular elimination
items.text_en: Definition of a modest person and the practice of regular elimination
items.desc_en: A baraisa defines a modest person as one who relieves himself at night in the same place as by day. The Gemara challenges this with Rav Yehuda's statement that one should train himself to go morning and evening to avoid needing to go far, and with stories of Rava and Rabbi Zeira who went far by day but not at night. The resolution is that the baraisa means in the same manner, not the same place, or Rav Ashi says it refers to a corner.

sub.desc_en: A baraisa defines a modest person as one who relieves himself at night in the same place as by day.

The Gemara objects by citing Rav Yehuda's statement that one should train himself to go morning and evening to avoid needing to go far, and by citing stories of Rava and Rabbi Zeira who went far by day but not at night.
The Gemara resolves that the baraisa means 'in the same manner' as by day, not the same place.
Rav Ashi offers an alternative resolution: even if the baraisa means 'in the same place,' it refers only to a corner, not the entire area.

items.text: The practice of regular elimination and a remedy for forgetting
items.text_en: The practice of regular elimination and a remedy for forgetting
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says one should train himself to go morning and evening to avoid needing to go far. Ben Azzai adds that one should go before sitting to study, and not sit and delay. If one forgets and sits and delays, his remedy upon standing is to recite a formula against witchcraft.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav rules that one should always train himself to eliminate morning and evening so he does not need to go far.
A baraita is cited where Ben Azzai similarly instructs to go early and late, and adds that one should go before sitting to study, not delay, or else sorcery will afflict him.
The Gemara asks: if one forgot and sat down and delayed, what is his remedy?
The Gemara answers: when he stands up, he should recite a formula against witchcraft.

items.text: Opening baraita and statements on proper conduct
items.text_en: Opening baraita and statements on proper conduct
items.desc_en: Ben Azzai teaches that one may lie on any bed except the ground and sit on any seat except a beam. Shmuel adds that sleep and excretion at dawn are like a whetstone to iron.

sub.desc_en: Ben Azzai rules that one may lie on any bed except the ground and sit on any seat except a beam.
Shmuel adds that sleep and excretion at dawn are like a whetstone to iron.

items.text: Bar Kappara's maxims and Karna's proverb
items.text_en: Bar Kappara's maxims and Karna's proverb
items.desc_en: Bar Kappara sells advice for dinars: eat when hungry, drink when thirsty, pour when your pot boils. Karna reads a Roman proverb about selling figs.

sub.desc_en: Bar Kappara sells maxims for dinars: eat when hungry, drink when thirsty, pour when your pot boils.
Karna reads a Roman proverb: sell your father's figs.

items.text: Abaye's instruction on modesty in the fields
items.text_en: Abaye's instruction on modesty in the fields
items.desc_en: Abaye tells the rabbis that when walking in the paths of Machoza to the fields, they should not look to either side, lest they see women sitting, which is improper.

sub.desc_en: Abaye instructs the rabbis that when walking in the paths of Machoza to the fields, they should not look to either side, lest they see women sitting, which is improper.

items.text: Rav Safra and Rabbi Abba: bathroom etiquette
items.text_en: Rav Safra and Rabbi Abba: bathroom etiquette
items.desc_en: Rav Safra enters the bathroom; Rabbi Abba knocks. Rav Safra invites him in, but Rabbi Abba rebukes him, citing a baraita about the Temple bathroom that shows one should not enter if occupied. Rav Safra thought it was a matter of danger, citing a baraita about a returning column causing dropsy.

sub.desc_en: Rav Safra enters the bathroom; Rabbi Abba knocks at the door.
After Rav Safra exits, Rabbi Abba rebukes him for not knowing the etiquette from the Temple bathroom.
The Gemara explains that Rav Safra thought danger was involved, citing a baraita about a returning column causing dropsy.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar and the Roman: a lesson from David and Saul
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar and the Roman: a lesson from David and Saul
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar is pushed by a Roman in the bathroom and leaves; a snake injures the Roman. Rabbi Elazar applies a verse about David sparing Saul, explaining that David told Saul he deserved death as a pursuer, but modesty saved him, referring to Saul entering a cave to relieve himself.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar enters the bathroom; a Roman pushes him out, and a snake injures the Roman instead.
Rabbi Elazar applies the verse 'וְאֶתֵּן אָדָם תַּחְתֶּיךָ' (I will give a man in your place), reading 'אָדָם' as 'אֱדוֹם' (Edom/Rome).
The gemara cites the verse 'He said: I could have killed you, but I had pity on you.'
The gemara questions the verse's wording: it should say 'וְאָמַרְתִּי' (I said) and 'וְחַסְתִּי' (I had pity) in first person.
Rabbi Elazar explains that David told Saul: 'You deserve death as a pursuer, but your modesty (צניעות) spared you.'
The gemara asks: 'What was that modesty?'
Rabbi Elazar cites the verse about Saul entering a cave to relieve himself, and explains that Saul covered himself like a sukkah (סוכה), demonstrating modesty.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina on disrespecting garments
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina on disrespecting garments
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina says that one who disrespects garments will ultimately not benefit from them, citing David cutting Saul's cloak and later not being warmed by clothes.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina states that one who disrespects garments ultimately will not benefit from them, citing David cutting Saul's cloak as the source.

items.text: Interpretations of the plague after David's census
items.text_en: Interpretations of the plague after David's census
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains that God rebuked David for calling Him a 'tempter', leading to the census and plague. Various sages debate what God 'saw' to relent: Jacob, Isaac's ashes, silver of atonement, or the Temple. The dispute concludes that the Temple is the likely answer.

sub.desc_en: רבי אלעזר (Rabbi Elazar) explains that God rebuked David for calling Him a 'tempter', leading to the census and plague.
The Gemara asks the meaning of 'עֵת מוֹעֵד' (the appointed time).

sub.text: Shmuel Saba in the name of Rabbi Chanina
sub.text_en: Shmuel Saba in the name of Rabbi Chanina
sub.desc_en: שמואל סבא (Shmuel Saba) in the name of רבי חנינא (Rabbi Chanina) answers: from the slaughter of the daily offering until its sprinkling.
רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) answers: until exactly noon.
רבי אלעזר (Rabbi Elazar) explains that God told the angel to take a 'great one' (רב) from Israel, and אבישי בן צרויה (Avishai ben Tzeruya), equivalent to the majority of the Sanhedrin, died.
The Gemara asks what God 'saw' to relent from the plague.
רב (Rav) answers: He saw Jacob our patriarch, as it is written 'וַיֹּאמֶר יַעֲקֹב כַּאֲשֶׁר רָאָם' (And Jacob said when he saw them).
שמואל (Shmuel) answers: He saw Isaac's ashes, as it is written 'אֱלֹהִים יִרְאֶה לּוֹ הַשֶּׂה' (God will provide Himself the lamb).
רבי יצחק נפחא (Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha) answers: He saw the silver of atonement, as it is written 'וְלָקַחְתָּ אֶת כֶּסֶף הַכִּפּוּרִים' (And you shall take the atonement money).
רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) answers: He saw the Temple, as it is written 'בְּהַר ה׳ יֵרָאֶה' (On the mount where the Lord is seen).

sub.text: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani
sub.desc_en: רבי יעקב בר אידי (Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi) and רבי שמואל בר נחמני (Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani) dispute: one says the silver of atonement, the other the Temple; the Gemara concludes that the Temple is the likely answer.

items.text: Laws of entering the Temple Mount and spitting in synagogue
items.text_en: Laws of entering the Temple Mount and spitting in synagogue
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the prohibition of entering the Temple Mount with a staff, shoes, or as a shortcut (kappendarya). Rava permits spitting in the synagogue by analogy to shoes. Rav Papa objects, citing the kappendarya prohibition. The baraita resolves the analogy, and Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda adds a kal vachomer from sackcloth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the term 'kappandarya' means.
Rava explains that 'kappandarya' means a shortcut, as its name implies.

sub.text: Rav Chana bar Adda in the name of Rav Samma
sub.text_en: Rav Chana bar Adda in the name of Rav Samma
sub.desc_en: Rav Chana bar Adda cites Rav Samma's explanation that 'kappandarya' is like saying 'instead of going around the rows, I will enter this one.'

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites Rabbah bar Avuha's ruling that one who enters a synagogue not intending to make it a shortcut is permitted to do so later.
Rabbi Avahu rules that if a path originally passed through the site, one is permitted to use it as a shortcut.
Rabbi Chelbo cites Rav Huna that one who enters a synagogue to pray is permitted to make it a shortcut, citing a verse from Ezekiel.
The mishna states that spitting on the Temple Mount is prohibited through an a fortiori inference.

sub.text: Rav Bibi citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Rav Bibi citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Rav Bibi cites Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that spitting on the Temple Mount even today is like spitting in God's eye, citing a verse.
Rava rules that spitting in a synagogue is permitted, drawing an analogy to shoes which are prohibited on the Temple Mount but permitted in a synagogue.

sub.text: Rav Pappa / Ravina / Rav Adda bar Matna's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa / Ravina / Rav Adda bar Matna's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa (or others) objects to Rava's analogy, arguing that spitting should be derived from the prohibition of a shortcut (kappandarya) instead of shoes.
Rava rejects the objection, stating that the tanna derives the prohibition from shoes, not from the shortcut.
The Gemara cites a baraita that lists prohibitions on the Temple Mount and derives the prohibition of spitting from shoes via a kal vachomer.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's alternative kal vachomer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's alternative kal vachomer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda offers an alternative kal vachomer from sackcloth before a mortal king to prohibit spitting before the King of Kings.

sub.text: Rav Pappa / Ravina / Rav Adda bar Matna's clarification
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa / Ravina / Rav Adda bar Matna's clarification
sub.desc_en: The objector clarifies that he meant to apply stringency both on the Temple Mount and in the synagogue, not to derive spitting from the shortcut.

items.text: Rava's resolution on synagogue conduct
items.text_en: Rava's resolution on synagogue conduct
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proposed analogy from the Temple Mount to the synagogue regarding shoes, and Rava offers a new derivation from 'your house' to permit rekika and shoes in the synagogue while prohibiting the kapandarya.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if one derives from the Temple Mount's prohibition of shoes, the synagogue should also be permitted in shoes, but one could instead derive from the kapandarya (a type of head covering) that it is forbidden.

Rava resolves the issue by deriving from 'your house' that just as one is particular about the kapandarya but not about rekika (spitting) and shoes in one's home, so too in the synagogue only the kapandarya is forbidden, while rekika and shoes are permitted.

items.text: All blessings in the Temple concluded with 'from the world'
items.text_en: All blessings in the Temple concluded with 'from the world'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all blessings in the Temple concluded with 'from the world' because they did not answer 'Amen' there, derived from Nehemiah 9:5. The Gemara explains that each blessing requires its own praise.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all blessings in the Temple concluded with 'from the world'.
The Gemara asks why the Temple blessings had this unique conclusion, and answers that it was because they did not answer 'Amen' there.
The Gemara cites Nehemiah 9:5 as a proof that 'Amen' was not answered in the Temple, and adds a verse about blessing God's name.
The Gemara resolves that each blessing requires its own praise, derived from the verse 'וּמְרוֹמַם עַל כׇּל בְּרָכָה וּתְהִלָּה'.

items.text: The source for greeting with God's name
items.text_en: The source for greeting with God's name
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the phrase 'and he says' from the Mishnah, citing Boaz's greeting and the angel's greeting to Gideon, and then the verse 'Do not despise your mother when she is old' to show that greeting with God's name is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by the phrase 'and he says' in the context of greeting with God's name.
The Gemara cites Boaz's greeting and the angel's greeting to Gideon, and then the verse 'Do not despise your mother when she is old' to prove that greeting with God's name is permitted.

items.text: Rava's interpretation of 'It is time to act for the Lord'
items.text_en: Rava's interpretation of 'It is time to act for the Lord'
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the verse 'It is time to act for the Lord, they have made void Your Torah' can be interpreted from beginning to end and from end to beginning: the reason for acting is that the Torah is voided, and the reason the Torah is voided is that it is time to act.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'It is time to act for the Lord, they have made void Your Torah' and introduces Rava's interpretation.
Rava states that this verse can be interpreted both from its beginning to its end and from its end to its beginning.
The Gemara explains: from beginning to end, the reason for the time to act is that the Torah has been voided; from end to beginning, the reason the Torah is voided is that it is time to act.

items.text: Hillel's and Bar Kappara's teachings on when to teach Torah
items.text_en: Hillel's and Bar Kappara's teachings on when to teach Torah
items.desc_en: Hillel the Elder teaches to scatter Torah when the generation loves it and to gather when it does not. Bar Kappara teaches to gather from the lowly and to be a man where there is no man. Abaye deduces that where there is a man, one should not act as a man, and the Gemara clarifies this applies when both are equal.

sub.desc_en: Hillel the Elder teaches that when the generation loves Torah one should scatter it, and when not, one should gather it, citing verses.
Bar Kappara teaches that when Torah is lowly one should gather from it, and where there is no man one should be a man.
Abaye deduces from Bar Kappara's statement that where there is a man, one should not act as a man.
The Gemara objects that Abaye's deduction is obvious.
The Gemara resolves that Abaye's statement is necessary only when both scholars are equal in stature.

items.text: Bar Kappara on the small section that all Torah depends on
items.text_en: Bar Kappara on the small section that all Torah depends on
items.desc_en: Bar Kappara teaches that the verse 'In all your ways know Him, and He will make your paths straight' is a small section upon which all Torah depends. Rava adds that this applies even to a matter of transgression.

sub.desc_en: Bar Kappara identifies the small section upon which all Torah depends: 'In all your ways know Him, and He will make your paths straight'.
Rava adds that this principle applies even to a matter of transgression.

items.text: Bar Kappara on teaching a clean and easy trade
items.text_en: Bar Kappara on teaching a clean and easy trade
items.desc_en: Bar Kappara teaches that one should always teach his son a clean and easy trade. Rav Chisda identifies this as needlework (or embroidery).

sub.desc_en: Bar Kappara teaches that one should always teach his son a clean and easy trade.
Rav Chisda identifies the clean and easy trade as needlework (or embroidery).

items.text: Rabbi's teachings on friends, guardians, and the nazirite
items.text_en: Rabbi's teachings on friends, guardians, and the nazirite
items.desc_en: Rabbi teaches three things: one should not have too many friends, one should not appoint a guardian in his house (citing Potiphar), and the section of nazirite is adjacent to sotah to teach that one who sees a sotah in her disgrace should become a nazirite.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi teaches that one should never have too many friends, citing the verse 'אִישׁ רֵעִים לְהִתְרוֹעֵעַ' (a man of many friends comes to ruin).
Rabbi teaches that one should not appoint a guardian in his house, citing the example of Potiphar who appointed Joseph and thereby came to sin.
Rabbi explains that the section of nazirite is juxtaposed to the section of sotah to teach that one who sees a sotah in her disgrace should become a nazirite.

items.text: Chizkiya and Rav Nachman on the juxtaposition of sotah and terumot
items.text_en: Chizkiya and Rav Nachman on the juxtaposition of sotah and terumot
items.desc_en: Chizkiya bar Parnakh in the name of Rabbi Yochanan explains that the section of sotah is adjacent to terumot and ma'asrot to teach that one who does not give them will eventually need the priest through his wife. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds that if one gives them, he will become wealthy.

sub.text: Chizkiya bar Parnakh in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Chizkiya bar Parnakh in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Chizkiya bar Parnakh in the name of Rabbi Yochanan explains that the section of sotah is juxtaposed to terumot and ma'asrot to teach that one who does not give them will eventually need the priest through his wife.

sub.text: Chizkiya bar Parnakh in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Chizkiya bar Parnakh in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: He cites verses to support the claim: 'אִישׁ אֶת קֳדָשָׁיו לוֹ יִהְיוּ' and the adjacent sotah passage.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds that if one gives terumot and ma'asrot, he will become wealthy, citing the verse 'אִישׁ אֲשֶׁר יִתֵּן לַכֹּהֵן לוֹ יִהְיֶה'.

items.text: Teachings on associating God's name with one's distress
items.text_en: Teachings on associating God's name with one's distress
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Berekhya in the name of Rabbi Elazar HaKappar teaches that one who associates God's name with his distress will have his sustenance doubled. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani adds that his sustenance will flutter to him like a bird.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Berekhya in the name of Rabbi Elazar HaKappar
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Berekhya in the name of Rabbi Elazar HaKappar
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Berekhya teaches in the name of Rabbi Elazar HaKappar that one who associates God's name with his distress will have his livelihood doubled, citing the verse 'וְהָיָה שַׁדַּי בְּצָרֶיךָ וְכֶסֶף תּוֹעָפוֹת לָךְ' (And the Almighty be your treasure, and precious silver unto you).
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani adds that his sustenance flutters to him like a bird, citing the same verse 'וְכֶסֶף תּוֹעָפוֹת לָךְ' (and precious silver unto you).

items.text: Teaching on neglecting Torah and strength in distress
items.text_en: Teaching on neglecting Torah and strength in distress
items.desc_en: Rabbi Tavi in the name of Rabbi Yoshiya teaches that one who neglects Torah will have no strength to stand in distress. Rav Ami bar Matna in the name of Shmuel adds that this applies even to one mitzvah.

sub.text: Rabbi Tavi in the name of Rabbi Yoshiya
sub.text_en: Rabbi Tavi in the name of Rabbi Yoshiya
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Tavi in the name of Rabbi Yoshiya teaches that one who neglects Torah will have no strength to stand in distress, citing the verse 'הִתְרַפִּיתָ בְּיוֹם צָרָה צַר כֹּחֶכָה' (If you faint in the day of adversity, your strength is small indeed).

sub.text: Rav Ami bar Matna in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Ami bar Matna in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Ami bar Matna in the name of Shmuel adds that this applies even to one mitzvah, as the verse says 'הִתְרַפִּיתָ' (if you faint) in any case.

items.text: The story of Hanina ben Ahi Yehoshua and his excommunication
items.text_en: The story of Hanina ben Ahi Yehoshua and his excommunication
items.desc_en: Rav Safra reports that Rabbi Avahu recounted how Hanina ben Ahi Yehoshua intercalated years and fixed months outside Israel. The sages sent two scholars to confront him, and after a debate, they declared him in excommunication if he did not comply.

sub.desc_en: Rav Safra reports that Rabbi Avahu recounted how Hanina ben Ahi Yehoshua went to the diaspora and intercalated years and fixed months outside the Land of Israel.
The sages sent two scholars, Rabbi Yosei ben Kippar and the grandson of Zecharya ben Kevutal, and Hanina praised them, citing the Mishnah about Zecharya ben Kevutal's service in the Temple.
Hanina began ruling leniently while the scholars ruled strictly, and when he denounced them, they responded that his rulings were already established and could not be overturned.
Hanina asked why they contradicted him, and when they said it was because he intercalated years outside Israel, he cited Rabbi Akiva as a precedent who did the same.
The scholars rejected the comparison to Rabbi Akiva, noting that Akiva left no equal in Israel, and they warned Hanina that if he did not comply, he would be excommunicated.

items.text: Opening narrative: the decree against the exiles
items.text_en: Opening narrative: the decree against the exiles
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a decree that if the exiles do not listen, they will be cut off from Israel. The people weep and affirm their portion in God, citing the verse that Torah comes from Zion.

items.text: Gemara's question on contradiction in rulings
items.text_en: Gemara's question on contradiction in rulings
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a sage can permit what another forbade, citing a baraita that a colleague cannot reverse a ruling. It explains that they held this to prevent followers from being drawn after the dissenting sage.

items.text: The gathering in Yavneh: Rabbi Yehuda's first homily
items.text_en: The gathering in Yavneh: Rabbi Yehuda's first homily
items.desc_en: The sages gathered in Yavneh and opened with honoring the host. Rabbi Yehuda then spoke about the honor of Torah, deriving from the ark that even Torah scholars who travel to learn are worthy of honor. The Gemara adds that God told Moses to return the tent, and Rava notes that Joshua still served.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's second homily: Torah is beloved daily
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's second homily: Torah is beloved daily
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda expounds on the verse 'Listen, Israel, today you have become a nation,' teaching that Torah is as beloved each day as when it was given. Rabbi Tanchum adds that skipping even one reading of Shema is like never reading it. The Gemara then interprets 'Hasket' to mean forming groups for study, citing Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina that solitary study leads to foolishness and sin.

items.text: Further interpretations of 'Hasket': self-mortification and silence
items.text_en: Further interpretations of 'Hasket': self-mortification and silence
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish teaches that Torah endures only through self-sacrifice, as per the verse 'This is the Torah: a man who dies in a tent.' Rava adds that one should first learn Torah and then reflect, interpreting 'Hasket' as silence before study.

items.text: The cream of Torah: from the house of Rabbi Yannai
items.text_en: The cream of Torah: from the house of Rabbi Yannai
items.desc_en: The house of Rabbi Yannai expounds on the verse about squeezing milk and anger: one finds the cream of Torah by sacrificing childhood learning; a student who remains silent when angered merits to distinguish blood; and one who remains silent twice merits to distinguish monetary from capital cases, as per Rabbi Yishmael.

items.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani: self-abasement for Torah
items.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani: self-abasement for Torah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani teaches that one who debases himself for Torah will ultimately be exalted, while one who plots will be silenced.

items.text: Homilies on honoring guests: Rabbi Nechemya, Rabbi Yosei, Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Homilies on honoring guests: Rabbi Nechemya, Rabbi Yosei, Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: Each sage expounds on the honor due to hosts of Torah scholars: Rabbi Nechemya from Yitro, Rabbi Yosei from the Egyptians, and Rabbi Eliezer from Oved Edom. The Gemara concludes with the blessing that Oved Edom received: eight daughters-in-law each bearing six children.

items.text: Opening verse about Obed-Edom's descendants
items.text_en: Opening verse about Obed-Edom's descendants
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse describing the descendants of Obed-Edom, who were blessed by God, as a prooftext for a previous discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse about Obed-Edom's descendants being blessed by God, as a prooftext for a prior discussion.

items.text: Rabbi Avin HaLevi on time and the individual
items.text_en: Rabbi Avin HaLevi on time and the individual
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avin HaLevi teaches that one who pushes against the time will be pushed by it, and one who yields to the time will have time yield to him.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avin HaLevi teaches that one who pushes against the time will be pushed by it, and one who yields to the time will have time yield to him.

items.text: The dispute between Rabba and Rav Yosef over precedence
items.text_en: The dispute between Rabba and Rav Yosef over precedence
items.desc_en: The Gemara illustrates the principle with the story of Rabba and Rav Yosef: Rabba was an 'uprooter of mountains' and Rav Yosef a 'Sinai'. When asked who takes precedence, the answer was that Rav Yosef (Sinai) comes first, but Rav Yosef did not accept the leadership, and he ruled only two and a half years.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute between Rabba and Rav Yosef, describing Rabba as an 'uprooter of mountains' and Rav Yosef as a 'Sinai', and notes that the times required them.
The community sends a query to the sages in Eretz Yisrael asking which of the two, Sinai or uprooter of mountains, takes precedence.
The sages reply that Sinai (Rav Yosef) takes precedence because everyone needs the 'master of wheat' (the one who knows the foundational sources).
Despite the ruling, Rav Yosef did not accept the leadership because the Chaldeans told him he would reign only two years.

items.text: Rabba's reign and its impact
items.text_en: Rabba's reign and its impact
items.desc_en: During Rabba's twenty-two years of leadership, even a laborer did not need to go home early, indicating great peace and prosperity.

items.text: Rabbi Avin HaLevi on the verse 'God of Jacob'
items.text_en: Rabbi Avin HaLevi on the verse 'God of Jacob'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avin HaLevi explains why the verse says 'God of Jacob' and not 'God of Abraham and Isaac', teaching that a person in distress should call upon the one most associated with the crisis, like a beam that enters its own thickness.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avin the Levi asks: why does the verse say 'God of Jacob' and not 'God of Abraham and Isaac'? From here we learn that the master of the beam should enter the thickness of the beam.
He answers with a parable: a person in distress should call upon the one most associated with the crisis, like a beam that enters its own thickness.

items.text: Benefiting from a meal with a Torah scholar
items.text_en: Benefiting from a meal with a Torah scholar
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avin HaLevi teaches that one who benefits from a meal where a Torah scholar is present is as if benefiting from the Divine Presence, as derived from the verse about Aaron and the elders eating before God.

sub.desc_en: רבי אבין הלוי (Rabbi Avin HaLevi) states that one who benefits from a meal where a Torah scholar is present is as if benefiting from the radiant splendor of the Divine Presence.
רבי אבין הלוי (Rabbi Avin HaLevi) cites the verse about Aaron and the elders eating before God, and raises the rhetorical question that they actually ate before Moses, not God.
The Gemara resolves that the verse teaches that benefiting from a meal with a Torah scholar is equivalent to benefiting from the Divine Presence.

items.text: Proper farewell: 'Go in peace' vs. 'Go to peace'
items.text_en: Proper farewell: 'Go in peace' vs. 'Go to peace'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avin HaLevi teaches that when parting from a living person, one should say 'Go to peace' (like Jethro to Moses), but when parting from the dead, one should say 'Go in peace' (as the verse says about Abraham).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avin HaLevi teaches that when parting from a living person, one should say 'Go to peace' (לֵךְ לְשָׁלוֹם), citing Jethro's successful farewell to Moses and David's failed farewell to Absalom as proof.
Rabbi Avin HaLevi adds that when parting from the dead, one should say 'Go in peace' (לֵךְ בְּשָׁלוֹם), citing the verse about Abraham's peaceful death.

items.text: From synagogue to study hall: receiving the Divine Presence
items.text_en: From synagogue to study hall: receiving the Divine Presence
items.desc_en: Rabbi Levi bar Chiya and Rabbi Chiya bar Ashi teach that one who goes from synagogue to study hall merits to receive the Divine Presence, and that Torah scholars have no rest in this world or the next, as they go from strength to strength.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Levi bar Chiya teaches that one who leaves the synagogue and enters the study hall to engage in Torah study merits to receive the Divine Presence, citing the verse 'ילכו מחיל אל חיל יראה אל אלהים בציון' (They go from strength to strength, every one of them appears before God in Zion).

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Ashi said Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Ashi said Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Ashi citing Rav teaches that Torah scholars have no rest in this world or the World-to-Come, as they constantly progress from strength to strength, citing the same verse 'ילכו מחיל אל חיל יראה אל אלהים בציון' (They go from strength to strength, every one of them appears before God in Zion).

items.text: Torah scholars increase peace in the world
items.text_en: Torah scholars increase peace in the world
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Chanina teaches that Torah scholars increase peace in the world, citing multiple verses that connect Torah study and peace.

sub.desc_en: רבי אלעזר (Rabbi Elazar) in the name of רבי חנינא (Rabbi Chanina) states that Torah scholars increase peace in the world, citing the verse 'וְכׇל בָּנַיִךְ לִמּוּדֵי ה׳ וְרַב שְׁלוֹם בָּנָיִךְ' (and all your children shall be taught of the Lord, and great shall be the peace of your children).

The Gemara adds a homiletic interpretation: do not read 'בָּנָיִךְ' (your children) but 'בּוֹנָיִךְ' (your builders), and then cites multiple additional verses—'שָׁלוֹם רָב לְאֹהֲבֵי תוֹרָתֶךָ' (great peace have those who love Your Torah), 'יְהִי שָׁלוֹם בְּחֵילֵךְ' (peace be within your walls), 'לְמַעַן אַחַי וְרֵעָי' (for the sake of my brothers and friends), and 'ה׳ יְבָרֵךְ אֶת עַמּוֹ בַשָּׁלוֹם' (the Lord will bless His people with peace)—to reinforce that Torah scholars are builders of peace.
